Ghana News.title: Ecobank JoyBusiness SME Fair 2026: Day One ends on high note as patrons urged not to miss remaining days
Ghana News.content:
The first day of the Ecobank JoyBusiness SME Fair 2026 has ended at Ghud Park, Accra Mall, with an impressive showcase of Ghanaian businesses, products and services, as patrons are encouraged to make the most of the remaining two days.

The three-day exhibition, which opened on Friday, November 13, and runs until Sunday, November 15, has transformed the venue into a bustling marketplace, bringing together businesses from the food, fashion, beauty, technology, agriculture, finance and lifestyle sectors.

Adding to the excitement are Joy Prime's KMJ and content creator Quecy Official, whose presence and engagement with exhibitors and patrons are helping bring the fair closer to audiences and create a lively atmosphere around the exhibition.

From the aroma of local spices and freshly prepared meals to colourful fashion collections, beauty products, electronic gadgets and household essentials, the fair offers visitors an opportunity to discover a wide variety of products under one roof.

A feast of Ghanaian products and enterprise

Food lovers have a lot to explore. Didi Shito, Corki Ventures and Gold Coast Foods' Sankofa Spices are showcasing spices and seasonings, while Manellah Foods offers cereals, Adjoor Ventures tuna products, and Yaapee Royal Foods, Nutrismart Ventures and Golden Parani a range of processed foods.

The beverage selection includes Fortune Spread from Wilmar Africa, soy milk from Delsoy, fruit juices from Orave Juices and Jussvina Drinks, natural cocoa juice from Koa Impact Commerce and coconut juice from Pinnacle Coco. Green Cup is also presenting beetroot, guava and pawpaw tea.

Shoppers can stock their kitchens with rice from MamsiJoy Ventures, fufu from Ellie Catering Services, yam from Martha's Yam Trading, fresh tomatoes from Farm Mate and farm produce from Orrab Farms. Flourish Foods Africa is showcasing grilled chicken and poultry products, while Ikam Plus offers corned beef and G-Way Investments tomato paste.

Mushroom General has processed mushrooms, Desco processed flour, and 97 Bakes and Evive Delight a selection of baked goods. Aladdin Bakery, Bliss Pop and Selis Satisfactory add snacks, popcorn and kenkey to the spread.

Fashion enthusiasts can browse clothing and accessories from Haute Xklusive, La Robe Classique, Utonez Clothier, Regy Couture, Kofikyere Klothing, JAT Couture and Kims Foods and Clothings. Asangenta has dresses, bags and hats, Shoes TE3 caters for different foot sizes, while Kinky Love Crochet showcases hair and wigs.

Beauty and personal-care products are also well represented, with cosmetics from Haus of Lush, RNS Beauty, Atlas Prime Merchantile, Leepoku Ventures and Chocho. Mist and Strands is presenting bath and body products, while Reed Diffusers Ghana and Esquicet Scents offer home-fragrance products, including diffusers and scented candles.

For the home, Sintex Tank is showcasing water storage solutions, Kemz Ceramics ceramic products, MGIG Suppliers powdered soap, and Liz Imports perfumes and home appliances. DBS brings housing and roofing solutions, Worafam Group of Companies safety wear, and Vital Vendors car essentials. Roses Enterprise and Mothercare, alongside Prestige Children's Palace, cater for mother-and-child needs.

Technology, finance and other services

The exhibition also features technology and digital solutions. Galop Sea Limited is displaying laptops and accessories, while Xfromo Hypermart has phones and accessories, including Google Pixel devices. Katon 360 Technologies is presenting a digital platform for SMEs, Solid Connect an app for artisans, and We Shop Africa and Ayuda their e-commerce services.

Ecobank represents the banking sector, with MTN showcasing telecommunications services. Insurance providers include, while Vaal Real Estate is presenting property-related services.

Travel and tourism businesses Grandeur Consult Travel and Tour and Astolinks are also participating, alongside the Ghana Export Promotion Authority (GEPA). Atlantic Meridian EV is showcasing electric vehicles, while Central University represents the education sector.

Other exhibitors include Greenhaul Solutions, which focuses on waste management and scrap procurement; T&C Farms and Atohfield, which operate in crop and animal production; Eldem Floral Services, offering fresh-cut flowers; Advantage GH Premium Apparel, providing printing services; Esbony Food Package, specialising in repackaging finished goods; and Gorgeous Vie Event Hub, which offers events and décor services. BB Brothers is showcasing canned wine, Golden Pride through Yao Consult represents liquor retail, while Kivo and Blessed 3 Ventures are also among the participating businesses. BB Chemist is promoting Relax Liver Salt.

A boost for businesses and shoppers

Beyond the range of products, the fair provides a platform for businesses to meet prospective customers, generate sales, increase brand visibility and build partnerships.

The 2026 edition, powered by JoyPrime, continues that mission by bringing businesses and consumers together in an engaging marketplace where visitors can discover local brands, access special offers and interact directly with exhibitors.

With Saturday and Sunday still to come, patrons are being encouraged not to miss the opportunity to explore the stands, meet the entrepreneurs behind the brands and support Ghanaian businesses.

Whether looking for fresh food supplies, a new outfit, beauty essentials, household products, electronic gadgets or business services, there is something to discover at the fair.

The Ecobank JoyBusiness SME Fair 2026 continues at Ghud Park, Accra Mall, until Sunday, November 15. Patrons are urged to visit, shop, engage with exhibitors and enjoy the experience, with KMJ and Quecy Official adding to the excitement.

Ghana News.title: Electorates must reduce financial demands on politicians – Krachi East NDC spokesperson
Ghana News.content:
Krachi East National Democratic Congress (NDC) Communications Officer, Peter Nlipah, has appealed to voters to reduce the financial demands they make on political aspirants, warning that excessive expectations during elections could undermine the delivery of development projects.

He says the growing expectation that politicians must offer money and other material incentives before securing electoral support places an unnecessary financial burden on candidates and could affect their ability to fulfil campaign promises once elected.

Speaking at the ‘Democracy Is Not For Sale’ programme held at the Dambai College of Education in the Oti Region, Mr Nlipah acknowledged that vote buying remains a major reality in Ghana's electoral process, with some voters openly demanding money from individuals seeking political office.

He explained that candidates who approach electorates to solicit their support are often confronted with demands for financial assistance, with some voters insisting that they must receive something in return for their votes.

According to him, the situation has become a challenge for political aspirants, who are sometimes compelled to meet these demands to improve their chances of securing electoral support.

Mr Nlipah observed that money which could have been invested in community development projects is often diverted to satisfy the financial expectations of voters during election campaigns.

He warned that this practice creates difficulties for politicians after they assume office, as the resources required to implement their campaign promises may have already been exhausted in the process of securing votes.

He said the situation could contribute to the failure of elected representatives to deliver on some of the development commitments they make to their constituents.

“It is true that vote buying is a reality in this country. When you go to the electorates to demand their support, when you are aspiring for a position, normally they demand money. They will tell you, ‘We will take something from you’,” he said.

He further explained that the financial demands often extend to delegates during internal party elections, putting additional pressure on aspirants to spend money that should ideally support development initiatives.

Mr Nlipah, however, stressed that voters also have a responsibility to help address the practice by reconsidering the financial expectations they place on political candidates.

He appealed to electorates not to make excessive demands on politicians, arguing that the more money candidates are compelled to spend to secure votes, the less financial capacity they may have to execute projects after winning political office.

"We want to just plead that electorates shouldn't demand so much from politicians. The more you demand from them, the higher their inability to be able to discharge their promises,” he cautioned.

He maintained that addressing vote buying requires a change in attitude among both political actors and the electorate, urging citizens to prioritise competence, accountability and the ability of candidates to deliver over immediate financial benefits.

The Democracy Is Not For Sale forum brought together residents, students and other stakeholders in Dambai to examine the practice of vote buying, its implications for democratic governance and the role citizens must play in protecting the integrity of Ghana's electoral process.

Ghana News.title: Justice Pwamang takes over as Ag. Chief Justice as Baffoe-Bonnie proceeds on leave
Ghana News.content:
Chief Justice Paul Baffoe-Bonnie has nominated Supreme Court Justice Gabriel Scott Pwamang to act in his stead during his absence from duty from November 12 to November 24, 2026.

The appointment is contained in a circular dated November 11, 2026, sighted by 3News.

In the circular, Justice Baffoe-Bonnie informed members of the Judiciary that he would be away from the jurisdiction for the period and would resume duty on Wednesday, November 25, 2026.

“In my absence, His Lordship Justice Gabriel Pwamang, the most senior Justice of the Supreme Court, will act,” the circular stated.

The notice was circulated to Justices of the Supreme Court, Court of Appeal and High Court, as well as Circuit Court Judges, Magistrates, Directors, Heads of Units and Registrars of Courts.

Copies were also sent to members of the Judicial Council, the General Legal Council and the Judicial Secretary.

Justice Pwamang’s nomination follows established judicial practice, under which the most senior Justice of the Supreme Court acts as Chief Justice when the substantive officeholder is unavailable.

He is expected to oversee the administration of the Judiciary and perform the administrative responsibilities of the Office of the Chief Justice until Justice Baffoe-Bonnie resumes duty.

The Chief Justice heads Ghana’s Judiciary and is responsible for the administration and supervision of the country’s courts.

Ghana News.title: NDC Deputy Youth Organiser aspirant Daniel Niibi outlines plans to give Greater Accra youth a stronger voice
Ghana News.content:
Daniel Niibi Afotey Odai, an aspirant for the position of Deputy Youth Organiser of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) in the Greater Accra Region, has outlined a series of proposals aimed at strengthening youth participation and improving support for party organisers.

Campaigning under the message, “Youth in Politics: From Spectators to Decision Makers,” Mr Afotey Odai says he wants to establish systems that will give young party members a greater role in decision-making and improve their access to opportunities.

His proposals include setting up a functional Greater Accra Youth Secretariat, creating a database of young people across the region’s 34 constituencies and introducing a 24-hour hotline to support youth organisers.

He is also proposing the appointment of a desk officer for every constituency and the establishment of a youth welfare scheme to provide support to organisers during illness, bereavement and other significant personal events.

Mr Afotey Odai says the proposals are intended to move the party’s youth mobilisation beyond election-related activities and create structures that support young people throughout the year.

The Nungua-based aspirant says his involvement in the NDC spans more than a decade, beginning at the branch and constituency levels.

He served for eight years as Deputy Youth Organiser for the Krowor Constituency, where he says he was involved in youth mobilisation, organising party structures and supporting grassroots activities.

He holds a degree in Political Science from the University of Ghana and is also a Chartered Manager.

Beyond party politics, Mr Afotey Odai is identified as the District Director of the Youth Employment Agency (YEA) in Krowor, where he works on connecting young people to employment and skills-development opportunities.

He also manages Nungua Royals FC, a role through which he says he uses football to identify and develop young talent.

His professional experience further includes work as a media consultant with the Multimedia Group, which operates Joy FM and Adom TV.

A central part of his campaign is the argument that young people should have a greater influence on decisions within the party, rather than being mobilised mainly for rallies, campaign activities and election-day duties.

He says the proposed youth database would help identify young people's skills and needs across the region, while the constituency desk officers would provide a direct link between local youth structures and the regional leadership.

The proposed welfare scheme, meanwhile, is intended to provide a support system for youth organisers beyond their political responsibilities.

“I am one of you. I have walked your road. I know your struggle. I will not forget you after the elections,” he says.

Mr Afotey Odai is seeking the number three position on the ballot in the NDC's Greater Accra Regional Youth Organiser elections.

His campaign is using the slogan #WeAreTogether.

Ghana News.title: Prophet Joseph Atarah releases new gospel single, ‘Formula’
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaian gospel musician Prophet Joseph Atarah has released his latest single, Formula, urging believers to remain steadfast in their faith regardless of their circumstances.

The song was produced by Dan Bassey, while its music video was directed and shot by Skyweb.

Speaking about the message behind the song, Prophet Atarah, leader of Believers Grace Crown Ministry International, said life’s circumstances could sometimes make people question God’s plan for their lives.

He said, however, that in God’s own time, He makes all things beautiful, often beyond human imagination.

“God’s blessings don’t follow a formula,” he said.

“You can’t copy someone else’s prayer, someone else’s fasting, someone else’s giving, someone else’s timeline, and expect the same result. What worked for them was for them,” he added.

Prophet Atarah noted that God deals with each person individually, knowing their story, struggles, timing and heart.

“Sometimes He blesses you through hard work. Sometimes through a closed door. Sometimes through waiting. Sometimes through a person you least expected. Sometimes He blesses you when you did everything right. Sometimes He blesses you even when you did everything wrong, just because of grace,” he said.

He urged believers not to compare their journeys with those of others, stressing that God’s blessings do not follow any formula and are often unpredictable.

“His plan for you is not a copy of another man’s plan. It is tailor-made. And when it comes, it will make sense why it didn’t come earlier, why it didn’t come like theirs, and why it had to come like this,” he said.

Formula is available on all digital music platforms.

Ghana News.title: Okyeame Kwame’s advocacy gets massive boost as BoG honours Ghana’s heroines
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaian musician Okyeame Kwame has welcomed the Bank of Ghana’s decision to honour prominent Ghanaian women on its newly unveiled cedi notes.

He has described the move as a fulfilment of his long-standing advocacy.

The musician has consistently argued that a nation that does not honour its heroes will have few, if any, young heroes to inspire future generations.

The new notes, which feature prominent men and women, honour three distinguished Ghanaian women:

Agnes Oforiwa Tagoe-Quarcoopome (GH¢1 note): A pioneering textile trader and market queen from Makola Market who inspired generations of women entrepreneurs and helped build early confidence in formal banking.

Justice Annie Ruth Jiagge (GH¢10 note): Ghana’s first female High Court judge in 1961, a former President of the Court of Appeal and a global human rights campaigner who helped draft the UN Declaration on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women.

Theodosia Okoh (GH¢50 note): The iconic designer of Ghana’s national flag.

Seeing the honour bestowed on the heroines, Okyeame Kwame said he felt fulfilled by his advocacy.

The musician appears to be extending his message of recognition and appreciation to others through his music. Earlier this year, he released Clap, a family-friendly reggae song with the chorus, “learn to clap for others, Pa Pa Pa.”

He followed it with a new song, Ayekoo (Big Up), released on 21 September, which also marked Kwame Nkrumah’s birthday.

Ayekoo means congratulations in the Akan language. On the song, Okyeame Kwame rides a dancehall beat, using lyrics and cadence to eulogise great men and women who have contributed to Ghana’s national development.

The personalities celebrated are drawn from politics, sports, entertainment and traditional leadership, among other fields.

The combination of wordplay and metaphorical delivery demonstrates the rapper’s experience without him having to say it. The song was produced by legendary producer Gomez Beats.

Its chorus is a smooth yet attention-grabbing melody that drives home the message through repetition: “big up, big up, big up, bibibibi, big up, big up, big up,” calling on listeners to respond, “Ayekooo.”

Jah Lead, the Afro-dancehall artiste who captured the hearts of Ghanaians with his hit song Lonely, was carefully selected to deliver the chorus, as Okyeame Kwame explained in an interview.

The song goes beyond entertainment. It is a culturally relevant audio-visual piece expected to resonate with many listeners.

Okyeame Kwame’s values are drawn from the ethos of his environment, but what stands out in the song is his recognition of five women who contributed to Ghana’s fight during the struggle for independence, as well as others who became formidable leaders after independence.

Names such as Naa Dedei Aryeetey, Mabel Dove Danquah, Susanna Al-Hassan, Ama Nkrumah and Theodosia Okoh are mentioned and appropriately celebrated.

He has also released a video that serves as an augmented reality representation of the entire experience, with Ghanaian culture on full display.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Eisenkot slams Netanyahu’s ‘racist’ campaign against Palestinian Israelis
World.content:
Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot has accused caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of fuelling a “racist and violent” campaign against Palestinian citizens of Israel during the elections.

Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming Israel’s new government, posted a lengthy social media update on recent developments in Israel on Friday.

“Arab citizens of Israel make up 21 percent of the total population. Since the start of the election campaign, they have faced a racist and violent campaign of delegitimisation fuelled by the outgoing prime minister and his circle for political reasons,” Eisenkot wrote on X.

“The prime minister of Israel is the prime minister of all citizens, including those who did not vote for him,” he said. “Arab citizens of Israel are part of the Israeli story. The attempt to marginalise them and smear them as a group is an anti-state act.”

In Israel’s October 27 elections, Eisenkot’s four-party alliance won 48 seats, while Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc secured 53, leaving both short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority. Arab-led parties, representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, won a record 19 seats.

Netanyahu repeatedly made unproven allegations of electoral fraud by Arab-majority parties – claims Israel’s own electoral authorities have rejected.

The caretaker leader has also repeatedly criticised Arab-led parties for refusing to describe Hamas as a “terror group” following the attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, despite all of the parties’ leaders condemning the Hamas-led assault.



“One can disagree with the representatives of the Arab parties, and one can even feel deep revulsion toward some of them, but one cannot, should not, and I will not allow an entire sector to be slandered,” Eisenkot said.

Arab-led parties have endorsed Eisenkot to replace Netanyahu. However, Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with those parties, which would give him a 67-seat bloc. Winning the backing of the two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats.

On efforts to form an emergency government, Eisenkot reiterated that he wants to fulfil the mandate as soon as possible, adding “it would be a grave mistake not to do so”.

Netanyahu weighs renewed strikes on Iran

Eisenkot, who ran as Netanyahu’s main rival, has six weeks to form a new government.

While Netanyahu may be politically weakened, the prime minister is reported to be weighing military action against Iran, despite a lack of enthusiasm from the United States, his own military establishment, and Eisenkot, who has demanded that Netanyahu avoid any new escalation unless it is critical.

In Friday’s update, Eisenkot said he had met with Netanyahu and his military secretary on Thursday to discuss the security situation but provided no details.

Earlier in the week, Eisenkot said that he was open to including Netanyahu in his coalition. Eisenkot suggested Netanyahu’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich was also welcome to join.

Eisenkot led Israel’s military from 2015 to 2019 and sat as an observer in Netanyahu’s war cabinet for the first eight months of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023.

World.title: The fight over Canadian steelworker jobs
World.content:
Stelco’s US owner blames Trump’s tariffs for layoffs, but its support for those same tariffs has raised questions.

Hamilton, Ontario, Canada – Chelsey Masteij had heard layoffs might be coming at Stelco, so she decided to use up some of her vacation days. She was making the most of the time off with her new dog when she got a call telling her not to come back to work.

The 34-year-old had spent years trying to break into the male-dominated steel industry before finally landing a job at the company’s Hamilton plant about three years ago.

She started as a general labourer in the cold-rolling department, later training to operate cranes and taking on shifts in the coke ovens.

The work was gruelling and physically demanding, but Masteij grew to love the routine and the close-knit community of coworkers she came to consider family. When she shared photos of herself with Al Jazeera, all in protective gear at the plant, she joked that she hardly had any pictures outside of work.

Masteij thought she might stay at Stelco until retirement. Instead, she was laid off on October 9.

The news hit hard, and she spent much of the next two weeks sleeping.

“I was in a complete mess,” she told Al Jazeera, her voice cracking as she recalled the experience. “I was kind of depressed.”

Now, instead of working 12-hour shifts, Masteij spends much of her time at home, cutting back on expenses while she collects employment insurance.

Masteij is among hundreds of Canadian steelworkers facing layoffs after Stelco’s American owner, Cleveland-Cliffs, announced in late September that it would temporarily shut down parts of its operations in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ontario.



Stelco blames the move on United States President Donald Trump’s tariffs, which it says have made it harder to sell Canadian steel to US customers, and on competition from cheaper foreign steel entering Canada.

But government officials and plant workers, including Masteij, are not convinced that is the whole story.

“Right now, there are a lot of lies going on with what’s happened,” Masteij said.

While US tariffs have hurt the Canadian steel industry, the union representing Stelco workers questions whether Cleveland-Cliffs is using difficult market conditions to serve its own business interests, with Canadian workers paying the price.

“Everyone knows we’re being used as pawns, that these layoffs weren’t necessary,” said Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, speaking to Al Jazeera at his Hamilton office.

The pressures facing Stelco

In June 2025, Trump doubled tariffs on steel and aluminium imports, including from Canada, to 50 percent, making them more expensive for US buyers.

According to Stelco, Canada’s exports of cold-rolled and coated steel to the US – used to make everything from cars to building materials – fell by 58 percent in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the quarterly average before the trade war.

But demand has also fallen in Canada, where the auto industry, a major buyer of the cold-rolled steel produced at the Hamilton plant, has also been hit hard by Trump’s tariffs, said Colin Mang, an assistant professor of economics at McMaster University in Hamilton.

“When they say that there is less demand for the product coming out of the Hamilton mill, that is correct,” Mang told Al Jazeera.

But it is not just Trump’s tariffs that Cleveland-Cliffs blames for Stelco’s problems.

During a July earnings call, CEO Lourenco Goncalves warned that the company might scale back production in Canada unless Ottawa did more to protect its steel industry from imports.

“And that will have consequences for employment in Canada, but will have a positive financial impact on Stelco and on Cleveland-Cliffs,” he said.

That was the first time Wells had heard jobs might be at risk. The union later offered to help Cleveland-Cliffs lobby Ottawa for stronger protections against foreign steel imports, believing Canadian workers might have more sway with the government.

“They never took us up on our offer,” Wells said.



Instead, the next call brought news of the layoffs.

As of Saturday, 175 workers at Stelco’s Hamilton plant had received layoff notices, with the announced cuts expected to affect up to 500 workers there and in Nanticoke.

Late last month, about 30 attended an information session the union organised in Hamilton, where they could learn about employment insurance and retraining opportunities.

Many were frustrated by the lack of clarity about how long the shutdown would last.

Some asked how their benefits would compare to their wages, while others wondered whether they would qualify for the full amount.

For workers who had spent decades at Stelco, another daunting prospect loomed: having to look for work for the first time in the digital era, competing for jobs with younger applicants as they neared retirement.

Some are already considering heading out west to find work.

“It’s hard for them to make those decisions,” Wells said, describing what he had been hearing from members. “Do I leave my family, go out west, make some money? Because they don’t know how long this is going to be.”

Masteij worries about what that could mean for Hamilton, a city where generations of families have worked in steelmaking, an industry that has shaped its identity for more than a century.

“I’m a steel city girl, and I can’t imagine the city without steel manufacturing,” she said. “We are losing tradesmen.”

Were the layoffs necessary?

But as workers grapple with what the layoffs mean for their families and their city, the union has been asking another question: whether these layoffs needed to happen at all – and it is not alone.

The US company has come under fire from the Canadian government, which is threatening legal action, accusing it of breaking promises it made when it bought Stelco in 2024.

Those included keeping at least the same number of unionised jobs and most non-unionised jobs in Canada, and pushing for trade policies that would benefit the steel industries in both Canada and the US.

Cleveland-Cliffs denies violating the agreement, saying it expects to meet its employment commitments for the year. It also maintains the layoffs are needed to “ensure the survival of Stelco” amid US tariffs, weaker demand and competition from cheaper foreign steel.

But the union and the government point to Stelco’s recent financial performance. Earlier this month, Goncalves reported the company’s strongest quarter since the acquisition.

“Mr Goncalves is not a victim,” Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly told Canada’s public broadcaster CBC, pointing to the company’s earnings. “He’s never made so much money.”

Experts have also challenged Goncalves’s claim that Canadian steelmakers are struggling because of “an avalanche of imports”.

Mang points out that nearly 80 percent of Canada’s cold-rolled steel imports come from the US, as does about half of the galvanised and painted steel coming into the country.



“What he’s trying to sell people on is the idea that there’s all this European or Asian steel coming into Canada,” he said. “This stuff is coming from his own country.”

The union and the government have also asked why, as Goncalves pushes for stronger protections in Canada against foreign steel, he has also been a vocal supporter of Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steel.

In testimony to US lawmakers in January, Goncalves argued that no country, including Canada, should be exempted from the steel tariffs. In an interview with Politico last year, he said he was “very happy” with the 50 percent tariffs on steel imports, adding, “I have my fingerprints on that 50 percent.”

Two countries, one company

For Wells, the irony is that Goncalves helped create the same conditions Cleveland-Cliffs now blames for the layoffs. He believes the company is using Canadian workers to pressure Ottawa to impose more restrictions on foreign steel, while also helping Trump argue that his tariffs are working.

Mang explained why Goncalves’ seemingly contradictory position might make sense for Cleveland-Cliffs.

“He wants trade barriers in both countries to seal off their domestic markets from each other and also from the rest of the world,” Mang said, “so that his companies in each country can benefit in their own domestic markets.”

Cleveland-Cliffs has been under growing pressure from Ottawa, which gave the company 15 days from October 22 to honour its commitments to Canadian workers or face legal action.

Amid that pressure, comments Goncalves made to CBC late last month appeared to support the union’s suspicions that the layoffs have less to do with tough market conditions and more to do with Cleveland-Cliffs’ broader business interests.

Asked why he supported tariffs on Canadian steel despite promises to protect workers and advocate for the Canadian steel industry when Cleveland-Cliffs bought Stelco, he said: “I bought Stelco because I could not afford anymore having Stelco flooding the market here in the United States to the detriment of my own company.”

The admission caught the attention of Joly, who said the comments could strengthen the government’s case against Cleveland-Cliffs if Goncalves meant that he had bought Stelco to keep its Canadian operations idle. She added that Ottawa could force the company to sell its Canadian assets.

On November 6, as Ottawa’s 15-day deadline expired, Joly asked Canada’s Competition Bureau to investigate the 2024 acquisition and whether the company’s conduct violated Canadian competition law.

“If negotiations and acquisition were conducted in bad faith, Canadians deserve to know. The company needs to face the consequences,” she said in a statement.

Cleveland-Cliffs maintains that it has complied with its obligations under the Investment Canada Act.

Goncalves has rejected the prospect of a forced sale but suggested he might sell Stelco himself in a year.

“I will sell the company after we operate the company for a while, and now that I know that I’m persona non grata in Canada, I will do that,” he told CBC.

In a statement to The Canadian Press news agency late last month, he said he hoped to bring laid-off workers back before Christmas.

“It will depend on Canadian customers buying Canadian steel, made by Stelco,” he said.

Al Jazeera contacted Cleveland-Cliffs for comment on the union’s allegations and Goncalves’s remarks.

What comes next for workers?

For Masteij, even as she waits to hear whether she will be recalled, she is preparing for the possibility that her time at Stelco is done. Her low seniority means she would be one of the last to be called back.



Masteij plans to use the time she is eligible for employment insurance to take a heavy equipment training programme, hoping it will open the door to other opportunities and give her something to focus on. The training could also help her if she returns to Stelco, which is still what she is hoping for.

For Wells, what is especially frustrating is how the company is treating workers, given the years of hard work and sacrifices many have made in their jobs.

“It’s not glamorous. You work shifts, nights, days, in the hot and the cold,” he said. “Our members miss Christmas meals with their families or their kids’ hockey games because they’re expected to work.”

“And that’s why this is particularly tough because that loyalty isn’t being repaid,” Wells added. “It’s actually being exploited, if anything.”

He worries about what a drawn-out legal battle could mean for those workers.

“Our members don’t have a lot of time,” he said. “We’re hoping things get settled as soon as possible.”

World.title: Car bombings in Russia kill military officer, injure ex-Ukraine PM adviser
World.content:
Moscow blames Kyiv for a series of car bombings that have targeted people linked to the war with Ukraine.

A car bombing in Moscow has critically injured an adviser to Ukraine’s former prime minister a day after a similar attack killed a military officer in St Petersburg.

The explosion on Friday was the latest in a series of bombings and shootings that have targeted people involved in the fighting in Ukraine. Moscow has blamed Kyiv for the attacks.

The Moscow explosion struck a car driven by Sergei Zavorotnyi, who previously worked as an adviser to former Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov, according to Russia’s Investigative Committee.

Zavorotnyi was hospitalised with injuries, the committee added. It did not identify possible suspects pending a criminal inquiry.

Azarov served as prime minister under Ukraine’s Moscow-friendly President Viktor Yanukovych, who was forced from office by protesters and fled to Russia in February 2014.

Azarov, who also lives in Russia, told state-run TV that he was “shocked” by the attack that left his former adviser critically injured. He said he believes Zavorotnyi was targeted because of his criticism of the Ukrainian government.

Zavorotnyi. 72, had worked as a journalist for Russia’s daily Komsomolskaya Pravda before becoming Azarov’s adviser. He wrote a book about Yanukovych’s ouster and ran an online outlet critical of Ukrainian authorities.

Russia’s REN TV channel said he lost his left arm, suffered multiple other injuries and was in a coma after the explosion.

Explosive devices triggered remotely

Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said an explosive device was reportedly planted under the man’s car and detonated remotely as he was driving on Friday.



“The investigative committee has already launched a criminal case into this explosion,” she said.

A day earlier, in St Petersburg, a military serviceman was killed by a bomb in his vehicle, according to Russia’s Investigative Committee. It did not identify the victim or say who could be behind the bombing.

The Fontanka news outlet said Thursday’s victim was a colonel, while other Russian online media said the victim was a senior air force officer.

Shapovalova said preliminary reports indicated that the victim was a military serviceman, rather than a colonel of the Russian Air Force.

Like the attack on Friday, he was also driving the car when the bomb went off, she added.

“In both cases an explosive device was triggered remotely, and it was planted under their car,” Shapovalova said. “Here in Russia, all the attacks are considered to be orchestrated by the Ukrainian side.”

Ukrainian authorities have not commented on either bombing.

World.title: Sixth victim confirmed in DC condo-related shooting in US, police say
World.content:
Police confirm sixth victim in DC condo shooting; suspect dead after barricading himself and starting a fire.

Share Sixth victim confirmed in DC condo-related shooting in US, police say on social media

Police have said a sixth person was shot on Thursday morning in Washington, DC, bringing the toll to one person killed and five wounded in an attack they believe was linked to a dispute over maintenance issues in a condo building.

In an updated statement, the Metropolitan Police Department said investigators had found a sixth victim, a woman, after officers initially located five other victims.

She was conscious and breathing with a “non-life-threatening gunshot graze wound”.

“The victim self-treated the wound,” police said.

Two women and two men were taken to hospital, all conscious and breathing.

James Stuart, the 46-year-old manager of the building in which the suspect lived, died at the scene.

Police believe the suspect, a 55-year-old doctor named Matt Wade Lambert, targeted Stuart while Stuart was doing his morning workout at the gym.

The shooting started just before 8am local time (13:00 GMT) at a VIDA Fitness gym in the city’s Logan Circle neighbourhood, about a mile north of the White House.

Police said Lambert shot Stuart inside the gym on the ground floor of the building before going back to his apartment on the seventh floor and firing on people below from his patio.

Five others, some of whom had been working at a construction site across the street. Police have not detailed the circumstances in which the sixth victim was shot.

The shootings unfolded in less than five minutes, according to interim police chief Jeffery Carroll.

Lambert then barricaded himself inside his apartment, where he talked to police negotiators over the phone. Police say he fired at least twice through the door while officers were outside, but no officers were injured.



He also broke the gas line connected to his fireplace and started a fire, which the building’s sprinkler system contained.

Police said Lambert spent most of the conversation with negotiators talking about the dispute with building management.

“Most of the conversation was about the homeowners associations and challenges with that,” said Carroll.

“While our negotiators were communicating with the suspect, they did hear a single gunshot,” he said, adding that Lambert then stopped talking.

When tactical officers forced their way into the apartment, they found him dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Police said inside the apartment, they found a shotgun, a rifle, and a handgun, all of which had been used in the shooting.

According to court records cited by The Associated Press, Lambert had filed a lawsuit alleging that he had not been able to enjoy his penthouse since 2024 because of mould, moisture and water problems that began after work had been done on the building’s exterior.

The lawsuit was ongoing, and Lambert appeared to have shared details of the dispute, including photos and an engineering report on an X account called ofMiceandMold.

His lawyer, Joel Braithwaite, told reporters on Thursday that the condo where Lambert had lived since 2017 looked like “a warzone” and that Lambert had spent more than $300,000 on the lawsuit.

World.title: US Treasury warns against rate hikes during US-Iran war energy ‘shock’
World.content:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called on the Federal Reserve not to hike interest rates because of an “energy supply shock” tied to the US-led conflict with Iran.

“I think the Fed should understand that this is an energy supply shock,” while the underlying US economy is very strong, Bessent said in an interview on CNBC on Friday.

“So I think that to hike too much into an energy supply shock when it’s coming down, these are very noisy numbers,” he said. “The Fed’s supposed to look into the future, not look in the rearview mirror.”

The central bank opted to maintain interest rates during its last policy meeting, leaving them at 3.75 to 4 percent. CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, forecasts an 89.4 percent chance that rates will be raised to 4.00–4.25 percent at the next meeting, scheduled for December 9.

Despite pressure from the White House to cut interest rates, the Federal Reserve has held them steady amid inflationary pressures stemming from the US-Israeli war on Iran. Since the conflict began, the Fed has maintained rates five times and raised them once.

Much of that pressure has come from rising energy prices. By September, energy prices had climbed 20.4 percent year over year. Although October’s energy price data has since been released, the Labour Department was unable to collect data in October 2025 because of last year’s government shutdown. As a result, it cannot provide a year-over-year comparison for October 2026.

Bessent’s remarks come amid a stronger-than-expected US jobs report, which bolsters the case for rate hikes. The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, according to the Labour Department’s release last Friday.



“I’m not going to tell the Fed what to do. I am going to say they should have an open mind,” Bessent said.

The Fed made three rate cuts over the same period last year, he noted.

“And now to reverse just based on an energy supply shock, a reversal in a dramatic way isn’t something that I would do if I were on the Fed. But I’m not on the Fed.”

Feeling the cost

Bessent’s remarks come as some top Fed officials are pushing for the opposite. On Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he planned to support a quarter-point increase at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting unless the core consumer price index — one of the central bank’s key measures for assessing the rate of inflation — came in at 0.3 percent or more.

“In that case, I believe a 50-basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting,” he said at a conference in London hosted by King’s Business School and the Money Macro and Finance Society.

The CPI report subsequently came out, showing a 0.4 percent monthly increase.

Consumers are feeling the rising costs at the petrol pump, as prices are declining but remain high. The average price for a gallon of petrol is $3.87 ($1.02 per litre), down from $4.34 ($1.14 per litre)this time a month ago, but still well above the $2.98 ($0.79 per litre) price recorded on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran.

World.title: Eisenkot Accuses Netanyahu of Fueling ‘Racist’ Hostility Against Arabs
World.content:
Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who is trying to form the next Israeli government, accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fueling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab citizens, in some of the strongest public criticism of his rival’s attacks on the community.

The comments were made days after Mr. Netanyahu delivered a divisive speech to the opening session of Parliament, or the Knesset, in which he referred to Arab lawmakers as “terror supporters” and “haters of Israel.” Diplomats and analysts condemned the remarks as a brazen display of hatred and incitement against Arab citizens, who make up about 20 percent of the overall population, and voted in massive numbers in inconclusive elections last month.

“Since the beginning of the election campaign, they have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimization, fueled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” Mr. Eisenkot said in a statement on social media.

“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story,” he said, adding that it was wrong to malign an entire community.

World.title: Caught Between Killers: Ebola on One Side, Islamic State on the Other
World.content:
Six months on, Ebola continues to hack a deadly trail across eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

When the outbreak was first detected in May, it resembled a single, giant blaze, with infections concentrated in a handful of towns in one province.

It has since morphed into a far bigger, more elusive foe, creeping into eight provinces and splintering into numerous hot spots as it moves through one of the world’s great rainforests.

Instead of one big fire, there are many now, scattered across a vast area about the size of Britain.

Health workers have corralled the virus where it was first detected, but infections are soaring elsewhere. Biakato, a small town deep in the rainforest, suddenly accounted for as many as one-quarter of new cases nationally. Yet its beleaguered residents were left almost entirely on their own, with dangerously little to defend themselves against the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

“We see the same mistakes as before,” said Dr. Jean-Jacques Muyembe, who helped discover Ebola in 1976 and now heads Congo’s National Institute for Biomedical Research. “It’s as if we were starting from zero. It’s very disappointing.”

And if that were not enough, the campaign to contain the epidemic has run into a terrifying new threat: the Islamic State.

World.title: The U.S.-Israel Relationship Is Broken. Here’s How Eisenkot Could Fix It.
World.content:
Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who has been given a chance to form Israel’s new governing coalition and replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is by no means assured of success.

But if he does take power, another hugely daunting challenge would immediately confront him: how to undo the vast damage done to Israel’s relationship with the United States, its closest and most important ally.

It’s hard to imagine things getting much worse.

Many Americans have turned against Israel over its devastating military campaign in Gaza, and even more so over its role in pressing for war with Iran, which led to soaring gas prices.

President Trump announced this month that he would cut off billions of dollars in annual U.S. military aid to Israel by the end of the year and blamed Israel in part for Republican losses in the midterm elections. Democratic control of Congress could quickly lead to sanctions on violent Israeli settlers and on new settlement construction in the occupied West Bank, as well as to new conditions on arms sales.

World.title: Study Hard, Get a Career and Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
World.content:
Britain didn’t introduce universal, free secondary education until 1944. In the United States, college was largely the province of the privileged few until the G.I. Bill opened access to veterans after World War II. Around the same time, the SAT created the first nationally standardized benchmark for admissions.

In countries whose economies developed later, the bargain took even longer to take shape. In India, the national college entrance exam was not introduced until the 1960s. In China, there is a long history of using meritocratic exams to select civil servants and other elites, but that system was disrupted by 20th-century reforms and the Cultural Revolution. The modern system was ushered in by Deng Xiaoping. In 1977 he re-established the national “gaokao” exam system as part of a post-Cultural Revolution rebuilding process. In the late 1990s, further reforms radically expanded university access.

For individuals, this access to education promised more money, more status or both. But for governments, it also offered political stability — a way to convince people to buy into society as currently structured, by promising the potential for advancement to the underprivileged without ousting those who had wealth and power already.

Are you a federal worker? We want to hear from you. The Times would like to hear about your experience as a federal worker under the second Trump administration. We may reach out about your submission, but we will not publish any part of your response without contacting you first.

Research has shown that the prospect of upward mobility — sometimes abbreviated as POUM — can make the poor less likely to demand redistribution. In China, merit-based selection for civil service jobs made people more willing to tolerate inequality, Hanzhang Liu, a political scientist at Florida State University, has found.

When people believed the system was meritocratic, they were more likely to attribute their failures to their own poor abilities, or to the high quality of the competition, she said. But when they did not believe so, those who lost out on jobs were more likely to consider the system rigged.

World.title: Europe Haggles Over Who Will Represent It in Talks With Russia
World.content:
“Europe really needs to pay attention,” President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine warned dozens of leaders from across the continent assembled in Dublin for a summit on Thursday.

European Union leaders were debating who should represent them on Friday over lunch. Mr. Zelensky is pushing Europe to choose someone by the end of the month, possibly as soon as a meeting of Ukraine’s allies next Thursday in Germany.

The discussions come as tensions run high. Ukraine’s domestic intelligence service, the S.B.U., said on Friday that the country’s forces had attacked a Russian warship this week. Analysts placed the warship in the Gulf of Finland, in northern Europe.

Even with such high stakes, challenges persist.

Small nations in the European Union do not always trust big ones to reflect their interests. Britain and Norway, which have a financial and security stake, are not part of the union. Eastern nations bordering Russia doubt that western ones understand the depth of the menace they face.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland said on Thursday, “Under no circumstances will we allow new security rules for this part of the world to be established over our heads, without Poland or Europe having a say.”

World.title: After Xi Purges China’s Generals, a Military Inquisitor Rises
World.content:
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, endorsed the expulsion of dozens of disgraced officials at a recent Communist Party meeting in Beijing, one man stood out as a clear winner.

Taking his new place at the front of the meeting was Gen. Zhang Shengmin, the somber-faced enforcer of Mr. Xi’s purges inside the military. He had been promoted to the Politburo, the party’s top leadership council, the latest step in his improbable rise from low-profile inspector to a position second only to Mr. Xi in China’s military hierarchy.

General Zhang has been the principal overseer of Mr. Xi’s campaign to purify the People’s Liberation Army. His latest elevation signaled that the investigations, indoctrination drives and loyalty tests could continue for years, as Mr. Xi searches for officers he believes are irreproachably loyal, experts and officials said.

“Twist the blade inward, with strict measures to cure disorder,” China’s main military newspaper said after the party meeting that was held late last month, referring to the continued discipline campaign.

World.title: Border Crossings Have Plummeted. Stephen Miller Isn’t Satisfied.
World.content:
Since President Trump resumed office, the number of illegal crossings at the U.S.-Mexico border has dropped to the lowest point in decades.

For one of Mr. Trump’s top policy advisers, that is not enough.

In conversations with both American and Mexican officials over the last several months, Stephen Miller has insisted that illegal border crossings must be reduced, according to officials in both countries familiar with the private conversations but not authorized to discuss them.

Mr. Miller’s goal, they said, is zero crossings. Mexican officials have said that, with a nearly 2,000-mile border, that is simply not possible.

In his new role as chief of staff, Mr. Miller is expected to continue driving that agenda.

One of the main forums for Mr. Miller’s demands has been his near daily calls with the U.S. ambassador to Mexico, Ronald ​Johnson, some of the officials said. On calls with staff, Mr. Miller, previously the deputy chief of staff, frequently rails about the number of border crossings, despite their low figures, the officials said.

World.title: One of France’s Most Popular Athletes Is Running for President
World.content:
When Teddy Riner, a judo champion and one of France’s most popular athletes, announced this week that he would run for president, it was less a game changer than a welcome diversion. For all of his appeal, Mr. Riner, 37, is unlikely to win the race to replace President Emmanuel Macron next spring.

Yet his quixotic candidacy reveals a hard truth about France’s presidential campaign. Five months before voters go to the polls, many are eager, even desperate, for a fresh face to upend a race that looks increasingly as if it’s on a glide path to the election of France’s first far-right government since World War II.

The main far-right candidate, Marine Le Pen, has held a commanding lead over all her rivals for months — a lead that has only been reinforced by weeks of protests, marred by violence, that have shaken France. The most prominent center-right candidate, Édouard Philippe, has faded in the polls as the unrest has sharpened the appeal of far-right calls for law and order and left-wing calls for social justice.

Another beneficiary of the upheaval is a far-left firebrand, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who now appears to be the likeliest candidate to advance into a second round against Ms. Le Pen in France’s two-round system. As things currently stand, French voters would be confronted with a choice between two poles of the political spectrum.

World.title: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
World.content:
Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.

Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues.

"What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said.

"The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs.

"One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in.

"You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."

The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.

Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".

He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.

Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.

"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.

"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.

In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners.

"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."

World.title: Watch: How a server outage took down Microsoft Teams and Outlook
World.content:
A Microsoft outage is affecting services including Teams, Outlook and AI software Copilot.

Microsoft has said the problem was caused by a higher-than-usual stress on its servers but that systems were now showing "early signs of stabilisation" as work continued on a fix.

The BBC's technology reporter Shiona McCallum explains what we know.

Read more about the Microsoft outage.

World.title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
World.content:
Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.

That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.

And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?

The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."

Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.

What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.

The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 â the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.

What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".

That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.

But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow.

"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week.

"Our proposals were almost laughed at.

"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."

The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire".

"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."

Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.

Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.

This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.

After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.

But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken.

"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

World.title: Nvidia scandal fallout widens as Trump's treasury secretary blames cabinet colleague
World.content:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed the Commerce Department, run by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec Nvidia chips, as the fallout from the scandal widens.

There is growing pressure on Lutnick across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions.

Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy.

Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it had been smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but is not on a list of firms that US companies are prevented from working with.

Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".
