"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.

Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.

World.title: German spies handed new powers to tackle 'hybrid threats' from abroad
World.content:
Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's parliament, the Bundestag, approved a major overhaul of its legislation.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who championed the bill, has called it a "reform of the century", necessary because of the increasing threats from foreign powers.

But the Left Party's security spokeswoman, Clara BÃ¼nger, said Dobrindt was creating a new German secret police.

The legislation gives numerous new powers to Germany's BND federal intelligence service, and its BfV domestic service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.

In the Bundestag, 309 MPs voted in favour of the new law on intelligence services, while 190 voted against and 71 abstained.

For historical reasons, German intelligence has mainly focused on gathering information rather than acting on it.

In future, German spies working for the BND, which is responsible for foreign intelligence, will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, including sabotage.

This could include paralysing the servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks, or even disrupting supply chains for weapons.

Agents for the domestic intelligence service, the BfV, will no longer to be limited to gathering information. For the first time they will be able to take protective action against property and IT systems, if specific threats are identified.

That means they will be allowed to dismantle or break explosives or weapons, divert or block data flows during cyber-attacks, delete or falsify data stored for malicious purposes, and plant false information on those involved.

World.title: African Miss Universe beauty queens in limbo as US visa restrictions bite
World.content:
Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secure a US visa.

Hall is due to represent Zimbabwe at the 75th edition of the Miss Universe pageant, with the winner set to be crowned on 24 November. But she has yet to obtain a visa to travel to the US territory.

"We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved," Hall said in a video posted on her Instagram page.

Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by the restrictions. Zambia has withdrawn its representative, Pamela Mubanga, from the competition because of US travel restrictions.

Contestants began arriving in Puerto Rico on 8 November for registration, fittings and other pre-pageant activities, putting pressure on Hall, and others including the representative from South Sudan, to secure their visas.

"Officially, today is the day I was supposed to be leaving for Puerto Rico for the 75th edition of Miss Universe," Hall said.

Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial US travel restrictions introduced under the Presidential Proclamation 10998, which took effect on 1 January 2026.

The measures suspend the issuance of visitor, student and exchange visas, as well as immigrant visas, to nationals of the affected countries. They also impose restrictions on other categories of non-immigrant visas.

In a statement, the Miss Universe organization in Zambia said Mubanga's situation was a consequence of the travel restrictions rather than individual circumstances.

"Unlike situations where a contestant's visa is denied due to personal circumstances, documentation or organisational challenges, Mubanga's situation is linked to the United States' presidential travel restriction affecting Zambia and other African countries," the statement read.

Mubanga, 25, a registered nurse, was crowned Miss Universe Zambia on 8 October and was due to represent the country at the international pageant.

The statement said five other African countries faced similar difficulties, although it did not name them.

Hall said she shared their concerns, adding that she had spent the past few weeks in South Africa trying to secure her visa.

"I am not alone in this predicament. Some of my African sisters are facing the same predicament, and I know exactly what they are going through," she said.

Miss Universe South Sudan also expressed uncertainty about her participation, commenting on Hall's video: "It is 50/50 whether we will make it, Miss Universe."

In another video posted three days earlier, Hall said she was still hoping to make it to Puerto Rico.

She captioned the video: "The fight to get Zimbabwe to Puerto Rico continues,"

The pageant's final is scheduled to take place at the JosÃ© Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan.

World.title: Democratic Senate leader Schumer set to face leadership challenge
World.content:
US Senator Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge to his position as US Senate majority leader from his fellow Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, as the party prepares to take control of Congress after sweeping the midterm elections.

Van Hollen, 67, said in a post on X on Thursday that Americans voted for change earlier this month and "to deliver, we need new leadership".

Schumer, 75, has led Democrats in the chamber since 2017, serving as both majority and minority leader. He was first elected to the Senate in 1999.

Following the midterms earlier this month, his position has come under pressure by some left-wing Democrats who see him as too moderate and part of the party establishment.

Responding to the challenge, Schumer, who represents New York, said he welcomes "any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead".

He added that he is "proud of what we've accomplished together" in the midterms, and he has "the votes to continue as Democratic leader".

The vote on Senate leader will be held behind closed doors in early December and the winner will assume the role on 4 January, when Democrats take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives after their midterms successes.

The move by Van Hollen, who represents Maryland, marks the most significant step by a high-profile Democrat to challenge the party's existing leadership following last week's midterms victory.

Announcing his plans to run on X, he wrote that Americans had called on the party to "unrig an economy rigged against working people".

In recent years, Van Hollen has taken positions popular with those on the left of his party.

In 2024, he supported restricting weapons shipments to Israel and criticised the Biden administration over its role in the war in Gaza.

In an interview with MS NOW, Van Hollen - who has served in the Senate for nearly a decade - acknowledged that he is an "underdog" but added that he believes the race is "very much in flux".

Independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed have both publicly come out in support of Van Hollen - while others have also called for new leadership.

In a post on X, Sanders said he believes Van Hollen "will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families".

El-Sayed said the challenger would bring "bold leadership" and lead with both "courage and experience".

Others Democrats have publicly backed Schumer.

Senator Jacky Rosen of Nevada said: "He has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment".

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said: "You will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position."

World.title: UN watchdog 'increasingly concerned' over uninspected Iran nuclear site
World.content:
The UN's nuclear watchdog has said it is "increasingly concerned" about a nuclear facility in Iran which it has not been allowed to inspect.

Iran informed the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) of plans to set up the uranium enrichment plant in the city of Isfahan a day before Israel began attacking its nuclear sites last June. The US joined the strikes later that month.

In a report seen by news agencies, the IAEA said it does not know the exact location or whether it contains nuclear material.

Since the start of the latest war, Iran has restricted IAEA inspectors' access to its nuclear sites, preventing the agency from verifying its enriched uranium stockpile.

Under a 2015 nuclear deal, Iran agreed to limit its enriched uranium stockpile to 300kg and enrichment to 3.67% purity. It subsequently exceeded both.

Before the June 2025 strikes, it had accumulated an estimated 441kg enriched to 60%, close to weapons grade.

The nuclear complex at Isfahan suffered extensive damage in US and Israeli strikes, particularly the parts above the ground. The condition of its underground facilities is not clear.

The IAEA believes much of Iran's highly enriched uranium was stored there.

"The Agency's lack of information about [Iran's] nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern... and needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency," it said in the latest report.

Iran announced plans for the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP) on 12 June 2025, shortly after an IAEA resolution which declared Iran had failed to meet its nuclear safeguards obligations.

Iran initially agreed to allow inspectors to visit the facility, but the inspection was cancelled after Israel launched attacks the following day.

The IAEA's latest calls come almost a year after it made a similar appeal to Iran. At the time it said it had only inspected some of the 13 nuclear facilities that were "unaffected" by the attacks and none of the seven that were.

The US and Israel said they attacked Iran's nuclear sites to prevent it developing nuclear weapons - something Iran has consistently denied seeking. It says its nuclear programme is for peaceful civilian purposes only.

World.title: Signals from Nigeria’s side of Lake Chad, By Samuel Aruwan
World.content:
On 7 November 2026, I listened with keen interest to the interview Alhaji Abubakar Gamandi, chairman of the Lake Chad Basin Fisheries Association of Nigeria, granted the BBC Hausa Service. As I translated it into English, I kept returning to his claim that armed groups now held six places on the Nigerian side of Lake Chad where troops had once been stationed. He spoke of fishermen who risk their lives to return to those waters because their families depend on what they catch. He also spoke of island communities where thousands of children have little opportunity to continue their education beyond primary school.

Speaking to Haruna Tangaza, he acknowledged the presence of the Nigerian Army, the Navy and troops of the Multinational Joint Task Force (MNJTF) at Baga. He said the Navy operated from the old fishing dam and covered that part of the lake. He then recalled where Nigerian troops had once been stationed farther into the lake. “On the Nigerian side, you cannot go to a single island and find soldiers stationed there. Back when there was peace, we had military bases. There were soldiers at Duguri and at Madayi. There was also Kaukiri, close to where that recent attack took place. Kaukiri is within six kilometres of the site. It too was a military base when there was peace. There were soldiers at Dogon Ciku, an army unit at Mari, and soldiers stationed at Shuwaram. Those were all military posts. When there was peace, the soldiers controlled all of them. Today there is not a single one left. The places I have just listed are all in Boko Haram’s hands.”

Tangaza asked, “As of this year, 2026?” Gamandi replied, “Yes, as of today, as we speak.” In March 2024, the International Crisis Group reported that Boko Haram’s JAS faction had taken Duguri and Shuwaram during its fighting with the Islamic State West Africa Province. Who held all six places when Gamandi spoke in November 2026 is a question for the Nigerian authorities to examine. In my view, the test of an operation on the lake is whether the authorities can maintain enough security for residents to return and earn a living.

He said the forces had yet to secure even the mainland, let alone the lake’s interior. He distinguished the waters and islands from the wider Lake Chad area, which includes places such as Monguno. That distinction matters to a fisherman deciding whether to return. He needs to know if he can reach his landing site and fishing grounds safely. On the Chadian side, Gamandi named Litri, Kaiga, Gubuwa and Kangalan as places where troops were stationed. He said Chadian authorities still held some islands where fishermen and farmers could work in peace. Since his community was driven out around 2013, he said, Boko Haram’s presence between Nigerian and Chadian positions had kept the route from Baga towards Baga Salla, Gubuwa and Kangalan closed to authorised civilian travel.

On the Nigerien side, he recalled that fishermen returned after a joint operation drove out rebels. He called it Operation Mikiya and tentatively dated it to 2000 or 2001. He said Nigerien troops did not establish posts on the islands. He described the lake interior off Kwatan Barwa, Kwatan Lailaya and Kwatan Karanga as the headquarters of Bakura Abu Umaima’s group. He mentioned Cameroon’s sector in the joint force but gave less detail about its presence on the islands. The question for the four countries is how much of the lake and its approaches their forces can cover together.

Gamandi estimated that there were more than 200 islands, with about 120 commonly used across the four countries. Some supported settlements with wells, mosques and weekly markets. He said there had been no comprehensive population count. Knowing how many people live on the islands would help the authorities decide where schools, clinics and public water points are needed.

He traced his own Hausa community’s settlement on the lake to around 1905 and to journeys for the Hajj. He mentioned people from Kebbi, Sokoto, Zamfara and Katsina who already knew how to farm and fish. He described the Kanuri, whom he calls Bari-Bari, as indigenous to the area and recalled that Buduma communities in parts of Chad, Niger and Nigeria raised livestock and fished. He credited Hausa settlers with developing commercial fishing and cultivating larger farms. Among those fishing on the Chadian side, he named the Buduma, Shuwa Arabs and Zaghawa. On the Cameroonian side, he mentioned the Masa.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Even in my own family today, there are Shuwa, Buduma and Bari-Bari relatives,” he said. “My own wife is Bari-Bari. We came together and became one extended family.” When trouble arose, he said, people could draw on relationships built over years of living and working together. A border closure can cut a fisherman off from a market and from family on the other side.

He said Chad had the largest share of the waters in use. He estimated that Nigerians accounted for about 80 per cent of fishermen on the Nigerien side, 60 per cent on the Cameroonian side and nearly 40 per cent on the Chadian side. That helps explain why restrictions in one part of the lake can affect families in another country.

“Sambisa may have the bigger name, but Lake Chad has a greater Boko Haram presence,” Gamandi said. He explained that people could catch fish for food and extract its oil for frying. He also spoke of animals that provide meat and fat, land that can yield a harvest in about three months, and drinking water within an hour’s walk. If his account is confirmed, fighters holding parts of the lake can obtain much of what they need where they are based, even when outside supplies are disrupted.

He described the terms under which people who still go to the islands are allowed to work. “There is no question of clashes now. Our people who are still there have to submit to them. If you do as they say, you can live there in peace. That means obeying their rules. You have to accept that they regard the place as part of their own territory. When you go in to fish, they tell you, ‘Stay away from that place. You can fish along this stretch. Anyone who crosses that boundary will be punished. Nobody is to bring us cigarettes, drugs or alcohol. Those things are forbidden in our territory. And if anyone wrongs another person and a complaint is brought to us, we will punish the offender according to what he did.’”

He also described how fighters restrict communication. “They hold the power and control everything. They tell you to leave your phone behind. They also tell you to keep news from town to yourself, including anything the soldiers have said, and to keep information about them from the soldiers. Those are the instructions they give you.” Restrictions on phones and contact with soldiers make it harder for residents to report threats.

Using data from the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, the Africa Center for Strategic Studies reported 880 deaths from violence against civilians linked to militant groups in the Lake Chad Basin in the year ending 30 June 2025. That was a 32 per cent increase over the previous year and the highest figure since 2016. In its August 2026 update, the Center reported that overall fatalities linked to militant violence in the basin rose by 60 per cent to 6,643 in the 12 months to mid-2026. It attributed most of that increase to battle-related deaths.

Where people cannot safely reach the police or courts, fighters can take it upon themselves to hear complaints and impose punishments. Control over fishing grounds, farms and markets also gives them a means of extracting money. The authorities should establish whether and where fighters impose levies on fishermen, farmers, herders and traders. Where collections are confirmed, they should cut off the revenue while protecting the people being made to pay.

Gamandi said that when an island settlement on the Nigerian side grew, the Lawan with jurisdiction would come and appoint a Bulama. The Bulama then exercised authority on the island, including in places where government officials rarely went. Anyone responsible for restoring civilian administration needs to understand how residents organised their affairs and whom they trusted.

He described the shortage of public services along the Nigerian stretch from Gamboru to Malam Fatori in Abadam Local Government Area. His emphasis was on settlements beyond the mainland. “Take the whole Nigerian side, from Gamboru to Malam Fatori in Abadam Local Government Area. Four local government areas border those waters. On the islands themselves, once you leave the mainland, you will hardly find a properly equipped school where children can learn. There are thousands of children there, yet there is no adequate school provision. Nor would you find a properly equipped hospital where people could get treatment.”

He acknowledged that some facilities had come after residents began to complain. “But given the number of people, the few facilities are barely felt.” He illustrated the disparity with a comparison. “A settlement may be 500 years old, yet if you count everybody, children and adults, you may find fewer than 200 people. It will have a school, a secondary school and everything else. Then you go to where people actually live in their thousands because that is where they can earn a living, and you find they have nothing beyond a primary school.”

He also spoke of inadequate electricity and water supplies. Families who could afford to make their own arrangements dug wells or sank boreholes. He saw the shortage of schools on the islands as one of the factors that helped Boko Haram’s ideology gain a foothold. “There are very many people living there, from different ethnic groups, and they were given no schooling. Everyone was left to their own devices. So when that ideology was brought in, people simply accepted it.” Borno State and the relevant local governments should establish which schools and clinics are functioning, what services they provide and whether families can reach them safely.

Gamandi recalled taking a photograph and a map to President Muhammadu Buhari and asking him to remember earlier fighting with Chad. He said Buhari had addressed troops from a boat by the landing at Doron Baga and told them that their next day’s meal would be brought to Kilbuwa. Buhari, he said, directed him and others to meet officials of the Department of State Services. The fishermen offered their knowledge of the islands and waterways. “We knew the area,” he said. “Countless young men from our communities made their living from fishing there and were eager to see the place cleared.”

“We went in and carried out that operation in 2017, as I said. It lasted only two or three months. Yet from 2017 to this day, no one has managed to get back to the places we reached in those three months.” Official records and accounts from others who took part can help establish how far the operation went and what followed. Fishermen still have knowledge the authorities can draw on, including which settlements rely on particular landing sites and what happens to trade when a route closes. They should be able to share it without putting their families at risk.

He explained why fishermen continued to go back even after the authorities declared the waters a war zone. “Now, the only people who go to those islands are those prepared to risk their lives. Our people who still go there to fish do so without official permission. The authorities have declared it a war zone. But ordinary people have to go in and find food. The authorities tried to stop them and couldn’t. People cannot stay away.”

He spoke of killings among those who went back. In better times, he said, the money from a catch fed families, sent children to school and helped relatives. Traders and people who process fish also depend on what fishermen bring ashore. Where restrictions are necessary, the authorities should explain where people can lawfully fish, land and sell their catch, and what help is available while their usual fishing grounds remain closed. A man with a family to feed will weigh an instruction to stay away against what his family will eat that week.

Gamandi also warned that a transfer of water into the lake could displace people living on the islands. He recalled that water levels fell sharply between about 1985 and 2000, then rose with the return of rainfall. He said fish were more abundant than he could remember. He recalled attending a summit on bringing more water into the lake while the late president was still in office. He also said he had raised his concerns about a water transfer in a BBC radio interview. The State House records that Nigeria hosted an international conference in February 2018 at which a transfer of water from the Ubangi River to Lake Chad was among the proposals discussed.

“We have counted more than 120 islands,” he said. “If you bring in enough water to restore the lake to its former level, I reckon about 70 of those islands would be submerged. If the water rises to the level people are talking about, where will the people who live on those islands go?” That estimate should be examined against the proposed water levels and the location of inhabited settlements. Families who have already lost homes or livelihoods to the fighting deserve to know whether such a project could displace them again.

The Nigerian government should ensure that its intelligence agencies examine Gamandi’s account in collaboration with the security forces and the relevant authorities in Borno State. They should establish who controls the six places he named, where armed groups obtain food and revenue, which routes they and their enablers use, and where civilians can travel safely. The review should draw on military and intelligence records as well as accounts from residents, fishermen and traders. Its findings should specify what action is needed and which authorities should take it.

The efforts of the Nigerian security forces on Lake Chad deserve commendation. More is required to fill gaps in security coverage and maintain control of the areas troops secure. In May 2026, the African Union Peace and Security Councilexpressed concern about Niger’s suspension of participation in the Multinational Joint Task Force and urged it to resume full participation. In October, Nigeria’s Defence Headquarters convened a forum on strengthening the force. Those efforts should lead to arrangements that the countries can put into practice on the lake and along its borders.

Nigeria, Chad, Niger and Cameroon should set aside their political differences and deepen existing intelligence sharing and cooperation. A return to full participation by Niger would help the four countries coordinate operations across the islands, waterways and land approaches. They should jointly identify the crossings used by fighters and their suppliers and agree on how to cover them. I have argued before that relentless pressure in areas occupied by terrorist groups can weaken their ability to operate. If fighters can cross a border when pressure mounts, they have another chance to regroup, replenish supplies and prepare attacks.

The state must establish a lasting presence in areas where people have been left without policing and basic services. Where armed men decide who can fish, hear complaints and punish those who disobey them, they have room to extract money, recruit and consolidate their hold. Once troops secure an area, the police and civilian authorities need the staff and resources to stay, and residents must be able to reach them safely.

A fisherman should be able to set out, sell his catch and come home safely without seeking permission from armed men. If someone threatens him or demands money from him, he should have somewhere to report it. His children should have a school to attend and a chance to continue beyond primary school. That is what a lasting state presence should mean to the people of the lake. As Gamandi said, “There is enough water. All we need now is peace.”

Samuel Aruwan is a postgraduate student in the Department of Mass Communication at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria.

World.title: DR Congo 2-0 Nigeria: Olympic Eagles suffer double blow in U-23 AFCON qualifier
World.content:
Nigeria’s Olympic Eagles suffered a 2-0 defeat to DR Congo in the first leg of their second-round 2027 Africa U-23 Cup of Nations qualifying tie in Lubumbashi on Friday, leaving them with a difficult task ahead of the return fixture.

A controversial ‘own goal’ by Samuel James and a strike from Filozofe Mabete handed the Congolese a two-goal advantage as Nigeria struggled to recover from a disappointing first-half performance.

The hosts took the lead in the 15th minute when James was adjudged to have turned the ball into his own net, putting Nigeria on the back foot.

The Olympic Eagles had an opportunity to open the scoring earlier when Victor Samuel found himself in a one-on-one situation with the Congolese goalkeeper in the ninth minute. However, he failed to convert the opportunity.

Nigeria’s problems worsened in the 35th minute when Mabete doubled DR Congo’s advantage with a well-taken free-kick, leaving the visitors with a difficult task heading into the break.

Nigeria also suffered an injury setback in the first half, with Zadok Yohanna forced off in the 30th minute.

Despite their efforts to get back into the contest, the Olympic Eagles could not break down the Congolese defence as the match ended 2-0.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

From Olympic glory to qualification struggles

The defeat adds to growing concerns about Nigeria’s recent struggles in the U-23 category, especially given the country’s impressive history in Olympic men’s football.

Nigeria made history at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, becoming the first African country to win gold in the men’s football competition.

Led by players including Nwankwo Kanu, Jay-Jay Okocha, Sunday Oliseh and Taribo West, the team defeated Argentina 3-2 in the final, with Emmanuel Amunike scoring the decisive goal in the 89th minute.

Nigeria subsequently reached the quarter-finals at Sydney 2000 before missing the 2004 Athens Games.

The Olympic Eagles returned to the podium at Beijing 2008, winning silver after losing 1-0 to Argentina in the final. They also claimed bronze at Rio 2016, defeating Honduras 3-2 in the third-place match.

However, their fortunes have declined since that achievement.

Nigeria failed to qualify for Tokyo 2020 after finishing third in their group at the 2019 U-23 AFCON in Egypt. The Olympic Eagles also missed Paris 2024 after losing 2-0 on aggregate to Guinea in the final qualifying round for the 2023 U-23 AFCON in Morocco.

The failure to qualify for Paris meant Nigeria missed a second consecutive Olympic football tournament, having last featured at Rio 2016.

The country has also experienced contrasting fortunes at the continental level. Nigeria won the inaugural U-23 AFCON title in 2015 but failed to qualify for the 2023 edition, which doubled as Africa’s qualifying competition for Paris 2024.

The current campaign therefore represents another opportunity for the Olympic Eagles to rebuild their continental standing and move closer to ending their Olympic absence.

READ ALSO: Olympic Eagles step up preparations with friendly against Grassrunners FC

Nigeria face uphill task in return leg

The result leaves Nigeria with a two-goal deficit to overturn in the return leg if they are to keep their hopes of qualifying for the 2027 U-23 AFCON alive.

Both teams will meet again on Tuesday, 17 November, at the Remo Stars Stadium in Ikenne, Ogun State.

The Olympic Eagles will need a significantly improved performance on home soil, particularly in attack and defensive organisation, to overturn the deficit.

A place at the 2027 U-23 AFCON in Egypt is the immediate target, but the stakes extend beyond the continental competition. The tournament will also serve as Africa’s qualification pathway to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games.

World.title: Genesis Energy wins two awards at Lagos Energy Summit, reinforcing commitment to power infrastructure development
World.content:
In recognition of its outstanding contributions to power infrastructure development, energy innovation and investment in Lagos State, Genesis Energy Holdings (GENESIS), a leading pan-African clean energy infrastructure development and asset management company, has received two awards at the 2026 edition of the Lagos Energy Summit, organised by the Lagos State Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources.

The awards presented to Genesis Energy Holding on the opening day of the Summit, at the Landmark Event Centre, Lagos, on Tuesday, 10 November2026, under the theme, “Lagos Energy Evolution: Transforming the Future.” includes the “Most Impactful Project (Power) Award” and the “Excellence in Energy – Summit Partner Appreciation Award.” The first was conferred on the company by Hon Sabur Akanbi Oluwa, Chairman of the Lagos State House of Assembly Committee on Energy and Mineral Resources, while the second award was conferred on the company by Hon. Biodun Ogunleye, Commissioner for Energy and Mineral Resources, Lagos State.

The recognition underscores Genesis Energy Holdings’commitment to advancing reliable electricity supply, developing critical power infrastructure and supporting the transformation of Lagos State’s energy sector through strategic investments and partnerships. Through its subsidiary, GELMAK Power Solutions Ltd, the company operates the Banana Island Local Grid Project in Ikoyi, Lagos, an integrated power generation and distribution network providing reliable electricity to residential and commercial customers.

Designed to reduce dependence on expensive and polluting diesel and heavy fuel oil (HFO) generators, the project currently records approximately 99% uptime. Its infrastructure capacity was recently doubled from 15MVA to 30MVA following the commissioning of an expanded substation, strengthening its ability to meet the growing electricity demand within the community.

Further demonstrating its commitment to expanding electricity infrastructure across Lagos State, GENESIS is developing Project Echo, the 260MW Ikorodu Power Project, in partnership with the Lagos State Government under the CLEM initiative. With the Lagos State Market Operator as off-taker, the gas-fired power project is designed to deliver reliable, grid-integrated electricity, strengthening power supply across Ikorodu and supporting the development of a more resilient electricity market. Once operational, the project is expected to improve electricity availability for households, businesses and industries, while stimulating economic activity and supporting the area’s continued development.

Commenting on the awards, Chairman and CEO of Genesis Energy, Mr Akinwole II Omoboriowo, said: “We want to extend our gratitude to Lagos State for giving us the opportunity to serve. We are most grateful for this recognition, which, for us, is both an honour and a call to action – a call to invest more. The business of energy is a very serious affair. Without energy, there can be no life. For us at GENESIS, it is not just a business; it is a lifelong commitment to uplifting our country and our continent, with Lagos State being at the forefront of that commitment.”

These investments reflect the Group’s alignment with Lagos State’s electricity sector reform agenda, particularly the objectives of the Lagos State Electricity Law 2024, which provides a framework for developing a competitive, transparent and commercially viable electricity market. Since its establishment in 2005, Genesis Energy Holdings has developed and financed clean energy projects across Africa, with operations and project footprints spanning 11 African countries.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The company deploys a diverse range of technologies, including solar photovoltaic (PV), battery energy storage systems (BESS), natural gas, wind, hydro and hybrid solutions, to develop reliable and sustainable energy infrastructure for businesses, governments and communities.

Its Nigerian portfolio includes the 84MW gas-fired power project at the Port Harcourt Refinery Complex, one of Nigeria’s largest licensed private off-grid power plants and NIDI project in Kano. In 2025, the Group further expanded its engagement in Nigeria through a US$500 million Memorandum of Understanding with the Katsina State Government for the development, financing, construction, operation and maintenance of major energy infrastructure projects across the State.

With a vision to “Light Up Africa One Community at a Time,” GENESIS remains committed to developing and deploying reliable, affordable and sustainable energy infrastructure that addresses the continent’s growing energy needs. Through strategic investments, innovative technologies and partnerships with governments and private-sector stakeholders, the company continues to advance energy access, strengthen energy security and support economic development across Africa.

World.title: Fani-Kayode presents Letter of Credence to Ramaphosa, formally assumes duty as ambassador
World.content:
Nigeria’s High Commissioner to South Africa, Femi Fani-Kayode, has presented his Letter of Credence to South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, marking the official commencement of his diplomatic assignment in the country.

Mr Fani-Kayode presented his letter to Mr Ramaphosa at the Sefako Makgatho Presidential Guest House in Pretoria, the official residence of the South African Presidency, on Friday.

The High Commissioner shared the development on X, describing the event as “great and historic.”

Letters of credence are formal diplomatic documents issued by a country’s head of state to confirm the appointment of a High Commissioner or permanent representative.

They officially introduce the envoy to the receiving authority, in this case, the South African president, and certify that the individual is empowered to speak and act on behalf of their nation.

Mr Fani-Kayode presented his letter of credence alongside ambassadors from 14 other countries. Each was formally introduced and given the floor to speak.

He pledged to strengthen diplomatic relations between both countries, describing the restoration of their historic friendship as a key priority of his diplomatic mission.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The envoy, also accredited to Lesotho and Eswatini, conveyed President Bola Tinubu’s goodwill to Mr Ramaphosa.

This comes amid tense relations between Nigeria and South Africa over xenophobic violence that forced many African states to evacuate their citizens residing in the country.

Mr Fani-Kayode had previously condemned violence against Nigerian nationals by South African security officials. He estimated that at least 30 Nigerians have been killed by the state’s police in the last four years. 12 Nigerians have also been killed since the start of the year.

In September, the High Commissioner said Nigeria’s patience was running thin.

Speaking at the ceremony, however, Mr Fani-Kayode recalled Nigeria’s support for South Africa during the struggle against apartheid, saying both countries shared a longstanding history of solidarity and friendship.

He described Nigeria and South Africa as major trading partners on the continent and stressed the importance of preserving their historical ties.

“Part of my job here is to reset that relationship, to come and build that bridge, and to ensure that whatever concerns we have, we can work them out and move forward together,” he said.

Mr Fani-Kayode added that closer cooperation between the two countries would strengthen Africa’s position and advance the interests of their citizens.

“If Nigeria and South Africa work closely together, the destiny of our great continent will be more secure,” he said.

The high commissioner also commended South Africa’s contributions to international diplomacy, particularly its role in BRICS, the Global South and the Group of 20 (G20).

He described South Africa’s engagement in global affairs as important to strengthening Africa’s representation on the international stage.

Meanwhile, Mr Fani-Kayode, on his X handle, complained that the South African presidential media team failed to live-stream his speech despite capturing those of the other ambassadors present.

“Of all the 15 introductions and speeches that were made and delivered this morning, only Nigeria’s was cut out,” he said. “To be clear, I repeat, we were the ONLY ones that were left out.”

“Clearly, some elements in South Africa do not want to hear what we have to say or see our faces, but we are here to stay as long as we are welcome and have the confidence of President Ramaphosa, which I am sure we do,” he noted further.

World.title: Still on the Minna mining misfortune, By Zainab Suleiman Okino
World.content:
Between the Nigerian government and citizens, the trust deficit is huge. Setting up a committee to unravel anything is viewed with suspicion. In our days in the Daily Trust newsroom, setting up committees was a butt of jokes among us. We called it the committee on snakes, in reference to a one-time US presidential aspirant, Ross Perot, who criticised the American bureaucracy’s penchant for setting up committees: “If you see a snake, just kill it. Don’t appoint a committee on snakes.”

Unfortunately, Nigeria has not done creditably well in this regard over time. The works of many committees are gathering dust on shelves across the country. When the Federal Government, through the Minister of Interior, Dr Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, set up the NSCDC committee to investigate the deaths of artisanal miners at the Niger State Command, skepticism greeted the idea. Yours sincerely was one of the members.

However, a lot of people also called to express their confidence and to say they would give us the benefit of the doubt, knowing I would not agree to suppress the truth. It turned out that all the committee members were enthusiastic, as was the eager public, and each came with his integrity intact and ready to fight any form of suppression of the truth or cover-up.

Five weeks later, the committee submitted its report with deep insights into the root causes of the tragedy that cost the lives of innocent people, and recommendations that, if properly implemented, could change the narrative for the NSCDC and other paramilitary agencies. The committee’s report is now public knowledge and awaiting the government’s next line of action, but before then, a bit of background suffices.

I waited a bit to see reactions to our findings, revelations, and recommendations. And I’m happy to note that, contrary to controversies that normally trail such efforts, a lot of people seem content with the outcome of ours and have expressed that much in their reactions and individual calls. I’m not surprised, though, considering the calibre and pedigree of the members, their inputs and commitment, and the man-hours poured into this sensitive public service concern.

Soon after the September 22nd inauguration, we hit the ground running literally, working till the evening of that day to herald the pressure-cooker work of the next few weeks. We outlined our work and administrative plans and timelines of the onerous task; the sequence of events, form of engagement, etcetera.

By the third day, we headed for the NSCDC headquarters in Sauka, Airport Road, where all the staff involved in Minna had been brought and detained. As a matter of courtesy, we met with the NSCDC Commandant-General and his management team. Our engagement and interrogation with the suspected staff in detention was one-on-one, starting from the lowest-ranking officer, and one by one, what transpired on the 15th and night of the 16th through to the morning of the 17th of September, when the bodies of 33 able-bodied young men were discovered , began to unfold. We interrupted this process and moved to Minna for a one-week field fact-finding mission.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Our one-week stay in Minna was eventful. The emir’s palace, where we met with most of the families of victims and survivors, felt like home. The emir played host to us and played his fatherly role to all the people who thronged his palace. His advice and words of encouragement were a morale booster to all.

A visit to the NSCDC command was a priority. We toured the scene of the crime and the entire NSCDC office, visited the mining sites around MI Wushishi Estate, and visited the state commands of the Police and DSS. Our first port of call on arrival was to Governor Mohammed Bago, who reiterated his commitment to finding the truth and encouraged us to do the same. Minna opened our eyes to new vistas. There we met an NSCDC top shot who was fingered through verbal confessions of those in detention in Abuja, but was seemingly shielded. His personal account collapsed in the face of overwhelming evidence and interrogation from our team. He was indicted along with some five others recommended for dismissal and prosecution.

*Back to the third leg of our investigation in Abuja, suspect interrogation continued. All suspects, including the former Niger State Commandant, Suberu Aniviye, appeared before us. The session climaxed with the appearance of the Commandant-General himself. Meanwhile, putting the reports together was Herculean, emotionally and physically draining, and tasking. It took a lot of high-level discussions, back and forth, even voice votes to arrive at some conclusions. So charged, yet democratic were those sessions that betrayal of trust and outsider interference were NOT tenable.*

To our relief, after an exhausting five weeks, the Minister of Interior and Nigerians received our report with excitement and a promise of implementation in its independent pristine copy. While we keep our fingers crossed and hope for restitution for victims’ families, I must express how delighted I was to have worked with some of the most patriotic and committed, I’ve ever met.

The committee members obviously had pedigree and names to protect, and therefore came with much vigour, credibility, and hunger to succeed. To think otherwise could not have been, considering the lives involved. Compromise was not an alternative as we maintained our independence. We all worked our hearts out, and the report was not even ready until late night on the eve of presentation on October 27.

I’m proud of the teamwork, collaboration, and collective resolve to ensure succour in the form of justice for the benefit of the poor victims of the Minna mining tragedy, who had the misfortune of being in the wrong place at the wrong time-the misfortune of being poor and unemployed, and the misfortune of being IDPs. Most of the victims were from some IDP camps scattered in parts of Niger State.

I’m also happy to have worked with highly placed professionals with capacity, who approached this important national assignment with zeal and tenacity. The background of our chairman is already in the public space as a retired Deputy Director-General of the Directorate of State Services, but there is more to him. Mr. Jonathan Kure, a thoroughbred, highly sought-after professional with an outstanding career in service, has a calm and disarming demeanour that can thaw ice-cold conflict. Under his leadership, all of us felt safe. He brought his competence, years of experience, and capacity to bear on the work and was able to manage the egos of nine highly competent and accomplished professionals.

Starting from an accomplished technocrat with a lot of wisdom, who retired some 14 years ago as a permanent secretary, Alhaji Idris Adamu Kuta knows all the rules and guidelines governing the public service sector and offered them appropriately. And guess what? None of us knew he retired from the mines sector and unarguably knows it like the back of his palms. But because he represented the Minna Emirate Council on the committee, he kept faith with the traditional institution whose view he must project, and he did admirably. Imagine such a self-imposed discipline! Incidentally, the Emirate Council availed us of everything we needed to do our job, including space and other conveniences.

Talking of a man of power, knowledge, and capacity, but still humble and calm, the Secretary to the State Government (SSG) of Niger State, Alhaji Abubakar Usman, represented the state on the committee and used the opportunity to showcase the kind of people Governor Bago has in his cabinet-capable, proficient and hardworking. Despite his busy schedules, he made sure to be present through crucial sessions and difficult decisions when his opinions were needed. The Minna triumvirate would not be complete without the mention of Liman Suleiman, the Secretary of the Miners Association representing the association on the committee. His quiet and gentle disposition belied his knowledge of the volatile but emerging powerful sector, as a former banker and businessman.

Dr George Agbakahi is an intellectual powerhouse – hardworking and determined, with the zeal to “crucify” offenders. He was fierce and made sure that no stone was left unturned to ensure justice for the Minna 33. Without moderation, and with his volume of intellectual input, we would have “written a whole book” on the incident. He was that passionate, even as he paid attention to details. AIG Hosea Hassan Karma (retd) is a big man not seeming conscious of his social status; he is a personification of humility. He went to the basics of policing responsibility by serving as our “IPO-in-Chief.” Through his untiring efforts, we were able to extract vital information needed to conclude our final verdict of culpability on some of the suspects.

Professior Mikhail Olayinka Buhari is the popular histopathologist who eased our job with his practical knowledge of science and medicine. He got to Minna ahead of us, and his precursory work is central to our conclusion that 33 and not 37 miners died. His hard work, steadfastness and professionalism so stood out that he earned the chairman’s constant commendation. Deji Adeyanju, a human rights activist and lawyer, though the youngest, was the most visible; he almost took the shine off our team. As an activist, he was easily recognised and given celebrity status. Deji applied his skills as a lawyer and interrogator, which proved very useful in getting the suspects to squeal and reveal information about the true situation of things, as if he were in a law court.

I’m still amazed at our camaraderie, but the unprecedented level of cooperation between the committee chairman and secretary, Professor Isa Hayatu Chiroma, still amazes me. A law professor, Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), and former director-general (DG) of the Nigerian Law School, he came with hands-on skills and administrative experience. Yet his loyalty to hierarchy and group decisions was impressive. Obviously well experienced and established in the workings of committees, Mr Chiroma is every secretariat’s delight. Versatile, organised, competent, and proficient, Chiroma’s expertise exuded in the secretariat’s decent outcome. He had sleepless nights putting various annexures, appendices, and documents together. On the cooperation between him and the chairman, they still owe me an explanation on whether they knew or had worked together in the past. The bond was seamless.

Zainab Suleiman Okino (FNGE) is chairperson of the Editorial Board of Blueprint. She is a syndicated columnist and was a member of the Independent Investigation Committee on the deaths of persons in NSCDC custody, Niger State Command, Minna. She can can be reached via [email protected]

World.title: US revokes over 6,000 visas in its birth tourism crackdown
World.content:
The US government is doubling down on its immigration control, with the State Department revoking over 6,000 visas belonging to foreigners engaged in or facilitating birth tourism.

The department announced on Thursday, through its X handle, that its Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force had revoked the visas of people identified as involved in the practice.

“The Department of State’s Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force has now revoked more than 6,000 visas from foreigners who engaged in or facilitated birth tourism,” the post read.

It also said the task force is still identifying and “holding accountable everyone involved in this illicit practice.” This implies that more visas are likely to be revoked over this practice in the future.

Birth tourism refers to travelling to another country, usually while pregnant, to give birth so the child can acquire that country’s citizenship or nationality by birth.

The latest action signals a wider crackdown on both participants and facilitators, including those who help arrange such travel.

Last month, the department announced that it had revoked over 4,000 visas, and that 700 of the revoked visas belonged to Chinese nationals.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The latest statement, however, did not provide a breakdown by nationality. As such, it remains unclear whether Nigerians were among those affected.

A core aspect of President Donald Trump’s “America first” policy and political campaigns has been a crackdown on immigration.

The US leader, during his presidential campaigns, pledged to increase deportations of people living in the country, restrict asylum and refugee admissions, and tighten both illegal and some legal immigration pathways.

Since resuming office, Mr Trump has implemented several policies aligned with this agenda. At the inauguration ceremony, for instance, he signed an executive order declaring illegal immigration a national emergency and ordered the speedy deportation of undocumented migrants.

The United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement crackdown on migrants has, in the past year, been criticised for human rights violations.

The Trump administration also imposed visa bans on several countries, including Nigeria.

It is also planning to introduce a policy requiring foreign nationals in the US seeking to change their status from temporary visa holders to permanent residents to return to their home country to apply for a Green Card.

World.title: I faked breast cancer to raise N13m – Blessing CEO admits
World.content:
Media personality and self-proclaimed relationship expert Blessing “Blessing CEO” Okoro has admitted to fabricating her breast cancer diagnosis in March.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that Blessing CEO sparked concern after sharing a series of emotional videos on Instagram, in which she claimed doctors diagnosed her with stage-four breast cancer.

However, Deborah Mbara, creative director of Delta-based makeup company Zazi Beauty Place, accused her of manipulating her medical report to deceive Nigerians.

The controversy prompted the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to arrest Blessing CEO. The commission subsequently arraigned her before Justice Yelim Bogoro of the Federal High Court in Ikoyi, Lagos.

The anti-graft agency filed a six-count charge against her, accusing her of obtaining money under false pretences and retaining proceeds allegedly connected to a fundraising campaign in which she claimed to have stage-four breast cancer.

The court subsequently remanded her to the Kirikiri Correctional Centre over an alleged ₦13 million cancer donation fraud. She later regained her freedom after spending months in detention on the case and other matters.

Faking cancer

Since her release, Blessing CEO has been active on social media and has denied allegations of drug use. However, during an interview with activist and social media personality Martins “VeryDarkMan (VDM)” Otse, she admitted that she falsely claimed to have cancer because she needed money to cover her shame.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

VDM posted the interview on his Instagram page on Thursday.

Blessing CEO explained that earlier medical examinations had detected a lump in her breast but confirmed that it was not cancerous. She, however, admitted that she deliberately portrayed the condition as cancer to attract financial assistance.

She said: “The pressure was too much, and that was where the cancer drama came in, and because of the pressure, I saw this embarrassment coming. Then I said to myself, What stunt can I pull? Then I pulled out the cancer. I don’t have cancer. The truth is, I had gone for a check-up a few months ago, and they found a lump on my boobs.

“It was not cancerous. So I took advantage of that, came to the media, cried for help, and said that the lump was cancerous. So people had empathy. I didn’t come out to beg for funds. I’m going to be very honest. I played an emotional game. I wanted funds, but I didn’t come out directly to ask for funds.”

Fans persuasion

Furthermore, Blessing CEO disclosed that she initially resisted the idea of appealing to Nigerians for donations until some of her fans urged her to give it a try.

She said her fans convinced her that being a celebrity should not prevent her from seeking public assistance, particularly when ordinary Nigerians had received similar support.

“First of all, I started by pretending like I wanted to sell my personal belongings, my car, my house. So, people had empathy. It was the fans that reached out to me, dear Blessing. If we can do this for an ordinary person who is not feeling well, why not you, as a celebrity, put out your account number? So that was when I put out my account number.

“The donations were rolling in. I was excited. One thousand, two thousand, three hundred, five hundred. I was honoured until VeryDarkMan came and said, ‘ You cannot be donating money for Blessings when there is no evidence. So he immediately made that video. The donation stopped”, she added.

She acknowledged that she regretted her actions.

World.title: Fela’s ‘Gentleman’ soundtracks ‘The Thomas Crown Affair’ trailer
World.content:
More than five decades after Fela Anikulapo-Kuti released “Gentleman”, the Afrobeat legend’s music has found its way into another international production, with the classic track featured on the soundtrack of the upcoming Hollywood film, “The Thomas Crown Affair.”

Amazon MGM Studios unveiled the official trailer on its Instagram page on Thursday, featuring the song in the upcoming heist thriller starring Michael Jordan.

The track provides the musical backdrop for several scenes in the trailer, introducing a new generation of international audiences to Fela’s music.

Fela released “Gentleman” in 1973 as the title track of his album of the same name. The song combines highlife rhythms, jazz-inspired horns and Afrobeat elements to criticise colonial mentality and the tendency to imitate Western lifestyles.

“The Thomas Crown Affair”

“The Thomas Crown Affair” will be released in cinemas worldwide on 5 March 2027.

Jordan leads the cast as Thomas Crown, a billionaire and art thief who plans an elaborate robbery to execute a revenge mission.

The film also features Adria Arjona, Kenneth Branagh, Lily Gladstone, Danai Gurira and Pilou Asbæk.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Arjona plays an insurance investigator who sets out to track down the Crown, while Branagh also takes on a key role.

Jordan’s adaptation introduces a different motivation for Crown’s actions compared with the previous versions.

In this instalment, the billionaire seeks to retrieve stolen cultural artefacts and return them to their rightful owners.

His mission sets up a tense cat-and-mouse chase with Bennet, a former FBI agent who joins the investigation into his activities.

The film is the third adaptation of the story, after the 1968 version, which featured Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway, and the 1999 remake starring Pierce Brosnan and René Russo.

John McTiernan directed the 1999 remake of “The Thomas Crown Affair”, featuring Pierce Brosnan as a wealthy billionaire who steals a priceless Monet painting from the Metropolitan Museum of Art out of sheer boredom.

René Russo plays Catherine Banning, an insurance investigator determined to catch him, while Faye Dunaway takes on a supporting role.

World.title: ‘We are not enemies’, Tinubu condemns political violence, warns perpetrators
World.content:
File image

‎By Johnbosco Agbakwuru

‎

‎President Bola Tinubu has strongly condemned violence in all its forms and reiterated his earlier directive to security agencies to go after those behind the dastardly acts, irrespective of their political leanings.

‎

‎President Tinubu, who frowned at the reported resurgence of violence in different parts of the country, said that being in different political parties or pursuing different ambitions does not make political actors enemies.

‎

‎In a statement he personally issued, titled “Let’s Shun Violence: Our Campaigns Must Be About Issues That Promote the Welfare of Our People,” the President ordered security agencies to confront thuggery and other anti-social and anti-democratic activities with full force.

‎

‎The statement read: “I have followed recent reports of violence accompanying political events in different parts of the country.

‎

‎“Every form of violence is condemned. Violence should never have a place in our political campaigns as we move toward the 2027 general elections.

‎

‎“Our campaigns should be about issues—a contestation of ideas that promotes the welfare of our people and the progress of our country.

‎

‎“As the leader of this country, I commit myself to a peaceful, free, and fair election, and I urge political leaders and supporters across party lines to conduct themselves responsibly.

‎

‎“I have said that being in different political parties or pursuing different ambitions does not make us enemies.

‎

‎“As Nigerians, we are members of the same household living in different rooms. Therefore, our politics must elevate human conditions and focus on national progress and development.

‎

‎“I want to reiterate my previous directive to the security agencies: be strict and firm against anyone who seeks to test our resolve and will to preserve public order.”

‎

‎President Tinubu said his administration is committed to an orderly and peaceful election, adding that all political parties and candidates should be protected and free to campaign anywhere in the country without molestation or fear for their safety.

‎

‎“We shall not tolerate any irresponsible conduct by politicians and their supporters,” he said.

‎

‎The President further added: “Security agencies are therefore authorised to confront thuggery and other anti-social and anti-democratic activities with full force.”

‎

World.title: Explained: Nigeria’s chances of qualifying for AFCON 2027 after beating Tanzania
World.content:
Super Eagles

Nigeria have boosted their chances of qualifying for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, AFCON after defeating Tanzania 3-1 in their latest qualifying fixture at the Godswill Akpabio International Stadium in Uyo on Friday.

The victory moved the Super Eagles to second place in Group L with six points, just one point behind leaders Guinea-Bissau, who have seven points.

Madagascar occupy third position with two points, while Tanzania sit bottom with one point.

However, Nigeria still have work to do to secure their place at the tournament, as only one additional qualification ticket is available in the group.

Tanzania have already secured their place at AFCON 2027 as one of the three co-hosts alongside Kenya and Uganda.

This means Nigeria, Guinea-Bissau and Madagascar are competing for the group’s remaining qualification spot.

Current Group L standings

What Nigeria need to qualify

1. Win their remaining matches

Nigeria must continue collecting maximum points in their remaining fixtures to strengthen their chances of finishing top of the group.

The Super Eagles have three qualifying matches left, including their return fixture against Tanzania on Tuesday, November 17.

A victory would keep them within touching distance of Guinea-Bissau and put additional pressure on the group leaders.

2. Overtake Guinea-Bissau

Guinea-Bissau remain Nigeria’s biggest obstacle in the qualification race.

With seven points, they currently enjoy a one-point advantage over the Super Eagles.

Nigeria must finish above them to secure the group’s only available qualification ticket.

3. Watch Guinea-Bissau’s remaining fixtures

Guinea-Bissau’s results in their remaining matches, particularly against Madagascar, could have a significant impact on Nigeria’s qualification chances.

Any dropped points by the group leaders would present the Super Eagles with an opportunity to move to the top of the standings.

4. Win the decisive March fixtures

After their November encounter against Tanzania, Nigeria will have two more qualifying matches in March 2027.

The Super Eagles are scheduled to travel to face Madagascar before hosting Guinea-Bissau in their final group fixture.

The two matches could ultimately determine Nigeria’s fate, particularly the home encounter against Guinea-Bissau, which may become a decisive battle for the group’s qualification ticket.

When will Nigeria’s qualification be decided?

The remaining qualifying fixtures will be played in November 2026 and March 2027.

Nigeria’s immediate assignment is the return fixture against Tanzania on Tuesday, November 17.

They will then face Madagascar away before welcoming Guinea-Bissau in March 2027 to conclude their qualifying campaign.

The Super Eagles will be hoping to enter those final fixtures in a strong position and avoid depending on other results to secure qualification.

The bottom line

Nigeria’s 3-1 victory over Tanzania has revived their qualification hopes, but Eric Chelle’s men cannot afford to become complacent.

With Guinea-Bissau still leading Group L, the Super Eagles must maintain their winning form, overtake the group leaders and finish top to secure their place at the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations.

World.title: AFCONQ: Arokodare scores brace as Super Eagles defeat Tanzania 3-1
World.content:
The Super Eagles of Nigeria bounced back to winning ways in their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, AFCON qualifying campaign with a 3-1 victory over Tanzania at the Godswill Akpabio International Stadium in Uyo on Friday.



Nigeria took an early lead through Alhassan Yusuf, who found the back of the net in the third minute to give the hosts a promising start.

However, Tanzania fought back and restored parity in the 36th minute after Wilfred Ndidi lost possession in midfield, allowing Msanga to capitalise on slack defending and make it 1-1.

The Super Eagles suffered another setback before the break when Ademola Lookman was forced off with an injury and replaced by Moses Simon.

Both teams went into half-time level, with Nigeria seeking to regain their advantage after the restart.

Super Eagles coach Eric Chelle introduced Tolu Arokodare and Chidera Usor at the beginning of the second half, replacing Alhassan Yusuf and Raphael Onyedika.

The changes paid off as Arokodare restored Nigeria’s lead in the 52nd minute with an excellent flicked finish to make it 2-1.

The striker completed his brace in the 60th minute, finishing off a move created by fellow substitute Nsor to extend Nigeria’s advantage to 3-1.

Chelle’s men maintained their two-goal cushion in the closing stages, although Arokodare missed an opportunity to complete his hat-trick.

The final whistle confirmed a 3-1 victory for Nigeria, giving the Super Eagles a boost in their quest for qualification for the 2027 AFCON.

World.title: FG’s ₦50,000 Relief Fund: How OPay Is Helping Nigerians Access Support
World.content:
The Federal Government’s ₦50,000 monthly relief fund under the National Emergency Relief and Stabilisation Intervention (NERSI) is designed to provide financial support to vulnerable Nigerians affected by economic challenges.

As one of the Federal Government’s approved payment partners, OPay is supporting the initiative by providing a convenient and secure digital platform through which eligible beneficiaries can check their status and receive their payments.

The partnership highlights the important role of trusted digital financial service providers in helping the government deliver financial assistance to Nigerians securely and efficiently. For eligible Nigerians who use OPay, checking their eligibility and accessing support can be done directly through the OPay mobile app or by dialling *955*20#. But who qualifies for the ₦50,000 NERSI relief fund, how can OPay customers check their eligibility, and what should beneficiaries know to avoid scams?

The National Emergency Relief and Stabilisation Intervention (NERSI) is a Federal Government programme designed to provide financial assistance to vulnerable Nigerians. Under the initiative, eligible beneficiaries are expected to receive ₦50,000 monthly to help them meet essential needs and manage financial pressures. The government is working with approved digital financial service providers, including OPay, to facilitate the payment of the funds to qualified beneficiaries.

OPay’s selection as one of the government’s approved payment partners reflects the importance of digital financial platforms in delivering public services and improving financial inclusion in Nigeria. As a regulated digital financial services provider, OPay offers an established and secure payment infrastructure that makes it easier for eligible Nigerians to access financial services. Through its platform, beneficiaries can conveniently check their eligibility and receive their relief payments, if qualified. OPay’s participation also reinforces its commitment to making financial services more accessible, reliable and secure for Nigerians.

The NERSI relief fund is intended for vulnerable Nigerians who meet the Federal Government’s eligibility requirements. However, having an OPay account does not automatically qualify a customer for the programme. The Federal Government is responsible for identifying beneficiaries and determining eligibility, while OPay provides a secure payment channel for qualified customers.

OPay customers can check their eligibility directly through the official OPay mobile app or USSD service. To check through the mobile app, customers should open their OPay app and check the homepage for the NERSI ₦50,000 relief notification. If they have been selected, a notification will appear. They can click on it and follow the instructions provided to proceed. Alternatively, customers can dial *955*20# using the phone number linked to their OPay account. If selected, they can follow the instructions displayed to accept the support.

Customers should note that OPay does not select beneficiaries or determine eligibility. The Federal Government makes these decisions. For further clarification, customers can contact the official NERSI support line on 0700-022-2222.

The Federal Government has explained that selected beneficiaries will receive an SMS requesting their consent before payment is made. Eligible OPay customers can receive their funds through their OPay accounts, subject to the programme’s guidelines

.

As more Nigerians seek information about the government relief fund, scammers may attempt to take advantage of unsuspecting individuals. OPay reminds customers to follow important safety guidelines to protect themselves. Customers should never share their PIN or OTP with anyone, as OPay will never ask for these details to process a relief payment. They should also avoid paying anyone to access the programme, as the NERSI initiative is free and requires no registration or processing fee.

Customers are further advised to avoid suspicious links promising access to the ₦50,000 relief fund, check their eligibility through the official OPay app and rely on verified government information. Anyone who encounters suspicious activities or requires clarification should contact the official NERSI helpline on 0700-022-2222. These precautions will help protect beneficiaries from fraud and ensure that government support reaches the intended recipients.

The Federal Government’s NERSI initiative demonstrates how collaboration with established digital financial service providers can support the delivery of essential services. As an approved payment partner, OPay is helping connect eligible Nigerians to government financial support through its secure digital payment infrastructure. Beyond this initiative, OPay continues to provide accessible financial services, including money transfers, bill payments, savings and business payment solutions.

OPay customers are encouraged to open their apps and check their homepages for the NERSI ₦50,000 relief fund notification. If it appears, they should click on it and follow the instructions to proceed. Alternatively, they can dial *955*20# and follow the instructions displayed. The Federal Government determines eligibility, and no payment is required to access the relief fund.

World.title: Man United captain Bruno Fernandes rejects second contract offer
World.content:
Fernandes

By Adegboyega Adeleye

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has rejected the club’s second offer to extend his contract, leaving negotiations over the Portugal midfielder’s future unresolved.

BBC Sport reports that Fernandes is out of contract at the end of the season, although United can extend his deal by 12 months, until 2028. The club wants to agree a new contract before using that option.

If no agreement is reached, United are expected to trigger the extension before January 1. Without it, Fernandes would be able to sign a pre-contract agreement with foreign clubs from that date, with six months remaining on his deal.

It is unclear when Fernandes rejected the offer. A resolution does not appear imminent amid the upheaval at Old Trafford: Michael Carrick was sacked on Thursday, while Mauricio Pochettino is expected to take over as head coach.

United will hope Pochettino’s arrival can persuade Fernandes to stay. The midfielder came close to joining Pochettino’s Tottenham in 2019, before moving from Sporting to United six months later. He has scored six goals in 13 appearances for United this season.

BBC chief football news reporter Simon Stone says Fernandes wants to compete for the biggest prizes and will want to see what impact Pochettino has at United. The club, meanwhile, must weigh the cost and length of a new deal against Fernandes’ recent drop in form after an outstanding previous season, when he broke the Premier League assists record and won major player-of-the-year awards.

Fernandes is 32, and a new contract could commit United to a substantial outlay over several years. Both sides may therefore have reasons to take their time, despite the club’s wish to keep its captain.

World.title: Meet the US family with five generations born on the same date
World.content:
An American family has entered the Guinness World Records after five consecutive generations were born on the same date, September 14, in a remarkable family coincidence spanning more than a century.

The Bell and Harlow family secured the record for the most generations born on the same day after the arrival of baby Arthur Bell on September 14, 2025.

Arthur’s birth extended a family tradition that began with his great-great-grandfather, Wilber Harlow, who was born on September 14, 1907.

The other family members who share the birthday are Wilber’s daughter, Addie Harlow, born on September 14, 1949; his grandson, Donald Harlow, born on September 14, 1972; and his great-granddaughter, Emma Bell, born on September 14, 1997.

Emma is Arthur’s mother, while Donald is his grandfather.

According to Guinness World Records, the family surpassed the previous record of four generations born on the same date, which had been jointly held by seven families.

The family said they had been aware of the unusual coincidence when four generations shared the September 14 birthday but delayed applying for official recognition because they hoped another child would continue the tradition.

Their wish came true when Emma’s second child, Arthur, arrived on the expected date, extending the record to five generations.

Speaking about the achievement, Emma said the family had always known they could hold the record but wanted to wait until they had a fifth generation.

“We kind of always knew that we held a record with four generations, we just never applied because we had that ambition to have the fifth on 14 September,” she said.

“And then it worked out!”

She added that the family was delighted to become the sole record holders rather than share the title with other families.

Arthur’s grandfather, Donald, also expressed his excitement, saying: “God works in beautiful ways.”

The family’s birthday tradition began in 1907 when Wilber Harlow was born. He later worked as a postmaster and owned the Harlow General Store in Brooks, Iowa.

On September 14, 1949, Wilber and his wife welcomed their daughter, Addie, on his birthday, beginning the remarkable sequence.

Addie later worked as a secretary for the Chief of Police in La Vista, Nebraska, for more than 20 years.

Her son, Donald, continued the coincidence when he was born on the same date in 1972. Donald subsequently welcomed Emma, who also arrived on September 14, 1997.

Although Addie died in 2023 before Arthur’s birth, the family had maintained the tradition of celebrating their shared birthday together, usually by visiting a restaurant and having a birthday cake.

Emma and her husband, Wyatt, said they became particularly excited when they realised their second child’s expected arrival date was September 14.

The family also noticed another unusual pattern in the sequence: the five generations alternate between boys and girls, following a boy-girl-boy-girl-boy pattern.

Emma described Arthur’s arrival as a remarkable coincidence, while Donald affectionately referred to the baby as their “miracle boy”.

The family also shares another geographical connection. Wilber and his wife married in Maryville, Missouri, the same place where Emma and Wyatt first met.

With Arthur’s arrival, the Bell and Harlow family have turned a birthday coincidence that began in 1907 into a Guinness World Records achievement spanning five generations.

World.title: Nigerian Navy releases 2026 Batch 39 recruitment shortlist [how to check]
World.content:
By Adegboyega Adeleye

The Nigerian Navy has released the shortlist of successful applicants for its 2026 Batch 39 recruitment into the Nigerian Navy Basic Training School and scheduled the recruitment examination for November 21.

World.title: U-23 AFCONQ: Nigeria suffer 2-0 defeat to DR Congo in first leg
World.content:
Nigeria’s hopes of qualifying for the 2027 Under-23 Africa Cup of Nations suffered a setback on Friday after the Olympic Eagles lost 2-0 to DR Congo in the first leg of their second-round qualifying tie.

The Nigerian side, led by Ikorodu City head coach Bright Osehai Ozebagbe and former Nigeria U-20 assistant coach Deniran Ortega, struggled to convert their early opportunities as the hosts secured a comfortable advantage ahead of the return fixture.

The coaching duo took charge in the absence of Super Eagles manager Eric Chelle, who was occupied with Nigeria’s senior national team preparations for their crucial Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against Tanzania.

Nigeria started brightly and nearly took the lead in the fourth minute when Victor Samuel’s effort missed the target.

The midfielder had another opportunity five minutes later after finding himself one-on-one with the DR Congo goalkeeper but failed to convert.

The missed chances proved costly as DR Congo took the lead in the 20th minute in controversial circumstances.

Nigeria goalkeeper Samuel James appeared to have been fouled by a Congolese player while attempting to collect an aerial ball during the build-up to the opening goal. However, the referee allowed the goal to stand.

The Olympic Eagles suffered another setback in the 30th minute when Brighton youngster Zadok Yohanna was forced off with an injury.

DR Congo doubled their advantage five minutes before the break through Felozefe Mabete, who produced an impressive free-kick to put the hosts firmly in control.

Despite their attempts to find a way back into the contest after the restart, Nigeria could not break down the Congolese defence, with the hosts protecting their two-goal advantage until the final whistle.

The result leaves the Olympic Eagles with a difficult task in the second leg, as they must overturn the deficit to keep their qualification hopes alive.

Nigeria will host DR Congo in the return fixture at the Remo Stars Stadium on Tuesday, where they will seek to secure an aggregate victory and advance to the final qualifying round.

The Under-23 Africa Cup of Nations also serves as the qualification pathway for the men’s football tournament at the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles.
