World.title: Why Bryson DeChambeau, Tom Brady, and other athletes are left empty after winning championships
World.content:
Some of the biggest names in sports have reached the pinnacle of success, only to discover that championships, trophies, fame, and fortune can't provide the lasting fulfillment they have been searching for. Many have wondered why they feel lonely, empty, and even depressed after major accomplishments.

Tom Brady, Bryson DeChambeau, Aaron Rodgers, Sean McVay, Michael Phelps, and more have struggled with this inner turmoil after major accomplishments in sports.

These men have won championships, accumulated millions of dollars, earned worldwide recognition and cemented their legacies in sports history. They are some of the most accomplished in their respective sports, yet despite all that success, they've publicly acknowledged something that should make all of us stop and think: Winning doesn't necessarily bring the lasting happiness, peace or fulfillment we expect it to.

Two-time U.S. Open champion Bryson DeChambeau is the latest example.

US PRESIDENTS CUP PLAYERS EXPLAIN HOW CHRISTIAN FAITH BUILDS FRIENDSHIPS AND PUTS GOLF IN PERSPECTIVE

During a recent appearance on the "Figuring Out with Raj Shamani" podcast, DeChambeau was transparent and vulnerable as he reflected on winning his first major championship at the 2020 U.S. Open and the surprising loneliness that followed.

After dedicating nearly his entire life to reaching that moment, he finally accomplished his dream. But the celebration eventually ended, and he found himself alone in bed with the trophy beside him.

"I gave 20 years of my life to do this and I did it. Well, now what do I do?" DeChambeau recalled.

He described waking up the following morning, realizing he'd won the U.S. Open, and almost immediately questioning what came next. What he had worked so hard for was fleeting.

"I'm in bed alone. I don't have my family with me. I don't have anybody around," he explained, describing the experience as a moment of vulnerability.

DeChambeau went on to explain how the experience forced him to reconsider his priorities, relationships and what he wanted his legacy to be, because he was realizing that being known as a U.S. Open champion only meant so much. What should have been one of the most satisfying moments of his life instead exposed a loneliness that a championship trophy couldn't fix.

DeChambeau continued: "I don't have somebody loving on me and giving me a kiss and a kid coming up on the bed and holding my hand and all that. Is that really what I want to do for my life? Is that one legacy I want to leave to? And so it really transforms you and makes you realize what life is about.

SCOTTIE SCHEFFLER'S CADDIE DETAILS CONVERSATION ABOUT POTENTIAL $1 BILLION LIV GOLF OFFER, WHY HE'D DECLINE

Interestingly, fellow golf superstar Scottie Scheffler expressed a nearly identical sentiment ahead of the 2025 Open Championship, explaining that even winning major championships doesn't provide lasting fulfillment.

"It's fulfilling from a sense of accomplishment, but it's not fulfilling from a sense of the deepest places of your heart," Scheffler admitted.

Quite the perspective and juxtaposition to DeChambeau, who had to find out the hard way.

Unlike DeChambeau, who described the loneliness of winning a U.S. Open without a wife or children to share it with, Scheffler has been outspoken about finding his ultimate identity and purpose in his Christian faith and his relationships with his wife and children.

In fact, Scheffler declared he'd rather be a great father than a great golfer, emphasizing that his faith and family take priority over his career. A very counter-cultural stance. It's a fascinating contrast between two of the world's best golfers: DeChambeau discovered that reaching the pinnacle of his sport left him longing for something greater, while Scheffler has already recognized that no trophy, paycheck or world ranking can satisfy the deepest desires of the human heart.

But DeChambeau is hardly alone.

In 2005, a 27-year-old Tom Brady had already won three Super Bowls when he made a remarkably similar admission during an interview with "60 Minutes."

"Why do I have three Super Bowl rings and still think there is something greater out there for me?" Brady asked.

His conclusion was that there has to be more than just being an accomplished quarterback.

Think about that. Arguably, the greatest quarterback in NFL history had already accomplished more than most athletes ever will, yet he still wondered whether there was something greater to pursue.

TERRY BRADSHAW OPENS UP ABOUT HIS 'DEMON IN THE NIGHT' DEPRESSION IN NEW MEMOIR

More than two decades later, that sentiment continues to resonate with other prominent sports figures.

Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay opened up about the same struggle during a September "60 Minutes" interview, which I previously wrote about for OutKick.

McVay admitted he'd convinced himself that winning a Super Bowl would finally make him happy. Instead, the championship exposed just how much of his identity and self-worth he'd attached to winning football games.

"The lies I told myself were, 'Once we win a Super Bowl I'll be happy,'" McVay admitted.

When the Rams followed their championship with a disappointing 2022 season, those insecurities became even more apparent. McVay seriously considered walking away from coaching for a broadcasting career before his wife challenged his thinking.

Aaron Rodgers has expressed similar concerns about finding identity outside of football. In a 2013 interview with Sports Illustrated, Rodgers emphasized that money couldn't buy happiness and that athletes needed to establish their identities beyond the game and the fame.

Years later, in the Netflix documentary "Aaron Rodgers: Enigma," the Super Bowl champion reflected on the unsettling question that followed reaching his ultimate professional goal: "Okay, now what?"

Even Michael Phelps, the most decorated Olympian in history with 28 medals, has spoken candidly about the emotional struggles that followed his greatest accomplishments.

Phelps revealed that he experienced periods of depression following multiple Olympic Games, describing the disorientation of spending years pursuing a goal only to feel lost once it was over. He has since become an advocate for mental health treatment, explaining that helping others means more to him than winning another gold medal.

Different sports. Different personalities. Different accomplishments. Yet a remarkably similar struggle.

Here's the reality: There's nothing wrong with pursuing greatness, working tirelessly toward a goal or celebrating the fruits of your labor. Sports provide some of the most inspiring examples of discipline, perseverance, sacrifice and excellence. Those are worth pursuing and celebrating.

But there's a difference between being passionate about what you do and allowing what you do to become who you are.

When your identity is built on winning, what happens when you lose? When your happiness depends on the next championship, what happens after you've won it? When your worth is measured by accomplishments, what happens when those accomplishments fade?

There's always another trophy to chase, another contract to sign, another record to break or another mountain to climb. But, if those things become the ultimate source of our happiness and identity, the satisfaction they provide will always be temporary.

While there are many books, philosophies, and worldviews, and intellectuals that have aimed to guide and warn us against the pursuit of worldly success as the ultimate goal, I believe the Book of Ecclesiastes says it best. King Solomon describes the emptiness of pursuing earthly pleasures and accomplishments apart from God. It's a lesson that remains just as relevant today. He calls it "vanity." It's essentially chasing after the wind.

As I wrote in my previous article about McVay, pursuing excellence in your career isn't a bad thing. Whether you're an athlete, accountant, plumber, or school teacher, you should aim to be the very best. But when your job, accomplishments or success become idols, they will eventually fail to provide the lasting fulfillment you're seeking. They can't be your primary source of meaning and fulfillment.

Personally, that fulfillment is found in Jesus Christ. My identity isn't in my job, my accomplishments, my failures or the opinions of others. It's in Him.

And while these athletes haven't all arrived at the same spiritual conclusions I have, or even you as a reader, their experiences point toward a truth worth considering:

You can win every award and trophy the world has to offer and still find yourself searching for something more.

Colonel Sanders is getting a frosty reception in the Italian Alps as KFC prepares to open restaurants in two upscale ski towns, sparking backlash from those determined to preserve the mountain villages' character and traditions.

The Kentucky-founded fast-food giant is set to reach new heights on Dec. 5, when two restaurants will open on the slopes of Cortina d'Ampezzo, a southern Dolomite resort village, and Madonna di Campiglio, an Alpine town in the Trentino region of northern Italy.

The move makes KFC the first fast-food company to operate on Italian ski trails.

KFC UNVEILS RADICALLY DIFFERENT RESTAURANT IN MAJOR COMEBACK PUSH

The Cortina d'Ampezzo location will be inside the Faloria Mountain Club, situated at an altitude of 2,123 meters, while the outlet in Madonna di Campiglio will be in the Piana di Nambino area at an elevation of 1,700 meters, The Guardian reported.

Along with Milan, Cortina d'Ampezzo co-hosted the 2026 Winter Olympics.

KFC has partnered with Super G, the company behind the après-ski bars at several Italian resorts, to launch the two new restaurants.

WHY KFC STOPPED CALLING ITSELF KENTUCKY FRIED CHICKEN — AND THE MYTHS THAT STILL WON'T DIE

Reactions have been largely negative.

"KFC should stay where it belongs! Not in our nature!" one person wrote on Instagram, expressing disdain that the restaurants would be within a UNESCO World Heritage site.

"In almost the entire Alpine region, it's now impossible to fly drones because they disturb the wildlife, and if I post my content on social media I attract inadequate and disrespectful people to the mountains," content creator Matteo Peroni said in a YouTube video.

"Does the smell of fried chicken not disrupt the wildlife and the balance that exists in the mountains? And doesn't a place like that bring inadequate people to the mountains?" he asked.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

In a statement to Fox News Digital, KFC said it "is proud to serve communities around the world and, wherever we operate, we work to be a respectful and responsible part of the community."

"We recognize the importance of the traditions and culture in Cortina d'Ampezzo, Madonna di Campiglio and the region," the statement said. "We are collaborating with local partners to deliver the experience our customers expect, while respecting the character of the location."

The KFC outlets could prove to be convenient and affordable slope-side dining options, and many restaurants on or around ski runs already use self-service lines to serve more guests quickly, according to Italian news outlet Corriere della Sera.

"This horror would weirdly improve the food situation in Madonna," one Instagram user wrote.

Overall, buckets of fried chicken and mashed potatoes don't seem to be eagerly anticipated in areas known for traditional dishes like regional pastas, dumplings, meats and cheeses influenced by Germany and Austria.

"This most northern region of Italy, which is home to Cortina d’Ampezzo and Madonna di Campiglio, has sparred its way into its own existence and identity for thousands of years and in the process has taken and borrowed its cultural and culinary influences from its conquerors and its steady habits," Colin Caplan, a food historian based in New Haven, Connecticut, told Fox News Digital.

It's not an impossible feat for fast-food chains to survive on the slopes. McDonald's has operated its McSki outlet, complete with the world's only "ski-thru" window, in Sälen, Sweden, since 1996.

World.title: Democrat Cindy Holscher defeats Republican Ty Masterson in Kansas governor’s race
World.content:
Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher has narrowly won Kansas’ race for governor, NBC News projected Thursday, extending the party’s hold on the office in the red state.

Holscher defeated Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, who was backed by President Donald Trump, to succeed two-term Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly.

While Trump carried Kansas — a state where registered Republicans outnumber registered Democrats nearly 2 to 1 — by double digits in the latest three presidential elections, polling had shown a close race down the stretch due mostly to voter frustrations with Trump and his handling of the economy. Democrats also benefited from increased attention on the traditionally conservative state as its Senate race tightened.

Kansas Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher. Evert Nelson / The Capital-Journal / USA Today via Imagn

Holscher’s victory came despite a nearly 3-to-1 Republican ad spending advantage in the general election, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

In the general election, Holscher aggressively tied Masterson to Trump, while also maintaining that she’d find areas to work with the administration.

“I think that’s a concern that [Masterson] has the ear of the administration, because the administration also has a hold on him. You won’t see Ty Masterson pushing back against bad policy, like tariffs that are hurting our farmers or the importing of beef that are hurting our ranchers,” she told local news station KMBC in October. She added that will also “work with folks” in the administration “to make sure we bring good things to Kansas.”

Masterson, who was endorsed by Trump, attempted to distance himself from the president on his website and in campaign materials. But his connection to Trump, who faced increasingly lower approval ratings in the traditionally red state, was unmistakable: the president came to Kansas over the last weekend before Election Day to campaign alongside Masterson and the Republican candidate in the state’s Senate race, Sen. Roger Marshall, who lost his re-election bid to Democrat Adam Hamilton.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson. Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty

Meanwhile, Holscher also prominently highlighted her opposition to new data center construction throughout her campaign.

“This field of Kansas sunflowers is under threat because big tech wants to build a day out of center. As governor, I’ll hit pause on data centers until we can set up firm guardrails to protect our communities and our budgets,” she said in one spot featuring her standing in a field.

Masterson has opposed a moratorium on data centers and has defended a 2025 law he voted for giving a sales tax exemption for data center investments. Holscher has called for a statewide moratorium on the new data center construction. Building the Future, a pro-data center super PAC, jumped into the race last month to boost Masterson.

Holscher’s win followed a primary that featured Democratic infighting. Kelly, who has maintained strong job approval ratings in the state, had endorsed Holscher’s Democratic primary opponent, state Sen. Ethan Corson, and issued stark warnings to voters about being “very concerned about the direction Kansas will go in” if Holscher were to win.

Holscher had run a more progressive-styled campaign, while Corson ran as a moderate. Kelly endorsed Holscher following the primary.

World.title: St. Patrick’s Day parade canceled in Florida thanks to state’s anti-DEI law
World.content:
A new anti-DEI law championed by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis that goes into effect next year has resulted in the cancellation of a St. Patrick’s Day parade.

The city of Delray Beach announced that it was pulling the plug on the popular 60-year-old spectacle — as well as the city’s annual Pride celebration — after it did a review of Florida Senate Bill 1134, which DeSantis signed into law and goes into effect on Jan. 1.

This new law, the city posted on an official website, “establishes restrictions on municipal funding, promotion, and official actions involving activities defined under the legislation as diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI).”

“Following a review of the legislation and its requirements, the City has determined that it is legally prohibited from organizing, funding, or promoting these events in 2027,” it said.

“Although the city is no longer able to fund these events, it does not prevent private entities from sponsoring these or similar events,” the city of Delray Beach posted on its official Facebook page.

Feeling the heat from his angry constituents, Del Ray Mayor Tom Carney posted on Facebook that “the city is working feverishly with multiple entities to ensure the 2027 St. Patrick’s Day parade goes on as scheduled!”

“The St. Patrick’s Day Parade isn’t just another parade,” Carney, a Republican of Irish descent, wrote. “It’s engrained in the DNA of the Delray Beach community... I’ve read your social media posts, received your emails and it is clear that the parade means as much to you in the community as it does to me.”

Notably, in his post, Carney did not mention whether he or any other city officials were working to salvage the Pride celebration.

Carney did not immediately respond to an NBC News request for comment.

There was also no immediate answer from DeSantis’ office on if Delray Beach officials might have misinterpreted the new directive when they cancelled the St. Patrick’s Day parade.

But the bill specifically bars counties, municipalities, public contractors, and grantees from using taxpayer money to fund events that celebrate “ethnicity.”

DeSantis, a Republican and likely GOP presidential candidate, has been leading the charge against DEI for a number of years.

Back in 2023, he signed a bill that defunded diversity programs at Florida colleges.

“If you look at the way this has actually been implemented across the country, DEI is better viewed as standing for ‘discrimination, exclusion and indoctrination,’ and that has no place in our public institutions,” DeSantis said at the time. “This bill says the whole experiment with DEI is coming to an end in the state of Florida.”

World.title: Alito says Supreme Court is caught between the president and a Congress that can ‘turn off the lights’
World.content:
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito expressed concern about Congress’ potential use of the power of the purse against the high court in remarks at an event in Washington, D.C., Thursday night.

Speaking with conservative author Mollie Hemingway at a black-tie dinner for the annual Federalist Society’s National Lawyers Convention, Alito said the judiciary is the “least dangerous” branch of the government, and is “vulnerable to the executive and to Congress because they are more powerful.”

“Congress can turn off the lights of the Supreme Court and stop everything from happening if they will not fund their activities,” he said. “And there are many, many, many other things that they can do, or at least try to do. So it is important to preserve the independence of the judiciary.”

Alito did not directly refer to the recent midterm elections, but the conservative stalwart’s remarks came shortly after Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in larger than expected numbers last week.

Despite the power dynamic, Alito said, that’s “not to say that the federal judiciary cannot be dangerous when it goes to strike.”

He referred to the court not as a “nuclear weapon” or a “500-pound bomb,” but a “hand grenade.”

“The hand grenade is the least dangerous, but that is not to say that is not dangerous,” Alito said.

While stressing the need for judicial independence in remarks to the audience of more than 2,500 conservative elected officials, lawyers, judges, and advocates, Alito also said he believes some federal judges have gone “far astray” in what he called recent “unjustified orders.”

That has helped lead, in part, to the rise of the controversial emergency docket over the past 10 or 15 years, said Alito, a nominee of George W. Bush. The Trump administration has had a very high success rate with the conservative majority on the so-called “shadow docket,” with interim rulings that have allowed the administration to move forward with immigration enforcement, the restructuring of the federal government and construction of a White House ballroom while underlying litigation is pending.

“Presidents have become very frustrated with their inability to get Congress to enact their legislative agenda, and so they have looked for ways to do as much as they can unilaterally with their own powers,” leading opponents to rush to court to try to block those orders, Alito said.

“The litigators, understandably, choose the districts where they think they are most likely to get the result they want. Their expectations are very often met,” he said, and “in some instances,” judges have issued “very sweeping and unjustified orders, stopping what the president wants during during the pendency of appeal,” a process that can take years.

“So, if at the end of that period it turns out that the district judge was wrong, the president, whoever it is, will have been prevented for most of a four-year term from implementing this, this, this initiative,” he said.

The lower court judges, he said, “are dedicated and they are skillful, but they’re not perfect, and they make mistakes. And in some instances, I think they have gone far astray.”

World.title: Top doctor for Congress resigns amid misconduct allegations
World.content:
Washington — Dr. Brian Monahan, the attending physician of the U.S. Capitol, has resigned from his post as lawmakers' top doctor, Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Thursday, amid allegations of misconduct.

"My understanding is he's resigned," Thune said.

One source familiar with the matter told CBS News that Monahan, a two-star Navy admiral, resigned after allegations of misconduct related to what he chose to do and asked the sailors under him to do in terms of providing care.

The resignation comes in conjunction with a report by the Defense Department's inspector general that found lax oversight of the Office of the Attending Physician.

The public version of watchdog report, while light on specifics and including numerous redactions, said investigators found a "gap in clinical quality management." The report found that some prescription drugs, including sleep aids and pain medication, were not properly inventoried or tracked.

These shortfalls, the inspector general said, could "result in OAP beneficiaries unknowingly assuming health and safety risks because clinical and prescribing practices were not monitored."

CBS News has learned the Navy is also conducting an inquiry into the Office of the Attending Physician.

Monahan has served as the attending physician since 2009. He is also a professor at Uniformed Services University in Bethesda, Maryland, and previously served as its chairman of medicine. He is certified by the American Board of Internal Medicine in internal medicine, hematology and medical oncology.

His removal was first reported by Punchbowl News. The Office of the Attending Physician did not reply to multiple requests for comment.

Since 1928, the Navy — through the Office of the Attending Physician — has been tasked with medical care of Congress, staff, the Supreme Court and visitors to the Capitol complex. In addition to administering minor first aid services and providing other general medical support, the office participates in planning for and responding to disasters that may involve the Capitol.

CBS News asked House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries on Thursday if he had any knowledge about the circumstances surrounding Monahan's dismissal. Jeffries said he did not but wants to ensure member health is protected.

The Navy Times reported military personnel in the office were pressured to endure 70-80 hour work weeks and do tasks "no one else wants to do ... like cutting a congressman's toenails or bringing their medication to their private residence at 3 a.m."

The inspector general's report included five recommendations for improving OAP, including designating an outside group to oversee quality control and establishing policies and procedures for OAP employees.

World.title: Brother of cartel leader "El Mencho" gets 22.5 years in prison
World.content:
Washington — The brother of the slain prominent cartel leader known as "El Mencho" was sentenced on Friday to 22.5 years in prison, after he pleaded guilty to drug trafficking and firearms offenses, the Justice Department said.

Antonio Oseguera Cervantes, 67, worked for cartels with his brother Nemesio Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, or El Mencho, who was killed by the Mexican army in February.

Antonio Cervantes, also known as "Tony Montana," pleaded guilty in July to conspiring to distribute five kilograms or more of cocaine and 500 grams or more of methamphetamine for importation into the U.S. He also pleaded guilty to using, carrying and possessing a firearm in furtherance of the drug trafficking conspiracy.

El Mencho co-founded and led the Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generación, also known as CJNG. Last year, the Trump administration designated the CJNG and other cartels as foreign terrorist organizations.

"For more than two decades, Antonio Oseguera Cervantes helped fuel one of the world's most dangerous drug trafficking organizations, flooding America's communities with deadly drugs while enriching himself and his associates," said Tysen Duva, the assistant attorney general for the Justice Department's Criminal Division, in a statement.

World.title: Criminal probe launched into cruise ship over potential "magic pipe"
World.content:
The MSC Poesia cruise ship, which was cleared to depart the Port of Miami on Thursday after being detained earlier this month, is under investigation for allegedly discharging oil illegally at sea, according to a U.S. official familiar with the probe.

The U.S. Coast Guard launched the criminal investigation into a so-called "magic pipe" case, in which a ship transfers its oil discharge into its gray water system. This is illegal under federal law.

Gray water — which includes anything from a sink or shower — can be discharged at sea as long as the ship is a safe distance from the shore.

The investigation could target crew members, the owner of the vessel, and whoever may have been directly involved and therefore potentially criminally liable, according to the U.S. official.

CBS News has reached out to MSC Cruises, which operates the ship, for comment.

The MSC Poesia was detained at the Port of Miami earlier this month after the U.S. Coast Guard, which has jurisdiction to inspect foreign-flagged vessels entering U.S. ports, "identified deficiencies with systems on board the vessel." At the time, MSC Cruises described the issue as a "regulatory matter" and no further details were provided.

More than 2,000 people were on board the MSC Poesia at the time of its detention, a source familiar with the matter told CBS News.

Using a so-called "magic pipe" could lead to hefty fines.

In 2016, Carnival's Princess Cruises was ordered to pay a $40 million fine for dumping oily waste into the ocean. It was the largest penalty of its kind at the time. The company also pleaded guilty to seven felony charges.

World.title: U.S. gave Singapore scant help with Alice Huang probe, source says
World.content:
Singaporean authorities seized the passport of then-Megaspeed chief executive Alice Huang in June 2025 and held it for eight months, preventing her departure while trying to engage the U.S. government to support their investigation into advanced Nvidia chips possibly being shipped to China.

One source with knowledge of the matter told CBS News on Friday the Singaporean government received no meaningful help from Washington during the time she was in the Asian city-state. This source said officials in Washington were "not forthcoming" in response to Singapore's requests for help, and no substantive assistance has been provided to date.

Singapore's government confirmed in a statement this week that it reached out to both the U.S. Department of Justice and the FBI for assistance with its investigation.

Alice Huang is the suspected Chinese spy at the center of the extramarital affair scandal that toppled Nvidia founder Jensen Huang from the helm of the global tech giant he built over three decades.

A screengrab from CTI video footage shows a woman identified by Reuters as Alice Huang attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, in black, at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan, May 22, 2025. CTI via Reuters TV

Since February 2025, Singaporean authorities have been investigating whether Alice Huang and Megaspeed worked with California-based Supermicro to ship the Silicon Valley firm's computer servers — equipped with advanced Nvidia chips — to China, the source told CBS News.

Alice Huang flew into Singapore in June 2025 for a voluntary interview with Singapore-based investigators from the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, according to the source.

The agency sits within the U.S. Department of Commerce and regulates the export of sensitive products on national security and economic grounds. The American authorities requested the interview, according to a Thursday statement by Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry, as part of a post-shipment verification check, a process used to determine whether imported products have reached their declared recipient.

Singaporean police also interviewed Huang on the same day as the U.S. officials, and made the decision to impound her passport.

The source said it was not known where Huang, a Chinese national, arrived in Singapore from in June 2025.

By February 2026, however, the Singapore Police Force had not charged Huang with any crime and had no option but to return her passport, the source told CBS News. She was barred from ever returning to Singapore, as authorities assessed that she had given "inaccurate information" to downplay her role at Megaspeed, as noted in the statement from the home ministry.

That statement was released four days after Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman who sources confirmed to CBS News was Alice Huang.

Singapore's investigation has focused on whether the then-Megaspeed CEO may have broken domestic law by lying about the details of purchases of computer servers from Supermicro, a San Jose-based technology company. The company's servers use Nvidia's advanced chips to run artificial intelligence software, data centers and cloud computing.

"The suspected domestic offenses pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offenses," Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry said in its statement this week.

Singaporean investigators have tried to determine the true ultimate destination of the Supermicro servers ordered by Megaspeed.

A second source familiar with the investigation told CBS News it is believed they may have been sent to Malaysia, but Singaporean investigators suspect "some or all" of them may then have been shipped onward to China. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.

Singapore's home ministry attempted to contact Supermicro, but the U.S. company only "provided limited cooperation," according to the home ministry statement.

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Malaysia kept Nvidia's chips and installed them in its own data centers, but then rented use of those centers to China, rather than physically shipping any chips to China.

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Friday that there was "no indication" any chips linked to the Nvidia-Megaspeed issue had been re-exported out of the country.

Beijing has dismissed the claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China." Asked Thursday about a Bloomberg report that she had returned to China, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters: "I do not have information on what you mentioned."

Since 2022, the U.S. has restricted the export of Nvidia's most powerful chips to China over national security concerns as the world's two biggest economies race for dominance in the AI sector.

The Singapore police first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025 to try to secure Supermicro's cooperation in revealing where its servers were ultimately ending up, repeating requests "on several occasions to the U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation," according to the Home Affairs Ministry's Thursday statement.

The second source confirmed to CBS News that Washington did not meaningfully engage with the requests for help on the investigation and said it "would be useful to know" what Supermicro declared about its exports to fulfill orders by Megaspeed, whether those products were registered as being bound for Malaysia, and whether some or all of those products were actually "bound for somewhere else," such as China.

The Singapore home ministry said in its statement that six other individuals linked to Megaspeed, in addition to Alice Huang, are wanted for questioning, but none have been in the country since the government launched its investigation in February 2025.

"One is a Singaporean citizen and the rest are foreigners," said the first person familiar with the case.

Singapore has charged five other people in a wider fraud conspiracy case related to the suspected transfer of Nvidia chips, including one Chinese man charged on Friday. The case was launched at the same time as the probe into Alice Huang and Megaspeed, the first source told CBS News, but it is separate.

"Singapore is committed to upholding our reputation as a trusted and reliable business hub. We will not allow companies or individuals to misuse Singapore's business environment to engage in fraud or dishonest practices," the home ministry said in its statement, adding that it would "conduct its own investigations independently, in accordance with our laws and based on the evidence available. We will cooperate with foreign authorities where appropriate, and take firm enforcement action wherever the evidence warrants it."

World.title: Boy found alive after 6 days lost in wilderness: "Grounded for life"
World.content:
A 17-year-old boy with autism was found alive Thursday after six days lost in eastern Australian woodlands.

The boy, whom police identified only as William, had begun camping with a teenage friend when he disappeared last Friday near Walhalla, a former gold-mining town 185 kilometers (115 miles) east of Melbourne, police said.

A police helicopter crew found him surrounded by wilderness lying asleep on a flat rock beside a creek, and he was later reunited with his mother. William was in good spirits and mostly in good health, the police statement said.

Video shot from the rescue helicopter showed he was shirtless and sunburned. He was wearing shorts and boots and was using towels as blankets.

"I'm just over the moon that he's alive," his mother, Elizabeth, told reporters. The AP has decided not to provide her family name to avoid identifying her son.

"And he's never leaving the house again. He's grounded for life. He's not going anywhere ever again," she joked.

Police video showed Elizabeth embrace her son after the rescue helicopter landed to complete its mission.

William was later taken to a hospital for his health to be monitored, police said.

"Amazingly, William is in good spirits and for the most part, in good health," they said in the statement.

In this image made from video and provided by the Victoria State Police 17-year-old William, center right, is embraced by his mother Elizabeth, while in a helicopter in Cowwarr, Australia, Nov. 12, 2026, after William spent six days lost in eastern Australian woodlands. Victoria Police via AP

William's family have said he has Level 2 autism. That requires "substantial support," according to the Australian advocacy group Autism360.

Such a person may have marked deficits in verbal and non-verbal social communication and rely heavily on routines and predictable activities. Disruption can cause significant distress.

The Southern Hemisphere spring weather had been mild for the past week in the alpine region where William was lost and there had been little rain.

Elizabeth had dropped off her son and his friend last Friday for a weekend of camping. William walked a short distance from the campsite to the drop-off location to collect more camping equipment but never returned to his friend, police said.

After becoming lost, William trekked for days up and down "some very steep terrain," Acting Police Inspector Jason Benbow said.

He spent the last two days where he was found at the creek, trapped by the steepness of his surrounds 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the his camp site, Benbow said.

"He woke up to the sound of the helicopter, gave them a thumbs up and they winched him to safety," Benbow told reporters.

The extensive police search for him involved more than 100 emergency services personnel and volunteers.

There have been other dramatic rescues in Australia's wilderness in recent years.

In 2025, a German tourist was found alive in Australia's remote Outback, 12 days after she went missing. She was found just a day after officials and local media said an Australian surfer, who had been feared lost at sea, was rescued after spending a night on an uninhabited island miles from where they had walked into the water.

In 2019, an Australian woman missing for three days was rescued after the SOS message she scrawled in the sand was spotted on a surveillance camera.

The successful rescues have included animals as well. Last year, a runaway dog was captured after a 529-day adventure in Australia as she roamed an island teeming with kangaroos, possums, koala bears and penguins.

World.title: Alex Murdaugh wants murder indictments tossed, saying agent lied
World.content:
Attorneys for Alex Murdaugh are expected in court Friday to ask a judge to throw out the original murder indictments for killing his wife and son, alleging the chief investigator in the case lied to the grand jury.

Murdaugh is facing a retrial on the murder charges after the South Carolina Supreme Court threw out his convictions and life sentence, ruling that a court clerk improperly influenced jurors against him during his 2023 trial.

Even if the longshot request to dismiss the indictments is granted by Judge Debra McCaslin at Friday's pretrial hearing, it may not stop or even postpone an April retrial for the disgraced lawyer. Prosecutors can seek another set of grand jury indictments as soon as next month, and defense attorneys said they won't stop them.

But a ruling for Murdaugh would be another rebuke of the chief investigator, State Law Enforcement Division agent David Owen.

A judge last year threw out a different murder case Owen was involved in because the dead woman's mother told the agent about a suicide threat her daughter made days before she died that Owen never relayed to prosecutors or defense attorneys.

Owen abruptly retired in 2024, not long after he was honored as State Law Enforcement Officer of the Year. He has acknowledged mistakes in the Murdaugh case, but denied intentionally misleading the grand jury.

Prosecutors said Murdaugh, 58, killed his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, on their sprawling property in the South Carolina Lowcountry in 2021. Murdaugh is spending decades in prison for stealing millions of dollars from clients, and has admitted in court that he is a thief, insurance cheat, bad lawyer and longtime opioid addict. But he denies being a killer.

Defense lawyers said that as prosecutors sought the indictments, Owen told the Colleton County grand jury that blood spatter was found on a T-shirt Murdaugh was wearing the night of the killings. An earlier report from state agents said there were no blood stains, and no such evidence was introduced at trial.

Murdaugh's lawyers have repeatedly pointed out how little evidence prosecutors have. No DNA or blood was found splattered on Murdaugh or any of his clothes, even though the killings were at close range with powerful weapons that were never found.

Owen also told grand jurors that the same ammunition load of buckshot in one chamber and large birdshot in the other used to kill Paul Murdaugh was found loaded in weapons all over the Murdaugh property, which wasn't the case.

Prosecutors have rejected allegations of deliberate misconduct, and wrote that "a single mistake is not bad faith." They said they have plenty of other evidence supporting the murder charges.

Owen told grand jurors about the video Paul Murdaugh recorded in which Alex Murdaugh's voice could be heard at the scene, contradicting his denials. Owen also told them about the family's mounting debts and how Murdaugh's schemes to steal from clients and his law firm were close to being discovered.

"Even if the defense is able to convince the judge that this chief investigator lied and the case should be dismissed, there's a lot of evidence here that does not relate to the chief investigator," legal analyst Jessica Levinson told "CBS Mornings" this week. "I think the prosecution would likely feel that they could bring a very similar case to the jury, hoping they would get another conviction."

Even with the original convictions overturned, Murdaugh remains in prison on separate financial crime sentences. The outcome of the murder case will not determine when he could be released.

Prosecutors previously argued that Murdaugh killed his wife and son because he thought the sympathy generated by the killings would buy him time to cover up his thefts.

World.title: The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue
World.content:
The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

In the weeks before Election Day, the Trump administration escalated its hunt for voter fraud and its pressure on election officials — especially in California — to crack down on illegal voting by non-U.S. citizens.

Now, with Election Day come and gone, election officials and civil rights attorneys are preparing for the administration to continue its search for noncitizens on state voter rolls, as well as what they see as intimidation tactics toward election officials.

"It's clear that there is this drive to try to conjure up facts that just don't exist. I don't think that's going to change," James Williams, county executive for California's Santa Clara County, told NPR. "So we fully are prepared to continue to deal with this."

Sponsor Message

In recent weeks, federal prosecutors announced criminal charges against dozens of people who are accused of voting or registering to vote without being a citizen. Yet compared to overall numbers of voters, noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. And since summer, the administration has touted what turned out to be grossly inflated numbers of noncitizens on state voter rolls.

In mid-October, federal officials alleged they had found 20,000 "likely" noncitizens on California's voter rolls. The Department of Justice sued the state to try to force election officials not to count ballots of voters whose citizenship had not been verified. A federal judge and a federal appeals court rejected the DOJ's requests, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene.

In the days leading up to Election Day, with the lawsuit pending, U.S. attorneys in California sent grand jury subpoenas to several counties, asking for records related to how local officials responded to DOJ's demands.

Though DOJ dropped its lawsuit last week, it has not rescinded these subpoenas.

"We have ongoing cases and investigations in various states surrounding voter process," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said at a Thursday press conference. "We are actively, and will continue to investigate election integrity cases criminally and civilly, and that wasn't expected to start or stop — no matter what the results of the election were last week."

toggle caption i Win McNamee/Getty Images

But recent unfavorable rulings for the Trump administration have created new obstacles for future federal attempts to intervene on state voter list maintenance.

Sponsor Message

"Do I think they will still keep at this? I do, but there are just a lot of court losses that are going to be really difficult for them to maneuver around," Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at Campaign Legal Center, told NPR. "They've hit substantial roadblocks because it's a lawless program that Congress has never authorized."

Recent court orders reaffirmed that states have the authority to run their elections and called into question the credibility of the federal government's data on noncitizens.

One key ruling, which came down the night before Election Day, found that DOJ and the Department of Homeland Security lack any statutory authority to distribute lists of purported noncitizens to election officials. In that order, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., wrote that taking that action also violates the Privacy Act. The federal government is expected to appeal.

In an earlier order in October, a different D.C.-based judge vacated the DOJ's project of requesting unredacted voter rolls from states, seeking to compare that voter data to federal databases, and instructing states to remove suspected noncitizens. The ruling found those actions were unlawful and disenfranchised eligible voters. The DOJ has appealed.

The Department of Justice declined to comment on litigation or future plans, but said in a statement, "The Department will continue to enforce federal election laws and will evaluate matters based on the facts and the law."

Looming criminal proceedings and subpoenas to election officials

Federal prosecutors have vowed to continue tracking down noncitizen voting cases, as have some local prosecutors. San Luis Obispo District Attorney Dan Dow is investigating the potential noncitizen voters federal officials flagged in his county. He has so far charged one individual.

"It has always been a crime but I've never had a noncitizen case referred to me. When we got 63 of them, we said, 'We will look at them,'" Dow told NPR. "It is our duty to uphold California law."

Sponsor Message

Loyola Law School professor Justin Levitt, who was a White House adviser on voting rights in the Biden administration, said he expects "a trickle of actual follow-through on actual cases" of noncitizens voting. "And that is also entirely consistent with everything we knew for decades — which is that this does happen, but it doesn't happen very often."

What remains to be seen is whether the Justice Department will retreat from the criminal threats federal officials have waged against local election officials, or try to escalate those further.

In letters delivered to every California county in October, DOJ officials warned: "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime."

President Trump added on Truth Social: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"

In the days before Election Day, officials in Los Angeles County as well as Bay Area counties, including Santa Clara and Sonoma, received subpoenas from their local U.S. attorney's office to turn over records this month.

In Sonoma, the subpoena is for records about an individual the DOJ alleges may have voted in a past election without being a U.S. citizen, as well as records about how county officials responded to DOJ requests to segregate ballots of people on its list of possible noncitizens, according to Sonoma County Counsel Joshua Myers.

The Oct. 21 subpoena sent to Los Angeles County, which was reviewed by NPR, requests records related to how the registrar-recorder's office screens for unlawful voting by noncitizens, as well as records responding to federal correspondence, including the demand to segregate ballots.

The DOJ said it does not comment on alleged subpoenas. But the substance of the subpoenas has raised questions about whether there may be a criminal probe targeted at counties.

Sponsor Message

Williams of Santa Clara County declined to speak about the subpoenas but said criminal threats against government employees who are trying to lawfully administer elections "strikes at the heart of what it means to live in a free society."

Looking forward, Williams said he is hoping for a way to productively collaborate with the federal government again.

"We should be aligned — federal, state and local government — in facilitating every citizen exercising their right to vote. And of course, we want voter rolls that don't include noncitizens," he said. "There's no disagreement about that."

Inflated and inaccurate lists

Another hurdle for the federal government's efforts to publicize purported noncitizens on voter rolls is the inaccuracies in its tallies so far.

Trump claimed in July there were 250,000 noncitizens registered in four states, including in California. But state officials pushed back on the data, and federal officials admitted the earlier numbers were a "ceiling" of potential noncitizens. In mid-October, federal officials had sent California its list of 20,000 "likely" noncitizens registered to vote in the state.

The federal government has never maintained a complete list of U.S. citizens. Trump administration efforts to cobble together citizenship data from various sources have led to naturalized citizens being mistakenly flagged as noncitizens, and data experts have warned the federal government's methodology in California was likely to also lead to false matches.

The weekend before Election Day, a federal judge allowed data experts from University of California Los Angeles' Voting Rights Project to analyze the DOJ's list of 20,000 names. The analysis found 42% did not appear on California's current voter roll and that naturalized citizens were on the list.

Separately, several California counties have noted the lists from DOJ were riddled with duplicates and obvious inaccuracies.

Santa Cruz County's top election official, Tricia Webber, wrote in an email that of the 81 people DOJ had listed as suspected noncitizens registered to vote in her county, "more than half are not registered in Santa Cruz County; some names do not match any person currently registered or previously registered," and some dates of birth "were wildly inaccurate with some dates appearing well into the future like 2044."

Sponsor Message

Even DOJ attorneys acknowledged in court hearings under questioning from judges that there have been flaws with federal lists of likely noncitizens.

U.S. District Judge David Carter, a Clinton nominee, who was presiding over the federal government's lawsuit against California, had planned to hold proceedings that would assess the accuracy of DOJ's lists. That will no longer happen since the DOJ dropped its lawsuit.

For Loyola Law School's Levitt, questions remain about whether federal officials violated the Privacy Act by using California voter roll data for this project without following required public notice procedures.

And with Democrats winning control of Congress, lawmakers could hold hearings that probe deeper into how federal officials came up with their list, said David Becker, the executive director for the Center for Election Innovation and Research.

"I think we're going to have some very serious scrutiny of the Department of Homeland Security and their methodology as they assisted the administration in its failed effort to try to demonstrate there was widespread noncitizen voting in this country," Becker said.

World.title: Does Europe regret its bet on U.S. defense?
World.content:
Does Europe regret its bet on U.S. defense?

You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

Fox has officially acquired Roku and there are CONSEQUENCES. For one, the " Marine Aquarium " screensaver will no longer be available. One person posted on the "Mildly Infuriating" subreddit: "I can't believe it I love my fish what am I gunna do."

Sponsor Message

toggle caption i Screenshot captured on Roku’s YouTube channel

The artist behind that screensaver, Jim Sachs, is NOT renewing his license due to Fox's acquisition. "It seems that Fox simply wants another venue for spreading their philosophy, which I consider repugnant. I can't stand the idea of my artwork being used to lure even one person down that rabbit hole," Sachs told Ars Technica . The licensing deal will have big personal consequences for Sachs, who relies on the $80,000 per year licensing deal. Another comment on the subreddit posted, "This is the last straw, Apple TV for me."

Coming up

The U.S. can't keep up with defense demand

How housing affects fertility rates in Spain

What Walmart stock has to do with the economy

News We're Watching

Did Europe make a bad bet on American defense tech? - Bruegel

What to Know: Over the past decade, European countries have become increasingly reliant on U.S. technology to support their air defense systems. We're talking fighter jets & missile defense systems like the Patriot, which can intercept ballistic missiles. It seemed like an obvious choice: these are high-quality pieces of technology, they're readily available, and buying American keeps the U.S. committed to European defense. Here's the problem: the whole "readily available" thing doesn't seem to be true. There is a MAJOR backlog of missiles while demand just keeps going up. That's due to both production delays and the U.S.' own military needs in Iran. PLUS!! European countries that bought technology like the Patriot are now locked in to American equipment. They can't just switch to another supplier to get missiles.

toggle caption i JOHN MACDOUGALL/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

Why this matters: You kind of want to know if you're not gonna get a few hundred missiles on time. While the U.S. is focused on the Iran war, threats from Russia still loom large in Europe. And now, many European nations are at the whim of these defense contracts panning out… having to put up with delays and higher costs. The article's authors look back and see a missed opportunity in 2022 for investment into homegrown systems: "Calls to Europeanise the funding and ordering of air defense systems were ignored and the strategic gap is now all too visible."

Sponsor Message

Business journalist and friend of the show Paddy Hirsch adds: "No one could have predicted the extent to which Trump would damage the relationship between the U.S. and Europe. But the fact is that Trump isn't the first president to beat the drum about European over-dependence on the US. He's just the first to really force the issue. And guess what? He was doing Europe a favor! Europe desperately needs to wean itself off the U.S. teat, and not just because of the unpredictability of a Presidential whim. But because there's no telling how U.S. and European interests will diverge over the next few decades."

Could more housing lead to a higher fertility rate? - Elcano Royal Institute

What to Know: Spain has one of the lowest fertility rates in the world. It's currently at 1.1, meaning 100 women birth 110 children on average. To maintain the current population, rates would need to sit at 2.1. Immigration has kept the population from dropping dramatically since 2000, but the author offers a DIFFERENT solution to Spain's childbearing woes: more housing. Spain, like many countries, has struggled with expensive housing: prices have risen 81% between 2015 to 2025. The average age of leaving the parental home in Spain is 30.2 compared to 23.8 in France and 24.1 in Germany. The author asks: could an influx of public housing incentivize partners to start families earlier?

How realistic is this?: There's no hard evidence in the Elcano article showing more housing actually leads to a higher fertility rate. That said, Planet Money co-host Jeff Guo says the evidence for this argument does look stronger outside the U.S. There was literally a paper about this topic IN SPAIN that came out a few weeks ago. The paper found a 10% rise in local housing prices LOWERS birth rates by about 3% for women 20-34. In fact, the authors deduced that higher housing prices account for roughly HALF of the 2014-2022 implied fertility rate decline. In short: more expensive housing = fewer kids.

Sponsor Message

Today's Indicator

The stock market might be the economy… just ask Walmart

If you HAVEN'T listened: We all know the old adage "the stock market doesn't equal the economy." Well, lately, maybe it does!! At least more than usual. The "new era" economy (AI, tech etc.) has an outsized impact on the growth of both the stock market AND economic growth. That's all well and good, except hyper-concentration means hyper-risk. If AI stocks start to tumble, it could have a negative chain reaction on the economy in a uniquely problematic way. Two non-profits in the episode warn that the AI bubble is a thing. In short, the economy depends on the market! A downturn there is more likely to mean an economic downturn too. Diversification is important, people.

LISTEN TO THE FULL EPISODE

If you HAVE listened: You know that the economic risk isn't just about a market downturn. It's about the impacts that follow. Consumer spending is driving much of economic growth, and that's led by wealthy spenders. Another downstream risk: pension funds hold debt related to the AI buildout, according to the report from the Open Markets Institute and Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund. They argue this has exposed pension funds and even ordinary workers to dangerous risk! Reporter Wailin Wong says, "That's something I wasn't able to get into in the episode, since we were focused on stocks and not debt. But certainly the credit markets are a huge part of this story too."

REST OF THE WEEK



In Our Spare Time

Reporter Ricky Mulvey read A Violent Masterpiece

It's a profane, no-holds-barred thriller. Jordan Harper wrote on TV shows in Hollywood before getting disillusioned with the industry and writing about some of its seedier parts in novels.

Sponsor Message

A Violent Masterpiece follows three storylines that converge around a suspicious death in a jail cell. It's Eyes Wide Shut meets LA Confidential.

Two things I really admire about Harper's work.

It's confidently modern. I think a lot of writers find more comfort writing about the distant past and allowing readers to find parallels to today. A Violent Masterpiece is confident and planted in the right now. Harper's razor-sharp writing style. He cut his teeth writing for television, so his work is well-structured and every word counts.

A Violent Masterpiece is a perfect book to rip through on a plane if you are traveling for the holidays. A genteel reader should stay far away, and sickos should pick it up. The story is far from perfect; you'll see why at the ending. I loved it.

World.title: How Sen. Chris Van Hollen plans to flex Democratic power on the foreign aid front
World.content:
How Sen. Chris Van Hollen plans to flex Democratic power on the foreign aid front

toggle caption i Nathan Posner/Anadolu



/via Getty Images

"We need new leadership," says Senator Chris Van Hollen, who on Thursday announced he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Democratic majority leader. Van Hollen has garnered support among Democrats for his sharp criticism of the Trump administration, including their upheaval of U.S. programs to promote health and end poverty around the world.

In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, two days before his announcement, Van Hollen spoke to NPR about his plans to "shine a light on all the harm and damage the Trump administration's done to our country and our interests around the world" — and what the Democrats hope to accomplish with foreign aid.

As the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee, which oversees the State Department and what's left of the United States Agency for International Development, he could have considerable sway over how Congress investigates and legislates on foreign aid.

Sponsor Message

This interview has been edited for clarity and length. NPR reached out to the State Department for comment but did not receive a response in time for publication.

You've taken a strong stand against the Trump administration's shakeup of foreign aid. You led protests against the dissolution of USAID and in a hearing last year told Secretary of State Marco Rubio that "People died because of those actions, mothers, fathers and children." You've also authored statements condemning a range of actions, including tying health aid to mineral deals. In the majority, what's the first step you'd take on the aid front?

Priority number one is to do an analysis of all the harm the Trump administration has done.

There have been very credible analyses showing that over 700,000 people around the world died between January 2025 and January 2026 because of cuts to USAID. If these trends continue, you're talking about millions of people dying in the coming years.

One of the great benefits of being in the majority, is you actually have a gavel and can call a public hearing, and use that as a spotlight to help educate people around the country.

We can do that to show the consequences of Elon Musk taking a chainsaw to USAID. I remember to this day a scene at the White House [in February 2025] when Donald Trump was at his desk and Elon Musk was standing behind him, and a reporter asked Elon Musk about the cuts to fighting Ebola, and Elon Musk's response was essentially, "Whoops, yeah, we missed that." And then he claimed that they'd restored it. Well, we know that they've not restored it adequately — there's good evidence that the current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo could have been better contained if the United States had not made big cuts to public health.

Sponsor Message

We can investigate what they did, not for the purpose of putting it back exactly as it was but understanding the damage that has been done, fully, with an eye toward reforming it.

You've already been speaking out against a lot of this in the minority. What kinds of actions can Democrats take as a majority that they couldn't before?

Being in the majority makes a big difference. Now we have many more tools available, specifically through the power of the purse.

One of the things the Trump administration has done is essentially sit on funds appropriated by the Congress for public health here at home but also for international health programs. So there's an example where we can much better safeguard the will of the Congress now that we're in the majority.

Can you give an example?

One of the things the Administration did was to rescind over $500 million in funds for global health. In other words, they cut it, and you had a rubber stamp majority in the Congress. Republicans, go along with that. You would never get Democrats to agree.

There's another ongoing example right now, which is a number of years ago, we passed about $1.5 billion in funds for [global] public health, and it appears that they're using those funds not for public health but to wind down USAID. So this is an area where we could say no, you may not use these funds to wind down USAID.

The administration has been ignoring a lot of these "no's" so far. What gives those "no's" more weight in the majority?

When we in Congress provide a sum of money, for say public health, we say this money should be spent on these specific items, like vaccinations or clinics. That's guidance, that's direction. It's technically called report language, and this report language used to be respected by Democratic and Republican presidents.

Sponsor Message

The Trump administration has ignored report language because it's not technically legally binding, and Republicans in the Congress have let them get away with it. And the more they let them get away with it, the more they do it.

So we're going to have to convert what used to be report language into real law to prevent this administration from taking those actions. We Democrats have been trying to do that, but since we've been in the minority, we haven't been able to get that passed.

What if the administration still tries to hold up funds or ignore or veto Congress' actions?

This has been a lawless president, and he's still in the White House. But being in the majority will give us more leverage. If we're able to codify the safeguards that would prevent the Trump administration from diverting funds from their intended purpose to something else, that would be legally binding. Then you can go to the courts and say, you know this isn't simply report language. This is not just guidance. This is legally required, and so that does provide the safeguards that we would need.

Now we may have a back and forth and fight with the administration over providing those safeguards, but we're in a much stronger position now than we have been.

If the Democrats win the presidency and keep control of Congress in 2028, would the fate of USAID be revisited? Might the agency return? Or are there parts of the Trump administration's global health policy that you think are worth preserving or building on?

I don't think there's anything the Trump administration has done that's worth preserving or building on. That does not mean that I'm in favor of simply returning to the status quo prior to this administration.

I am a big believer that the role that USAID performed was both helpful to protecting the health of Americans but also helpful to developing good relations with other countries and the people of other countries. I think we need to develop our plan for how we perform this very important role as part of our foreign policy and as part of our health policy. But I'm not saying we would just go back exactly to the way USAID was.

Sponsor Message

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: Manchester United names USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino as its manager
World.content:
Manchester United names USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino as its manager

toggle caption i Omar Vega/Getty Images

Mauricio Pochettino, who took over an ailing U.S. men's national soccer team in 2024 and led the squad to a Round of 16 finish in the 2026 World Cup, is departing to take over as coach of famed Manchester United.

Pochettino was the highest-profile manager the U.S. had ever hired. His aggressive attacking style of play won praise from his players and fans alike. At the 2026 World Cup, the USMNT finished first in its group and won its first knockout-round game since 2002. Pochettino's three wins were the most at any World Cup by a USMNT coach.

As a player, he represented Argentina in the 2002 World Cup and played in soccer leagues in Spain and France. As a coach, he managed some of Europe's most recognizable clubs: Tottenham Hotspur, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain. Last August, he signed an extension to lead the USMNT through the 2030 World Cup, giving him a full four-year cycle to build the team into a true contender.

Sponsor Message

Pochettino will lead the U.S. for two more games — against Haiti in the coming days — before departing for Manchester United.

World.title: Nvidia CEO steps down. And, Sen. Chris Van Hollen to run for majority leader
World.content:
Nvidia CEO steps down. And, Sen. Chris Van Hollen to run for majority leader

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down following reports of his extramarital affairs, the company's board announced. The company's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has been appointed interim CEO. The company launched an investigation after allegations surfaced that Huang had an affair with one of its clients, who U.S. intelligence officials concluded had been recruited by China's top spy agency. In an email to Nvidia staff, Huang admitted to cheating on his wife and promised to cooperate with the investigation. Nvidia's share price fell sharply Wednesday after the news of his second affair with an Nvidia executive came to light. Huang was widely considered an important business leader in the U.S. and had close ties to President Trump.

toggle caption i Sean Gallup/Getty Images

🎧 Huang was the face of Nvidia, but Kress has also played a prominent role , NPR's John Ruwitch tells Up First. She is well-known within the company and among investors and business partners. Taking over during a crisis presents immense challenges, especially since Nvidia is a key player in the AI economy. The company produces the most widely-used chips powering the AI revolution, Ruwitch says. Kress must balance the short-term fallout from Huang's downfall while navigating Nvidia's long-term strategy. The strong demand for Nvidia's products is expected to continue as AI usage rises. Ruwitch says one remaining question is how much trust and flexibility the board will give Kress in her leadership.
