Taking over during a crisis presents immense challenges, especially since Nvidia is a key player in the AI economy. The company produces the most widely-used chips powering the AI revolution, Ruwitch says. Kress must balance the short-term fallout from Huang's downfall while navigating Nvidia's long-term strategy. The strong demand for Nvidia's products is expected to continue as AI usage rises. Ruwitch says one remaining question is how much trust and flexibility the board will give Kress in her leadership. 🎧 Huang's resignation may also have consequences for the U.S. government. NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben says the scandal is raising questions for the White House and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Commerce handles imports and exports, and Kurtzleben says one big question is whether the U.S. should have more tightly restricted the chips it exports. Lawmakers from both parties want to know when Lutnick knew that Huang was in contact with a suspected Chinese asset, and what he did or didn't do in response.

Sponsor Message

White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have been busy this week working on a new security framework between Russia and Europe and seeking to end the war in Ukraine. They led peace talks in Abu Dhabi, met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and then traveled to Ireland to meet with Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.



🎧 During their visit with Putin, both sides noted progress on the humanitarian track of negotiations, according to NPR's Charles Maynes. Kushner sees potential for a new security framework between Russia and Europe to help end the war, but Putin remains unyielding in public comments. Putin has accused Europe of prolonging the conflict through military support for Ukraine and ruled out European peacekeepers as part of any deal. Despite this, Witkoff said Putin had agreed to include Europeans in future talks, though the Kremlin didn't confirm it.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has announced he will challenge New York's Chuck Schumer for the Senate majority leader position. Following recent midterm victories, Van Hollen said voters desired a "change from the status quo." Elected to the Senate in 2016 after more than a decade in the House, the 67-year-old progressive gained national attention last year for lobbying for the release of Kilmar Abrego Garcia after his wrongful deportation to a prison in El Salvador. His announcement comes as progressive activists and some Democrats push for the 75-year-old Schumer's replacement. Schumer has been in the role since 2017 but faced criticism from the Democratic base for failing to confront Trump vigorously during a funding dispute in early 2025.

Sponsor Message

Life advice

toggle caption i filadendron/Getty Images

It's once again time to plan your Friendsgiving or Thanksgiving. You might be wondering: should you stick with your classic turkey recipe or spice things up? What about decorations — mini gourds or a stunning sunflower centerpiece? Let Life Kit help you decide with some fresh ideas to bring flavor, color and a touch of calm to your gathering.

🦃 Use "magical questions" to ignite engaging conversations with guests. Questions like "What's the weirdest thing you've found in your pocket?" can break the ice and reveal personalities in group settings.

🦃 If you're hosting, choose three moments to be fully present. You can't do everything on your to-do list, so focus on what matters most, like decorating the Thanksgiving table, serving turkey and watching the game.

🦃 Place holiday decor in the entryway to make a strong first impression. A simple centerpiece, like a thrifted glass vase filled with pinecones or cranberries, can create a festive feel.

🦃 Engage all of your guests' five senses with cozy touches like a velvety blanket on the couch, a crackling candle and decorative gourds.

Spice up your menu with new crowd-pleasing Thanksgiving recipes, including a salt-and-pepper roast turkey breast and pull-apart garlic bread. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Weekend picks

toggle caption i Bruce Glikas/Getty Images

Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:

🍿 Movies: Gentle Monster follows a loving couple who move to a farmhouse and whose peace shatters when the husband is accused of a crime. Léa Seydoux, who plays the wife named Lucy, discusses her first "complex" lead role in English with Morning Edition.

📺 TV: The new show Cupertino follows two Silicon Valley lawyers whose new firm represents the underdog, takes on big tech and grapples with the complexities of AI.

📚 Books: Journalist Mona Chalabi spent five years following 10 Americans of different economic standings to uncover what it takes to feel financially secure. Her book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are, delves into the elusive nature of financial security.

Sponsor Message

🎵 Music: Rappers Lil Baby, Jack Harlow and SOB x RBE offer three ways to relight a flickering star and chart a path toward creative restoration through their respective albums, released today.

🎭 Theater: School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play wraps up its Broadway run this week. To celebrate, it will have paid livestreams on The League of Live Stream Theater's website. Set in a 1986 Ghanaian boarding school, the play humorously tackles themes of girlhood and beauty standards.

❓Quiz: Did you actually pay attention this week, or did you just scroll past the headlines? Prove it.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images North America

Existing home sales fell to 3.75 million in October, marking an 8.8% drop from last year — the lowest sales in 16 years, according to the National Association of Realtors. For more than 60 years, researchers at the University of Virginia have identified children with past-life memories. A new study suggests that those who died violently or unexpectedly are reincarnated more quickly than others. (via WBUR) The American Cancer Society has recommended routine prostate cancer screenings for the first time. The group says that blood tests, especially for high-risk groups like Black men and those with a family history, could save lives.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Happy World Kindness Day! Check out our kind photos of kindness to humans -- and cats
World.content:
Happy World Kindness Day! Check out our kind photos of kindness to humans — and cats

toggle caption i Tuane Fernandes/The Everyday Projects/Everyday Brasil

Editor's note: Today, November 13, is World Kindness Day!

Kind-minded organizations from various countries came up with the idea and announced it on November 13, 1998. (And the date stuck.) The goal is kinda obvious — do something kind!

It doesn't matter if it's a modest action. One of the founding groups is the Small Kindness Movement of Japan. And no kind deed is too small to acknowledge. One year, the Japanese movement gave an award to a cabbie who pulled over to clear trash bags off the road lest they cause an accident. According to a report in the Christian Science Monitor, the cab driver humbly said it was "no big deal."

So on Friday, November 13, 2026, try a little kindness. To inspire you, we've talked to folks whose lives were changed by kindness — and asked the photojournalists of The Everyday Projects, a global network, to submit pictures that capture a kind moment. Animal lovers will be happy to see photos of kindness toward animals as well as an image of a support donkey — a reminder that animals can be kind to us humans, too.

toggle caption i Henitsoa RAFALIA

toggle caption i Andres Yepez/EverydayEcuador

Let's start with a simple yet profound story about a snack.

Sponsor Message

Back in 2004, Maymunah Yusuf Kadiri , a neuro-psychiatrist and mental health advocate in Nigeria, was a young doctor working in the emergency room at the Lagos State University Teaching hospital. One night sticks in her mind. It was chaos. There were accident victims everywhere. She recalls the blood, the cries and her own exhaustion.

"I hadn't eaten for over 12 hours, and my hands were shaking," says Kadiri, who was 28 at the time. "Then an elderly cleaner, one of those invisible heroes in hospitals, walked up to me with a small nylon bag." Inside was a biscuit and a sachet of water.

"Doctor," she said, "you need small strength to save people."

"It sounds simple, but I'll never forget it. That biscuit tasted like hope. Her kindness reminded me that healing isn't only about medicine, it's about humanity," says Kadiri. "As a psychiatrist, I've seen it over and over: People don't just heal in hospitals, they heal in human connections."

And while one isolated act of kindness may seem random, it can lead to much more.

toggle caption i Ana Caroline de Lima

toggle caption i James A. Rodriguez/James Rodriguez / Everyday Latin/James Rodriguez / Everyday Latin

Huguette Diakabana remembers when she had to drop out of school at age 10 — until a mysterious donor came to her rescue. Her family was planning to emigrate to the U.S. from Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of Congo) and couldn't afford school fees. They figured she'd make up the year later. She had a different idea: "I put on my previous year's uniform and sat outside under the street window of my would-be classroom." One day, the director invited her inside. Diakabana realized someone must have paid her school fees, but who?

Sponsor Message

Returning to the school years later, Diakabana discovered it was a school guard. She wanted to repay him. "He told me to help others when I could, so I launched a scholarship program," says Diakabana, who now lives in Switzerland and is co-founder of The Luminous Agency, which focuses on digital literacy.

Dr. Junaid Nabi, a physician-scientist who conducts research in health care technology at the RAND School in Washington, D.C. and is a senior fellow at the Aspen Institute, says he's come to realize that kindness isn't actually a trickle in the ocean. An act of kindness is more like dropping a stone that creates expanding ripples, he says.

"There are studies that illustrate how kindness spreads through social networks in measurable ways. When we are kind to someone, they don't just feel better — they become 25% more likely to help others."

One such investigation described how kindness can be contagious. It was sparked by reports of an outbreak of kindness on a cold December morning in 2012. A stranger picked up the tab for the coffee order of the next customer in the drive-through line at a Tim Hortons coffeehouse in Winnipeg, Canada. And that customer picked up the tab of the person behind him. In the end, 226 customers passed on this act of kindness.

The study authors, citing other examples of "pay it forward" kindness at fast food restaurants and their own experiments encouraging subjects to help others, write: "Why, in the absence of external sanctions and opportunities for reciprocation, do people help strangers? One possible explanation is that helping is driven by receiving or observing help. In other words, generosity towards strangers may be socially contagious."

toggle caption i Ana Caroline de Lima

toggle caption i Paulo Ermantino/Everyday Social Justice

Don't talk yourself out of it

It might sound contradictory, but researchers studying the psychology of altruism, kindness and giving have uncovered this curious paradox: Sometimes, people can be kind-hearted, have a genuine desire to help someone, but in spite of that, not give at all.

Sponsor Message

Marta Serra-Garcia, a professor of economics and strategy at the Rady School of Management in the University of California, San Diego, is one of the authors of the study Give Enough or Not at all.

"There's a growing body of work in economics and psychology trying to understand altruism. Altruism is a result of a feeling of empathy and the emotion of feeling warm and well when you help others. We know people are altruistic, but we're trying to understand when, why and how," she says.

The study, published in the September Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, revealed that people may prefer to give nothing rather than donate an amount they consider too small — even when those on the receiving end would welcome whatever they can get.

"It seems like an odd thing," Serra-Garcia says in an interview over a video call with NPR. "You're generous, but because you want to do the right thing, you might end up not giving at all, out of concern that your gift would be viewed as inappropriate or might even offend the other person."

In one experiment in the study, givers tended to overestimate the minimum amount recipients would consider acceptable.

"We tend to think there are givers and non-givers," says Serra-Garcia. "The people who give are the generous and kind ones, the non-givers are just not generous." But the study indicates otherwise.

"That perception of appropriateness makes them think, "I'd rather not give at all, although I'm a generous person," says Serra-Garcia.

toggle caption i Amnon Gutman

toggle caption i Alan Eason/Everyday Africa

Nature or nurture?

And where does kindness come from? Are you born with it? Or can you learn to be compassionate and empathetic?

Jeff R. Temple , a professor and psychologist with UTHealth Houston, says kindness is a central thread running through his studies on healthy relationships among adolescents and young adults.

Sponsor Message

"In our intervention work — including with the Fourth R program and other school-based curricula — we teach adolescents to practice perspective-taking, to express care even during disagreement and recognize the impact of their words and actions. These are essentially the behavioral expressions of kindness."

Such kids are less likely to bully others because they know what healthy relationships are like, he says.

toggle caption i Alan Eason/Everyday Africa

A ripple effect

And let's not forget that kindness can change not only the life of the recipient of the kind deed but of the kind person, says Nabi, who offers this anecdote.

In the 2013 Savar building collapse in Bangladesh, where 1,040 garment workers were crushed under concrete. Rescue workers managed to pull out 2,400 people from the rubble two weeks after the collapse. Nabi arrived at the disaster site as a Red Cross volunteer, expecting to gain experience in trauma care. Instead, he says, the experience changed his psyche, teaching him about the nature of true kindness.

In the 2013 Savar building collapse in Bangladesh, more than 1,000 garment workers died and thousands were injured. Nabi arrived at the disaster site as a Red Cross volunteer, expecting to gain experience in trauma care. Instead, he says, the experience changed his psyche, teaching him about the nature of true kindness.

"In the midst of chaos, with bodies awaiting identification, kindness came down to being present during others' darkest moments," says Nabi. "I performed CPR on workers I knew wouldn't survive and when I couldn't save someone, I stayed by their side, holding their hand."

"Before Savar, I was mechanistic, rushing through clinical work like tasks," he recalls. "The image of workers who had embraced each other as concrete crushed them — that final act of human kindness in the face of death — shattered my callousness completely."

When he returned to the hospital, he listened to patients differently, giving them more of his time. He also urges doctors to volunteer for humanitarian causes to practice compassion.

Sponsor Message

"Kindness, I learned, is about showing up completely for another person's suffering," Navi reflects, "and letting that experience fundamentally change who you are."

So if you began reading this story with the thought that World Kindness Day is … a gimmick … it is a gimmick imbued with heart and hope.

It's a good reminder to practice kindness more, Dr. Kadiri says. "And here's the beautiful part: When someone receives kindness, they don't just feel better, they become better." They may be inspired to perform their own act of kindness. And that, she says, makes the world a kinder, better place too.

Your turn: Readers! Have you ever had a life-changing moment because of an act of kindness. Share your story with us by emailing globalhealth@npr.org. We'll consider all submissions for a follow-up story. Be sure to tell us how to contact you if we are interested in featuring your anecdote.

Special thanks to the photojournalists of The Everyday Projects, who shared their beautiful images of kind moments for this story.

Kamala Thiagarajan is a freelance journalist based in Madurai, Southern India. She reports on global health, science and development and has been published in The New York Times, The British Medical Journal, the BBC, The Guardian and other outlets. You can find her on X @kamal_t

World.title: Nvidia's interim CEO inherits risky AI bets and a legal mess
World.content:
Nvidia's interim CEO inherits risky AI bets and a legal mess

toggle caption i Markus Schreiber/AP

A suspected intelligence scandal, reports of multiple extramarital affairs and the abrupt departure of one of Silicon Valley's most influential CEOs. It's been a dizzying week for Nvidia and the AI industry.

Jensen Huang helped bankroll the AI boom. Now, after 33 years at the helm of the leading company in AI, he's out, leaving questions about the future of an industry that has relied heavily on his company's financial backing. Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO.

Sponsor Message

"Nvidia has put itself basically in a position of being a bank, backstopping everything," Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and longtime AI researcher, told Morning Edition.

He was describing circular financing: Nvidia invests in AI companies that then use the money to buy Nvidia's chips. OpenAI, Anthropic and CoreWeave have relied on that funding, he said, even as many AI businesses struggle to turn a profit.

"Jensen was kind of a swashbuckler, willing to make bets of arbitrary size," Marcus said.

Unlike Huang, whose background is in engineering, Kress comes from finance and appears more cautious about making large financial bets, potentially changing how Nvidia backs the wider AI industry.

Kress will also have to contend with potential federal and congressional investigations into Nvidia's dealings involving China, leaving her to "clean up that mess," Marcus said.

He said lawmakers need answers about what information Huang may have shared with Alice Huang and why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had not intervened earlier.

"Why didn't Lutnick shut some of this down when he was asked to?" Marcus said.

Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.

The radio interview was edited by Simone Popperl and the web copy was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Stelco recalling 175 laid-off workers at Hamilton steel plant
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hamilton steelmaker Stelco is recalling 175 workers that had been laid off earlier this fall.

Stelco made the announcement in a news release on Friday, saying that the workers would be back in the factory by Dec. 1. The company also indicated that it would retroactively pay the workers for the time they were laid off.

The American parent company, Cleveland-Cliffs, announced in September that it planned to lay off as many as 500 workers as it idled certain steel production at Stelco.

The federal government said that any move to lay off workers would violate "binding commitments" Cleveland-Cliffs made when it bought Stelco in 2024.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly wrote to the Ohio-based company in mid-October, demanding that it reverse the layoffs or face possible legal action.

Cleveland-Cliffs originally cited U.S. tariffs, weak demand for Canadian steel and competition from imported steel products as its reasons for the planned layoffs. Stelco's Friday statement also cited those issues, but said the company had been granted reassurances from its customers.

"Our customers have committed to support our Hamilton finishing operations despite the lack of response from the federal government to address the shortfalls in their tariff-response program and the continued flood of offshore imports of galvanized products that have eroded our domestic market," the statement said.

WATCH | Joly on the future of Stelco: Ottawa plans to force sale of Stelco if Cleveland-Cliffs doesn't respond by end of day: Joly | Duration closed caption 1:17 Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said on Friday that she plans to ask a court to order U.S. steel company Cleveland-Cliffs to sell Ontario-based Stelco if she doesn't hear from them by the end of day. She said the federal government has this power because Cleveland-Cliffs is in breach of the Investment Canada Act. Joly made the comments before Stelco announced it would recall 175 laid-off workers on Dec. 1.

The government says Cleveland-Cliffs agreed to keep the number of unionized employees at 2024 levels through to 2029 in its original purchase agreement.

Just prior to Stelco's announcement, Joly said she would be seeking a court order for Cleveland-Cliffs to divest from the Hamilton plant if she didn't hear from the company by the end of the day.

Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves told CBC's Power & Politics late last month that he originally bought the Hamilton plant to stop it undercutting his U.S. business.

"I bought Stelco because I could not afford anymore having Stelco flooding the market here in the United States to the detriment of my own company," Goncalves told host David Cochrane.

Joly said Goncalves's comments were a "shocking admission" and asked the competition bureau to investigate whether Cleveland-Cliffs had run afoul of the Competition Act.

World.title: Feds, Ontario offering Stellantis 'aggressive package' to keep Brampton auto plant open
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal and Ontario governments are mounting a last-ditch effort to save the Stellantis auto plant in Brampton by pitching the company possible survival "scenarios" and offering an "aggressive package" of support to make it happen.

Rather than hold a news conference to announce this latest step, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly revealed the plan in Woodbridge, Ont., at another announcement.

"We've put an aggressive package to Stellantis to prevent the sale. And we are still in solution mode to prevent the sale," Joly said in response to a reporter's question about the future of the plant.

Joly said the next move is for her, Unifor — the union representing workers at the plant — and Ontario Minister of Economic Development Vic Fedeli to meet with Stellantis global CEO Antonio Filosa to pitch the plan.

Fedeli said Unifor has come up with more than one scenario for how the sale can be stopped and the plant "kept warm" until new Stellantis product lines can return.

"They have brought forward some suggestions. These are men and women who have built products at Stellantis's Brampton plant for decades. They know exactly what needs to happen in that plant," Fedeli said.

$2.5B auto support package

In October, the federal and Ontario governments announced an $8.7-billion support package for steel, critical mineral and auto sectors, with $2.5 billion earmarked for the auto sector over two years.

Fedeli said the financial support for Unifor's suggested "scenarios" will be paid for out of that fund.

"Not all of it, of course, but part of it is available for this solution," Fedeli said.

In 2022, the Trudeau government promised to inject up to $529 million in Stellantis plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., to help them increase production of electric and gas-powered vehicles.

More than 2,000 workers at Stellantis's Brampton plant have been out of work since the company halted operations in 2023 to begin that retooling process so the facility could produce the Jeep Compass.

But Stellantis paused the retooling effort in early 2025, announcing in October of that year that the Jeep Compass would be built at the Belvidere Assembly Plant in Illinois instead.

WATCH | Joly says feds have 'levers' for Stellantis case: Joly says feds have 'levers' around Stellantis plant sale — but not what they are | Duration 1:01 Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Friday that Ottawa has 'levers' to pull with Stellantis because of financial support the government provided to support key facilities. The Liberal government wants to keep the Brampton, Ont., assembly plant and jobs tied to it, Joly said, but did not offer specifics around what is being offered or how they plan to proceed.

The plant's future in Brampton had been left in limbo until Monday, when Stellantis announced it was selling the facility to Canadian armoured ⁠vehicle maker Roshel Inc..

"When it comes to Stellantis our position is clear: they cannot close the plant," Joly said. "If they would, we would sue them … and they're on the hook for hundreds of millions of dollars."

Last December, CBC News confirmed that the federal government had given $222 million to the Canadian arm of Stellantis between 2023 and 2025. CBC News asked the federal government for the most recent total but has yet to receive a response.

But in a statement on Thursday, Stellantis Canada CEO Trevor Longley said the company will only return subsidies to the government to the tune of $24 million.

"Documents are clear, contracts also are clear. The Brampton facility of Stellantis is linked to the Windsor plant and also the battery investments, that's why I've said and I continue to say Stellantis is on the hook for hundreds of millions of dollars," Joly said Friday.

President of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association Flavio Volpe says that according to Stellantis's product plan, it still has four vehicles for the 2029 model year that have not been assigned to a plant.

"Let's stop the sale, keep the plant warm and then work on landing those products here," Volpe told CBC News.

World.title: Avril Lavigne welcomes baby girl
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian pop-punk princess Avril Lavigne has welcomed her first child — a baby girl — with an unnamed partner.

"Our Mini F--king Princess has arrived 🎀👑🍼🩷," Lavigne shared in a post on Instagram, accompanied by a carousel of photos, including one of her and her mystery partner holding the newborn's hand, and another of a row of three pairs of classic checkered slip-on Vans — lined up in a row on a skateboard.

Lavigne, 42, hasn't revealed the baby's name or who her father is; the Sk8er Boi singer is not publicly linked to anyone at the moment.

Lavigne has been married twice in the past to fellow well-known Canadian musicians: Sum 41 frontman Deryck Whibley (2006–2010) and Nickelback's Chad Kroeger (2013–2015). She was also once engaged to American rapper Mod Sun, and has been previously linked to Tyga, Brandon Davis, Wilmer Valderrama and Brody Jenner.

Her latest release came in 2024 in the form of a career-spanning greatest hits album, including 20 songs across her seven studio albums — everything from Complicated to Girlfriend to Head Above Water.

Love Sux, her most recent studio album, was released in 2022 and produced by Mod Sun, Travis Barker and John Feldmann.

While Lavigne has not toured in 2026, she embarked on a 69-show Greatest Hits Tour starting in Vancouver in 2024. The run included 13 stops across Canada, concluding at the All Your Friends Festival in Oro-Medonte, Ont., in June 2025.

World.title: They called her 'Mommy': Vulnerable senior dies after 2 strangers take over her life
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Dorelia Licorish didn't know where she was. Her confusion came after she was asked a simple question by a Toronto judge presiding over a video court hearing last May.

"Are you in Guyana right now?"

Licorish, an 86-year-old Toronto resident who was in the South American country at the time, turned to the two men with her.

"I'm supposed to say yes?"

"Yes," one of them responded.

A provincial agency had gone to court to get legal guardianship over Licorish, arguing she was mentally incapable and the men were taking advantage of her financially.

Back in Canada, members of her family had been searching for Licorish. They called police after they hadn't been able to reach her for weeks and her house looked abandoned.

Less than six months after that call, Licorish died in hospital from an infected bedsore so deep her pelvic bone was exposed. The two men with her in Guyana are living in her Toronto home. Police have laid no charges.

Licorish’s nieces, Susanne Perch, left, and Andrea Phillips-Beckles, right, are seeking answers from police about what happened to their aunt. (Krista Hessey/CBC)

An investigation by CBC's the fifth estate into Licorish's death reveals that even when government agencies and law enforcement are alerted to a case of suspected elder abuse, they can fail to protect the most vulnerable seniors.

Licorish's family believe she was neglected by the men who had moved in as tenants before declaring themselves her caregivers.

"I would like to get justice for her because [the police] didn't take anything seriously at all," said Andrea Phillips-Beckles, Licorish's niece.

Watch the full documentary, "They called her 'Mommy,'" from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m .

Mistreatment of older adults is on the rise, experts say, as Canada becomes a " super-aged" country this year, with one in five people aged 65 or older.

While rates of elder abuse are not tracked nationally, a 2022 study by University of Toronto researchers found one in 10 Canadians over age 65 experiences some form of elder abuse — physical, financial or sexual — every year, and racialized and cognitively impaired older adults are at higher risk.

"Dorelia's story is one that's being played out in so many places, among so many individuals each and every day in our country, and this issue is only growing bigger," said Dr. Samir Sinha, geriatrician and clinician scientist a t Sinai Health System and University Health Network in Toronto.

"What's preventing this from happening to you?"

An undated photo of Licorish. (Krista Hessey/CBC)

Beloved auntie

Licorish immigrated to Canada from Barbados in the early 1960s. She was sharp-witted and fiercely independent, her family and friends said. She did not have any children of her own, but after her sister died, raised Phillips-Beckles.

"She was one vibrant, vibrant woman," Phillips-Beckles said.

Licorish worked as a nurse at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health on Queen Street West in Toronto for decades before retiring.

Christiana Egi, Licorish's former nursing colleague and close friend of 35 years, told the fifth estate she noticed Licorish was displaying memory problems as early as 2018.

WATCH | Remembering an independent woman: Remembering a much-loved family member | Duration closed caption 2:02 Dorelia Licorish is remembered by her friends and family as a fiercely independent woman who loved fashion, travelling and gardening.

In early 2024, Licorish told Egi that a married couple, Daniel Gopie and Elton John Rambarrat, had moved into her basement and were helping her around the house.

"I was like, 'I hope this is for real, that something doesn't happen.'"

The first red flags for Licorish's family came in June 2024. Licorish's landline had been disconnected and a second cousin received word the new tenants had said the house was now in their name.

The cousin showed up at Licorish's home in Toronto with police, but Licorish got angry and asked them to leave.

Daniel Gopie, left, Licorish and Elton John Rambarrat in an undated photo. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)

A month later, she gave Rambarrat and Gopie powers of attorney over her property and personal care — giving them control of her finances and health should she be deemed incapable. Then she signed a will leaving all her assets to them, including her million-dollar Toronto home.

When Phillips-Beckles went to the home in August 2024, she says Licorish didn't immediately recognize her and the men never left her aunt's side. One of the men told her Licorish's will is "bulletproof."

"He started calling her 'Mommy,' and then she said, 'These are my sons from God.' I said, 'No, they're sons from the devil,'" Phillips-Beckles said.

Legal documents in question

In September 2024, Ontario's Office of the Public Guardian and Trustee (OPGT) began looking into the relationship between Licorish and her tenants after receiving a tip from a real estate lawyer.

The OPGT is a provincial agency tasked with safeguarding the interests of mentally incapable Ontarians.

The lawyer told the agency he had been asked to add Rambarrat and Gopie to the title of Licorish's property. He refused after Licorish could not recall the men's names.

In a 120-page affidavit filed in Ontario Court of Justice, the OPGT detailed what allegedly happened after Rambarrat and Gopie moved in. The men said they had met Licorish at her church and she allowed them to live in the basement rent-free in exchange for helping her with shopping and chores.

They began going with Licorish to appointments with her longtime family doctor, court records show. The doctor told the OPGT that after an appointment in September 2024, she asked Licorish about the men and the powers of attorney document they had shown her, Licorish was "very surprised" and didn't remember signing it.

An undated photo of Gopie, left, Licorish and Rambarrat. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)

Her family doctor wrote she had "concerns with Ms. Licorish's memory" and had booked a mini-mental status exam. However, Rambarrat cancelled the appointment. In medical notes from August 2025, doctors wrote Licorish had a history of dementia but it is unclear when it was first diagnosed.

In an interview with the fifth estate, the men said Licorish did not have dementia and was capable of granting them powers of attorney and creating a will that named them sole beneficiaries.

"The lawyer did the will. She did think it was fine and we didn't see it as a problem; it's something [Licorish] wanted to do," Rambarrat said.

The lawyer, Veena Pohani, told OPGT that while the three had "an unconventional relationship," she did not see signs of abuse and Licorish appeared happy.

Pohani declined to be interviewed for this story, citing client-solicitor privilege.

Rambarrat says lawyer Veena Pohani created the powers of attorney documents and will for Licorish. (veenapohani.com)

While a dementia diagnosis does not necessarily mean someone is incapable, lawyers have a duty to ensure clients have the mental capacity to understand the legal decisions they are making and that they are not being pressured by outside forces, according to the Ontario Law Society.

Pohani told the OPGT Licorish was capable of making these decisions, although no information is included about how she determined that.

Allegations of financial abuse

Banking records submitted in court show a dramatic change in Licorish's spending around the time the men entered her life. Thousands of dollars in ATM cash withdrawals and near-weekly alcohol purchases quickly depleted her modest pension and drove her account into overdraft.

Rambarrat and Gopie were added to Licorish's accounts in early October 2024. They cashed out some of her investments and withdrew money from her line of credit a few weeks before they took Licorish to their home country of Guyana for the first time.

Undated photos of Licorish with Gopie and Rambarrat in Guyana. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)

Bank staff wrote to OPGT that Licorish told them she "trusts them fully" and the transactions were completed with her consent.

However, about six weeks later, Licorish told OPGT investigators that she was not aware of withdrawals in the thousands.

Rambarrat and Gopie deny using Licorish's money for their own purposes and say they used it for home repairs.

However, when asked by OPGT investigators, they could not provide a receipt.

Family tries to intervene

Over 18 months, Licorish's family members made multiple calls to Toronto police, voicing concerns about the men's relationship with their elderly relative.

Body camera recordings and records obtained through the Freedom of Information Act show police treated multiple reports as "family disputes."

The fifth estate also learned police went to Licorish's house in March 2024, the same month the men allegedly moved in, and noticed she had cognitive issues.

Court records also reveal Gopie, who became Licorish's main caregiver, pleaded guilty to two assault charges in 2013 and 2018, unrelated to Licorish. Yet, police took no action to intervene.

Retired Durham police detective Martin Franssen, who specialized in suspected cases of elder abuse and reviewed the OPGT court file, says Licorish's case is "textbook."

He says Gopie's criminal history and Licorish's vulnerable mental state should have alerted officers to look into the situation more.

"This is the future of Canada — based on the changing age demographics — and we have to change our ways."

OPGT goes to court, Licorish goes to Guyana

In October 2024, the OPGT filed a notice in court to remove Rambarrat and Gopie as Licorish's powers of attorney for property and for the agency to take over her financial affairs.

However, seven months passed before OPGT submitted evidence.

By then, the men had taken Licorish to Guyana for a second time. All three attended a virtual court hearing to assign Licorish a lawyer who would be tasked with discerning her wishes.

In the audio recording of the hearing, obtained by the fifth estate, the OPGT's lawyer said the agency went to court "hastily" and did more investigative work after speaking to Pohani.

The lot in New Amsterdam, Guyana, where sources say Rambarrat and Gopie intend to build a house. (Krista Hessey/CBC)

The men told the judge they were in Guyana because they are building a house. They said they brought Licorish with them because they were her caregivers and it wasn't safe for her to be left alone.

The men spoke for Licorish until the judge asked if there was anything she wanted to say.

"I don't want them to leave me," she replied weakly.

Franssen says it is common in predatory relationships involving older adults for the perpetrator to quickly make the victim feel dependent upon them, making it less likely that they will report the abuse.

"If cognition comes into play … they may not even realize it's being done, but they will believe, in a lot of cases I've seen and dealt with, that they have that reliance on that individual."

The fifth estate spoke to several residents who saw and interacted with Licorish while she was in Guyana. Fearing retaliation, CBC News agreed not to identify them.

Multiple sources questioned how well Licorish was being cared for because Gopie would drink heavily, sometimes becoming intoxicated with Licorish. They said the three of them stayed in a dilapidated home where several other people connected to Rambarrat also lived.

Sources say the men and Licorish stayed at this house for weeks alongside several other members of Rambarrat’s family. (Krista Hessey/CBC)

During the trip, Licorish grew too weak to leave the house independently and would be left alone for hours, several sources said.

The men deny this, saying she was on vacation and well-cared for. They say she only visited the rundown home during the day and slept elsewhere.

The fifth estate has learned that when Licorish returned to Canada in July 2025, the lawyer assigned to her at the court hearing was unable to obtain instructions, though there was no explanation as to why.

"We have a system that, as designed, can't act quickly enough," Sinha said. "We don't have the luxury of time in these cases."

Licorish's final months

Upon returning from Guyana, Licorish's mental and physical health had declined, Licorish's friends and family said. She became bedridden after a brief hospitalization in August for a swollen knee and began receiving visits from personal support workers and nurses.

Partial records from the province's home-care agency, Ontario Health atHome, obtained by the fifth estate show Licorish had a pressure injury on her tailbone on Oct. 5, 2025. Nursing notes say the men were not "willing and able" to care for the wound.

The Victorian Order of Nurses, a non-profit nursing agency, was authorized to send someone to tend to the bedsore every three days.

A nurse reported to Ontario Health atHome Rambarrat had assisted him with turning Licorish because she would not allow the male nurse to touch her and he advised Rambarrat to turn Licorish frequently.

That same nurse said on Nov. 5 he requested a specialist to come to look at the wound because it was getting bigger and deeper. However, it's unclear if that occurred.

Licorish was unresponsive when she arrived at Scarborough General Hospital on Nov. 7, 2025. (Submitted by Susanne Perch)

On Nov. 7, 2025, Licorish was rushed to Scarborough General Hospital after a nurse found her unresponsive, medical records show.

She had gone into septic shock, a reaction to an infected Stage 4 bedsore, the most severe rating, that was oozing brown liquid and had a foul smell. Doctors also noted "profound dehydration" and high blood sugar levels.

When asked why he or Gopie did not take Licorish to the hospital sooner, Rambarrat said they deferred to the health-care professionals caring for Licorish.

Both S.R.T.-Med-Staff, the agency sending PSWs to care for Licorish daily, and the Victorian Order of Nurses did not respond to detailed questions, citing privacy laws.

The men, as Licorish's attorneys for personal care, had a legal duty of care to her, retired police detective Franssen said.

"Why didn't you pick up [and call] 911? Why did you need a health-care professional to walk in that day and turn to you and say, 'I suggest you call 911?'"

Licorish died on Nov. 21, 2025, 10 days after the men agreed for her to be moved to palliative care.

Sinha says her death was preventable.

"If she arrived at the hospital sooner, she may still be alive."

Because of her passing, the OPGT's case in court was dismissed.

Police close the case

Licorish's family only found out she was in hospital after a cousin driving by her house saw an ambulance out front. When they became aware of Licorish's condition, they called Toronto police again. This time, they alleged the men neglected Licorish and begged police to investigate.

In May, six months after Licorish's death, Toronto police detectives informed the family they had closed the case.

Toronto police declined interview requests, saying in a statement they conducted a thorough review of the circumstances surrounding Licorish's care, finances and death.

"The investigation included the examination of extensive medical, home care and other records, consultation with multiple parties involved in her care.... Following that investigation, no evidence was identified to support the laying of criminal charges," a media spokesperson wrote.

Multiple members of Licorish's extended family called Toronto Police Service's 43 Division about Rambarrat and Gopie's relationship with their elderly aunt. They accuse the police of not taking their concerns seriously. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Family members are in the process of contesting Licorish's will, arguing she wasn't mentally capable at the time of signing.

Rambarrat and Gopie say Licorish's family did not care for her and they are entitled to her house.

"I'm obligated to get something," Gopie said in an interview. "Does nobody come and clean her piss? Clean her shit? Do anything for her?"

Phillips-Beckles has a binder of files and contacts she's been collecting as she tries to piece together what happened to her aunt.

"I can't wrap my head around it at all, that she's gone and how she went," she said. "She shouldn't have gone that way."

World.title: Canadian women pass stern test from Czechs at hockey worlds, advancing to semifinals
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada is through to the semifinals of the women's world hockey championship, but not without facing a few anxious moments against Czechia.

Renata Fast's second-period goal stood as the winner as Canada held off the Czechs 3-2 in the quarterfinals on Friday in Herning, Denmark.

"We have a lot of respect for Czechia; they played a great game," Canada defender Erin Ambrose said. "I think we did a good job five-on-five; we had a lot of attempts on net, a lot of shots on net, but they played desperate and blocked a lot of shots."

Sarah Fillier and Rebecca Leslie also scored for Canada, which went undefeated in four games with a plus-25 goal differential in pool play. Eve Gascon made 14 saves at KVIK Hockey Arena.

Kristýna Kaltounková replied with a pair of power-play goals, and Noemi Neubauerov tallied two assists as Czechia scored more than one goal against Canada for the first time in six encounters in all competitions.

Klara Peslarova stopped 38 shots in the Czech net.

"From the start, we wanted to set the standard of being physical, going hard on them, going to the net, but also being strong in our zone, and I think we did that well. I'm very proud of my team," Kaltounková said. "It's a testament to our team's strength that we're knocking on that door to beat the North American team."

WATCH | Canada fends off feisty Czechs in quarterfinals: Canada holds off Czechia to advance to women's world championship semifinals | Duration closed caption 0:55 Renata Fast scored the eventual game-winning goal, as Canada defeated Czechia 3-2 to advance to the semifinals of the women's world championship in Denmark.

Canada will face Finland in Sunday's semifinals. The Finns, who fell 2-0 to Canada in Group B action, blanked Germany 6-0 on Friday.

In the other quarterfinals, the United States was scheduled to play Denmark while Sweden faced Switzerland later Friday.

After a goalless first period, Canada struck twice early in the second. Fillier scored 1:29 into the period when she pounced on a loose puck in front of the net, then Leslie ripped a wrist shot past Peslarova on the power play at 4:12.

Kaltounková scored on a net-front scramble to cut the deficit at 11:01, but Fast restored Canada's two-goal lead with a point shot at four-on-four play before the period finished.

"I didn't think it'd be the game-winner," said Fast, Canada's captain for the game. "I thought we'd keep it at 3-1 or score more goals, but I'm happy that it found its way to the back of the net."

Kaltounková, who was selected first overall by the New York Sirens in the Professional Women's Hockey League 2025 draft, beat Gascon off a rebound five minutes into the third period for her second of the game.

The 24-year-old later took an elbowing penalty, putting Canada on the power play with 83 seconds remaining.

World.title: 15 United Conservative constituency presidents won't sign agreement to publicly back Alberta referendum result
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Presidents of 15 United Conservative Party constituency associations say they won’t sign a revised code of conduct requiring them to publicly respect and abide by the result of a provincial referendum on national unity.

In a letter obtained by CBC News, the locally elected constituency board presidents say they disagree the party has the authority to change the code of conduct without members voting on the change. Four of the people listed on the letter told CBC News the letter was authentic.

The presidents, who are from constituencies in Edmonton, Calgary and beyond, also say such a demand doesn’t belong in a code of conduct, and contradicts an existing code provision that protects their freedom of expression.

“I believe they've overstepped their boundaries, and really I wanted it just to go away,” said Robert Such, president of the UCP constituency association in Calgary-Klein, whose name is on the letter.

In an interview on Thursday, Such said he has a strong sense of western alienation and is glad Alberta held an October referendum on whether to hold a second, binding referendum on the province pursuing independence from Canada.

“I'm happy it's done,” he said. “Let's move on to bigger things. Some people just can't stop litigating this.”

Days after three-quarters of voters who cast ballots in the Oct. 19 referendum indicated they wanted Alberta to remain in Canada, Premier Danielle Smith said in a video message to fellow UCP members that anyone who publicly represents the party must abide by Alberta voters’ federalist wishes.

Smith said that would include any candidates running for the party, UCP board members and the presidents of constituency associations in the province’s 87 ridings.

Earlier this week, the party’s executive director sent all constituency association presidents a new non-disclosure agreement and code of conduct document to sign by Friday.

UCP spokesperson Dave Prisco told CBC in an emailed statement that the party is "going to work with people respectfully," but it expects UCP leadership to honour the party's position.

"The position of our party has not changed. We will respect and honour the referendum results, and a strong Alberta within a united Canada is our position. We expect anyone in a leadership role to uphold that. Our focus remains on the priorities of Albertans."

Demand conflicts with UCP’s ethos: political scientist

Such said he thinks there’s little the party can do, which is why he felt comfortable declining. If the party cancels memberships in response, “We’re just electing the NDP,” he said.

Such said he does not think the party is rife with members who will continue the push for independence from Canada. He said his Calgary constituency association is more concerned with finding a high-quality candidate that appeals to urban, federalist voters for Oct. 18, 2027, the fixed election date.

University of Calgary political science Prof. Lisa Young said she believes the party board’s requirement for local leaders to back the referendum result conflicts with the UCP’s culture.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks to party faithful at the United Conservative Party annual general meeting in Calgary, Saturday, Nov. 4, 2023. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

“It’s a party that very much values the idea of bottom-up, grassroots influence on government, on the party leader,” she said in an interview.

To introduce such a rule, the party could ask members to vote on a motion at its upcoming annual general meeting in Calgary, starting Nov. 27, Young said. However, she noted leaders may be afraid members won’t support it.

She said it’s possible the annual general meeting will be a “fractious event” instead of the type of cohesive gathering one might expect before a provincial election.

“I think you're going to see a lot of mobilization from the floor trying to push back against this sort of new top-down set of rules from the party leadership,” Young said. “Who will win coming out of a contest like that?”

Even if an attempt at forcing a unity message from party representatives leads members to leave the party — or be forced out — Young doesn’t think it’ll be a huge setback.

Elections Alberta figures show the UCP has so far raised $5.2 million in donations for the first three quarters of 2026, and this total may not include all constituency level contributions.

The Opposition Alberta NDP has reported nearly $3.6 million in contributions during the same period.

Young said she believes it's a bigger risk if a contingent of UCP members defect to another political party organized enough to garner votes, which could then split right-leaning voters.

“Smith is going to face a difficult election coming up,” Young said. “She's got to be thinking about that, because she's not doing particularly well in the polls while she's also fighting on another front with her own party.”

World.title: Richard Neil found guilty in 1990s 'woodland rapist' cold case
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story contains details of sexual assault against children.

A three-decade search for a predator dubbed southern Ontario's "woodland rapist" has ended with a Toronto man convicted of kidnapping and sexual assault.

A jury at the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Brampton on Friday found Richard Neil guilty of a total of 17 offences in connection with three brutal attacks on children in public parks in 1992, 1994 and 1995.

Two boys, aged 8 and 10, and a 15-year-old girl each told police they'd been lured into wooded areas, tied up and raped by a stranger. The victims all said they'd been forced to drink the assailant's urine.

Once DNA evidence showed the same unknown suspect had carried out all three attacks in the Ontario communities of Kitchener, Brampton and Oakville, police launched an urgent search to identify the man and catch him.

Nearly 30 years went by without a significant break in the case — until advances in forensic technology led to Neil's arrest in 2024.

Richard Neil leaves a Brampton, Ont., courthouse on Oct. 16. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

At the time, police announced there may be more victims.

The 67-year-old Neil, a British-born former Canada Post and UPS driver, had homes in Toronto and Victoria, B.C.

The divorced father of three insisted he wasn't involved in the 1990s assaults. But the evidence — including DNA, fingerprints and Neil's interest in urine-drinking — was hard to dispute.

It took the jury less than four hours of deliberation to unanimously accept the Crown's version of events.

Neil will be sentenced at a later date.

"There's some relief of course, mixed with a little bit of disappointment that we couldn't catch him at the time," retired Halton Regional Police Det. Sgt. Graham Barnes told CBC News.

A Halton Regional police officer is seen in 1995 holding a composite sketch of the then-unknown child sex predator dubbed the 'woodland rapist.' (CBC)

Longtime cold case

The case long baffled investigators from the Peel, Halton and Waterloo regions, who formed the Project Woodland task force in 1995. As the manhunt made headlines at the time, the media labelled the unidentified attacker the "woodland rapist," given his pattern of violence.

A composite sketch of a man — based on descriptions provided by the victims — was distributed to law enforcement agencies across the province and nearby U.S. states.

Officers canvassed Oakville neighbourhoods nightly in 1995 and reportedly received more than 1,300 tips over the years. Neil's trial heard that the Centre of Forensic Sciences in Toronto had looked at 310 persons of interest in total — to no avail.

At one point, Barnes, the former lead detective said he even hired a Texas-based firm to see if a Russian satellite had captured an image of a licence plate on an SUV linked to the attacker.

WATCH | DNA on underwear worn as a mask helped identify Neil: DNA on underwear worn as mask helped identify alleged child rapist | Duration closed caption 1:58 Warning: Story contains details of sexual assaults against children | 31 years after a teen girl was forced into the woods and attacked in an Oakville, Ont., park, a jury has been shown underwear worn as the assailant’s mask. A forensic scientist testified that DNA on the underwear matched the accused, Richard Neil, who is on trial for a series of sexual assaults against children in the 1990s.

By 1999, police speculated the assailant could be dead.

But Crown attorney Shazin Karim told the jury police finally identified Neil as a suspect in recent years thanks to genetic genealogy analysis conducted in the U.S.

The investigative technique — which involves comparing crime scene DNA to genetic data voluntarily submitted to direct-to-consumer genealogical services — was unavailable to police in the 1990s.

One of the victims previously told CBC News that according to investigators, the breakthrough was made possible after one of Neil's relatives submitted their DNA to an ancestry-type website.

The victim, who was 10 when he was assaulted in Brampton's Norton Place Park in 1994, said he was "shaking" when he was told of Neil's arrest.

"I felt overwhelmed with joy, then sadness," he said, "as I started to recall the memories of that day."

In September 1994, Peel Regional Police said a boy was walking through Brampton's Norton Place Park when he was approached by a suspect and lured to a nearby wooded area, where he was sexually assaulted. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Neil's trial before Justice Rosemarie Juginovic began in early October. The jury heard contemporaneous police interviews of the three victims, who were not required to testify. Their identities are covered by a court-ordered publication ban.

Three horrific attacks

The unsolved attacks on children sent shockwaves through southern Ontario communities in the 1990s.

On Aug. 21, 1992, an eight-year-old boy told police he'd been approached by a man offering to show him a collection of bikes in a wooded area of Kitchener's Idlewood Park. The man later pulled out a pocket knife and tied the boy's foot to a tree before sexually assaulting him.

On Sept. 29, 1994, the 10-year-old boy reported a similar attack in the Brampton park. He said he was forced to drink urine from a bottle and perform sex acts on the man.

The jury in the trial of Richard Neil was shown this image of a two-litre pop bottle recovered from the scene of a brutal attack on a 15-year-old girl at Wildwood Park in Oakville, Ont., on Aug. 31, 1995. The girl told police the unknown assailant forced her to drink urine from the bottle. (Ontario Superior Court of Justice)

Then, on Aug. 31, 1995, a 15-year-old girl recounted another violent incident with further similarities, including the use of a bottle for urine-drinking. The court heard she was held at gunpoint and also made to snort cocaine.

Prosecutors said forensic analysis showed it's "20 quadrillion times more likely" that DNA collected at the three crime scenes belonged to Neil, rather than another, random person.

The jury was told Neil's fingerprints matched those lifted from two shopping bags and a two-litre pop bottle located at Wildwood Park in Oakville, where the girl was assaulted.

What's more, Karim, the Crown attorney, said images, videos and messages seized from Neil's electronic devices demonstrated he has "an interest in urine-drinking."

Neil acknowledged having a "simple fetish" for urine, insisting "it's actually quite common." He said he had only "engaged in that act" with consenting adults.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.
