De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: International News Briefs for Friday, November 13, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Friday, November 13, 2026.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen Will Challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate Majority Leader

Nov 13, 2026

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen said Thursday he will challenge New York’s Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader when Democrats retake control of both chambers of Congress in January. This follows historic gains for Democrats in last week’s midterm elections. They’ll now control at least 255 seats in the House of Representatives and 55 in the Senate. This is Senator Van Hollen speaking on MS NOW.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen: “And it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption and his wars and his cruelty. It was also about a call for a larger change to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people and that’s fueled by a corrupt political system. And the call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual. And to do that, I think we need new leadership.”

Van Hollen is the first Democratic senator to launch a leadership challenge since 1994. His bid was quickly endorsed by Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Vermont independent Senator Bernie Sanders.

Youth Climate Activists Protest in Chuck Schumer’s Office to Demand New Senate Leadership

Nov 13, 2026

Image Credit: Sunrise Movement

More than 50 young activists with the Sunrise Movement were arrested Thursday after hundreds of protesters staged a sit-in inside Senator Chuck Schumer’s Washington, D.C., office. Activists are pushing for new Democratic leadership in the Senate after nearly a decade under Schumer. They also want Democrats to abolish the Senate filibuster. Children also participated in the action Thursday as many of the protesters held signs that read “The filibuster kills,” “Stop the climate crisis,” and “Schumer: Step up or step aside.”

Sunrise Movement activist 1: “Chuck Schumer and establishment Democrats are more scared of the voices of young people than of the climate crisis.”

Grace: “The American public is tired of the same old politics, and we’re ready for real change.”

Sunrise Movement activist 2: “Chuck Schumer would rather listen to billionaires than young people.”

Sunrise Movement activist 3: “Chuck Schumer doesn’t listen to us. He listens to corporate money, specifically coming from AIPAC. Over $400,000 have been invested into him.”

Jamie: “I chose to do this because when I was in high school, I saw the places I love burn to the ground because of the climate crisis. As I’ve grown older, I’ve seen American tax dollars go to burning and bombing Gaza.”

Grace: “I think everybody, including young people the most, can see the writing on the wall at this point, right? And we’re all saying the ship needs to be going in this direction.”

Nvidia’s Colette Kress to Serve as Interim CEO as Jensen Huang Resigns Amid Scandals

Nov 13, 2026

Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned. The chip maker says its longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO while Nvidia’s board of directors searches for a permanent replacement. Huang stepped down as Reuters reported he’d had an intimate relationship with a second employee, whom Reuters did not name. That follows reports that Huang had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence officials claim was spying for Beijing as part of a Chinese intelligence operation seeking to acquire advanced computer chips, which are banned by U.S. export controls. Huang reportedly helped the alleged spy acquire at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips for China via a Singapore-based cloud computing company called Megaspeed International. Meanwhile, Bloomberg reports Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before House lawmakers in a closed-door hearing later this month. Nvidia has lost nearly $2 trillion in market capitalization since its all-time high in early October. We’ll have more on this story after headlines.

Microsoft Outage Disrupts Communications for Millions Across 74 Countries

Nov 13, 2026

In more technology news, Microsoft is scrambling to fix a major outage that’s disrupted communication for millions of people across at least 74 countries since Thursday morning. The outage has cut off access to Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and the AI assistant Copilot.

Iran Says It Blew Up U.S. Early-Warning Radar as Trump Declares, “We Don’t Need a Deal with Iran”

Nov 13, 2026

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it destroyed a U.S. early-warning radar system in Bahrain in retaliation for a U.S. strike on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran. Officials also claimed four attacks on oil tankers in ​the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, following strikes on a pair of supertankers one day earlier.

Iran’s attacks came as President Trump on Thursday sidelined Vice President JD Vance as the top U.S. negotiator with Iran. Trump said in a social media post he’d directed Vance to instead focus on fighting what Trump called “corruption and crime” in Democratic-controlled cities and states. Trump wrote, “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

Houthis Claim Fresh Attacks on Saudi Oil Facilities Including East-West Pipeline

Nov 13, 2026

Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement, known as the Houthis, has claimed fresh attacks on oil infrastructure and an air base in Saudi Arabia. A Houthi spokesperson said targets included the Yanbu oil facility on the Red Sea, an Aramco facility in Riyadh and a pumping station on the East-West Pipeline, which is Saudi Arabia’s main route for shipping oil past Iran’s blockade on the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, the Arab League warned Thursday that a Houthi siege of the southwestern Yemeni city of Taiz is leading to a humanitarian disaster, with “acute shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicines and medical supplies.”

Russia and Ukraine Continue Deadly Strikes as U.S. Envoys Meet Putin and Zelensky

Nov 13, 2026

Russia and Ukraine traded drone and missile attacks overnight, despite a diplomatic push by the Trump administration that’s purportedly seeking an end to the conflict. The violence came after President Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, followed by a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin. Both Russia and Ukraine agreed to a prisoner swap that Zelensky called the largest since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Meanwhile, Zelensky has accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of once again restricting service to Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink internet satellite constellation, which Ukraine uses for drone attacks.

Infant Dies of Hypothermia in Gaza as Calls Grow for Israel to Allow Imports of Winter Supplies

Nov 13, 2026

Image Credit: Deutsche Presse-Agentur GmbH

In Gaza, a Palestinian infant has died from hypothermia after Israeli attacks left his family displaced and living in a tent in Khan Younis. Kinan Ahmed Raqiq was just 9 months old. His death came as Israel continued to impose severe restrictions on imports of fuel and winter supplies into Gaza. U.N. humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher says 150,000 tents remain stuck in warehouses at Gaza’s borders, even as some 350,000 displaced Palestinians face heavy rain, flooding and plummeting temperatures. On Thursday, a group of 49 nations issued a joint call for Israel to ease restrictions on shelter, fuel, water, sanitation and medical supplies to Gaza. The United States did not sign the statement. This is Britain’s ambassador to the U.N., Sarah MacIntosh, speaking from U.N. headquarters.

Sarah MacIntosh: “As winter sets in, far too many people in Gaza are still without adequate shelter and risk exposure to hypothermia, respiratory infections, waterborne diseases and other preventable illnesses. Constraints on the entry of critical shelter items and other life-saving supplies continue to prevent humanitarian organizations from responding at the scale required.”

In more news from Gaza, a Palestinian was killed by Israeli gunfire east of Gaza City earlier today. That followed an Israeli strike on a car near the gate of Al-Shifa Hospital which killed one person and left several others critically wounded. That attack came as Palestinians in Khan Younis held funerals for a ​surgeon, a teenage boy and four other Palestinians killed when an Israeli airstrike targeted southern Gaza’s Nasser Hospital complex. We’ll have more on that attack, and the latest from Gaza, later in the broadcast.

ICE Detention of USF Professor Draws Protests and Demands for Her Release

Nov 13, 2026

Image Credit: University of San Francisco

In California, community members are demanding the release of beloved nurse and University of San Francisco professor Ann Lawani, who was detained by ICE nearly two months ago. Lawani is originally from Nigeria and has lived in the U.S. since 2007. She was reportedly at home in Lodi, still wearing her pajamas, when ICE agents showed up at her door in early September, taking her to a local holding facility. Then she disappeared from ICE’s database for three days, with her older brother telling The New York Times, “It was the worst time of my life, knowing she had been siphoned into an abyss and there was nothing I could do about it.” Lawani is now being detained thousands of miles away at an ICE jail in Basile, Louisiana.

Protesters in San Diego Demand ICE Release 8-Year-Old Haitian Boy to Relatives

Nov 13, 2026

Hundreds of protesters, including teachers and elected officials, rallied outside San Diego’s federal building Thursday, calling for an 8-year-old Haitian boy to be reunited with his relatives. He was taken into federal immigration custody after a check-in last week. The boy is a third grader at a local elementary school. His family and advocates say they do not know his whereabouts.

23 Immigrants Died of Medical Neglect in ICE Custody in First Year of Trump’s Second Term

Nov 13, 2026

Image Credit: GEO Group

Nearly two dozen immigrants died in the custody of ICE during the first year of President Trump’s second term due to medical neglect. That’s according to findings by the San Francisco Chronicle, which obtained internal ICE investigations into the 29 deaths that occurred in 2025. ICE’s own documents admit immigration jails failed to provide emergency medical care. In some cases, ICE jail staff even mocked or ignored people who requested help and who later died.

At least 62 immigrants have died in ICE custody since Trump’s return to office. In response to the abuse, immigrants jailed across the nation have staged hunger strikes and other peaceful actions. This week, the publication L.A. Taco reported at least 24 people detained at the Adelanto ICE jail in California’s Mojave Desert started another hunger strike — the second so far this year. Meanwhile, another hunger strike at the Northwest ICE jail in Tacoma, Washington, is also ongoing. Hunger strikers at both facilities have reportedly faced threats, including being transferred to other ICE jails across the country. Both Adelanto and Northwest are operated by the for-profit prison company GEO Group.

NYC Mayor Mamdani Orders Inspections at 100 Sites After Deadly Building Collapse in Brooklyn

Nov 13, 2026

Here in New York, tenant advocates are demanding justice after what they described as the preventable collapse of an apartment building in Brooklyn that killed at least eight people, including two children, and injured at least 23 others Wednesday. Among the victims were two construction workers from Ecuador and Guatemala; a food delivery worker and Amazon worker, who were relatives from Guinea in West Africa; and two young cousins from Colombia.

The publication amNewYork reports the collapse may have been caused by corner-cutting by subcontractors and developers working on an adjacent construction site where crews were digging a pit for a new massive, multi-story development. In the wake of the collapse, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said five contractors and developers connected to the disaster are associated with about 100 other sites across New York, and that the Department of Buildings would immediately begin inspecting those sites.

The executive director of NYS Tenant Bloc, Sumathy Kumar, said in a statement that the tragedy “stresses the urgency of taking buildings out of the hands of bad landlords who are looking to make quick profits at the expense of people’s safety” and “highlights the need for dignified, high quality housing built with union labor, which is why we are fighting for social housing across the city and state.”

Read more news here on Havana Times.

World.title: I Had Fun Killing My Protagonists!
World.content:
When Christopher Columbus landed on Cuba’s northeastern coast in 1492, it was probably near Gibara, where I took this photo.

By Jenny Cressman

HAVANA TIMES – In my first three diary columns, I did a lot of reminiscing about my early trips to Cuba. Now, however, I think it’s time for something different. Since I concluded my last column with comments about reincarnation, I’ll start there.

The short stories in my latest book, Kat of Nine, are linked by reincarnation, although that isn’t revealed until the fourth story in the nine-tale collection. As I began writing these stories, I did not initially intend to link them. In fact, I hadn’t even planned on writing a collection! It was just an interesting activity to occupy me during COVID.

I wrote the first story because I’d read a lot about Cuban history and one thought kept rumbling around in my mind: What would native inhabitants of the island have thought when they witnessed Christopher Columbus arrive? I’ve ruminated on this in other books and articles I’ve written but, this time, I decided to delve into the concept more fully. And, because it was the time of COVID, I had time to ride that train of thought.

Since I’d written a trio of romance-adventure novels from the perspective of the protagonist, it seemed natural to write in the first-person narrative style again. I put myself in the head of a young woman watching from shore as Columbus’ trio of ships sail into view. The first paragraph in her story summarizes her recollections. Then, the story shifts to present tense, as she experiences the initial arrival of Spanish sailors.

From there, her tale leaps forward to key moments that occurred at later times in her life. Eventually, she meets Hatuey, an iconic figure in Cuban history; his story always intrigued me! The end of the story is, essentially, her end. This scene is set soon after the protagonist witnesses Hatuey being burned.

Because the stories are linked by reincarnation, I don’t think I need to declare a “spoiler alert” when I point out that all but the last protagonist had to die. In writing these short stories, I enjoyed the challenge of finding different ways to kill off my beloved characters! But, I must admit, I cried as I wrote about the demise of each Kat of Nine heroine.

When I read excerpts at book events, I sometimes provide “trigger warnings” regarding violent incidents. I don’t like violence but, in this case, my desire for authenticity superseded my own way of living. Cuba’s past was not a pony ride through the park. Spanish conquistadors were brutal, as were many who came later in the island’s centuries of domination.

I commissioned Cuban artists to provide illustrations for each of the stories in Kat of Nine. This dramatic piece by Manuel Olivera Alvarez (MOA), is aptly entitled “The Conquest.”

But, let’s get back to “1492,” the first story in Kat of Nine. Here’s an excerpt:

…My memory of that day, that time, is a little jumbled. I was just a girl then; now, I am a woman. I recall feeling anxious and excited as we gathered on the beach and watched the ships approaching. Their white sails flapped like the wings of a bird that is settling to roost for the night. We waited impatiently. Finally, a small boat was dropped from one of the big boats and we could see movement, black shapes against the sun.

The small boat began to come toward the shore. When it arrived on the sand, amid the waves, some men from our group ran forward to help them. Together, their men and ours dragged the boat up onto the beach so that their leader would not get wet when he stepped out. We could tell immediately who their leader was. Even if he had not been wearing a big hat and a coat with shiny buttons, we would have been able to tell. He had the bearing of someone in charge. He waved his hand to command action and his men jumped.

Our leader did not have a fancy hat and did not behave like that, but he stood tall when he stepped forward to greet these peculiar people. He calmly spoke our customary words of welcome. I don’t remember exactly what was said but I remember the feelings. Excitement fluttered in my chest. I was eager to get close and find out who these strangers were, where they came from and why they were here, but I was timid and nervous. I stayed back a little, off to one side, with some of the other young girls.

These men – there were no women – looked very different from us, and even smelled different. They had on many layers of clothing and I could tell they were hot. The beads of sweat popped out on their foreheads and slowly slid down their faces, causing their skin to glisten. They were not smiling. They looked very uncomfortable. Were they afraid of us? I had the impression they might be, at first. But, soon, I think they understood that we were not dangerous. We were just curious…

While our leader tried to communicate with theirs, the rest of us coyly looked each other over. We tried to be careful in our visual assessment because we did not want to cause offence, but one of my friends was a little more bold. She crept closer to a pair of men at the edge of their group who were sitting on a log, so I followed. When these men noticed us near them, they become interested. They sat up straighter and looked directly at us. But, they didn’t just look at our faces. Their eyes ran up and down our bodies. One said something to the other and licked his lips. I didn’t understand the words but I knew what he was thinking. I grabbed my friend’s arm and whispered that we should go back to our families now.

After those first men left, we did not see any big boats for a long time. We had not expected them to return….

The back cover of my book, Kat of Nine, gives you a brief summary of what the nine stories in this collection are about.

[Watch for my next column in approximately two weeks. If you like my writing here, you’ll probably enjoy Kat of Nine / Kat de Nueve – all text is in both English and Spanish. You can find it on Amazon or at locations in Muskoka, my ‘hood.]

Read more from the diary of Jenny Cressman here on Havana Times.

World.title: US Immigration Judge Denies Asylum to Stateless Nicaraguan
World.content:
Former political prisoner Jairo Lenin Centeno Ríos. Photo: Carmen Aguirres / Nicas Libres Ya

Javier Centeno, one of 222 Nicaraguan political prisoners banished to the US in 2023, was denied asylum on the basis of Ortega-Murillo’s bogus drug charges.

By 100% Noticias

HAVANA TIMES – On November 10, 2026, a US immigration judge denied Jairo Lenín Centeno Ríos the right to political asylum. Centeno was one of 222 political prisoners the Ortega regime exiled to the United States in February 2023 and subsequently stripped of their citizenship. Stateless, he now faces the threat of deportation back to Nicaragua or to a third, unknown, country.

The court’s decision was announced on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, during a hearing held via video call from the Folkston D. Ray Detention Center in Georgia, where Centeno remains in immigration custody. Javier now fears being sent back to the country where he was imprisoned and from which he was expelled.

Meanwhile, he remains in an ICE detention center, leaving his four minor children in Nicaragua without the financial support he provided them.

Decision the result of baseless drug charges filed in Nicaragua

The Nicaraguan, originally from León, claims that the decision was based on a drug trafficking conviction handed down in Nicaragua, even though a United Nations report declared his detention arbitrary.

In statements to the Nicaraguan newspaper LA PRENSA, on Wednesday, November 11, the former political prisoner explained that the judge rejected his request for protection, given the criminal record resulting from his imprisonment in Nicaragua. The judge termed him a danger to the United States due to the crimes for which he was convicted by Nicaraguan authorities, despite the attempts of his defense team to explain the circumstances of his imprisonment in Nicaragua and subsequent exile.

Centeno maintains that the Nicaraguan regime’s drug charges were bogus, used by the regime to politically persecute him. He is now in a state of uncertainty, as he has already received a deportation order that he has refused to sign, and is waiting for his attorney to file an appeal.

From Exiled Political Prisoner to ICE Detainee

Centeno was arrested by the Ortega regime on September 14, 2018, during the period of repression that followed the outbreak of massive anti-government protests. He was released on December 30, 2019, under the regime’s unilateral Amnesty Law, but was recaptured on February 26, 2020 in a manner the Nicas Libres Ya website termed: “arbitrarily and illegally, and without a warrant in a raid at his grandmother’s house.”

Centeno remained in a Nicaraguan prison until February 2023, when he was among the 222 political prisoners the Nicaraguan authorities released and transferred to the United States under an agreement with the Biden administration. Almost immediately afterwards the Ortega-Murillo regime ordered all members of that group to be stripped of their citizenship. Centeno, like many of the others, remains stateless.

Arrested and detained by ICE despite the conclusions of the UN Working Group

After arriving in the United States, Centeno tried to rebuild his life. He began working in the construction industry as a welder.

However, on July 27, 2026, he was once again arrested – this time by agents of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) while he was at a beach in Maryland, spending a day off with his partner, Conny Martinez. He was subsequently transferred to Georgia, where he remains in detention.

One of the most significant aspects of the case is that Centeno’s detention in Nicaragua was examined by the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention. In its Opinion 69/2023, adopted during the session held from November 13 to 17, 2023, the international body analyzed the situation of 23 individuals imprisoned in Nicaragua, including Jairo Lenín Centeno Ríos.

The document concluded that his detention was arbitrary and contrary to the guarantees recognized in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. In its analysis, the Working Group also identified serious violations of the guarantees to a fair trial in the case of Centeno and other individuals included in the opinion.

This conclusion constitutes a documented international precedent regarding the irregularities of his imprisonment in Nicaragua. Unfortunately, the United Nations’ ruling does not automatically lead to the granting of asylum in the United States. The immigration decision depends on a separate procedure, subject to US law, within a US political administration that has moved to deport as many immigrants as it can.

According to Centeno, his attorney presented to the judge both the political nature of his imprisonment and the fact that he was stripped of his nationality, but neither of these arguments were given the weight he had hoped for.

Detention leaves his Nicaraguan children without economic support

Beyond his immigration status, Centeno faces the anguish of being unable to financially support his four minor children, who remain in Nicaragua. Before his arrest, he worked as a welder in construction and, as he explained to LA PRENSA, was the children’s primary financial provider.

Since his arrest by ICE in July, he has stopped sending them money.

In the interview, he expressed concern about his children’s needs and the possibility of remaining in detention for a longer period. He is particularly concerned for how his Nicaraguan family can sustain the costs associated with their studies if he continues in detention. This is the dilemma of many in ICE detention: while he fights to obtain legal protection in the United States, he leaves his children without economic support.

Fears Being Sent to Nicaragua or to a Third African Country

According to a report published by LA PRENSA, on Tuesday, November 10, Centeno received a deportation order that calls for his return to Nicaragua or the possibility of sending him to a third country in Africa.

The former political prisoner stated that he has not signed the document because he fears the consequences of returning to Nicaragua, where he was imprisoned for reasons he considers political.

He also expressed his opposition to the possibility of being transferred to an African country, given the difficulties he already faced in adapting to a new life after several years of imprisonment.

His concern is compounded by the revocation of his Nicaraguan citizenship, a measure that has affected numerous opponents and critics of the Ortega-Murillo regime.

The existence of a deportation order does not necessarily mean that his expulsion has already been carried out or that the transfer will be immediate. The situation will depend on pending legal proceedings and the appeal decisions of immigration authorities.

In this case, Javier’s defense team will seek to overturn the court’s decision while he remains in custody in Georgia. He is currently seeking support from human rights organizations and bodies that could help resolve his situation.

Centeno’s situation raises questions about the legal options available to people who were expelled from their country, lost their nationality, and now face deportation proceedings in the United States. It also raises questions about whether convictions handed down by governments accused of political persecution should be considered valid evidence in immigration proceedings.

In Javier Centeno’s case, there is a United Nations ruling documenting the arbitrary nature of his imprisonment, but it is not yet publicly known whether that information was fully considered in the U.S. immigration decision.

The Nicaraguan reiterates that he did not arrive in the United States on his own initiative, but rather as part of a group of political prisoners transferred from Nicaragua in February 2023.

The fear of returning to Nicaragua, the uncertainty surrounding his immigration status, and concern for his four children are all part of a situation that, as he told LA PRENSA, has deeply affected him.

The outcome of his appeal will determine whether he can continue to seek protection in the United States or whether he will face new deportation proceedings.

Seven of the 222 Nicaraguan ex-prisoners revictimized by ICE

According to a September 18th article in the Nicaraguan news site Confidencial, seven of the group of 222 have been newly detained by ICE. One was released, one has been ordered deported to Ecuador, and – at the time of the article – the others, including Centeno, were awaiting resolution of their cases.

First published in Spanish by 100% Noticias and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Nicaragua here on Havana Times.

World.title: Cuban Regime Crackdown on Cell Phone Signal Boosters
World.content:
The use and importing of cellphone signal boosters is prohibited in Cuba.

By Yenys Laura Prieto (El Toque)

HAVANA TIMES – The Cuban government is calling for “citizen surveillance” of unauthorized equipment but offers no solutions to the island’s telecommunications network deficiencies.

In a post on its official Facebook page, Cuba’s Ministry of Communications urged residents to report the installation of cell phone signal boosters without legal authorization. The warning comes as thousands of users struggle with the state telecommunication monopoly Etecsa’s poor network coverage. Those who attempt to improve their reception on their own risk fines and confiscation of their equipment.

Government control also extends to satellite connections. According to the newspaper 14ymedio, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs sent a notice to diplomatic missions warning that they are prohibited from importing or using Starlink devices. The communication was reportedly addressed to foreign embassies and international organizations accredited in Havana.

Meanwhile, stepped-up repression continues. The arrest of a community activist sparked a neighborhood protest in Guamuta, part of the town of El Cobre in Santiago de Cuba. Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano had been distributing food to people in need. Following his detention, a group of women accompanied by their children took to the streets to demand his release. According to opposition activist Jose Daniel Ferrer, as of November 10, Yoel remained detained at the provincial headquarters of State Security in Santiago de Cuba.

Published in Spanish by El Toque and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.
