The investments are expected to improve the company’s ability to service hotel chains while supporting its growing retail distribution network. Alongside the capital expenditure, the company is investing in brand marketing and staff development, while reviewing its operating costs to improve efficiency.

“We look at every line item, and we see where it must add value to remain in our books,” Grant said.

Despite the disruption caused by Hurricane Melissa, Everything Fresh is anticipating improved business as hotel properties resume operations and demand strengthens ahead of the winter tourism season.

“Demand is exciting; we have concluded negotiations with RIU and increased volumes on that side in Jamaica,” Grant said.

He noted that some hotels that had been operating below capacity following the hurricane were gradually returning to normal operations, providing scope for increased business in the final quarter of 2026 and into 2027.

For its 2025 financial year, Everything Fresh reported revenue of $4.17 billion, an increase of $489.97 million, or 13.3 per cent, compared with the previous year. Jamaica accounted for the largest share of the increase, contributing $428.3 million, or approximately 87.4 per cent, to group revenue growth. Revenue from the Jamaican operation rose 14.8 per cent to $3.33 billion, up from $2.9 billion in 2024. The Bahamian operation contributed the remaining $61.7 million, representing approximately 12.6 per cent of the group’s revenue increase. Revenue from the territory rose eight per cent to $840 million, compared with approximately $770 million in the previous year.

Everything Fresh distributes meat, dairy products and fresh produce to customers across its markets.

World.title: BROADER SCOPE
World.content:
Arnett Gardens goalkeeper Alesha Robinson (left) and Sara Needham of Los Perfectos vie for the ball during the Jamaica Women’s Premier League first-leg semi-final match at UWI Mona Bowl on May 16, 2026. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Despite the imminent introduction of relegation and promotion in the Jamaica Women’s Premier League (JWPL), Professional Women’s Football Jamaica Limited (PWFJL) Chairperson Christina Hudson believes the move will significantly raise the standard of the competition and strengthen women’s football locally.

The JWPL has operated without a promotion and relegation system since 2008, instead using a league and play-off format. However, the limited number of clubs with active women’s teams has resulted in changes to the competition, with clubs entering or withdrawing depending on their circumstances.

That is expected to change with the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) planning to introduce a National Women’s Tier Two competition next year which would see the return of a second division in women’s football for the first time in nearly two decades, since the former Women’s ‘A’ League.

The Jamaica Observer has learnt that the plan has been in development for several months, with a host of teams expressing interest in joining the competition and ultimately earning promotion to the JWPL. An early 2027 start date has been proposed and would end before the completion of the 2026/2027 JWPL season.

A reliable source told the Observer that Waterhouse FC, three-time JWPL champions who did not return to the competition in 2023 following the COVID-19 pandemic, Montego Bay United and Tru-Juice FC are among six or seven clubs expected to participate in the Tier Two competition. All three clubs also field teams in the men’s Jamaica Premier League.

The Observer has learnt that a club from St Ann, separate from Mount Pleasant Football Academy, is also interested in joining the competition.

When contacted, JFF President Michael Ricketts didn’t confirm the exact details but told the

Observer that the federation is leaning towards a 2027 start date following further consultations with relevant stakeholders.

“It depends on how serious these teams are and even a shortened version would serve the programme well, so definitely we’ll be looking at that and we’ll make an announcement in that regard soon,” he said.

“We will need to look at those teams that would have given an indication that they want to play football and once you meet with them and they are serious, then we could very well have this Tier 2 but we are super excited.”

Hudson believes the planned introduction of the Tier Two reflects the growth of the JWPL, which has been managed by the PWFJL for the past two seasons.

“I think that this is super exciting [and] I think that shows the power of what we have been doing,” she told the Observer.

“So for the very first time this season, the top two winners of the Tier Two will be promoted to the Jamaican Women’s Premier League and the bottom two of the Jamaican Women’s Premier League will be relegated to Tier Two.”

Although relegation could present a challenge for clubs in the revamped JWPL, Hudson believes the introduction of the system will raise the competitiveness and commercial appeal of women’s football.

“I think it can only benefit the quality of the football that we’re seeing. All of the benefits that the Jamaican Women’s Premier League gives or builds out in each season for our clubs is something that is renewed season to season,” she said. “So the clubs get to benefit from being a part of the league for that season and then a new club that comes along will also benefit in their new season, so I don’t think that there’s any downside to the relegation and promotion system.”

“People have been saying that the bottom half of our league is not overly competitive. So now that clubs have this goal that if you’re not making it in the top, you might lose your spot. I think it’s definitely going to push teams at the bottom half of the table to want to improve the quality of the football that they’re playing so that can only help us because obviously the more exciting football and the better quality football that we’re seeing on the pitch, the more people will want to come out and watch the games.”

The JWPL is set to kick off next month with 12 teams including Frazsiers Whip who will be looking to defend their title for a fourth straight year.

World.title: Why Europe failed to find a superhero to take on Putin
World.content:
The push to identify one representative to speak for Europe was understandable. The appeal of having a single, respected leader taking the reins is largely based on a desire to project European strength and unity — as well as an interest in making negotiations with Russia, the U.S. and Ukraine efficient and effective.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy himself said this week he wanted Europe to identify within days who will take its place in the talks, and suggested he’d prefer it was one person (he even indicated that he had a preference, though would not reveal a name).



He didn’t get his way. Instead, leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, decided that the “E5” made up four big EU countries ― Germany, France, Poland and Italy ― and the U.K., plus officials from the European Commission and Council, would take the work forward as a team.

Technical discussions

The search for a top representative to fill Europe’s seat at the negotiating table at the next round of peace talks had become a political obsession in Brussels that missed at least two big points.

The first is that the leadership level is not currently where the negotiations are at. Talks this week in Abu Dhabi were technical discussions between senior officials. The big political players like Putin and Zelenskyy were not there, never mind Trump. Russia sent a Kremlin aide to lead its team and Ukraine tasked its intelligence chief with making its case.

If these officials make progress toward a deal, leaders will no doubt want to get involved. Ultimately, it will be leaders who sign any peace agreements that follow — and there’s no limit on the number of EU presidents or prime ministers who could join such a meeting as signatories or guarantors of the final deal.

The next thing that needs to happen, according to both Ukraine and the U.S. envoys mediating the talks, is for Europe to join the discussion with Russia — at this technical level.

World.title: Le Pen offers to meet Zelenskyy in Brussels
World.content:
Marine Le Pen delivers a speech during a visit of the "Salon Made in France" at Parc des Expositions of Porte de Versailles, in Paris on November 13, 2026. | Geoffroy van der Hasselt/ AFP via Getty Images

The Ukrainian leader wants to persuade the far-right leader to continue supporting Ukraine if she becomes president of France.

PARIS — Far-right leader Marine Le Pen said she would be prepared to hold talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Brussels, in the wake of her promises to stop French financial aid to Ukraine.

Speaking on the sidelines of a trade fair in Paris, Le Pen said a meeting in Brussels would be “justified” because “the topic of Ukraine financing is rattling Europe.”

“The German chancellor is starting to threaten people, it’s starting to be an issue in Europe and it would be interesting to discuss this,” she said in a reference to Friedrich Merz’s threats to cut EU funds for countries who refuse to support Ukraine financially.

World.title: Microsoft outage renews European calls to detox from US tech
World.content:
Mensch didn't specifically address the Microsoft outage, which lasted nearly 24 hours and affected millions of users in 74 countries. Still, the shutdown of key tools like Outlook email and Teams messaging impacted plenty of the tech and government leaders gathered in Dublin to chart Europe’s AI future.

French President Emmanuel Macron closed the day with a post on X: “Our independence cannot be outsourced. It must be built here at home, in Europe,” he wrote. "When it comes to artificial intelligence, too, Europe has everything it takes to compete. We have no time to lose.”

An EU diplomat present at the leaders' talks said that "we need to pick up speed, permitting and investment to compete on the world market, to have sovereignty."

Tech sovereignty, including control over the cloud, chips and models that power AI, has been a rallying cry of the second mandate of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and was one of the key agenda items at Friday's gathering of the leaders of the EU's 27 member countries.

"We have outsourced too much of our digital infrastructure to actors outside the EU," Finnish European Parliament lawmaker Aura Salla said in a press release Friday following the outage. She suggested that government contracts specifically "must support European technology."

Others zoned in on the risk created by relying on digital infrastructure controlled by a couple of large companies.

World.title: Ex-Labour MP accused of sexual harassment joins Plaid Cymru
World.content:
In 2023, five women alleged that Davies, a former Commons select committee chair, subjected them to unwanted sexual attention, both physical and verbal, after coming into contact with them through his work as an MP. Davies had the whip suspended as a Labour MP immediately after the allegations were made public but remained a member of the party until 2025.

When the claims against Davies were first reported by POLITICO, he said he did not “recognize” them, adding: “If I have inadvertently caused offence to anyone, then I am naturally sorry.”

In these instances, the women had raised concerns about his behavior informally but had not complained in writing.

At least two women later filed official complaints with the Labour Party, resulting in an investigation lasting more than a year.

Davies was not eligible to stand as a candidate in the 2024 election because he was suspended, and quit the party ahead of a planned hearing on his conduct in 2025. As a result, the hearing never went ahead.

The former MP for Swansea West argued in the article published Thursday that the party engineered his removal as a candidate for factional reasons. “I was made to wait 23 weeks without any complaints. When complaints were made, they were ‘to support other women’ who had not made any complaints. None were reported to Parliament,” he said.

World.title: EU countries to announce deportation hub deal with Rwanda
World.content:
The countries previously confirmed that they aim to close the first deals to set up the off-shore centers in 2026, with plans to make them operational as of next year.

The deportation hub in Rwanda would function as a pilot project and deals with other countries and involving other EU countries are likely to follow.

A recent reform of EU rules made it possible for EU members to cut deals to set up such deportation hubs with other countries on the condition that they meet international human rights standards.

Specifics of the scheme, including the nationalities of the people that would be moved to the hubs, their living conditions there and oversight of the deal, all depend on the agreement countries cut.

But human rights groups have warned that the hubs risk opening the door to human rights abuses, far removed from EU oversight or recourse.

Plans by the Conservative British government plans to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda were slapped down by the U.K. Supreme Court in 2023, which ruled the scheme unlawful. After coming into power in 2024, the Labour government shelved the plans, with then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer calling the Rwanda plan “dead and buried.”

The U.K. had aimed to move people to Rwanda to process their applications remotely, whereas the incoming deal of the EU countries would target people who have been ordered to leave the bloc’s territory.

Seb Starcevic contributed to this report.

World.title: What Vladimir Putin won in Abu Dhabi Ukraine peace talks
World.content:
The ambitious aim apparently now agreed between Washington and Moscow is to discuss all the issues together. And then to “find a pathway to settle them all at the same time,” Jared Kushner explained to reporters in a post-talks briefing in the UAE’s capital. Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, was representing the U.S. in the talks, along with Steve Witkoff, a real estate investor who is Trump’s special envoy to the Middle East.

So much for sequencing — generally seen by experienced diplomatic negotiators as crucial to any successful peace talks. And so much, too, for starting with a ceasefire or the tiresome breaking down of complex issues into discrete and manageable tasks to try to move things along while raising confidence and inspiring trust.

To be sure, Russia and the United States won’t be able to strike a deal on their own. Ukraine will get a say, and European leaders have already pushed back against Trump’s big, beautiful deal, rejecting any attempt by the White House and the Kremlin to reshape the continent’s security architecture.

Russia’s Foreign Affairs’ Minister Sergei Lavrov delivers a press-conference following the Collective Security Treaty Organization meeting in Moscow on November 10, 2026. | Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images

But it has been a longstanding Kremlin goal to get the U.S. to agree to the “let’s talk about everything” strategy, a process that will succeed in “diverting attention from what really is the critical issue, and that’s the war on Ukraine,” said Eugene Rumer, who served on the U.S. National Intelligence Council under President Barack Obama.

Rumer told reporters in a briefing that the lack of sequencing speaks volumes and is a hallmark of Russian diplomacy which aims at “muddling any situation.”

It’s difficult to quibble with his pessimism. Russian President Vladimir Putin has a long track record of using peace talks to delay, obfuscate and exhaust opponents as he continues doing whatever he wants — all the while insisting that everything is interconnected and must be solved all at the same time.

World.title: Whitehall to increase face-to-face job interviews after surge in AI applications
World.content:
In the most extreme cases, entire applications — even virtual interviews — appeared to have been generated by bots and not human beings, the official added.

There is at least one case in which civil servants became so suspicious during a virtual video call that the candidate was not a real person that they terminated the interview early.

The official said the civil service plans to move away from personal statements — and for flagship recruitment schemes, leaders are looking at reintroducing compulsory face-to-face interviews.

Fewer personal statements

The changes are likely to form part of a wider review of Whitehall which Romeo is due to deliver to Prime Minister Andy Burnham by summer 2027.

Romeo said in her annual lecture on Tuesday that she planned to “strip back and simplify” Whitehall recruitment to attract the most talented people from all backgrounds, adding she wanted to end “formulaic job ads, generic interviews and slow processes.”

This includes scrapping “success profiles,” a core feature of the civil service’s bureaucratic recruitment process. A new selection framework is due to be launched from April 2027.

World.title: EU institutions survive Microsoft outage unscathed
World.content:
Microsoft on Friday morning said recovery was still uneven. "At this time, we have no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident. We will continue to treat this with urgency until full mitigation," it said.

At the European Commission “the impact ... is very limited and does not affect our operations,” spokesperson Thomas Regnier told POLITICO. He said the outage had a “minor impact on a limited number of applications, such as the slowness of SharePoint.” Outlook and Teams were “fully operational,” Regnier said.

The Council of the EU, which gathers representatives of national governments, also carried on work: Outlook and Teams were “working on our side,” a Council official told POLITICO, declining to give more details on the institution’s IT setup.

The Parliament's press service said in a statement to POLITICO that it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation as a precaution.

The outage is exposing the reliance of companies and governments on Microsoft services — an issue that has also been a longstanding concern in Europe among proponents of keeping more control over IT and digital infrastructure.

In October last year, a similar outage of Amazon Web Services servers prompted immediate calls for Europe to boost its tech sovereignty.

World.title: Russia sends major business delegation to Kabul for business talks with the Taliban
World.content:
Russian deputy prime minister Alexei Overchuk was welcomed by a guard of honour when he arrived in Kabul on Thursday with a delegation of 70 Russian business people to conduct business talks with the Taliban government, Afghan officials said.

 

Overchuk met Taliban prime minister Mohammad Hassan Akhund, the deputy prime minister for economic affairs Abdul Ghani Baradar as well as foreign minister Amir Khan Muttaqi.

According to a statement by the Afghan government published on X, Abdul Ghani Baradar described to the Russians Afghanistan's potential for economic development and investment, pointing to "strategic location, abundant resources and a workforce of 24 million people".

Abdul Ghani Baradar invited Russian companies to invest in agriculture, mining, constructions of roads, railways and factories, and to create a special economic zone in Afghanistan, while expressing his wish to expand exports of Afghan agricultural products to Russia.

The deputy prime minister also asked Russia to "provide the necessary facilities for Afghan products to be supplied to Russian markets and to cooperate in reducing transport and transit costs".

A Russian news agency quoted Alexei Overchuk as saying that the Russian delegation represent companies that are already operating in Afghanistan and that "many others want to start operating in this country."

Overchuk said that the companies represented in the delegation work in the fields of transport, logistics, agriculture and pharmaceuticals and that the Afghan government is interested in Russian chemical fertilisers, as well as in "building fertiliser production plants on Afghan soil".

Overchuk estimated that trade between Russia and Afghanistan in the first eight months of 2026 had more than doubled, reaching over 349 million dollars.

Russia officially recognised the Taliban government in July 2025, being the only state to have taken such a step since the Taliban seized power in August 2021, after the withdrawal of the United States.

Although no country other than Russia has formally recognised the new Afghan regime, the Taliban authorities have so far held high-level talks with many states and have established specific diplomatic and economic relations with some governments.

World.title: France and Germany near deal on De Cos for ECB top job as EU confirms two candidates
World.content:
Two candidates have been put forward to replace Christine Lagarde at the helm of the European Central Bank, an EU official said on Friday, as EU leaders gathered in Dublin for an informal summit.

 

Spanish daily El País also reported that France and Germany were finalising a deal on the central bank's top jobs, with Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos as the favourite to become the next president.

The official did not name the two candidates, but as Euronews previously reported, the contenders are Pablo Hernández de Cos and former Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot.

The Eurogroup confirmed both nominations last week.

European Council President António Costa updated leaders on Friday morning and aims to begin consulting the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council at the EU summit on 26 November, the official said.

A new deadline of 18 November has been set for nominations to fill the other two vacancies on the central bank’s six-member Executive Board, which runs the ECB day to day. The posts are chief economist and head of market operations, both significant roles in the leadership.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron are currently in "intensive" talks to negotiate the candidates.

In Dublin, Merz told reporters that agreements were in sight but not yet final, and that he needed a few more days to consult his coalition partners before presenting Germany's proposal next week.

Who gets what

France leans towards Hernández de Cos, a former Bank of Spain governor whose more moderate stance on monetary policy suits a country under fiscal strain, El País reported.

He would be the first Spanish economist to lead the ECB.

Spain's Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo told Euronews on Monday that Hernández de Cos' expertise and ability to build consensus made him an ideal candidate.

The proposed deal would give Berlin the chief economist post and Paris the seat of Germany's Isabel Schnabel, who is in charge of market operations, German business daily Handelsblatt reported.

Merz's office wants Princeton University economist Markus Brunnermeier for the role, which is seen as the ECB's second most important job, the newspaper reported.

Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks during a press conference at the EU Summit in Dublin, 13 November 2026 AP Photo/Virginia Mayo

He would be the first German chief economist since Jürgen Stark left at the end of 2011, replacing Ireland's Philip Lane, whose term ends in May.

If Knot won the presidency instead, France would take the chief economist post and Germany would keep the market operations portfolio, Handelsblatt added.

Either way, a Franco-German deal would probably mean both posts would go to the eurozone's two biggest economies.

A German government spokesperson said Berlin wanted "adequate" representation in the ECB's leadership and expected a deal by the end of the year.

A vacancy in Basel

Picking Hernández de Cos would also free up the top job at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), where he has been general manager since 1 July 2025.

Owned by central banks around the world and based in Basel, Switzerland, the BIS is often called the "central bank of central banks".

His departure would create another senior vacancy, and the BIS Board of Directors would choose his successor.

With Schnabel due to leave the ECB on 3 January for a role at the IMF, three of the Executive Board’s six members are due to leave in less than five months.

Governments are therefore negotiating the posts as a package.

World.title: Iran MPs debate possible shift in nuclear doctrine and exit from NPT
World.content:
Iran’s nuclear doctrine is generating a heated debate in the Islamic Republic’s parliament and power circles as the United States and Israel designated Iran’s capability to develop a nuclear weapon as the primary objective of their war on Iran.

 

Kamran Ghazanfari, a member of Iran's parliament, told Euronews on Friday that building nuclear weapons is far more essential for Iran that neutralising what he called “"US and Israeli propaganda against the Islamic Republic."

"When America and the Zionist regime have repeatedly threatened us with the use of nuclear weapons, we cannot be indifferent to this issue, as it is a threat that targets all the people of Iran and our very existence,” Ghazanfari said, adding that “they are enemies and have shown that they will not refrain from any crime so we cannot say 'God willing they will not use nuclear weapons against us'. We must confront them,” the Iranian lawmaker said.

He called on Iran’s leadership that “we must review the nuclear doctrine of the Islamic Republic so that the enemy knows that if it seeks a nuclear attack on Iran, it will face a reciprocal response from Iran,” adding that “just as since the Second World War until now none of the countries that possess nuclear weapons have used these weapons against each other because they fear that the other side will carry out such an attack against them, the Islamic Republic must also create deterrent power."

Ghazanfari does not see the lack of nuclear submarines and bombers capable of carrying nuclear weapons as undermining the Islamic Republic's nuclear deterrence, stating that missiles are also a solution to carry nuclear warheads.

But a former Iranian lawmaker, Heshmatollah Falahatpisheh, told Euronews that even if Iran had several nuclear warheads it would still lack nuclear deterrence, stating that "I find it unlikely that nuclear deterrence is part of our country's strategy because nuclear deterrence has three components: having an atomic bomb, a deterrent nuclear balance, and the ability to deliver the final blow. Those who think nuclear deterrence is created simply by having an atomic bomb are mistaken."

In a telephone call with Euronews, he said that "I really do not know whether the country has an atomic bomb or not, but, as far as I was aware, Iran's nuclear programme was peaceful, and even its possible military dimensions were closed by the JCPOA so that Iran's case would be removed from Chapter Seven of the UN Charter.”

“In my view Iran's military strategy is a conventional strategy, and this strategy has been fairly effective. I also find it unlikely that what Iran’s Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei meant when he said that Iran has certain things was an atomic bomb," Falahatpisheh said.

Kamran Ghazanfari, however, believes that when the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council says that "we have something", he is referring not to an ordinary weapon but to a "special weapon".

He said that Iran is trying to formally withdraw from the Treaty of the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), the landmark international treaty whose objective is to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons and weapons technology.

"I infer that this change of doctrine has in practice already happened. In parliament we are also pursuing withdrawal from the NPT, and last year some members of the presiding board of parliament blocked it, but MPs are still pressing for this plan to be put on the open floor, although a series of obstruction efforts are still preventing the plan from reaching the floor, Ghazanfari said.

But Heshmatollah Falahatpisheh considers the withdrawal from the NPT to be laying the groundwork for future wars against Iran, stating that "Iran's relations with the NPT have in practice been destroyed and whether Iran remains in the NPT or not depends on the nature of relations between Iran and America.”

“The discussion of Iran leaving the NPT does not help Iran's national interests because leaving the NPT amounts to hiding part of Iran's nuclear programme,” Falahatpisheh told Euronews, adding that Iran’s “Supreme National Security Council has not agreed to the MPs' triple-urgency bill to withdraw from the NPT, otherwise this plan would have been put before an open session of parliament."

Meanwhile on Thursday, Iran’s Assembly of Experts also called for examining the issue of Iran's withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

In a statement, the assembly, whose main task is oversight of the performance of the leadership, said that "examining the issue of withdrawal from the NPT, reviewing the country's defence doctrine and creating the necessary deterrence has become an unavoidable necessity and has turned into a public and national demand."

Finally, in announcing Iran’s latest position on the NPT membership, Iran's Foreign Ministry stressed that the Islamic Republic still remains committed to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.

World.title: Berlin clan boss Issa Remmo appears as 'state guest' at EU Parliament event
World.content:
Clan boss Issa Remmo from Berlin took part in a conference of imams at the European Parliament in Brussels, as first reported by the Jüdische Allgemeine. The fact that the head of a clan, which in Germany is associated with an apparently endless list of offences, appears in Brussels as a state guest is seen as a slap in the face not only to the German justice system.

 

Photos show him listening to the speeches and applauding when the discussion turns to the fight against antisemitism. Yet his extended family in the Berlin district of Neukölln is hardly a symbol of successful integration and acceptance of Germany's basic values.

Serious crimes time and again

The 58-year-old is regarded in Berlin as the head of the so-called Remmo clan. The Remmo clan is estimated to have around 500 to 1,000 members, while the core family around its head, Issa Remmo, in Berlin, comprises around 103 people.

The immediate family circle around clan boss Issa Remmo lives predominantly in Berlin-Neukölln. Not all relatives are criminals. However, part of the extended family has repeatedly come to notice for serious offences. In 2023, five young men from the Remmo clan were convicted of the spectacular jewel theft from the Green Vault in Dresden.

Imam meeting in Brussels

According to information from the newspaper "Bild", Issa Remmo took part in the anti-Islamism conference at the EU Parliament at the invitation of French EPP politician Céline Imart and imam Hassen Chalghoumi. Chalghoumi is known as an interfaith bridge-builder and a clear opponent of terror.

The topics of the meeting were the fight against Islamism and antisemitism.

According to the report, the hosts initially knew nothing about Remmo's clan background. Imart later apologised to everyone who may have been hurt by his participation.

In the group photo of the organisation ELNET (European Leadership Network), which aims to improve relations between Europe and Israel and apparently organised the meeting alongside French conservative MP Céline Ismart, Remmo is clearly visible.

Jewish, Christian and Muslim religious representatives took part in the conference.

According to the Jüdische Allgemeine, Issa Remmo spoke in Brussels with French author of Jewish faith Marek Halter about antisemitism and said: "I am not an imam, but I can say one thing: we are all brothers in this world. Let us all live together, together. Where is the problem? Love will win, and terror will lose."

According to Remmo, there should no longer be any antisemitism, and Marek Halter agreed with "Inshallah".

Clan boss Remmo overshadows the Left party's election campaign in Berlin

Issa Remmo recently made headlines for attending an election party of the party Die Linke in Berlin-Neukölln. His son Firas is said to have communicated beforehand via chat with Left Party Bundestag member Ferat Koçak.

The Left party in Berlin-Neukölln insisted that it has neither political nor personal ties to Remmo. He stated in several conversations, including in Brussels, that he was disappointed with the Left party.

World.title: Azerbaijan intensifies its European engagement at the EPC Summit
World.content:
Azerbaijan is set to increase and diversify its energy supplies to Europe, beyond the current 10 EU member states, Azerbaijan’s president Ilham Aliyev announced on Thursday during the 9th European Political Community Summit in Dublin.

 

Aliyev held talks with European Council President Antonio Costa during the EPC summit to discuss the long-term energy contracts “in the context of continuing successful cooperation between Azerbaijan and the European Union in gas supplies,” an Azerbaijani presidency statement said, while Costa declared that “the resumption of negotiations on a new EU-Azerbaijan agreement is good news for our citizens.” The EU-Azerbaijan Strategic Partnership in the Field of Energy was established in 2022.

Commenting on the meeting, Costa emphasized the two-way benefits the EU-Azerbaijan cooperation declaring that “this has been an important year for EU-Azerbaijan relations,” adding that “with peace between Azerbaijan and Armenia now a reality, the EU is also investing to ensure that people across the region benefit.”

President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev met with President of the European Council António Costa in Dublin president.az, November 2026

Aliyev said that Azerbaijan increased its gas supplies to the European Union from 8 billion cubic meters to 13 billion cubic meters, which accounts for nearly half of Azerbaijan’s exports, and that with the discovery of new fields, the South Caucasus country plans to increase gas supplies further.

The cooperation is now also focusing on renewable energy, a strategic national objective for Azerbaijan, with Aliyev highlighting the agreement reached between Azerbaijan, Georgia, Turkey and Bulgaria on exporting renewable energy to the European markets.

Azerbaijan’s president said that the gas pipeline stretching from Baku to Italy, passing through the territories of seven countries and supplying 10 European Union member states via interconnectors in Bulgaria, was currently operating at full capacity, and that Baku intends to continue expanding its transported volumes.

Costa and Aliyev also said that the European Union’s assessment of the Nakhchivan railway project would be completed soon and that they discussed the developments of transport links and connectivity within the global Middle Corridor project connecting Asia to Europe through the South Caucasus and Central Asia towards the Black Sea, a fast-developing alternative to the Strait of Hormuz crisis for the global supply lines.

Costa invited Aliyev to Brussels to continue the discussions on EU-Azerbaijan’s cooperation given the South Caucasus country’s role in Europe’s energy supply and security.

Strategic partnership with the UK

Azerbaijan’s president Ilham Aliyev and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham signed a Joint Declaration on Strategic Partnership between Azerbaijan and the United Kingdom, during the EPC Summit in Dublin.

With the UK being the largest European investor in Azerbaijan’s economy, historically driven by BP's Caspian operations, the new strategic framework focuses on defence and security cooperation, expanding trade and investment, renewable energy, infrastructure as well as artificial intelligence, advanced technology and others.

British officials said relations have now reached a historic milestone and both leaders committed to expanding mutual trade, defence cooperation, and private-sector investment ties under the new accord.

With Russia watching on, the UK and Azerbaijan agreed to “strengthening cooperation in defence and security in support of regional peace and stability” (...) “across a broad spectrum of security priorities, in response to evolving security challenges and threats.”

The two sides also agreed to “support the development of the Middle Corridor, alongside transport, logistics and infrastructure projects that facilitate cross-border trade and investment.”

Securing the Ukrainian grid and drone agreements

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a “detailed discussion” with President Aliyev during the EPC summit, focusing on emergency support for Ukraine's battered energy grid ahead of the harsh winter and post-conflict reconstruction strategies.

Zelenskyy confirmed that contracts were signed under the so-called “Drone Deal,” an ongoing bilateral drone agreement, saying that “we are working to scale up orders,” adding that “relations between our countries are developing.”

Zelenskyy also thanked Aliyev for Azerbaijan's humanitarian assistance as officials confirmed an ongoing €1.35 million emergency grid support package from Baku, comprising heavy electrical equipment and generators.

Total Azerbaijani humanitarian aid to Ukraine has now reached €48 million, focusing on civilian energy infrastructure and medical rehabilitation.

Ukraine’s president also noted that Kyiv is closely analysing Azerbaijan's post-conflict reconstruction across Karabakh and the East Zangezur regions, as the Ukrainian government views Baku's massive infrastructural overhaul as a viable blueprint for its own eventual post-war recovery.

The two leaders also discussed expanding economic and trade relations, including private-sector economic cooperation, with Zelenskyy saying that “we value the fact that companies are staying and continuing to work for our people, often despite Russia’s vile attacks.”

Advancing Armenia-Azerbaijan peace process

Building on their historic peace process, Azerbaijan’s president Ilham Aliyev held new talks with Armenian prime minister Nikol Pashinyan on advancing their peace consolidation, border delimitations, water cooperation and interconnection of electricity grids as well as more confidence-building measures.

The two leaders also discussed the progress of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) connectivity project, including the planning of its railway and highway components.

Since November 2025, a total of 105,000 tonnes of cargo have been transported to Armenia through the territory of Azerbaijan.

Prime Minister of the Republic of Armenia Nikol Pashinyan and President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev in Dublin for the EPC summit president.az, November 2026

Broadening European engagement

President Aliyev met with Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis for talks on upgrading the Southern Gas Corridor's infrastructure in the context of Azerbaijani-Greek bilateral relations, anchored by the Trans Adriatic Pipeline (TAP).

President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev and Prime Minister of the Hellenic Republic Kyriakos Mitsotakis in Dublin for the EPC summit president.az, November 2026

Aliyev also held talks with Moldovan President Maia Sandu on energy cooperation and on strengthening Moldova’s energy security as well as economic and trade ties with a particular focus on the agricultural sector.

President of the Republic of Moldova Maia Sandu and President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev in Dublin for the EPC summit president.az, November 2026

Azerbaijan’s president met his Romanian counterpart Nicusor Dan for the first time to discuss energy and connectivity projects, focusing on linking the Caspian and the Black Seas.

Dan said in a post on X that “we focused on deepening our Strategic Partnership, advancing key energy and connectivity projects, and pursuing an ambitious shared political and economic agenda,” adding that “our cooperation, linking the Caspian and the Black Sea, has strong potential to grow.”

Aliyev also held energy talks with Bulgaria’s prime minister Rumen Radev and Czech prime minister Andrej Babis.

World.title: The dangers of revising Europe's security architecture
World.content:
Experts warn against revising Europe's security framework because they say it would mean granting Moscow its longstanding wish of renegotiating postwar security on the continent.

European leaders have so far found compromises in response to many of US President Donald Trump's demands.

But they were surprised to hear Trump say that he raised Europe's security framework with Russian officials.

"It's going to be a big agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House last week.

He said that deal might include all of Europe. But what he meant by "all of Europe" was not clear.

US envoy Jared Kushner also wrote that Europe and Russia had struggled to establish a sustainable security framework for more than 30 years.

Kushner said he was looking at a "broader" European architecture before he flew to meet with Russian and Ukrainian representatives in Abu Dhabi.

European diplomats immediately pushed back on Washington's approach to secure a peace deal in Ukraine because they feared that a peace settlement could restore Russia's sphere of influence and undermine NATO.

"We ​already have European security ​architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their ​respective roles. We ​must make sure Ukraine is integrated ‌into ⁠this architecture," said Kaja Kallas, the European Union's foreign policy chief.

The issue with revising Europe's postwar security framework

Russia made clear during talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week that they were keen to discuss a broader European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.

"Phrases about the European security architecture are certainly Russian talking points and not only talking points but, to a degree, part of a media propaganda effort that Russia makes to frame the war as it wishes to frame the war," said Michael Kimmage, a historian of the Cold War.

Russian leaders, including Vladimir Putin, have long alleged that the US and NATO repeatedly violated pledges they made in the early 1990s not to expand the alliance into the former Soviet bloc.

They have seen NATO's enlargement during this period as having put them in a humiliating position in which they could do very little.

At the same time, in the 1990s, the European project saw the birth of the European Union, the single market that ensured the free movement of goods and people across member states, the Schengen agreement for border-free travel, and the euro.

The core idea was to extend peace across the continent.

"Europe can mean so many things, but the European project was not designed for war. It was designed for peace," said Kimmage.

During this period, there were even suggestions of Russia becoming a NATO member.

But that relative period of stability changed after Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Russia wants to redraw all of this by force. And I think that that's fundamentally unacceptable to Europe with all the diversity and variations that you get within the European landscape on what's acceptable and not acceptable. I think the large-scale redrawing of borders by force is just not the European project," said Kimmage.

"So to the extent that the redrawing of borders by force is the lifeblood of Russian foreign policy, and I think that's a pretty easy case to make, Russia and Europe are at an impasse," he said.

What was to happen to Ukraine's security?

The Trump administration very quickly turned to making sure that "existing European security institutions" would be intact, with Jared Kushner having said late Thursday that the next round of negotiations would include "our European partners."

Kushner, along with Steve Witkoff, flew to Moscow to talk to Putin after talks in Abu Dhabi. Then they flew to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Kushner had earlier Thursday signaled some "really incredible" postwar plans for Ukraine, saying that it could not be concluded without Europeans at the table.

"We should not allow a diktat from Russia that would result in some kind of neutralization or significant reduction in the military forces of Ukraine going forward, because that would make Ukraine very, very vulnerable to future aggression and pressure coming from Russia," said Hiski Haukkala, the director of the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.

That would mean that Ukraine would also be completely dependent on the security guarantees that the US or Europeans are able and willing to provide.

"We are supporting Ukraine because we are supporting international law and the basic norms of decency and international security when it comes to European security architecture. And this is the vantage point from which we are operating," he said.

The European Union has repeatedly pointed to some of the basic treaties that Russia broke, including:

The UN Charter

The Helsinki Act of 1975, which established the ten core principles of European security, including the non-use of force or threat against territorial integrity.

The Charter of Paris for a New Europe that built on Helsinki commitments

The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), which was one of the few multilateral security forums where the West and Russia engaged.

The Budapest Memorandum of 1994 in which Russia, the US and the UK provided security assurances to Ukraine and others in exchange for them giving up their nuclear weapons.

"Russia walked away from these principles and smashed them to pieces in the process. And they are not interested in reinstating the previous security architecture order. They want something different in its stead. And as long as this is not on the table, the Russian form of negotiation is to wage war. War is a form of bargaining," Haukkala said.

"And they are signaling strategic intent to change the makeup of European security, to subdue Ukraine and to change the very essence of European security," he added.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Volodymyr Zelenskyy after having met Vladimir Putin in Moscow. Image: Peter Morrison/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

What is the way forward?

Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for European Affairs in the George W. Bush administration, said Russia is very good at sticking to its demands.

He said Russians know how to negotiate and "right now, they are not negotiating," referring to talks in Abu Dhabi.

Some experts said there was no possibility of having a new security architecture with the Russians at this point because there was no trust or common vision to align with Russia at the moment.

Others like Balazs Jarabik, an expert on post-Soviet politics, said that Russia was part of the European security architecture whether Europeans liked it or not.

"And the question is whether it's included as our enemy. Obviously, Russia is not going to be a partner, right? We have to find a modus operandi to reduce the risk of a horizontal escalation and potentially a bigger European war, even a bigger one than what we have now."

A host of European leaders on Friday rejected the Russian demands to discuss Europe's security framework as well, with a spokesperson for the German government saying that Berlin was looking to host a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" to secure funding for Ukraine's defense and reach a unified position regarding future peace talks.

World.title: EU leaders urged to 'act now' to stay AI competitive with US, China
World.content:
EU leaders in Dublin were called on by an AI executive to move quickly in the tech race with the US and China. EU official Metsola, however, expressed frustration with the idea that the bloc is behind in AI development.

European Union leaders met in Dublin on Friday at the first ever summit on artificial intelligence (AI). The meeting came at a critical moment, as the bloc seeks a unified policy on the rapidly evolving technology.

The meeting took place in Dublin's Convention Center, which was also the meeting place of the European Political Community summit this week.

Mistral's CEO Mensch urges EU to 'act now'

French AI company Mistral's CEO Arthur Mensch, as well as Nobel-prize winner and researcher Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI," spoke to EU leaders at the summit.

"Europe has all the technology and the talent to lead the AI race," Mensch said during the event. "What it needs is speed, financing and a strong coordination between member states."

Mensch urged the leaders to "act now" to stay competitive with the US and China in regards to AI development.

"AI is the most important technology of our time," European Council ‌President Antonio Costa said in a post on X regarding the summit. "Europe must make the most of its benefits, from higher productivity to better public services. We must also manage the risks and changes it will bring — and help set global standards for responsible governance and safe, human-centric AI."

The summit took place at a time of mounting worries about the emerging technology, which promises to transform ‌industries, labor markets and societies.

It also came in the wake of a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents in recent months and the wider discussion about how the technology could harm humanity.

Tech leaders behind the technology have also fallen under scrutiny. As recently as this week, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign after it was revealed that he had been in a relationship with a Chinese spy and a direct report in his company.

Finding Europe's role in the AI revolution

During the summit, a discussion occurred about where Europe fits in within the AI movement.

European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said she frustrated with the notion that Europe had "somehow lost the AI race."

She noted that the EU has "world-class talent, technological expertise and industrial experience to lead in AI."

"What we need now is to ensure that our ideas have the financing they need to grow and succeed in Europe," she added.

Will AI laws protect us? EU AI Act explained To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said there is a "dark side" to AI.

"We can all already see this in the battlefield in Ukraine, where you have drones equipped by artificial intelligence to really train to find anybody to kill," Kallas, the former prime minister of Estonia, said at the event.

Leaders face questions on how to unlock AI's potential, how to catch up with China and the United States in the race for the technology, but also how to protect against the risks it poses to individuals and businesses.

The governments of Estonia and Finland wrote in a letter ahead of the summit that Europe must "establish EU-level arrangements for responding to serious AI incidents," calling for "developing advanced AI and governing it responsibly."

World.title: What's going on with the polar vortex?
World.content:
Observations show the ring of fierce winds that rotate at the Earth's North Pole has changed direction. Scientists say it's a historic disruption and the earliest reversal on record. What could it mean for the weather?

High up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons. This is the polar vortex.

If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere.

Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.

Earliest vortex disruption on record

It's not yet clear how the current disruption to the polar vortex will affect the Northern Hemisphere winter, but scientists agree it is a record-breaking event.

"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told the AFP news agency.

The French meteorological agency Meteo-France, meanwhile, called it "an unprecedented event."

The early breakdown of the vortex "really increases the chance of cold air outbreaks across the latitudes where most of the densely populated population centers are across the Northern Hemisphere, US, Europe and East Asia," Judah Cohen, a climatologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology told AFP.

When the polar vortex is detabilized, it can send a blast of freezing temperatures further south Image: Adam Glanzman/Getty Images/AFP

What exactly is the polar vortex and how does it work?

The polar vortex is an enormous band of cold, low-pressure air that spins counterclockwise around the North Pole, about 10 to 50 kilometers (around 6 to 30 miles) above the surface.

It's closely connected to the jet stream, another band of powerful winds just below the vortex. The jet stream forms a boundary where the cold Arctic air meets warmer air from the tropics and subtropics.

The vortex can sometimes be a tight circle, keeping the coldest air locked around the North Pole over winter. It can also form uneven waves that dip southwards. And as it changes in strength and shape, that can influence the atmosphere below and alter the position of the jet stream, which drives the weather on the ground.

So, if the jet stream is more "wavy," and plunges south, it may also allow freezing Arctic air to spill southward.

One of the biggest influences that can provoke this kind of disruption is known as "sudden stratospheric warming." This is when temperatures in the polar stratosphere rise dramatically within a few days, causing the vortex's strong westerly winds to weaken.

This can push the vortex off its spot at the North Pole, make it split apart into multiple rings, or — as is happening now — cause the westerly winds to change direction.

It can take several weeks for the vortex to recover.

What does this mean for winter weather?

A previous polar vortex disruption contributed to the deadly Great Texas Freeze in February 2021, which caused more than a week of freezing temperatures that sparked power outages and killed hundreds of people.

But bone-chilling cold isn't a foregone conclusion. The Met Office, which is the UK's national weather and climate service, stresses that what's happening with the polar vortex can nudge odds in that direction, but it's not a switch that turns cold weather on and off.

Other weather patterns can also influence the outcome.

For example, there's a possibility El Nino, which is associated with milder winters, could "moderate or modify" the impacts, Cohen told AFP. But he added this was not certain.

The El Nino weather phenomenon, caused by the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is currently intensifying and is expected to peak at the end of the year. The ongoing event has been classified as exceptionally strong and is disrupting weather around the globe.

Some research has also linked the rapid warming of the Arctic driven by climate change to increasing disruptions to the polar vortex. That means that, even as the planet warms, some areas may still experience more severe cold spells. But this connection is not conclusive and is still debated by scientists.

World.title: Ice hockey: Russia threatens against Canada and Germany over exclusion from tournaments
World.content:
A fortnight after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two tournament hosts.

"Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.

"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak added after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.

"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada."

Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak was the Soviet Union's top netminder in the 1970s and early 1980s Image: Yuri Kochetkov/SNA/IMAGO

Canada refuses to bend on junior tournament

The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed on Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to play in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Canadian Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden said in a statement. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Following last month's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling, in which it said that the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient – the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.

Norway then said it had been bumped from the World Juniors and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated that they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.

Men's tournament with Russia 'effectively impossible'

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14. With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible."

However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport said on Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the (German) ice hockey federation (DEB), nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a World Championship anywhere."

At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport—and ice hockey in particular—find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship."

Munich's Olympic bid and the IOC's new stance on Russia

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hardline on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

For now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to pointing the way forward for the men's tournament in Germany next May.

World.title: Why does El Salvador's Bukele have troops in Haiti?
World.content:
Haiti's Prime Minister congratulating El Salvador's President for a gang crackdown in Haiti has shone a light on the relationship between the two countries. What's going on, and where does the US stand?

Haiti has been engulfed in crisis since 2018, with protests, a presidential assassination and widespread gang violence bringing the country to its knees.

But earlier this week, Haiti's Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime hailed a major win in the battle against the violence, thanks to "the commitment of the Salvadorean forces in the fight against gangs."

El Salvador's President, Nayib Bukele had earlier said a joint task force between the countries had "destroyed" what he called "the house of Lanmo San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters." He also tweeted out an as-yet unverified video of helicopters firing on a sprawling property.

Why are troops from El Salvador in Haiti?

A number of Salvadoran troops have been stationed in Haiti, nearly 2,000 kilometers from their homeland, since the beginning of 2025, mostly in an attempt to curb gang influence.

Last month, Bukele dispatched more than 2,000 troops and special forces to Haiti, ostensibly to rescue four Salvadorans who were ambushed on October 18 and have not yet been found.

How the West messed with Haiti To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Writing on social media platform X, Fils-Aime thanked the Salvadorean military for helping "the fight against gangs." The two nations are, he added, working alongside the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), in an attempt to "regain control of the territory and restore state authority."

The GSF has been operating in Haiti since 2016. But there are doubts to the legitimacy of El Salvador's presence.

"Where the lines are and where the coordination begins and ends between a bunch of distinct entities and security forces is a huge concern about how this actually plays out, and El Salvador are trying to frame it as their choice, their action," Jake Johnston, a Haiti expert and director of international research at the Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR) in Washington, told non-profit news agency The New Humanitarian this week.

What is the current situation in Haiti?

A UN report about Haiti released on Thursday described "bloody turf wars, sexual violence and other horrors, noting that serious violations and abuses continue to be committed across the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area and in the Artibonite and South-East departments."

It further found that between July and September 2026, at least 1,167 people were killed and 459 injured, with more than half of that violence stemming from "ground or aerial operations carried out by security forces against gangs, sometimes with the support of a private military company using drones."

Salvadoran troops in armored vehicles patrol the streets of Haiti Image: Fildor Pq Egeder/REUTERS

For many observers, this chaos is a major part of the appeal for Bukele, who appears to wish to export his mano dura (iron fist) policy on to foreign soil. The policy saw gang members jailed on a huge scale and a significant drop in the murder rate of a country once notorious for homicide. But Romain Le Cour Grandmaison, a Haiti expert from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, told DW earlier this month that Haiti's gang problem is more entrenched. He says using the same tactics as in El Salvador may not have the same result.

"Haiti does not currently have the conditions to replicate the Salvadoran model: Its prisons were emptied in 2024, its justice system is largely paralyzed and criminal groups resemble militias more than gangs, with territory, taxes, weapons of war and political networks that protect them," Le Cour Grandmaison said.

Does El Salvador have US support?

Despite El Salvador being on Donald Trump's list of "shithole countries" that the US president disparaged in 2018 in notorious remarks which he later partially denied, relations between the US and El Salvador have improved markedly during Trump's second term.

Nayib Bukele has tried to position himself as an ally to Donald Trump Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance

The number of migrants deported to El Salvador from the US rose by 98% at the start of 2026 and Le Cour Grandmaison said the US plays "a central, albeit very discreet, role in public life" in El Salvador.

Bukele's move to position himself as an ally of Trump has seen the US president offer him a level of endorsement and autonomy to do what Bukele deems necessary to protect El Salvador's security and that of its troops.

"He said that he has a big problem with Haiti. I said: 'Look, you're running your country. You have to do what you have to do,'" Trump said in November.

World.title: Iran targeted US radar system in Bahrain
World.content:
Iran claimed it struck US radar systems in Bahrain, while the US said it had intercepted the attacks. Clashes continue in the Strait of Hormuz, as the war remains in a state of de-escalation.

Iran said its forces hit a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday. However, the US military denied the claims and said it shot down two Iranian attack drones.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) initially said in a statement that its air force targeted and destroyed the radar on the island of Bahrain.

They claimed this was a retaliatory attack in response to an US attack on a telecommunications tower in the Iranian county of Sirik, on the shores of the Strait of Hormuz.

Several hours later, the US military's Central Command, denied the IRGC's claim that the radar was destroyed and said it stopped two "one-way attack drones" targeting Bahrain by the militant group.

It reported no casualties or damage.

How serious are Iran's new threats of retaliation? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Where does the Iran war stand?

Iran war, started by the US and Israeli strikes on February 28, is currently undergoing a de-escalation as main issues remain unresolved.

Both US and Israel are holding off major attacks as they held elections over the last weeks.

On the other hand, Tehran has continued seeking to control the Strait of Hormuz, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, while continuing to attack ships it considers unauthorized users of the waterway.

Iran conflict: Could a new phase of the war be imminent? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait in the area where reports of burning ships came through.

Before the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump said on October, "We may do another little Epic Fury," referring to US-Israeli strikes, without giving any timeframe.

Trump is expected to meet Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at an APEC leaders' summit in China next week and discuss ending the ​war in Iran.

Pakistan-mediated peace talks between the US and Iran on April failed to reach a conclusion.

World.title: Beijing faces its Russia dilemma amid talk of Xi-Trump-Putin summit
World.content:
China is forced to tread carefully as it considers hosting a meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump. While the optics are sure to favor Moscow, Beijing is risking its image at the global stage.

An unprecedented meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States could be happening on the sidelines of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen next week.

China has yet to confirm that the meeting will take place. However, a Chinese Foreign Ministry official recently told the press that Beijing was "in communication" with relevant parties. In Moscow, a Kremlin representative said work on "coordination" was underway.

The clearest indication about the potential summit came from US President Donald Trump last weekend. Talking to reporters at a Florida airport, Trump said he "thinks" one of the meetings planned for APEC will be with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Trump, Putin or Xi: Who really runs the world? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Is the world set for a 'new Yalta'?

Despite the lack of official confirmation from either Beijing, Moscow, or Washington, the media has already dubbed the potential trilateral summit a "new Yalta," invoking the optics of the US, UK, and Soviet Union convening at the end of World War II and deciding on the new geopolitical power balance in the Crimean resort town.

The Yalta summit saw Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill represent the three main victorious powers of WWII Image: RIA Novosti/SNA/imago

At the same time, nobody seems to be quite sure what the three leaders would talk about if China agrees to host the trilateral summit at APEC.

In his brief remarks to reporters on Sunday, Trump avoided mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine when asked about the possibility of the meeting, bringing up only "Iran" and "denuclearization" as possible talking points.

The Chinese Foreign Ministry reported "no information" when questioned earlier this week about the potential substance of talks.

End of campaign to isolate Putin?

A three-way meeting with a photo op would be a big diplomatic win for Russia's President Putin. Since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Kremlin chief has faced years of diplomatic boycott by Kyiv's allies, most notably the US under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.

Putin first pitched the idea of a trilateral summit last month during a call with Trump. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Putin wanted the meeting to discuss an end to his war in Ukraine.

For the US, the president standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of America's foremost rivals could be a bad look, although Trump has already made a show of personally greeting both leaders with a red carpet at different points during his second term.

As host, China is in an even trickier position. While Russia and China are broadly aligned on many issues, Beijing does not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm China's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.

EU wary of being left out of Ukraine talks

The Chinese government is also working to rebalance economic ties with the EU. The European powers would likely bristle at a summit hosted by China and discussing the war in Ukraine without Kyiv or Brussels present at the table.

Europe seeks role in Ukraine peace talks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"China is clearly uneasy about the possible trilateral meeting with the US and Russia, and although Beijing has shifted its position from saying nothing to admitting that the three powers are in contact, the vagueness of these declarations seems deliberate," Alicja Bachulska, Asia policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW.

"Beijing is aware of the potential negative optics of the 'Yalta 2.0' framing, even if this historical comparison is inaccurate and does not reflect current geopolitical dynamics," Bachulska said.

She notes the trilateral meeting could "trigger further escalation in the already worsening relations between China and the EU" if Ukraine is discussed with no Europeans in the room.

For China, there is also little to gain in terms of optics. Images of Xi standing with Trump, the leader of Beijing's top rival, and Putin, Beijing's partner in opposing the US, could present an awkward look.

"Even if the meeting only yields a photo opportunity, it could nevertheless severely erode China's image," Bachulska added.

Beijing and Moscow stick to 'no limits' partnership

Putin and Xi have met some 40 times since the Chinese president came to power in 2012.

The two neighboring countries have grown especially close following the declaration of "no limits" partnership accord in early 2022. The move was announced by Xi and Putin on the sidelines of Beijing Winter Olympics, just weeks before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The current Russia-China ties are deeper than they have been in decades.

At the core of the axis between the two nations is a long-term strategy to contain US power while fostering an alternative global order both Moscow and Beijing can use for their own ends.

China helping Russia from the sidelines

Throughout the course of the Ukraine war, which is nearing the end of its fifth year with no solution in sight, Beijing has quietly provided Russia with crucial market for energy exports, while supplying technology and so-called "dual-use" goods.

While China did not explicitly provide Russia with weapons, its exports included high-tech components that could be used for modern weapons systems like drones.

Russia needs China trade more than ever To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Officially, Beijing maintains neutrality on the Ukraine war and has refused to take responsibility for its outcome.

"China is more interested in reforming global governance in ways that reflect its preferences and red lines while preserving a collegial appearance," Aurelio Insisa, senior analyst at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.

Even if China agrees to host the meeting, it will likely avoid framing it as three top powers making decisions for the rest of the world, according to Insisa.

"Embracing the 'G3' narrative would undermine its image as a champion of the Global South and developing countries. It is also worth noting that Beijing has shown no interest in engaging with the one pressing issue that could realistically be addressed in such a trilateral format: nuclear disarmament," he added.

What are the actual limits of China-Russia axis?

In a report published in August, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC), painted China as a "decisive enabler" of Russia's war in Ukraine.

Beijing was "converting Moscow's dependence into lasting military, technological, economic, and geopolitical advantages while avoiding the obligations of a formal alliance," according to the US body.

However, the commission also noted there were limits to Beijing's strategic support, and intelligence and security concerns remain a constraint on deeper cooperation. The report emphasizes the relationship is more of a strategic alignment than an alliance, with deep mistrust remaining in some key areas.

Russian defense firms, for instance, have accused Chinese companies of stealing intellectual property. Beijing, on the other hand, is concerned with Russia's growing strategic relationship with North Korea, which has reduced Pyongyang's dependence on China.

Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China and Russia also differ on nuclear doctrine. While Beijing maintains a longstanding "no first use" policy, Moscow uses nuclear threats as part of its strategy.

China getting a 'privileged vantage point' on Ukraine war

But for now, the benefits of alignment remain.

MERICS' analyst Insisa believes the cooperation between Russia and China will largely continue within this year's framework, including Russia providing energy and potentially transfering military technology in the "few remaining areas where it retains an advantage."

"China, in turn, will continue to supply dual-use technologies, purchase Russian energy, provide Moscow with a measure of diplomatic cover, and — more importantly — offer channels for circumventing Western sanctions," he added.

Notably, China will also get a "privileged vantage point" on how the battlefield in Ukraine is evolving land warfare.

"Strategic distrust between the two sides, particularly Russia's concerns about economic dependence on China, will continue to limit the scope of their cooperation," Insisa said.

World.title: Cyber attacks and hybrid warfare: Germany gives sweeping powers to its police and intelligence services
World.content:
Drone sightings and cyberattacks have heightened security concerns. How are the police preparing to meet these challenges? And how do intelligence services plan to counter threats from both domestic and foreign sources?

Germany's intelligence agencies have been given wide-ranging new powers. The lawmakers in the Bundestag agreed to a reform package on Friday.

Under the new rules, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), Germany's foreign intelligence service, will be allowed to respond to cyberattacks by foreign powers with counterattacks of its own. The range of possible measures is broad, from deleting and manipulating data to disabling entire systems and, if necessary, even destroying physical weapons such as drones that could be deployed against Germany.

Under certain conditions, the agencies will also be permitted to enter homes and business premises covertly, for example, to prepare surveillance operations. They will, however, not be allowed to use force against people. An independent oversight board is to be established to monitor the agencies.

Opposition lawmakers specializing in domestic policy warned against granting powers that are too broad.

Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Separation of powers hampers procedures

The president of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch this week again pointed out that today's hybrid attacks pose a new challenge to the organizations safeguarding the country's security. At his organization's annual meeting in Berlin this week, he said the "hybrid attacks" are challenging the "separation principle," which means that the police conduct investigations while intelligence services gather information. The exchange of data between the two is permitted only under strict conditions.

Münch has long objected to this strict division of responsibilities. He has been calling for expanded powers for the police and closer cooperation with the domestic intelligence agency, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, which is responsible for countering espionage and sabotage.

The separation principle results from lessons learned from the Nazi dictatorship, when the Secret State Police (Gestapo) operated largely outside judicial constraints and served as the regime's central instrument of terror, used to oppress and murder Jews, Sinti and Roma, homosexuals, communists, social democrats and many others. The Allied powers that defeated Nazi Germany in World War II then decided that the police and intelligence services should remain institutionally separate and be granted different powers.
