World.title: Temporary no longer: Ukrainian refugees in Poland confront the long term
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Leo Greenberg Speaking to Fox News in late October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky admitted a widely known but uncomfortable truth: Ukraine needs its refugees back. “We need 9.5 million people – who lost their homes, who are abroad, everywhere – we need them to come back to Ukraine…to rebuild their country,” he said. Zelensky: We need 9.5 million people who lost their housing, who are abroad everywhere — we need them to come back to Ukraine, just to live and to build their country. pic.twitter.com/Xu2Ld4eGOu — Clash Report (@clashreport) October 21, 2026 Unfortunately for Ukraine, all signs point in the opposite direction: Ukrainians abroad are deferring or abandoning thoughts of return. A large proportion of those refugees – almost one million of them – live in Poland, where Ukrainians, including migrants who arrived before 2022, have provided an economic and demographic boon. But their continued stay has also posed social and political challenges, as a country with no history of mass immigration grapples with the new reality of a sizable non-citizen minority. This has left the refugees themselves in a state of limbo: torn between a homeland that wants them back, and to which many would like to return, but where conditions do not allow for it; and an adopted home where they have created new lives but where social tensions and logistical hurdles have meant persistent uncertainty. A new reality sets in When Solomiia Pischana, a Ukrainian woman in her late twenties, fled from Kyiv to Poland in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, she hoped to go back that same year. When Kyiv was secured by Ukrainian forces, a return seemed possible. In late 2022, Pischana started travelling back home to see family and friends. “I was really living between two countries. I thought a lot about going back.” Yet quickly, a new reality set in on her visits: “In winter it became basically impossible to stay there – the constant explosions.” In Poland, by contrast, “everyone put the emphasis on helping me, on helping Ukrainians.” In a photo essay, we look at the lives of three of the million or so Ukrainian refugees who remain in Poland one year on from Russia's invasion: Liudmyla, a mother; Vlad, an amputee soldier; and Viktoria, a high-school student https://t.co/kdOpEgt2LB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2023 For many Ukrainians, Pischana’s story will feel familiar. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Poland became the main waystation for Ukrainians on their way out. Millions crossed the border, and while many went on to other destinations in Europe and beyond, initially more than one million remained in Poland. The Polish state reacted quickly, assigning more than a million special identification numbers for Ukrainian refugees – known as “PESEL-UKR” – and enrolling them in the same housing and benefits systems used by Polish citizens. So too did Polish society, with a majority of Poles working in some way to assist Ukraine or arriving refugees, and many hosting refugees in their homes. Around 77% of Poles have been involved in helping refugees from Ukraine, for which purpose they spent around €2 billion out of their own pockets, a new study by @PIE_NET_PL has found https://t.co/xWu8JWNMui — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2022 For Ukraine, the exodus of around six million refugees meant a raft of problems. Some 650,000 military-age men left the country, while schools had to figure out how to provide remote instruction for two million children abroad. Most of all, the refugee crisis worsened Ukraine’s demographic challenges. Before 2022, Ukraine’s population of 42 million had already been shrinking and ageing. Now, Ukraine’s minister for social policy estimates that just 22-25 million people remain in Ukrainian-controlled territory. Two thirds of Ukrainian businesses are short of workers. Initially, many hoped for a brief war. But, as the reality of a long, grinding conflict dawned, it became clear that Ukraine could no longer plan for an imminent influx of able-bodied adults: surveys by Kyiv’s Centre for Economic Strategies show that the proportion of refugees intending to return dropped from 74% in November 2022 to 43% in January 2026. “Rather chaotic” attempts to connect with refugees This reality has meant that, while Ukraine needs its people back, it also knows that it cannot compel people to return to a life defined by rolling blackouts and the ever-present threat of drones and ballistic missiles. As a result, Ukraine’s efforts to encourage and support refugee return have been haphazard and limited. Ukraine has one deputy minister, Ilona Havronska, who is armed with just 150 million hryvnia (13.1 million zloty, €3 million) in this year’s state budget to maintain connections with refugees abroad and support their return. Havronska has sought to create a network of “Unity Hubs,” paid for by foreign governments, where Ukrainian refugees can confer with trained consultants about returning home. Such facilities have opened in Stockholm, Prague and Berlin, with the latter receiving 5,000 visits since opening in May. ⚡️Ukraine, Germany agree to open 'Unity Hub' for Ukrainian refugees in Berlin. "This is a professional space that brings together community, business, and cultural initiatives," National Unity Minister Oleksii Chernyshov said.https://t.co/rlTq3MpOd0 — The Kyiv Independent (@KyivIndependent) February 15, 2025 So far, however, no hub has opened in Poland, whose interior ministry told Notes from Poland: “To be frank, the Ukrainian side, Minister Havronska, they haven’t approached us much about this recently.” Ukraine’s other major effort, a digital platform called “Dodomu” (“Homeward”), allows users to make a return plan and check off items on a digital to-do list, such as transferring medical files, verifying IDs, and registering children in Ukrainian schools. Since launching in June, Dodomu has been used by 4,500 people in Poland, of whom 600 have completed a questionnaire about their possibility of return. Ukraine’s efforts to reach out to refugees abroad have been “rather chaotic”, according to Olena Babakova, a Polish-Ukrainian journalist and researcher who studies migration. However, a survey by the UNHCR suggests that it may not make much difference: Ukrainian refugees ranked “support for return” as less important to their decision-making than security, economic opportunities, and housing in Ukraine. Nevertheless, for older refugees and those from now-occupied territories in eastern Ukraine, large numbers cited additional information as one of their key needs. Valentina Bryl, a Ukrainian who has lived in Poland since before 2022 and is now an HR specialist in Wrocław, notes that returning to Ukraine would mean she would have to “start everything from the beginning – my job, my life. It’s not just about safety.” So while Bryl says that she visits Ukraine often – taking the 25-hour rail journey from Wrocław to Kharkiv to see her husband, who is serving at the front – she hasn’t made use of Dodomu or thought about the Unity Hubs. She has no intention of moving back. From welcome to wariness in Poland Yet for the million or so Ukrainian refugees in Poland, as well as the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian economic migrants who came before 2022, a growing consideration is not only the conditions in Ukraine, but also the environment they face in their adopted homeland. Poland welcomed refugees in 2022 and has supported them since. It has also benefited economically from their presence, with Ukrainian refugees estimated to have raised national GDP by 2.4% in 2025. Ukrainian refugees boosted Poland’s GDP by 2.4% in 2025, the equivalent of €21.5bn, according to a report by the UN @Refugees agency and @Deloitte At the same time, their growing presence in the labour market had no negative impact on employment or wages https://t.co/lcsuIwBzpy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026 However, there have been growing social and political tensions. During the 2025 presidential election, even liberal candidates proposed restricting child benefits for Ukrainian refugees. The eventual winner, right-wing candidate Karol Nawrocki, in one of his first acts as president, vetoed an extension of Ukrainians’ temporary protections, before signing a revised extension that restricted benefits. Those political changes reflect shifting attitudes in society. A June 2026 report from the Institute of Political Critique (IKP) described last year’s election campaign as a “Rubicon”, citing testimony from Ukrainian refugees that the public environment had become more hostile and historical issues had surfaced. Pischana told Notes from Poland that, while she is “surrounded by good people” in Poland, she has noticed that “old topics like the Volhynia massacre are coming up much more”, referring to the mass slaughter of Poles by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two. “Just walking down the street and speaking Ukrainian, it’s started to feel a bit more dangerous,” she added. Police data show that the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year than in the same period of 2025. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 Myroslava Keryk, who leads Ukraiński Dom, a hub that provides services to Ukrainian refugees in Warsaw, told Notes from Poland that her staff have faced growing harassment. She described a slew of AI-generated videos depicting them demanding Poles pay greater taxes to support refugees, as well as sexualised, fake accounts made of her employees on online apps. Poland’s government has condemned the recent spate of hate crimes and accused the opposition and Nawrocki of stirring up such social vitriol. Meanwhile, it has begun preparing for Ukrainian refugees’ longer-term stay. Ukrainian refugees’ current PESEL-UKR status is tied to the EU’s temporary protections, now set to expire in March 2028. So this year, the government introduced a new “CUKR” status, valid for three years of residence after it is granted. Some 75,000 Ukrainians have already submitted applications. President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill ending the special status granted in 2022 to Ukrainian refugees, who will now be treated on the same legal basis as other foreigners. Nawrocki said he is "ending the era of unconditional privileges" https://t.co/BzY7wrdl49 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 20, 2026 This new status, however, is only a step on the path to long-term stability. CUKR, unlike most refugees’ current “UKR” status, counts toward the five years of legal stay required to apply for long-term EU resident status. However, its three-year duration means holders need to secure two additional years of legal protection in Poland before applying for long-term residency. Polish state policies have not always made things easy for refugees. New restrictions on benefits and on travel outside of Poland have made refugees careful. Despite that, many appreciated the legal and logistical clarity of Poland’s approach, typified by the new CUKR status. Refugees’ primary fears have concerned their social environment, not their legal status. Babakova put it neatly: “Ukrainians in Poland feel very connected to Ukrainian society, but not the state. At the same time, they have come to trust the Polish state, but not Polish society.” The citizenship question At the same time, a growing number of Ukrainians are thinking of obtaining citizenship, which would allow them to travel more freely and vote in Polish elections. An August survey of Ukrainian refugees in Poland found that a plurality (35%) listed obtaining citizenship as the “most desired form of assistance” to make their lives easier. In 2025, a record 19,000 foreigners, more than half of whom (10,000) were Ukrainian, were granted citizenship in Poland. Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago. Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 But since then, Poland has moved to restrict access to citizenship – to make it “an earned privilege, not a formal certificate”, in the words of the interior ministry. The plans include extending the required period of legal residence from five to eight years, requiring a loyalty declaration, mandating advanced knowledge of Polish, and introducing an exam on Polish history and values. Pischana wants to become a Polish citizen: “I’ve thought that it would be logical […] I’ve lived for years in Poland. I know the language.” She added that her university thesis focuses on Polish history: she’s writing a comparison of Ukrainian and Polish songs with political or social themes, from the 1980s to the present day. Kamil Kisiel, deputy director for the department of internal affairs and migration at Poland’s interior ministry, told Notes from Poland that the new citizenship laws, soon to be announced, will be tough: “For now, being more restrictive is the way to go, so that we can manage people’s expectations”. The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Kisiel was also up front that the Polish government does not envision many Ukrainians in Poland becoming citizens. No more than a few tens of thousands of Ukrainians have obtained Polish citizenship in the past decade, and those who arrived in 2022 are not yet eligible to apply. Instead, Kisiel highlighted, “long-term EU residence is…the sort of stability people should expect”. Karina, a Ukrainian woman who has been in Poland since she was 15 and did not want her surname published, says that she wants Polish citizenship as it offers “a chance to travel around the European Union, go to Spain. You can also go to America, because a Polish passport gives you visa-free travel; unfortunately, with a Ukrainian one you can’t.” Head in Poland, heart in Ukraine Barring a major change in the course of the war, Ukraine may even become one of the countries, including Ireland and Armenia, whose diasporas are as large or larger than their domestic population – a scenario that Havronska, the Ukrainian deputy minister, told Notes from Poland she is planning for. At the same time, social tensions and citizenship restrictions in Poland reflect the fact that refugees are challenging Poland’s identity: since the eradication and movement of Jews, Ukrainians and Germans during and after World War Two, Poland has been a largely monoethnic nation, accustomed to one language, one faith, and one national identity. The approximately 1.5 million Ukrainians in Poland have changed that. For Pischana, her head is in Poland while her heart remains in Ukraine, saying that she feels more attached to the culture of her homeland. “It’s a pity I can’t develop in my own country, because there’s room to do it there,” she says. For Bryl, it’s been harder to keep close to Ukraine: “I have work, I have other responsibilities…You no longer want to read, you don’t want to get angry at some bad news”. At the beginning, she said, she felt she had a fully Ukrainian life – just one that was put on pause. But, she adds, “when it’s already been going on for five years, and it’s still unknown how long it’ll go on, well, it’s hard to keep it on pause.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland dismisses Russia’s claim of breaking up Polish spy network as “disinformation”
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. After Russia announced that it had dismantled a Polish spy network and arrested two alleged agents, Poland has dismissed the claims as “disinformation” and a “provocation”. On Wednesday, while Poland was celebrating its national Independence Day, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) announced that it had “disrupted the activities of an intelligence network of the Polish special services operating in Kaliningrad”, a Russian exclave that borders Poland. It claimed to have detained two “agents”- one working for Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW), the other for the Internal Security Agency (ABW) – who had been “collecting and transmitting information about military personnel and facilities” and “the socio-economic situation in the Kaliningrad region”. The FSB added that seven Polish citizens and three Russians who had had contact with Polish intelligence agencies had been “officially warned”, and that the Polish citizens had been banned from entering Russia. The agency also published a film containing images of alleged suspects being detained and various documents and telephone messages in Polish. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the arrests would not further worsen relations with Poland given ties between the two countries “essentially do not exist right now,” reported the RIA news agency. In a statement on Wednesday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for Poland’s security services, said that he regarded the Russian announcement “as yet another provocation and act of disinformation”, especially as it had been released on Polish Independence Day. He added that he would not comment further and “appealed to everyone not to amplify hostile narratives or play into Russian propaganda”. Speaking to news website Wirtualna Polska, Maciej Wewiór, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, said that Poland was working to verify the information announced by the FSB. However, he urged “extreme caution” when dealing with such claims from Russia. “Let’s not fall for Russian propaganda and become pawns in this game,” he said. Jako rzecznik ministra koordynatora służb specjalnych nie komentuję materiałów zamieszczanych w sieci przez rosyjskie służby. 🛑 W dniu Narodowego Święta Niepodległości traktuję je szczególnie jako kolejną prowokację i dezinformację. 🛑 Apeluję o niepowielanie wrogiej narracji i… — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) November 11, 2026 Polish fact-checking and investigative journalism service OKO.press also raised doubts about the material shared by Russia. It notes that the alleged Polish-language phone messages released by the FSB have unnatural wording and appear to have been translated from Russian. It also points out that the footage showing the alleged detentions appears to have been recorded much earlier, judging by the green folliage on trees. This assessment was echoed by Stanisław Żaryn, who served as spokesman for the security services from 2016 to 2022. He said that “fabricated propaganda materials” were clearly “prepared in advance” and “fit the Russian security services’ ongoing campaign against Poland”. “It should be assumed that, in its operation against Poland, Moscow will resort to fabricated evidence, and today’s FSB statement will be used to legitimise earlier accusations against Poland of preparing an attack on Kaliningrad,” he added. #InfoAlert. Kolejna rosyjska prowokacja. FSB twierdzi, że rozbiła polską siatkę szpiegowską pracującą w Obwodzie Królewieckim. Analiza komunikacji rosyjskiej wskazuje, że mamy do czynienia z zaplanowaną sekwencją działań informacyjnych. Wpisuje się ona w stałe oddziaływanie… pic.twitter.com/s6bTV9pIK8 — Stanisław Żaryn (@StZaryn) November 11, 2026 The FSB’s announcement came a week after Poland announced that it had detained and charged six people – five Poles and one Russian – suspected of running an operation to illegally supply Russia with military components, which were smuggled over the border into Kaliningrad. Poland also sent additional security personnel to its regions along the Russian border this month following intelligence reports suggesting a planned act of sabotage or other provocation there. Prime Minister Donald Tusk later claimed that “individuals with flashlights” had been spotted at the border but “we very quickly mobilised the appropriate forces and managed to prevent a provocation”. Poland recently launched a special operation along the Russian border after receiving information that acts of sabotage may take place there in the coming days. For more, see our report from yesterday:https://t.co/RVaXb6SQJI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 3, 2026 Poland has seen a sharp rise in cases of espionage and sabotage carried out on behalf of Moscow in recent years. The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined. Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe. In response, Poland has successively closed down all of Russia’s consulates on its territory, prompting Russia to do the same with Polish consulates in a tit-for-tat move. World.title: Poland indicts Ukrainian man for assisting in rail sabotage on behalf of Russia
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish prosecutors have filed an indictment against a Ukrainian man accused of working on behalf of Russian intelligence and assisting in last year’s sabotage of a rail line in Poland. The accused, who can be named only as Volodymyr B. under Polish privacy law and is pictured above, will stand trial for espionage, sabotage and causing the risk of a major transport accident. He could face up to life in prison if convicted. Prokurator z mazowieckiego wydziału PZ PK skierował do Sądu Okręgowego w Warszawie akt oskarżenia przeciwko Volodymyrowi B. w śledztwie dotyczącym aktów dywersji na torach kolejowych, do których doszło jesienią 2025 r. w miejscowości Mika i Gołąb. ⬇️https://t.co/N2vK7thpKe — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) November 12, 2026 In November last year, the Polish authorities discovered acts of sabotage on two sections of a rail line running between Warsaw and the eastern Polish city of Lublin. In one case, a device containing military-grade C4 explosive was detonated in an apparent attempt to derail a freight train near the village of Mika. However, it caused only minor damage to the floor of the train. The following day, in the nearby town of Puławy, a passenger train carrying 475 people had to brake suddenly due to damage to the line. However, no one was injured. Soon after, Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced that the perpetrators had been identified as two Ukrainian citizens working on behalf of Russia. They had entered Poland from Belarus and then fled back across the border immediately after the incident. In December, Interpol issued red notices for the men, identified as Yevhenii Ivanov and Oleksandr Kononov. However, the pair remain at large. Meanwhile, a third Ukrainian man, Volodymyr B., was detained in Poland a few days after the sabotage and was charged with assisting in carrying out the attack. In their statement regarding the indictment of Volodymyr B., published on Thursday, the National Prosecutor’s Office says that he assisted Yevhenii Ivanov in conducting reconnaissance of the area, selecting a place to plant the explosives and installing recording devices and metal elements on the rails. “These actions created an imminent threat of a disaster, threatening the lives and health of many people and significant property damage,” wrote prosecutors. “Their goal was to seriously intimidate many people and influence public opinion.” They also say that Volodymyr B. was “participating in the activities of Russian intelligence”. The most serious charge he faces is for acts of sabotage on behalf of foreign intelligence, a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of ten years, ranging up to life. Interpol has published red notices for two men that Poland says were responsible for carrying out the sabotage of a rail line last month on behalf of Russia The pair immediately fled to Belarus after the incident and their current location is unknown https://t.co/RnahHDQkC8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 18, 2025 Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe. Such actions have often been carried out by Ukrainians and Belarusians. Last month, the trial began of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. This week, Poland announced that it had detained and charged two Ukrainians accused of carrying out espionage and acts of sabotage on behalf of Russia. World.title: Polish deputy foreign minister charged over alleged misappropriation of millions of zloty
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish deputy foreign minister has been charged with misappropriating millions of zloty entrusted to him and taking steps to prevent creditors from recovering money owed to them. Prosecutors say that Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski used the money for personal expenses and to buy three apartments in Warsaw. His wife has also been charged in the case. Both of them deny the allegations, and Bartoszewski says he “will defend the truth and my good name”. Prokurator z mazowieckiego wydziału PZ PK przedstawił posłowi na Sejm RP Władysławowi Teofilowi Bartoszewskiemu dwa zarzuty: przywłaszczenia powierzonych mu środków pieniężnych znacznej wartości oraz udaremnienia zaspokojenia wierzyciela. Komunikat: ➡️ https://t.co/EXZ3NsovBh pic.twitter.com/Lmp2f3Bw2r — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) November 10, 2026 The case dates back to before Bartoszewski had entered politics. In 2019, he became an MP for the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL). In 2023, after PSL became a junior partner in the current ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk, he was made deputy foreign minister. From 2004, say prosecutors, Bartoszewski was entrusted with managing the assets of Polish art collector and philanthropist Andrzej Ciechanowiecki, who was Bartoszewski’s godfather and a friend of his late father, Władysław Bartoszewski, a former Polish resistance fighter, Auschwitz prisoner, and later foreign minister. From 2005, Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski, who has waived his right to anonymity in the case, also managed funds belonging to the Non Omnis Moriar Foundation, linked to the collector. According to prosecutors, Bartoszewski used some of the money to buy and renovate three apartments in Warsaw between 2005 and 2006. From 2009, Ciechanowiecki began asking Bartoszewski to account for the funds, but he allegedly failed to do so and began avoiding contact with Ciechanowiecki. In 2012, Ciechanowiecki and the foundation terminated their agreements with Bartoszewski and demanded the return of funds, say prosecutors. The following year, they filed a lawsuit demanding that Bartoszewski pay them around £1 million, 7.2 million zloty, €650,000 and $76,000, plus interest. According to prosecutors, Bartoszewski then took steps to prevent the money from being recovered. A company owned by him and his wife sold three apartments in Warsaw, after which the couple disposed of their shares in the company. His wife also donated a property to their underage children. “As a result of these actions, Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski and his wife possess no assets from which the creditor’s claims could be satisfied,” prosecutors said. In March 2024, a Warsaw court ordered Bartoszewski to pay the foundation more than 13.2 million zloty, plus interest. Prosecutors note that the judgment is not yet binding as an appeal is still pending. Od półtora roku sąd nie wyznaczył terminu apelacji w sprawie Władysława Teofila Bartoszewskiego — dowiedział się Onet. Sąd pierwszej instancji nakazał wiceministrowi spraw zagranicznych zwrot aż 13 mln zł, jakie powierzył mu jego chrzestny https://t.co/JzPwcJG4KU — Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) November 4, 2025 Meanwhile, in 2023, representatives of the Ciechanowiecki Collection Foundation at the Royal Castle in Wawel, which now holds the assets of Ciechanowiecki (who died in 2015), filed a notification to prosecutors of alleged crimes committed by Bartoszewski and his wife. Earlier this year, the prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, asked parliament to lift Bartoszewski’s immunity so that prosecutors could bring charges against him. However, he voluntarily waived it on 6 October. At the time, Bartoszewski told newspaper Fakt that he “absolutely does not feel guilty” and “the evidence confirms this”. He also claimed that there is “a political element to my case”, though he did not elaborate further. Sejmowa komisja regulaminowa opowiedziała się we wtorek za uchyleniem immunitetu posła PSL Władysława Teofila Bartoszewskiego w związku z wnioskiem prokuratury w sprawie podejrzenia popełnienia przez niego między innymi przestępstwa przywłaszczenia mienia.https://t.co/ydA0jNNUQ8 — tvn24 (@tvn24) October 6, 2026 On Tuesday this week, prosecutors announced that they had charged Bartoszewski with misappropriation of funds of significant value – £1 million, €405,000 and 6,683,705 zloty – entrusted to him by Ciechanowiecki and the foundation. The offence carries a prison sentence of between one and 10 years. A second charge concerns allegedly taking steps to prevent or reduce the recovery of money owed to a creditor. It carries a prison sentence of between three months and five years. Prosecutors say that, on the same day, they “brought similar charges” against Bartoszewski’s wife and that both of the accused denied guilt. Wiceszef MSZ Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski oświadczył, że nie przyznaje się do popełnienia zarzucanych mu przez prokuraturę czynów. Zapowiedział, że będzie bronił prawdy i swojego dobrego imienia "tak długo, jak będzie to konieczne". https://t.co/tGodfs9Gzi — Interia (@Int_Wydarzenia) November 10, 2026 In a statement issued later on Tuesday, Bartoszewski issued a statement rejecting the allegations and saying that he “will defend the truth and my good name in every instance, for as long as necessary”, reports the Polish Press AGency (PAP). “I am convinced that both the criminal proceedings and the ongoing civil proceedings will confirm my arguments and rights to my property,” he added. “I consistently maintain that all actions related to the acquisition of the real estate were consistent with the original will of Andrzej Ciechanowiecki expressed at the time of their purchase, and the premises were intended to constitute permanent financial security for my family.” Asked whether the prime minister would dismiss Bartoszewski following the charges or wait for a court ruling, government spokesperson Adam Szłapka said that the deputy minister “is currently on leave and decisions regarding this matter will be made upon his return”. World.title: Annual Polish Independence March passes through Warsaw
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The annual march held in Warsaw to mark Poland’s Independence Day has passed through the city without major incident. This year’s event took place amid heightened security following the deadly terrorist attack in Kraków just four days earlier. Hundreds of thousands of people, including President Karol Nawrocki, marched through the city amid a sea of white-and-red flags. The event, which is organised by nationalist groups, also acted as a display of unity among the right-wing and far-right opposition ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections. Figures from the more liberal government, as always, avoided the march. Prime Minister Donald Tusk celebrated Independence Day hundreds of kilometres away in the city of Szczecin, where he issued an invitation to the opposition-aligned Nawrocki to visit his home for talks. This year’s Independence March was held under the slogan “Polak w Polsce gospodarzem”, which translates roughly as “Poles are in charge in their own country”. The slogan was chosen to “emphasise our opposition to foreign influences on Poland and underscore that Poland should be a nation-state without mass immigration”, said Rafał Buca, the march’s spokesman. “In Poland, Poles should rule – not some foreigners, not the European Union, not big corporations.” On the morning of the march, the organisers shared an image showing Tusk as a puppet of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. “Time to cut the strings of foreign influence,” they declared. Czas odciąć sznurki obcych wpływów i marionetkowych decyzji! W naszym własnym kraju to my – polscy obywatele – jesteśmy jedynym suwerenem i to my ustalamy reguły! 🇵🇱 POLAK W POLSCE GOSPODARZEM! pic.twitter.com/8Htr8s0klx — Marsz Niepodległości (@StowMarszN) November 11, 2026 The main organisers of the march are associated with Confederation (Konfederacja), a far-right group that sits among the opposition in parliament. But it is attended by a wide range of people, from the mainstream right through to the radical right. Leading figures from other opposition parties, including the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), centre-right Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) and radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), were present, as well as Nawrocki, who last year became the first Polish president to attend the march. A member of the march’s organising committee, Marcin Osowski, told broadcaster WNET that around half a million people were at today’s event. The municipal authorities, which are under the control of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, later put the figure at around 250,000. That would make today’s Independence March the largest ever other than the one in 2018, when a broader event was organised to mark the centenary of Poland regaining its independence after World War One. The opposition was aiming to show a united front amid their ongoing protests against the recent takeover of the constitutional court by a group of government-backed judges and ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections, at which they hope to unseat Tusk’s government. “It’s about showing our strength and, at the same time, for this march to be a springboard for the election campaign,” said Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of PIS, during the march, quoted by the Niezależna news website. “Unity is important.” Meanwhile, one of the leaders of Confederation, Krzysztof Bosak, told the crowd in a speech that, “while we have different experiences and views, under the white-and-red flag we form one community”. “Next year, we must turn this community into an election victory…We must remove the current clique from power and form a pro-Polish government,” he declared. “We do not accept the violent takeover of state institutions. We demand respect for the law.” Na Marszu Niepodległości jesteśmy u siebie! Przyjeżdżamy z różnych stron, mamy różne doświadczenia i poglądy, ale pod biało-czerwoną flagą tworzymy jedną wspólnotę. Każdy jest w niej potrzebny. Także ten, kto dziś czuje się samotny, odrzucony i traci poczucie sensu. Ta wspólnota… pic.twitter.com/L5pYU1RVv0 — Krzysztof Bosak 🇵🇱 (@krzysztofbosak) November 11, 2026 However, Confederation’s other main leader, Sławomir Mentzen, shared a picture of himself at the march in front of a banner showing images of both Tusk and Kaczyński crossed out, alongside the word “Reset”. While Bosak’s nationalist faction of Confederation is seen as more amenable to the idea of working with PiS to form a potential future coalition government, Mentzen’s libertarian faction is less enthusiastic about the idea. In the past, the march has sometimes seen violence, with participants clashing with police. However, in recent years it has generally passed peacefully, and that was again the case today. The city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaszkowski, who is a deputy leader of KO, said on Wednesday afternoon that, other than the illegal use of pyrotechnics (such as a flare held up by Mentzen), the march was proceeding without incident. Local authorities in Warsaw had put in place additional security measures following Saturday’s terrorist attack in Kraków, in which a 24-year-old Polish man, Michał Oksiński, killed six people and injured over a dozen more by shooting an AR-15 rifle from his car. Oksiński’s rampage was quickly brought to a halt in a shootout with armed police, and he died from his injuries on Monday. On Tuesday, the justice minister revealed that evidence uncovered so far shows “strong traces of right-wing extremism” in Oksiński’s activity. There are "strong traces of right-wing extremism" in the activity of the man who carried out the mass shooting in Kraków, says Poland's justice minister. His search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist https://t.co/UhVbkWSaCq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026 Tusk, meanwhile, celebrated Independence Day in the city of Szczecin in northwest Poland. “All of us, without exception, are responsible for ensuring that Poland remains strong, secure, free and independent forever,” said the prime minister. “Everyone who holds Poland in their hearts must understand that independence, freedom and a secure republic are a common good.” Tusk noted that, since the recent crisis around the constitutional court broke out, Nawrocki has refused his offer to meet and discuss how to find a solution to a crisis that has pitted judges appointed under the former PiS government against those chosen by the current ruling coalition. The prime minister today renewed that offer, inviting Nawrocki and his family to visit Tusk’s home in the build-up to Christmas. “We must be able to discuss things together, without bitterness, without hatred,” said the prime minister. Note: This article has been updated to include the official estimate of attendance at the march. World.title: Poland and US sign statement of intent on strengthening defence industry cooperation

Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, have signed a statement of intent on strengthening cooperation between their defence industries. “Today, we are taking the next steps in our alliance,” declared Hegseth, while Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the move signalled that Poland is now “not only a model ally…but has become a strategic partner of the United States”. The Polish defence minister added that he would also push for equipment jointly manufactured by Poland and the US to be eligible for EU defence funding. “Poland is the US ambassador in the EU,” he declared. Wicepremier W. @KosiniakKamysz z #Waszyngton: to chyba moja najważniejsza i przełomowa wizyta w USA. To moment, w którym mogę powiedzieć, że Polska jest nie tylko modelowym sojusznikiem, ale stała się strategicznym partnerem USA. pic.twitter.com/75xdgzIaG0 — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) November 10, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz was welcomed by Hegseth in Washington to discuss a range of issues relating to security cooperation. A major item on the agenda was Poland’s desire for a new permanent US military base on its territory. After the meeting, Kosiniak-Kamysz told reporters that there was a “green light from the Pentagon” for the base, with the final decision now resting with the White House. He said that was expected to be made in early December. Hegseth, meanwhile, praised Poland for embracing the “NATO 3.0” concept, under which the US wants Europe to take on more responsibility for its own defence. “Poland is building one of the most formidable armies in Europe, ready to secure and defend its territory,” said the Secretary of War, who noted that Warsaw is “leading by example” with its high levels of defence spending. Hegseth also welcomed the fact that Poland is investing significantly in US equipment, including Abrams tanks, F-35 fighter jets, Apache helicopters and Patriot air-defence systems. “You are building a fully modernised, interoperable force, and our two nations are…giving military cooperation industrial depth as well,” said the secretary of war. Hegseth also reaffirmed Washington’s desire for a peace deal in Ukraine and “encouraged Kosiniak-Kamysz to continue Poland’s steadfast support of Ukraine”, said Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell. American defense technology is driving innovation and creating new opportunities for transatlantic industrial cooperation.@USAmbNATO Matthew Whitaker, Assistant Secretary of Commerce David Fogel @CommerceGov and @USAmbPoland Tom Rose met with Deputy Minister of Defence… pic.twitter.com/5etw1L3X5A — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) November 10, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the statement of intent he had signed with Hegseth was aimed at ensuring more US equipment was manufactured and maintained in Poland itself, including technology transfers. He also said that he wants to secure European funds for jointly produced US equipment. The EU’s SAFE programme of defence loans, for example, largely excludes US manufacturers. “We want American equipment manufactured by Polish-American companies to benefit from European funding. I will present such a position next Tuesday at the meeting of EU defence ministers,” said Kosiniak-Kamysz. “Poland is the US ambassador to the EU.” The meeting between the two defence secretaries also coincided with the Transatlantic Defence Industry Access Forum, which brought together 70 Polish and 80 American firms, with the aim of strengthening ties between the two countries’ defence industries. W ostatnich dniach dobra decyzja o utworzeniu w Polsce centrum serwisowego rakiet Patriot, a dziś podpisaliśmy kolejne porozumienie z USA, które przyspieszy współpracę naszych przemysłów zbrojeniowych. In July, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles. In May, an agreement was signed to establish a centre in Poland for servicing the engines of Abrams tanks. That same month, President Donald Trump announced that his country would station an additional 5,000 troops in Poland, prompting Warsaw to formally request the establishment of a new US military base, which President Karol Nawrocki has suggested should be called “Fort Trump”. World.title: Two Ukrainians charged with spying and sabotage for Russia in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has detained and charged two Ukrainian citizens accused of carrying out espionage and acts of sabotage on behalf of Russia. The men, aged 24 and 25, were allegedly paid to conduct reconnaissance of critical infrastructure and military facilities across Poland. They are also accused of setting fire to several vehicles with the aim of stoking anti-Ukrainian sentiment. Funkcjonariusze Agencji Bezpieczeństwa Wewnętrznego zatrzymali w Mińsku Mazowieckim dwóch obywateli Ukrainy w wieku 24 i 25 lat podejrzanych o szpiegostwo i prowadzenie działań dywersyjnych na zlecenie rosyjskich służb specjalnych. ▶️ Mężczyźni rozpoznawali i robili zdjęcia… pic.twitter.com/G3i8hEsBHT — Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 10, 2026 The suspects were detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) on 3 November in Mińsk Mazowiecki, a town just outside Warsaw, the capital. ABW officers also searched their residences and other locations connected to the investigation, seizing data storage devices and narcotics. According to investigators, the suspects were tasked with setting vehicles on fire after changing their licence plates to ones used by Ukrainian military vehicles. This was “aimed at fueling anti-Ukrainian sentiment”, says the National Prosecutor’s Office. Prosecutors have charged the men under Poland’s espionage law with working against Poland on behalf of a foreign intelligence service – a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of five years – and sabotage on behalf of foreign intelligence, which is punishable by 10 years to life. At the prosecutor’s request, a court ordered both suspects to be placed in pretrial detention for three months. In recent years, Poland has seen a huge rise in cases of espionage and sabotage carried out on behalf of Russia. The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined. Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 Last month, a Polish man was jailed for five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of an airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. Shortly afterwards, the trial began of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage. World.title: Bohemian Burlesque Festival Returns to Prague for Its 10th Anniversary
World.content:
The Bohemian Burlesque Festival returns for its 10th anniversary, bringing four nights of international performances and a daytime market to Ostrava (already sold out), Brno, and Prague.

The festival, the largest burlesque event in the Czech Republic, will welcome a record 100 performers from 20 countries for this year’s edition. The programme combines classic burlesque, cabaret, contemporary performances, and vintage glamour.



This year’s theme is French-inspired, with three of the festival’s guest performers and headliners coming from France. Artists from Finland, Lithuania, and Estonia will also join performers from across Europe and beyond, alongside Czech talent.

Two major international names lead the programme. Medianoche, originally from New York and raised in Spain, is one of the industry’s best-known performers and won the prestigious Miss Exotic World title in 2017. Representing France, Chanelle de Mai is an acclaimed performer and costume designer known for her elaborate acts and precise choreography.

They will be joined by French special guests Vicomte Harbourg and drag performer Chantaaaal.

Prague will host three festival events over two days, all taking place at Hotel Belvedere in Prague 7.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Bohemian Burlesque Festival (@bohemianburlesquefestival)

The programme opens on Friday, November 20, with Bohemian Cabaret Prague, a gala evening featuring international headliners, professional performers, and local artists. The show starts at 20:00, with doors opening at 19:15.

On Saturday, November 21, the festival continues with the Bohemian Market, running from 12:00 to 18:00. Visitors can browse vintage clothing, accessories, jewellery, lingerie, and burlesque-inspired fashion.

It is also a great opportunity to enjoy plenty of burlesque at an affordable price: tickets cost just CZK 350, making it a good alternative for those who miss out on the evening shows.

The programme also includes fashion shows, retro hair and makeup services, photo sessions, discussions about body image, interviews with festival guests, and performances by 24 emerging burlesque artists. A pin-up competition, live singer, and magician are also planned.

The weekend concludes with Bohemian Queen Night, the festival’s closing gala, starting at 20:30. Twelve performers from around the world will compete for the titles of Bohemian Queen and Bohemian Princess, as well as the Best Costume Award.

A new feature for 2026 will give audience members the opportunity to vote for their favourite performer in an Audience Choice Award. Festival headliners and special guests will serve as judges and perform during the second half of the evening.

Both evening shows will feature a raffle and a Best Dressed Audience competition, with prizes for visitors who arrive in their finest outfits.

World.title: Prague Adds Special Trams and More Metro Services for Letná Demonstration
World.content:
Prague is preparing for a large demonstration at Letná on Sunday, November 15, with additional public transport services planned to accommodate the expected crowds.

The city will increase the frequency of trains on all three metro lines and introduce two temporary tram routes, numbered 40 and 44, to help transport participants to and from the demonstration.



Organized by the Million Moments for Democracy (Milion chvilek) movement, the event is expected to attract thousands of people from across the Czech Republic. Organizers are anticipating a record turnout.

The additional tram services are intended to ease pressure on regular routes, particularly around Letná and neighbouring districts.

Metro services will run more frequently between 11:30 a.m. and 7 p.m. on Sunday.

Tram 40 will operate from approximately noon until 7 p.m., running every five minutes. It will connect Letná with all three metro lines, travelling from Palmovka through Florenc, Vltavská, Hradčanská and Dejvická before terminating at Červený Vrch.

Tram 44 will also run at five-minute intervals, but only from noon until approximately 3 p.m. Starting at Špejchar, the route will pass through Strossmayerovo náměstí and Výstaviště towards Nádraží Holešovice. It will then continue around Holešovická tržnice, pass Vltavská and return to Letná.

The second route is intended primarily for passengers arriving on Metro Line C.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Milion chvilek pro demokracii (@milionchvilek)

Despite the additional services, transport authorities warn that overcrowding and delays are likely, particularly at Hradčanská, Vltavská and Nádraží Holešovice stations and on connecting tram routes.

According to Prague 7 authorities, the busiest periods are expected shortly before the demonstration starts and immediately after it ends. The greatest pressure on public transport is anticipated before 2 p.m. and at around 4 p.m.

Tram Disruptions Elsewhere in Prague

Passengers should also expect changes to regular tram services in central Prague.

From approximately 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., trams will be temporarily suspended in the area between Palackého náměstí, Národní divadlo, Jiráskovo náměstí and Myslíkova Street.

Tram lines 5 and 17 will be diverted via Karlovo náměstí during this period.

Road Restrictions and Changes to Letná Ice Rink

Drivers heading towards Letná should also expect traffic restrictions and temporary road closures in the surrounding area. The city recommends avoiding car travel to the demonstration and allowing extra time for journeys.

World.title: James Blunt Announces Prague Concert as Part of European Tour
World.content:
British singer-songwriter James Blunt will return to Prague on March 5, 2027, for a concert at O2 universum.

The performance is part of his Airplane Mode Tour, which will see him travel across Europe in support of his upcoming album.

Best known for international hits including “You’re Beautiful,” “Goodbye My Lover” and “Wisemen,” Blunt last performed in Prague three years ago, when he played at Forum Karlín.



His upcoming show will combine songs from his new record with the tracks that established his international career.

Blunt rose to international fame with his debut album, Back to Bedlam, released in 2004 after he left the British Army. Before pursuing music, he had attended the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst and served in Kosovo.

The debut album became a major commercial success, featuring three of his best-known songs: “You’re Beautiful,” “Goodbye My Lover” and “Wisemen.” It went on to rank among the 20 best-selling albums in UK history and earned Blunt several major industry honours, including Brit Awards and MTV Europe Music Awards, as well as five Grammy nominations.

His second album, All the Lost Souls, followed in 2007 and included “1973,” which topped music charts in more than 20 countries.

Titled Airplane Mode, the new album is scheduled for release on November 6, 2026, through Atlantic Records. The 12-track record has been introduced by the single “Tastes Like Summer,” followed by “Weight of It All,” a song addressing the pressures of modern life.

The European tour will run through February, March and April 2027, with Prague among its scheduled stops.

Tickets for the March 5 concert are available through Ticketportal and Ticketmaster.

The concert is organised by Charmenko Czechia.

World.title: What to Know About Czechoslovakia’s Velvet Revolution
World.content:
On Nov. 17, 1989, student protesters filled the streets of Prague. It was eight days after the fall of the Berlin Wall, and the same tide of freedom that had swept Berlin seemed to have come to the Czech capital.

Police tried to beat back the demonstrators, hoping to tamp down the demand for freedom, but the people seemed to have grown immune to the brutality of the regime; the show of force only galvanized the resistance.

The students were joined in the coming days by Czechoslovak citizens of all ages. By Nov. 20, a half-million Czechs and Slovaks filled Prague’s streets and took over Wenceslas Square. The Communists were forced out. By the end of 1989, Czechoslovakia was on its way to having an elected President for the first time since 1948.

The events of those world-changing days would come to be known as the Velvet Revolution. But, while the Velvet Revolution was over relatively quickly, it had been decades in the making.

The Failed “Prague Spring”

In January of 1968, the USSR gave the leadership of Czechoslovakia to someone new: Alexander Dubček. Dubček had fought against German forces during WWII, joining the communist party in his country after the end of the war. He rose through the ranks, serving in the parliament and general assembly as part of a new generation of Slovak communists.

Compared to his successor, the Stalinist Antonin Novotny, Dubček was liberal. Within months, he implemented governmental and economic reforms and allowed citizens increased freedom of speech, including freedom of the press. The people of Czechoslovakia embraced the changes and the period of Dubček’s liberalism became known as Prague Spring.

Like the spring, it was fleeting. By August of 1968 the Soviet Union had enough. A more liberal Czechoslovakia was a threat to its regional power and could signal weakness on the world stage.

Over half a million Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia; Soviet tanks rolled through the narrow streets of Prague, crushing mostly student-led protests. Soviet loyalist Gustav Husak replaced Dubcek and returned the country to an authoritarian communist regime — but something had changed.

Jan Palach

The following January, Jan Palach, a Charles University student in Prague, entered a suicide pact with several fellow students. They were determined to protest the Soviet invasion and combat growing despondency among citizens after the takeover.

On Jan. 16, 1969, Palach climbed the steps of the National Museum near the bustling train station on the edge of Wenceslas Square. There he doused himself with gasoline and lit a match.

In his suicide note, he signed his name as “Torch Number 1” — suggesting more self-immolation and protests to come. (Jan Zajic became “Torch Number 2”; though he couldn’t be directly linked to the original pact, Zajic participated in group hunger-strike after Palach’s death and was part of the resistance.) Palach lived for three days in a hospital after sustaining burns to 85% of his body. Amazingly, he still managed to give interviews. He spoke softly, his voice rough and halting.

When asked why he had done what he did, Palach replied that he wanted to voice opposition to the Soviet invasion and “make people wake up.” He died three days later.

The Velvet Revolution

In the decades that followed, Communist rule in Czechoslovakia continued, and the resistance, although forced underground, continued to grow too. By 1989, intermittent uprisings throughout Warsaw Pact countries, the increasing militarism of Soviet governments across the region and slowing economic growth within the Eastern Bloc set the stage for revolution.

In neighboring Poland, Lech Walesa, Anna Walentynowicz and workers of Lenin Shipyards in the Polish city of Gdańsk founded the Polish trade union Solidarność — Solidarity. Strikes and non-violent civil disobedience tactics employed by Solidarity paralyzed Baltic seaports.

In January 1989, 20 years after Jan Palach’s death, the clandestine resistance movement formed after the Soviets crushed the promise of Prague Spring planned what they dubbed “Palach Week.”

For the first time since Palach’s self-immolation, they would go to the place where he fell in Wenceslas Square for as public memorial and protest against the ongoing Soviet occupation. Nearly 5,000 people came out the first evening of that week — an unthinkable number since the Prague Spring. It set the stage for what became known as the Velvet Revolution.

That autumn, after a simmering year of protests and the fall of the Berlin Wall, students organized another protest. They chose Nov. 17, the 50-year anniversary of the killings of Prague students by invading Nazi troops.

The English phrase “Velvet Revolution,” which the European Parliament Directorate-General for Translation credits to Czech dissident Rita Klímová, signifies the idea that the revolution was brought about without violence — even though the larger process was not always peaceful. Soldiers beat protesters, used water cannons on the crowd and made numerous arrests.

A writer named Vaclav Havel was arrested that night. In 1968, Havel had been in Liberec, a small town outside the capital, when Soviet tanks rolled into his native Prague.

Before the regime was able to shut down Liberec’s radio station, Havel broadcast several speeches advising fellow citizens to engage peacefully but be prepared to defend themselves, encouraging them to remain loyal to the liberal ideals of the Spring and to resist and persist. So by the time the protests began in 1989 he was a well-known dissident turned leader of a coalition of opposition movements, the Civic Forum.

But when the government-controlled newspaper Rudé Právo tried to paint the jailed Havel as a symbol of a supposedly failed freedom movement, it backfired tremendously. By Nov. 28, after constant protests and workers’ strikes, the Communists announced they would cede power, and the parliament then removed the one-party provision from the constitution.

In December, Havel’s name was put forward as the Forum’s candidate for interim president. Two months later, in February 1990, in a speech to a joint session of the U.S. congress, Havel expressed his own disbelief that he was even nominated — yet by that point, he stood before the body as President of Czechoslovakia all the same.

In 1990, the country’s first open and free national elections were held. Havel retained his seat until the Velvet Divorce — the peaceful dissolution of Czechoslovakia into the Czech and Slovak Republics in 1992 — at which point he stepped down. He then served as President of the Czech Republic from 1993-2003.

World.title: Expat Next Door: How One Entrepreneur Is Making Flower Delivery in Prague Easier
World.content:
Originally from Ukraine, Valentyn moved to the Czech Republic in 2015, worked his way into the IT industry and eventually launched Pinflower, a platform connecting customers with the best local florists in Prague.

His journey to becoming a tech entrepreneur didn’t start in an office. After arriving in the Czech Republic in 2015, Valentyn initially settled in Brno, where he worked night shifts in a bakery and washed cars. In 2017, he entered the IT industry through technical support before moving into software engineering.



The idea for Pinflower came from a frustrating experience. While looking for a bouquet for a friend’s birthday, he couldn’t find anything suitable at his usual flower shop. Delivery would take hours, so he ended up driving across Prague himself.

He wondered why there wasn’t a simple way to see which nearby florists had bouquets available, compare prices and arrange pickup or delivery.

Rather than wait for someone else to solve the problem, he built the platform himself, working on it in his spare time. Pinflower launched in July 2026.

Local florists, one platform

Pinflower brings together local flower studios in Prague, allowing customers to compare bouquets, prices and delivery options in one place. The platform makes it easier to find flower delivery in Prague without having to browse individual shop websites.

Unlike anonymous delivery services, every arrangement comes from a named local florist. Customers can choose a specific bouquet or select the Florist’s Style option, allowing the florist to create something inspired by a reference image.

The platform is available in English, Czech, Ukrainian and Russian, making it easier for foreigners to order without having to call a shop or speak Czech. Customers can also arrange deliveries to Prague from abroad and pay by card, Apple Pay or Google Pay.

Another key feature is real-time delivery availability. The system considers each florist’s opening hours, bouquet preparation time and delivery area before showing customers when an order can arrive. One of Pinflower’s partner studios also offers 24/7 flower delivery in Prague, subject to availability.

Ordering flowers through ChatGPT

Since October, Pinflower has also allowed customers to arrange orders through ChatGPT and Claude.

Instead of browsing the website, customers can describe what they need, specify their budget and provide a delivery address. The AI assistant checks available bouquets, prices and delivery times before preparing the order. Customers then receive a secure payment link.

The founder sees this as part of a broader shift in online shopping, where people will increasingly start with a conversation rather than a search engine.

What’s next?

For now, the priority is expanding Pinflower’s network of Prague florists, with other Czech cities potentially coming later.

But the long-term ambition goes beyond flowers. The founder envisions bringing together local bakeries, gift makers and other small businesses, allowing customers to organise celebrations and surprises through a single platform.

The idea is to make it easier to support local businesses while using technology to simplify everyday tasks.

World.title: Prague to Mark 37 Years Since Velvet Revolution With 160 Events
World.content:
Prague will mark the 37th anniversary of the Velvet Revolution on November 17 with more than 160 events taking place along Národní Street as part of this year’s Korzo Národní celebrations.

Organised by the association Díky, že můžem, the annual event will bring together concerts, theatre performances, public discussions, exhibitions and activities exploring democracy and freedom.



This year’s programme carries the motto “Let’s Not Stand on the Sidelines. Democracy Relies on Each of Us.” The organisers say the message reflects growing concerns about declining trust in society and the challenges facing democratic institutions.

One of the central moments of the celebrations will take place at 17:11, when the traditional song Modlitba pro Martu (A Prayer for Marta) will be performed from the balcony of the Metro Palace.

This year, the performance will form the finale of a theatrical production titled DŮM VŠECH (House for All), which begins at 17:00. Visitors unable to gather directly beneath the balcony will be able to watch the performance on large screens along Národní Street or through a live broadcast.

The day’s programme will begin earlier, with the popular Velvet Brunch, a charity event held directly on the street between 10:00 and 13:00. At 13:00, members of the Czech Radio Children’s Choir will perform the national anthem.

Other events include live podcasts, musical performances and discussions on social issues. Among the scheduled speakers and performers are Markéta Foukalová, Martin Brunner, Václav Kopta and Vietnamese community representative Quang Luong.

Havel, the Vietnamese community and Věra Čáslavská

Several parts of this year’s celebrations will focus on important anniversaries.

The programme will commemorate the 90th anniversary of the birth of Václav Havel, the playwright and former Czech president.

His legacy will be explored through the traditional Václav Havel’s Living Room, titled “For Vašek”, at Platýz Palace. Actors including Vojtěch Vondráček and Taťjana Medvecká will read texts dedicated to Havel.

Another anniversary concerns the Vietnamese community, which marks 70 years in the Czech Republic. The programme will include Lost in Translation, a discussion bringing together three generations of Vietnamese residents to examine questions of identity, belonging and life between cultures.

The celebrations will also remember gymnast Věra Čáslavská, ten years after her death. Her life and the relationship between sport and politics will be examined through a special lecture aboard the Educational Tram and a live recording of the Outsider podcast.

World.title: FlixBus Launches Direct Route Between Prague Florenc and Airport
World.content:
FlixBus will introduce a direct bus connection between Prague’s Florenc Central Bus Station and Václav Havel Airport on November 12.

The new service will operate 13 times a day in each direction, with the journey taking approximately 30 minutes.

The first bus will leave Florenc at 3:40 a.m., while the last departure is scheduled for 10:40 p.m. From the airport, services will run between 4:15 a.m. and 11:15 p.m.



Ticket prices will depend on demand and departure times. According to the FlixBus website, the usual fare is around CZK 79, including the booking fee. The cheapest tickets start at CZK 69, while some departures cost up to CZK 89.

The company expects the route to attract business travellers in particular. Passengers will have access to Wi-Fi and power outlets on board.

BusAir joins the competition

FlixBus is not the only company expanding its airport connections. A separate private service, operating under the name BusAir, began running between Prague’s city centre and the airport in late October.

Operated by UBUS, the service offers eight departures a day in each direction, with buses running every two hours. A ticket costs CZK 125 and remains valid for 24 hours.

Due to renovation work on the ceiling at Prague Main Railway Station and traffic restrictions on the city’s main arterial road, BusAir currently departs from Opletalova Street, close to the station. On the way to the airport, it also stops at Hradčanská metro station on Line A.

Both new services are entering a market where the main competitor is the Airport Express, operated by Prague Public Transit Company (DPP).

The Airport Express runs more frequently than the private alternatives, with departures every 20 to 30 minutes during the day and hourly services overnight. It is also currently the only direct bus connection between the city centre and airport operating throughout the night.

Standard Prague public transport tickets are not valid on the service. A single adult ticket costs CZK 200, although passengers can get a lower fare when purchasing it together with a train ticket.

World.title: Říčany Named Czech Republic’s Best Place to Live for Ninth Year
World.content:
Říčany has been named the best municipality in the Czech Republic for quality of life for the ninth consecutive year, retaining its position at the top of a nationwide ranking ahead of Prague.

The Central Bohemian town, located southeast of the capital, again led the Quality of Life Index compiled by the Obce v datech project. The ranking assesses 206 Czech municipalities with extended administrative powers.

At the other end of the table, Orlová in the Karviná District ranked last, while nearby Karviná finished second from bottom.



The geographical divide remains clear: the 14 highest-ranked municipalities are all located within 50 kilometres of Prague or Brno, while many of those at the bottom are found in former industrial and border regions, particularly in the Moravian-Silesian and Ústí nad Labem regions.

There have nevertheless been signs of improvement in parts of the Moravian-Silesian Region. Over the past eight years, Odry, Kopřivnice and Hlučín have each climbed by around 40 places in the ranking.

The picture is less positive in the Ústí nad Labem Region, where only six of the region’s 16 assessed municipalities have improved their position since 2018. Roudnice nad Labem was the only municipality in the region to record a substantial rise.

Pohořelice Makes the Biggest Leap

Pohořelice, in the Brno-Country District, has recorded one of the most striking improvements since the index was introduced in 2018. The town has climbed from 117th place to fifth this year.

Nepomuk, in the Plzeň Region, has made an equally large jump of 112 places and now ranks 24th. Kuřim has moved up 65 positions to 15th, while Mnichovo Hradiště has risen 46 places to 18th.

According to Jan Havránek of AQE Advisors, which developed the project, municipalities do not need to perform at the top in every category to improve their overall ranking.

For around half of the 30 municipalities that have improved the most, the stronger results were linked to a younger population, population growth and, in many cases, longer life expectancy.

The Quality of Life Index evaluates municipalities across several broad areas, including health and the environment, material security and education, and relationships and public services.

World.title: PM Magyar: Meeting with Ukrainian President Zelensky could take place in Transcarpathia as early as November
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has held talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin, with the two leaders discussing a possible meeting in person. Magyar said the meeting could take place in Ukraine’s Transcarpathia region as early as the end of November.

Speaking by phone to public radio Kossuth on Friday, while attending an informal meeting of EU heads of state and government in Dublin, Magyar said he had spoken to Zelensky for 10–15 minutes on Thursday. They also discussed the possibility of meeting face to face.

Transcarpathia rather than Budapest or Kyiv

“Transcarpathia came up as a possible location, rather than Budapest or Kyiv. The foreign ministers are currently discussing the arrangements, and the meeting could even take place at the end of November,” Magyar said.

The prime minister also outlined his diplomatic engagements in the Irish capital. The European Political Community summit was held on Thursday, while an informal EU summit was scheduled for Friday. Magyar said he had also met the Secretary General of the Council of Europe, as well as the prime ministers of Armenia, Luxembourg, Kosovo and Ireland, and the President of Switzerland.

Hungary could benefit from pharmaceutical manufacturing returning to Europe

Commenting on his recent visit to Berlin, Magyar highlighted the opportunities for Hungary in the pharmaceutical industry, which has a long-standing tradition in the country.

He described it as a major opportunity that Germany and several other European countries are considering bringing the production of strategically important goods back to the EU and its single market, partly because of transit and supply chain problems.

Péter Magyar and Volodimir Zelensky at the EU Summit on 18 June 2026. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

Fuel prices and inflation remain under control, Magyar says

Asked about fuel prices in Hungary, the prime minister said the average price of petrol had fallen below HUF 600 per litre, close to the previous protected price. Diesel had also become cheaper following a significant decline in global crude oil prices.

He added that the government had taken steps to prevent diesel shortages and petrol station closures, particularly to protect hauliers and motorists who rely on diesel-powered vehicles.

Magyar also said inflation had not been this low for a very long time. He argued that the increase from 1.6% to 2% was relatively small, while food prices had actually fallen. Both the government and the National Bank of Hungary are planning for 3% inflation next year, which he described as “perfectly healthy”. He added that eurozone countries would be pleased with inflation of 2–2.5% or even 3%.

On economic growth, Magyar said the government was working with realistic and achievable figures in both the 2026 and 2027 budgets.

He attributed the economy’s modest 0.1% growth in the third quarter to drought, which caused more than HUF 800 billion in damage to agriculture alone, weighing on overall economic performance.

The government continues to forecast growth of 1.7–1.8% for 2026, as it did previously. The figure formed the basis for its 2.4% growth projection for next year. Both the European Commission and the central bank expect higher growth, Magyar noted.
