Magyar hits back at Orbán’s criticism of the budget

Responding to criticism of the budget by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, Magyar said he did not believe he should concern himself with interviews given by someone whose former government had seen half its members placed in pre-trial detention or arrested, or whose own family members had faced allegations of human trafficking.

Magyar insisted that his government had presented a well-founded budget. He accused the previous administration of delivering no economic growth during its final four years, bringing Hungary the highest inflation in Europe and allowing the prices of certain food products to double.

Istanbul Convention ratification could reach Parliament soon

The prime minister also announced that a parliamentary resolution on ratifying the Istanbul Convention could be submitted to Parliament without delay.

He said the government’s strategic cabinet had discussed amendments to the criminal law package he had partly announced on Wednesday. The Ministry of Health had also been consulting on changes to the so-called foetal heartbeat decree for months and had been working on a proposal for several weeks.

Magyar added that various ministries had already drawn up measures to support pregnant women, remove the prescription requirement for emergency contraception and tackle period poverty. Ratification of the Istanbul Convention would be the final step in this process.

Responding to criticism of the convention, he argued that women experiencing domestic or relationship violence do not care whether the term “gender” appears in an international agreement. He also pointed out that men can be victims of violence in relationships.

Magyar rejected criticism from former Health State Secretary Péter Takács, who had claimed the previous day that, because of Magyar’s alleged inferiority complex over his ex-wife and Zsolt Hegedűs’s supposed lack of backbone, 14-year-old girls would be able to take emergency contraceptive pills “like sweets”.

The prime minister stressed that many unwanted pregnancies had occurred precisely because women could not obtain the medication without a doctor’s prescription.

Mistaken agent-file disclosure has dealt a blow to public trust

Magyar was also asked whether the credibility of the government’s efforts to open up communist-era secret agent files had been undermined by the mistaken identification of Sándor Lezsák, a Fidesz politician and prominent member of the democratic opposition before the regime change, as a former network operative.

The prime minister said the legislation on opening the files had been developed jointly with archivists and historians and subsequently passed by Parliament. Some MPs from Fidesz and the Christian Democratic People’s Party (KDNP) had also voted in favour of it.

He stressed that the archives fall under Parliament’s authority, not that of the government. The head of the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security (ÁBTL) had accepted responsibility for the error and apologised, as Magyar himself had done in his capacity as prime minister.

Asked whether ÁBTL Director-General Gergő Bendegúz Cseh should remain in his position, Magyar said that, in his personal opinion, he could not continue in the role, adding that Cseh himself did not wish to do so.

However, he argued that a responsible leader should not walk away before the mistake has been addressed, saying that one should not “abandon a sinking ship”. Nevertheless, he made clear that Cseh would not continue his work.

Magyar acknowledged that millions of people had been waiting for the secret agent files to become public and that the recent mistake had dealt a blow to the process.

He maintained that the intention behind the initiative had been right and that everyone involved had done their best to ensure it went smoothly, although this had unfortunately not happened. The government had been addressing a 36-year-old failure to act, he concluded.

World.title: Budapest’s two biggest Christmas markets open today – here are the dates, opening hours and what to expect
World.content:
The festive season has officially begun in Budapest, as Advent Basilica and Vörösmarty Classic Xmas both open their gates on 13 November. Visitors can look forward to Hungarian handicrafts, festive food, spectacular decorations and plenty of Christmas magic until the beginning of 2027.

Budapest’s two biggest Christmas markets opened today

Budapest’s two best-known Christmas markets have officially opened today, 13 November, welcoming locals and tourists alike to enjoy the festive atmosphere in the heart of the Hungarian capital.

Located at St Stephen’s Basilica and Vörösmarty Square, the markets are among the city’s most popular winter attractions. Both will remain open over the Christmas period and New Year’s Eve, although their opening hours will vary on certain holidays.

Advent Basilica: Christmas magic in front of St Stephen’s Basilica

The award-winning Advent Basilica returns with nearly 100 Hungarian craft exhibitors, a wide selection of festive food and a spectacular Christmas setting.

Visitors can expect a beautifully decorated Christmas tree, illuminated decorations, a canopy of lights and the popular light projections on the façade of St Stephen’s Basilica. Further festive programmes will also take place throughout the event.

The market has been voted Europe’s most beautiful Christmas market four times, according to its organisers.

Opening dates: 13 November 2026 – 1 January 2027

General opening hours:

Monday–Thursday: 11 am–10 pm

Friday–Saturday: 11 am–11 pm

Sunday: 11 am–10 pm

Special opening hours:

24 December: 11 am–3 pm

25–26 December: 11 am–8 pm

31 December: 11 am–3 am (New Year’s Day)

1 January: 11 am–6 pm

More information is available on the official Advent Basilica website.

The Christmas market at at St Stephen’s Basilica. Photo: Facebook/Advent Bazilika

Vörösmarty Classic Xmas: festive traditions in the heart of Budapest

The Vörösmarty Classic Xmas also opens today, transforming one of Budapest’s most beautiful central squares into a festive meeting point.

The market will feature craft exhibitors, traditional Christmas treats and a small railway, offering an extra attraction for families visiting with children.

Opening dates: 13 November 2026 – early January 2027

General opening hours:

Monday–Thursday: 11 am–9 pm

Friday–Saturday: 11 am–10 pm

Sunday: 11 am–9 pm

Small railway opening hours:

Monday–Friday: 2 pm–8 pm

Saturday–Sunday: 11 am–8 pm

Special opening hours:

24 December: 10 am–2 pm

25–26 December: noon–6 pm

29–30 December: 11 am–9 pm

31 December: 11 am–3 am (New Year’s Day)

Please note that the craft exhibitors and small railway will operate for the last time on 28 December. The small railway will open at 2 pm on 26 December.

For further details, visit the official Vörösmarty Classic Xmas website.

Two Christmas markets, one festive Budapest experience

Whether you are looking for Hungarian handicrafts, traditional seasonal food, spectacular light displays or a family-friendly programme, both Christmas markets offer plenty of reasons to explore Budapest during the festive season.

The two locations are also within walking distance of each other, making it easy to visit both in one evening. For tourists and locals alike, they are a great starting point for discovering Budapest’s Christmas atmosphere.

World.title: Former FM Szijjártó reportedly helped deliver Russian smear material targeting Tisza politician to Hungary
World.content:
Hungary’s former foreign minister Péter Szijjártó reportedly coordinated with the Kremlin to bring Russian intelligence documents to Budapest, detailing efforts to discredit Tisza politician István Kapitány ahead of the 2026 election. The revelations come from a new book by investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi.

The Russian intelligence services allegedly worked to undermine the Tisza Party and strengthen Fidesz’s electoral position by spreading compromising material about István Kapitány, a former senior Shell executive who joined the opposition party. According to Friends with Benefits (“Barátság extrákkal”), the book by investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi, Szijjártó received several reports from Russia detailing these operations.

According to Telex’s summary, the documents were reportedly delivered through Hungarian diplomats based in Moscow and Belgrade, following coordination between Szijjártó and the Russian government.

Russian intelligence produced AI videos targeting Kapitány

One of the documents described a campaign to discredit Kapitány through a series of articles and manipulated videos. Russian officials reportedly claimed they had used publicly available information about his career at Shell, where he served as a vice-president responsible for developing the energy company’s subsidiaries, including those in Russia, between 2014 and 2024.

The material also included links to Hungarian-language websites and AI-generated videos allegedly showing Kapitány and his associates celebrating the outbreak of the war against Iran at a private party.

The apparent intention was to portray them as wealthy oil investors profiting from rising energy prices caused by the conflict. One of the Russian reports claimed that the video had reached 160,000 people on TikTok.

The campaign’s message echoed accusations frequently used by Fidesz: that Tisza politicians were wealthy, lived abroad and prioritised their personal financial interests over Hungary’s, allegedly supporting wars and higher energy prices while planning to abolish the country’s utility price cuts.

However, the strategy was reportedly less about maintaining a consistent political message and more about creating confusion, flooding the information space and undermining voters’ trust.

Hungarian ambassadors were asked to transport Russian documents

According to Panyi’s book, the first document discussed in detail reached Budapest on 23 March 2026 through Norbert Konkoly, Hungary’s ambassador to Moscow.

A few days later, Szijjártó reportedly asked him to collect another package of documents from the Russians.

Konkoly refused, expressing discomfort with what had effectively become a regular courier service between Moscow and Budapest.

The book suggests that the ambassador was already uneasy about the Hungarian government’s increasingly close relationship with Russia and Szijjártó’s frequent visits to Moscow.

Following Konkoly’s refusal, Szijjártó turned to Hungary’s ambassador in Belgrade, József Magyar, who reportedly delivered Russian documents to Budapest on 27 March and again shortly afterwards.

Some of the material referenced articles published on websites known for spreading pro-Kremlin narratives. One example was an article on Kárpáthír questioning Kapitány’s connections to Shell, BlackRock and the Tisza Party.

Campaign reached 18 countries, but its effectiveness is questionable

The Russian documents reportedly described an extensive international operation. According to the reports cited by Panyi, Russian intelligence distributed 64 pieces of material across 18 countries, targeting Kapitány’s reputation.

Articles and related content allegedly appeared on websites in the Netherlands, Italy, Germany, Luxembourg and Nigeria, among other countries. Russian reports claimed that the materials generated 2.9 million views, with subsequent publications adding another 486,000. However, the actual reach of these campaigns is difficult to verify.

The operation also included claims that Kapitány had discussed shutting down the Druzhba oil pipeline with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as well as allegations that a Tisza victory would lead to cuts in social benefits.

Interestingly, Russian operatives reportedly produced contradictory propaganda for different audiences. In materials aimed at Ukrainian readers, Kapitány was even portrayed as an agent of the Kremlin.

The timing of the Russian reports and Fidesz’s own campaign communications also raises questions. Several government and Fidesz attacks on Kapitány appeared after Szijjártó had reportedly received the Russian material.

Former Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó and Sergei Lavrov. Photo: Facebook/Szijjártó Péter

Was there a coordinated plan to keep Orbán in power?

While the Kremlin’s interest in keeping Viktor Orbán’s government in power clearly aligned with Fidesz’s political objectives, the precise extent of coordination between the two sides remains unclear. According to Panyi, a Hungarian intelligence officer told him after Fidesz’s election defeat that if an agreement had existed, Orbán would certainly have known about it.

The book also contains claims suggesting that parts of the Hungarian leadership had considered requesting Russian assistance to remain in power. One source from the Ministry of Defence described a ten-point plan based on escalating levels of Russian support.

“It was an escalation ladder: it was about what level of Russian assistance we would request,” the source reportedly explained.

The plan allegedly included seeking help from the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence service, at around the third stage. According to the source, this meant that considerably more aggressive measures had also been contemplated.

Although the Russian operation’s actual impact is still uncertain, the revelations raise serious questions about the extent of Moscow’s involvement in Hungary’s 2026 election campaign and the relationship between Russian intelligence and the former Hungarian government.

World.title: New documents reveal Orbán’s brother offered cooperation to former FM Péter Szijjártó
World.content:
Further documents linked to Hungary’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs have emerged, shedding light on the relationship between Áron Orbán, the brother of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, and former Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó. One email from 2023 shows Áron Orbán offering to cooperate with Szijjártó and recommending his newly appointed chief adviser. Two other documents reveal an earlier request for a personal meeting and a visit to the ministry in 2016.

György Velkey, Parliamentary State Secretary at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, published the documents on Facebook. He said he and his colleagues began searching the ministry’s records for material related to Áron Orbán after the former prime minister’s brother was detained on suspicion of human smuggling. They found several emails of interest and decided to make three of them public.

Áron Orbán recommended his chief adviser to Szijjártó

One of the documents is an email sent in September 2023, in which Áron Orbán directly offered cooperation to Péter Szijjártó, who was foreign minister at the time. Introducing himself as a chief executive, Orbán also presented a newly appointed chief adviser to the minister.

Velkey obscured the adviser’s name, citing personal rights, although he suggested in his post that it would not be difficult to work out who the person was.

In the email, Áron Orbán said the adviser had been appointed because of his achievements in education, training, IT, centralisation and consolidation projects. He asked Szijjártó to place his trust in the adviser and contact him not only when planning and implementing projects but also when preparing decisions.

Orbán described the proposed cooperation as a strategic step that could help ensure the high-standard implementation of the objectives set. According to Velkey, Szijjártó forwarded the email to his immediate colleagues.

Earlier request for a meeting with the ministry

Another email, dating from July 2023, shows Áron Orbán asking Eszter Gyarmati, then the ministry’s Administrative State Secretary, for a personal meeting. The proposed discussion concerned strategic cooperation in education, IT and security technology services.

Orbán’s chief adviser was also expected to attend. However, the published correspondence does not establish whether the meeting eventually took place.

The third document dates back further. It records that Szijjártó received Áron Orbán at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on 27 May 2016. Tamás Menczer was also among the recipients of the related correspondence.

At the end of his Facebook post, Velkey hinted that more ministry documents concerning Áron Orbán could emerge. He concluded with the words “To be continued”, suggesting that further revelations may follow.

World.title: Heavy rainfall brings Hungary November’s average in a single day
World.content:
Large parts of Hungary received exceptionally heavy rainfall on Thursday, with several weather stations recording the equivalent of the country’s entire average November precipitation in just 24 hours. The downpours also brought a new national daily precipitation record.

Record amount of rain reached Hungary

According to Hungary’s national meteorological service, HungaroMet, more than 30 millimetres of downpour fell across extensive areas, while some locations in the north recorded over 50 millimetres. The average monthly precipitation for November is 48.6mm, meaning that several measuring stations reached or exceeded this amount in a single day.

Kékestető recorded 59.9mm in the 24-hour period, while both the Gerecse hills and Balassagyarmat received 55.9mm, according to data shared by HungaroMet.

A month of precipitation in one day

The heaviest recorded downpour was in Tardos, in Komárom-Esztergom County, where 66mm fell on Thursday, 12 November. This set a new national daily precipitation record, surpassing the previous high of 61mm, measured in Letenye in 1997.

HungaroMet said several weather systems arriving from the west brought successive waves of rain to the Carpathian Basin. Rain initially affected mainly southern areas before the extensive precipitation zone associated with Cyclone Charles moved across the country, delivering widespread and substantial rainfall.

World.title: Budapest metro line to undergo maintenance this weekend
World.content:
Budapest’s M2 metro line will operate on a shortened route this weekend due to scheduled track maintenance, with replacement buses running between Deák Ferenc Square and Déli Railway Station.

M2 metro line to undergo maintenance

According to the Budapest Transport Centre (BKK), the changes will begin at 10 PM on Friday, 13 November, and remain in effect throughout Saturday and Sunday, 14–15 November. During this period, metro trains will run only between Örs vezér Square and Deák Ferenc Square.

Passengers travelling between Deák Ferenc Square and Déli Railway Station will be able to use replacement buses marked M2. The buses will cross the Margaret Bridge and also serve Kossuth Lajos Square and Batthyány Square.

Alternative routes for passengers

At Kossuth Lajos Square, passengers heading towards Déli Railway Station should board in Alkotmány Street, while those travelling towards Deák Ferenc Square should use the stop on Bajcsy-Zsilinszky Road. At Batthyány Square, buses towards Déli Railway Station will stop in Csalogány Street, near the junction with Fő Street. Replacement buses heading towards Deák Ferenc Square will stop in front of the church.

To reduce disruption between Buda and Pest, the 4–6 tram service will run more frequently throughout the weekend. The BKK recommends that passengers travelling to Széll Kálmán Square use the 4–6 tram, changing at Blaha Lujza Square. Those coming from Hűvösvölgy or Óbuda and heading towards the city centre are also advised to take the tram.

Plan ahead with BudapestGO

Passengers travelling from the Pasarét area to the city centre, or from around Astoria to Buda, can use bus 5. Travellers heading from Buda to the M3 metro line are advised to take the 4–6 tram and change at Nyugati Railway Station. Those arriving by train can transfer to the M4 metro at Kelenföld railway station.

The BKK advises passengers to check their journeys using the BudapestGO app, which provides real-time public transport information and route planning, as well as ticket and pass purchases.

World.title: Fallen tree disrupts key international rail route between Budapest and Vienna; trains rerouted

Train services between Bicske and Herceghalom have been suspended, with passengers facing significantly longer journey times and replacement bus transfers. According to MÁV, the disruption is expected to continue until the afternoon.

The fallen tree reportedly struck both tracks’ overhead wires and also fell partly onto a train arriving at the station. The S10 service that left Győr at 7:38 am for Budapest’s Déli railway station was unable to continue beyond Bicske Lower.

Railway maintenance underway

The incident comes as MÁV carries out maintenance work along the Budapest–Győr–Hegyeshalom railway line ahead of the December timetable change.

Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy said around 26 kilometres of track were being maintained, with speed restrictions removed or prevented on nearly three kilometres. The work is expected to eliminate restrictions currently adding up to 12 minutes to journey times.

More than ten locations between Budaörs and Hegyeshalom are involved, including Bicske, Tatabánya, Tata, Almásfüzitő, Komárom, Győr and Mosonmagyaróvár. The programme includes moving at least 8,000 tonnes of crushed stone, replacing wooden sleepers with reinforced concrete ones at three sets of points, and renewing sections of track.

The aim is to reduce technical disruptions, improve punctuality and make train services more reliable.

World.title: Police fail to identify women who attacked blind man in Budapest shopping centre
World.content:
Police have suspended an investigation after two women allegedly tried to rob a blind man with a guide dog in a Budapest shopping centre, assaulting him when he resisted. The suspects have not been identified.

Two women attacked a blind man

The incident happened during the summer and was reported by RTL Híradó on Thursday, 12 November. The Baráthegyi Guide Dog School Foundation has now shared video footage of the attack to highlight the vulnerability of people with disabilities.

The victim, Dániel Klabacsek, is a young man with multiple disabilities, including visual impairment, autism and a mobility disability. He was accompanied by his guide dog, Vidra (meaning “otter”), when he encountered the two women at a busy shopping centre in Budapest.

According to his account, the women offered to help him find his way to the metro. He accepted, but instead of taking him there, they led him to the rooftop of the building. He later asked them to help give his dog some water.

One of the women sat him down on a bench and started talking to him before unclipping his waist bag. When he noticed, she reportedly claimed she only wanted to check how much money was inside, then returned it.

Klabacsek subsequently asked the women to escort him back into the building. The situation escalated in the lift, where one of them tried to take his bag again. When he resisted, the women allegedly forced him down and repeatedly banged his head against the lift wall.

According to the victim, one of the women also shouted: “Don’t resist us, you dog!”

Klabacsek said he was deeply affected by the experience and struggling to process what had happened. At one point, he shouted for help inside the shopping centre, but nobody came to his assistance.

Investigation suspended

Klabacsek eventually filed a police report on the advice of his guide dog trainers. The foundation said it released the footage to draw attention to the vulnerability of people with disabilities and the importance of protecting them.

Police told RTL that the investigation into suspected robbery was suspended in mid-October because officers had been unable to establish the identities of the alleged perpetrators. 24.hu also reported that the investigation had been suspended, giving late October as the date.

The two women have therefore not been identified, and no suspects have been brought to justice in connection with the incident.

World.title: Week in Review: To Be Or Not To Be
World.content:
Last week, the European Commission released its annual progress reports on the EU accession hopefuls. But in Serbia’s case, the report was more about backsliding on reforms than on progress, reflecting a tortuous year for the country.

In her interview for Balkan Insight, Dragana Djurica, head of the European Movement in Serbia, takes stock of where Serbia’s EU accession process stands. Optimistically, she argues that the bleak report could act as a roadmap for reform in the country after the recent change of power.

World.title: EU, UK ‘Concerned’ as Kosovo Moves Against Hague Court’s Powers Again
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Protest in Pristina against the verdict convicting four high-profile Kosovo Liberation Army figures , October 1, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

The European Union and United Kingdom have warned Kosovo MPs to seek international advice as they review an amended law aimed at curbing the powers of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers on Friday.

The legislation was initiated by the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, after the Hague-based war crimes court convicted PDK ex-leader Hashim Thaci and three other wartime Kosovo Liberation Army officials who fought for liberation from Serbia’s oppression, sparking outrage among Kosovo Albanians.

The EU Office in Kosovo said that “the amendments raise serious concerns regarding Kosovo’s international obligations and compliance with basic rule of law principles, in particular judicial independence, the protection of victims and witnesses, the continuity of procedural rights, and effective accountability”.

In a statement on Facebook, the EU also said that the amendments “also raise concerns regarding their constitutionality”, and stressed “the need for prior consultations before any adoption, in line with Kosovo’s international obligations”.

The British Embassy in Pristina echoed these concerns, saying in a statement on Facebook that “we fear that the proposed amendments will do nothing to serve Kosovo’s essential interests and will undermine its relations with international partners and supporters”.

The British Embassy encouraged MPs to “take the time for further consultations internally and with the EU and other international allies to find a better solution”.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers is a hybrid court that is located in The Hague and staffed by internationals but is part of Kosovo’s judiciary. It was established in 2015 to try former Kosovo Liberation Army fighters, under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies.

The establishment of the Specialist Chambers was initiated in an exchange of letters between Kosovo’s President and the EU, making it an international agreement, and therefore the EU requires consultations for any changes in its legal framework.

MPs initially voted for the amended law in a rushed procedure on October 6, under pressure from protests that turned violent outside the parliament building and the need to push through the urgent last-minute election of Kosovo’s new president to avoid the continuation of a political crisis that had lasted almost two years.

The vote followed weeks of protests after the four former KLA leaders were convicted of the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder.

Hashim Thaci and Jakup Krasniqi were sentenced to 25 years in prison each and Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi received 18 and 13 years respectively. An appeal is expected.

Given the uncertainty over whether the Hague court will indict anyone else, the effect of the proposed legislation is uncertain, however.

Kosovo MPs are also undecided on whether the bill in its current form is adequate.

On Thursday, at the Parliamentary Commission for Legislation, MP Vigan Qorrolli from ruling party Vetevendosje argued that a redraft is needed.

“Our position as the political majority is very clear; we believe that a new legislative initiative – drafted with care and through joint parliamentary participation – would be the most responsible way to address this issue,” Qorrolli said.

However, PDK MP Blerta Deliu-Kodra said that, following discussions with other political parties, “we have agreed to pass the bill, but there is no consensus on amending it. We must proceed with the bill as it stands, and subsequently, we will enter the amendment process.”

World.title: Eight Key Defendants in Istanbul Municipality Mass Trial Freed From Custody
World.content:
Eight defendants in the Istanbul Municipality trial walked free on Friday after a court ordered their release late on Thursday despite prosecutors demanding that all detained defendants remain behind bars.

Those freed included Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu’s lawyer, Mehmet Pehlivan, and Fatos Pinar Turker, manager of Istanbul Municipality’s media company. The decision brought relief in opposition circles, although Imamoglu and other defendants remain in prison.

“I am happy, of course, but also saddened. My brother and my friends are in prison. I want them to regain their freedom soon,” Pehlivan said on Friday after leaving prison.

Turker also focused on those who remained detained: “My only wish is to reunite with my daughters. My thoughts are with the other friends who remain imprisoned,” he said.

Mayor Imamoglu, who is also the main opposition presidential candidate for the next election, is one of the 46 defendants still in custody after the eight were released. A total of 436 people have been indicted in the case, accused of involvement in corruption. They insist that the charges are politically motivated and false.

During the latest hearing, Imamoglu again denied the prosecution’s claims and criticised its reliance on secret witnesses.

“This pile of rubbish built on a secret witness has collapsed. There is not a single tangible witness,” Imamoglu told the court, demanding his release.

Defence lawyers and opposition figures have challenged the use of secret witnesses in the case and demanded the release of those being held, pending trial.

Over the last few years, dozens of opposition mayors and hundreds of party members have been arrested on corruption and terror charges.

Imamoglu was arrested on March 19, 2025. The prosecutor’s office is demanding a 2,352-year prison sentence for him. Imamoglu denies all the accusations.

Opposition politicians, rights groups and international organisations have said the government is using the judiciary to crush its political rivals in what they call an unprecedented crackdown.

World.title: After the Protests: Bulgaria as a Cautionary Tale
World.content:
“The situation is not better, not worse. It’s just the same,” said Vesislava Tancheva, spokesperson for Bulgarians United for One Goal, the civic association behind the protest outside the Russian embassy and which also demonstrated against the previous government. It goes by the acronym BOETS, which in Bulgarian means ‘fighter’.

One thing is different, however – the scale of the protests.

In November and December 2025, tens of thousands of Bulgarians took to the streets across the country. The collapse of the ruling coalition led by the centre-right GERB party, the dominant party in Bulgaria since 2008, was portrayed in media reports as a success story.

Twenty-two-year-old law student Aleksandar Tanev saw firsthand how quickly Gen Z can mobilise. After a few demonstrations, he and some fellow students founded Students Against Mafia. They were soon inundated with requests from young people across the country to join.

A year on, however, Tanev says “it was not enough”.

“This corrupted management that ruled Bulgaria for more than 15 years is responsible for our cities, our roads, our education,” Tanev told BIRN. “They are guilty, but we vote for them. We need to understand our responsibility.”

He was echoed by Asen Lazarov, 27, another of the young people who took to the streets last year and co-founder of the NGO Active Politics, which aims to make politics more accessible to young people.

“Protests are a way to express your democratic participation, but they should not be the final step,” he said. “We should expect more from the politicians that we’ve elected.”

At a time when social movements in France, Albania, Spain or Serbia are challenging the political establishment, Bulgaria offers an instructive case study.

Governments change, system remains

World.title: Democracy Digest: Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary Pick Fight with Berlin Over Ukraine Aid
World.content:
Hungarian PM Peter Magyar also criticised the idea of linking Ukraine’s financial support to the ongoing EU budget talks during a visit to Germany this week. “I would like to express, diplomatically and politely but nevertheless firmly, that I do not consider it a good idea to link the European budget, which is ultimately about the EU itself, in any way to another issue,” he said at a press conference with Merz in Berlin, where he otherwise heralded a new beginning in German-Hungarian bilateral relations after years of frosty ties under his predecessor Viktor Orban. Magyar also delivered the renowned State of Europe speech organised by the CDU-affiliated Konrad Adenauer Foundation. Speaking in German, he did not spare Europe’s governing elites, accusing them of having “lost contact with the people”, nor Brussels, which had detected the problems Europe was facing but had been unable to find solutions in recent years. The PM also warned against radical movements offering easy solutions to problems but, in fact, merely end up dividing and polarizing Europe and serving the interests of outside, often hostile forces. His view of the EU sees a gradual shift back towards nation states, which, in his words, know better what their societies need. He also pleaded for cheaper energy sources – though stopped short of saying they should be Russian – and for strengthening the continent’s industrial fabric and competitiveness, and stepping up the fight against illegal migration and climate change.

Fico’s mood this week was not helped by his government losing its parliamentary majority. The prime minister, who spent years demanding early elections whenever his opponents found themselves in the same position, now seems prepared to govern without one. The numbers became clear on Wednesday, when a controversial amendment to the Criminal Procedure Code received just 75 votes in the 150-seat parliament. Two MPs around the recently dismissed environment minister and lawmaker Tomas Taraba voted against it, while former coalition MP Jan Ferencak abstained. The amendment sought to restrict the use of testimony from cooperating defendants. Prosecutors and anti-corruption groups warned that it could undermine ongoing criminal cases, including the “Purgatory” police corruption trial, in which high-profile Smer politician and former police chief Tibor Gaspar is a defendant. Gaspar denies the legislation was intended to help him personally in his legal disputes. Things went wrong again that afternoon. A bill to abolish postal voting from abroad was derailed because none of its sponsors appeared to present it. Under parliamentary rules recently introduced by the coalition itself, the proposal could now be delayed for six months. Gaspar, who was chairing the session and is also among the bill’s sponsors, wants that interpretation reviewed. Fico once had little patience for governments relying on independent MPs. He accused former PM Mikulas Dzurinda of buying support and demanded early elections when Iveta Radicova and Eduard Heger struggled with their majorities. In 2006, he described opaque deals with independent MPs as one of the gravest attacks on parliamentary democracy since 1989. His own coalition now has 75 dependable MPs. Fico says he will negotiate with Taraba’s group and accepts that some bills may fail. Smer still insists this is not a minority government.

World.title: High Bank Fees Hamper Albania’s Crackdown on Cash
World.content:
In Tirana’s 9-Katëshet neighbourhood, people queue for ice cream at 100 lek a scoop.

Previously, the ice cream parlour only accepted cash, but the growing number of tourists among their clientele, many of whom don’t carry cash, has forced the business to start taking bank cards too.

If you pay by card, however, the price is 125 lek.

“We don’t make any extra profit from this,” the woman behind the counter said. “It’s the fee charged by the bank that provides us with the card payment service.”

World.title: On a Bosnian Mountainside, a Quiet Exodus Leaves Only the Elderly Behind
World.content:
As All Saints’ Day approached, Dubravka Jurisic sat down in her home in Straza and counted its residents.

She ran a finger down the handwritten pages where for years she has kept a record of births, deaths and who lives where in this village on the slopes of Mount Majevica, in the far northeast of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Reaching the end, she declared: “Seventy-one people currently live in the village.”

That’s less than half the number counted the last time Bosnia held a census, in 2013. Then, authorities registered 188 residents of Straza, part of Srebrenik municipality, though census totals can include Bosnian citizens who have lived abroad for years. In January 2017, Jurisic made her own count: 138.

Between 1991 and 2013, the population of Srebrenik municipality as a whole shrank from 40,882 to 39,678. The town of Srebrenik itself grew by roughly 1,400 residents. The villages, in other words, are emptying faster than the town.

Those who remain are, by and large, elderly. While Srebrenik municipality is majority Bosniak, Straza is Catholic Croat. Many of its residents hold Croatian passports, easing their departure since Croatia joined the European Union in 2013.

“Before the war, there were about 100 unmarried young men in the village,” said Jurisic, 52, referring to the 1992-95 war in Bosnia during the collapse of federal Yugoslavia. “Today we don’t have a single one.” According to Jurisic, the youngest resident is already a teenager.

World.title: Bulgarian economy grew by 0.6% in Q3 2026 – flash estimate
World.content:
Bulgaria’s economy grew by 0.6 per cent in the third quarter of the year, the National Statistical Institute (NSI) said in a flash estimate on November 13. In real terms, gross domestic product (GDP) in Bulgaria in July-September was 35.51 billion euro.

Year-on-year, the economic growth in the third quarter was 2.5 per cent. NSI is due to announce preliminary growth figures for the quarter on December 4.

The flash estimate’s seasonally-adjusted data showed domestic consumption increase by 1.4 per cent during the third quarter, and it was 6.3 per cent higher on an annual basis. Gross fixed capital formation shrank by 0.8 per cent in July-September, and was 0.5 per cent lower compared to the third quarter of 2025.

Exports fell by four per cent compared to the second quarter of the year, and were 5.5 per cent lower compared to the third quarter of last year, while imports shrank by 4.8 per cent on a quarterly basis and were down one per cent year-on-year.

The country recorded a trade surplus of 357.2 million euro in the third quarter, the equivalent of one per cent of GDP, NSI said.

World.title: Defence Minister: MiG-29s and F-16s will guard Bulgaria’s skies ‘on rotational basis’ in 2027
World.content:
Bulgarian skies will be guarded on a rotational basis by MiG-29s and F-16 fighter jets in 2027, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told a November 13 news conference about the defence budget for next year.

Stoyanov did not explain what is meant by rotation, but he said that in 2027, F-16s will only be on duty during the day because they are not certified and prepared for night flights.

He made it clear that the military will continue to rely on the nearly 40-year-old Soviet MiG-29 fighter jets, without it being clear how many of them are still operational, where spare parts will be obtained, and where they will be repaired and tested for safety.

At the same time, Stoyanov spoke of problems surrounding the use of the new US-made F-16 fighter jets. Bulgaria has already acquired eight of them and is waiting for another eight, which will probably arrive in Bulgaria in 2029, a delay from the initial schedule.

The first eight F-16s will also be modified. For example, they must be equipped with the new AN/ALQ-254(V)1 Viper Shield electronic warfare suite.

This is a mandatory electronic warfare package because it is related to the survival of the F-16 against modern radars and electronic threats. Stoyanov said that the US had given an assurance that the Viper Shield systems would be delivered and installed in 2027.

In addition, according to Stoyanov, the already trained Bulgarian pilots are prepared for air-to-air mode, not air-to-ground, that is, they cannot hit ground targets.

The repair of the engines, as well as the repair of maintenance units for the MiG-29 aircraft , is to be ensured.

“There is no way we can continue to fulfill our functional obligations, including our obligations to Nato structures, without the MiG-29 aircraft,” Stoyanov said.

There are also two new projects included in the new budget. They are related to the maintenance of the F-16. One is specifically for the maintenance of the F-16, and the second project is for the acquisition of additional missile armament for the aircraft.

As to when the F-16s can do duty fulltime, Stoyanov said that this could happen when the Viper Shield systems are received. But he added that the necessary pilots must also be available.

The draft budget of the Defence Ministry for 2027 envisages expenditures amounting to 2.23 per cent of gross domestic product.

The total planned finance for defence spending amounts to 3.151 billion euro, which is an increase of 17 per cent compared with 2026.

“The largest increase is in capital expenditures – from 868 million euro this year to over 1.223 billion euro next year,” Stoyanov said. This represents 40.83 per cent of the ministry’s budget budget.

“This is a budget for accelerated modernisation. With Nato’s requirement for a share of capital expenditures above 20 per cent, we exceed 40 per cent,” he said.

Stoyanov said that Bulgaria is working on many projects, both under the SAFE loan mechanism and from the Bulgarian budget.

This includes the acquisition of seven new three-coordinate (3D) radars , a coastal anti-ship missile system from the United States , French Caesar self-propelled artillery systems (SAU), German Iris ground-based air defence systems, 155 mm shells, vehicles, multiple launch rocket systems, drones.

The budget envisages purchasing six firefighting aircraft.

“We are working on the implementation of a project to acquire up to six firefighting aircraft. If the procedure passes without appeals, there is a possibility that the first two will be delivered by the end of 2027, after which the procedure for their absorption will begin,” Stoyanov said.

Stoyanov said that new projects will also be launched with national funds, including modernisation of the avionics of the C-27J Spartan transport aircraft and maintenance of the MiG-29.

It is also planned to acquire new small arms, unmanned aerial systems and space-based platforms; for reconnaissance and surveillance of land and sea targets, strike and FPV drones.

Personnel costs are maintained, with an additional four million euro to compensate for the increase in the minimum wage.

Military personnel will welcome the new year with frozen salaries, due to the freezing for the second time of the automatic increase tied to the average salary. ” If we increase salaries, we have to cut capital expenditures , ” Dimitar Stoyanov said recently.

To fill the shortage in the Bulgarian military, a target of 27.5 million euros from the central budget has been earmarked for the appointment of new military personnel.

At the same time, the resources saved from the dismissal of over 400 employees in the Ministry’s administration this year are being redirected to positions in the military formations.

Stoyanov hopes to recruit at least 1000 new military personnel in 2027, but he made it clear that he is not very optimistic.

The military itself admits that in some units there is even a 25 per cent shortage of personnel, with the situation being the worst in the army.

The Defence Ministry has tried to patch things up with initiatives such as “Be a Soldier” and with changes in the law to introduce so-called voluntary service, but in practice there has been little positive result and the personnel gap remains.

(Archive photo of Bulgarian Air Force Mig-29s, a Spartan and F-16s: Defence Ministry)

World.title: Opposition parties slam PM Radev over ‘reservations’ on Dublin declaration on European security
World.content:
In statements on November 13, opposition parties slammed Bulgarian Prime Minister Roumen Radev over Bulgaria’s position to support “with reservations” France’s initiative on key principles of European security, presented in Dublin.

While some media reports said that Bulgaria was alone among EU countries in not signing the declaration, the website of the President of France showed Bulgaria among the signatories, and the Bulgarian government information service said that the country had supported it, with reservations about the preamble.

Daniel Mitov, an MP for Boiko Borissov’s opposition coalition GERB-UDF and a former foreign minister, said that Bulgaria continues to pursue an unclear foreign policy.

“It was not clear again what he (Radev) signed, what he did not sign and with what reservations,” Mitov said.

“We have Schrödinger’s foreign policy again – we are both there and not there. They never explained what these reservations are,” he said.

“Obviously, Prime Minister Radev is not talking to Bulgarian citizens through such explanations. He is talking to his masters in the Kremlin and giving them a signal that he is actually defending their interests in European formats,” Mitov said.

Borissov said: “Did we sign the declaration or didn’t we? I didn’t understand! German media says we didn’t, the Elysee Palace says we did”.

Ivailo Mirchev, co-leader of opposition coalition Democratic Bulgaria, said: “This is yet another ‘hybrid’ position from Bulgaria—we have joined, yet we haven’t joined”.

“Mr. Radev is clearly afraid of Russia. We ought to treat our partners as a true ally would,” Mirchev said.

Radev, speaking on November 13, said that Bulgaria supported the declaration with reservations only regarding the preamble.

“And we support the declaration in its working part, where we have clearly expressed principles for joint efforts to counter organized crime, terrorism, hybrid attacks, the production and distribution of drugs, and countering illegal immigration,” Radev said.

“But we also take into account that negotiations are currently underway, finally at a high diplomatic level, for a peaceful solution to the war in Ukraine. It is here that we think that the language of common European documents should reflect the dynamics of these political processes, especially when it comes to negotiations,” he said.

“That is why we also expressed reservations about the preamble of the declaration, so that these formulations correspond to these dynamics. So that we can have a broader scope of dialogue and not exclude peaceful solutions in their entirety.”

Radev said that in the earlier versions, there was a formulation about the importance of the negotiations in Abu Dhabi “and that we should support them, then that disappeared, dropped out”.

“We insist on having such a text, to take it into account and not to narrow the field for dialogue and the options for finding a solution. We supported this declaration with reservations only in the preamble. What we have reservations about – these are the formulations in light of the negotiations that have already begun. This is an adopted document by Bulgaria and we welcome it, my reservations to the preamble are recorded.”

Regarding Bulgaria’s position on a new EU loan for Ukraine, Radev said: “Our position is clear – we support all efforts for peace”.

“I do not accept the imposition of the position for peace from a position of force, because we saw a year and a half ago, when I stated it, that this will only lead to more victims, more destruction and an even greater escalation of the conflict, which is already a risk not only for Europe, but for the entire world,” he said .

“We must take into account that Bulgaria, unlike other EU member states, is the country with the largest historical community in Ukraine. And we are deeply concerned by the fact that Bulgarians continue to die in this war every day,” Radev said.

“And that is why we want peace to be restored as quickly as possible. The task of our government is to help our compatriots in Ukraine live in peace as soon as possible, but also to have access to education, healthcare, electricity, and heating during this transitional period. And this will not be solved by investing in military means.”

Radev again referred to Bulgaria being in an excessive deficit procedure, as he has before when speaking about assistance for Ukraine.

“We are in an excessive deficit procedure. We have problems with the reserves in the state. And we have no way in this situation to provide financial resources, but in no case do we hinder the decisions of other member states,” he said.

“Whoever decides to help and invest financial resources in whatever they decide. So we are not blocking anyone in this situation,” Radev said.

“We are ready to talk about mechanisms that will guarantee that these funds will not go to weapons, but to humanitarian activities, to support with electricity, to medical activities, and this is very important for us – we want to see mechanisms that will target these funds, if we invest such as a guarantor, to go specifically to our community. It is compactly expressed in several regions of Ukraine,” he said.

(Photo: government.bg)

World.title: War of words follows consumer watchdog action against retail chains in Bulgaria
World.content:
A war of words lasting days has followed action by Bulgaria’s consumer protection body against retail chains in Bulgaria, with the row inevitably also attracting political comments.

As The Sofia Globe reported on November 9, Bulgaria’s Consumer Protection Commission (CPC) said that it had fined supermarket chain Kaufland Bulgaria 75.7 million euro, citing “unfair trade practices towards Bulgarian food producers”.

The regulator announced three violations against suppliers: pressure to reduce delivery prices, unfair deduction of fees for services, and unjustified delay in price increase negotiations. The decision is subject to appeal in court.

The chain rejects the accusations, claims that the total added value they generate for the state is almost 14 billion euro and it is preparing for a legal battle.

Mihail Petrov, CEO of Kaufland Bulgaria: “And if Kaufland goes on a bobsled ride down, then the bankruptcy of Corpbank will seem like a spring breeze to them. Kaufland has a lot of loans, a lot of suppliers, it has 8,800 employees and stop practicing on it. I can’t wait to go to court and turn the CPC’s act into dust”.

The retail chain’s director’s warnings about a possible outflow of investments prompted a sharp response from Economy Minister Alexander Pulev, who described Petrov’s tone as arrogant and said that the government would not give in to such warnings.

“We are not at war with retail chains, we are at war with unfair trade practices,” Pulev said.

The FMCG (Fast Moving Consumer Goods) market is quite profitable, quite liquid, even if there is an outflow in the market position of a chain, this vacuum will be filled literally within a few weeks by their competitors,” he said.

“Before threatening the Bulgarian state, let this gentleman open the statistics and look at the fact that literally the latest data for this year show a 100 per cent growth in foreign direct investment in the country, so I am calm, I have no reason for any concern about this type of arrogance,” Pulev said.

On Facebook, Prime Minister Roumen Radev’s Progressive Bulgaria ruling party said: “No matter how big you are, you are not above the law.

“When he (Petov) makes an analogy with CorpBank, the Kaufland manager confuses the law with lawlessness,” Progressive Bulgaria said.

“No one is stronger than the state when it applies the law to protect the rights of its citizens. Such declarations only confirm the correctness of the control bodies. Instead of arguments, we hear threats,” the ruling party said.

The Confederation of Independent Trade Unions in Bulgaria (CITUB) also expressed serious concern about the public statements by the management of Kaufland Bulgaria .

CITUB said that it does dispute the company’s right to defend its interests through legal means, but it is unacceptable for the jobs and fate of employees to be used as an argument to exert pressure on state institutions.

“Every company has the right to defend its interests in court. At the same time, CITUB considers it unacceptable for the jobs and fate of workers to be used as an argument for putting pressure on state institutions in connection with the exercise of their legal powers,” the trade union organisation said.

Ivailo Mirchev, an MP for opposition coalition Democratic Bulgaria, said that Petrov’s statement was arrogant and unacceptable.

Instead of scaring with catastrophic scenarios, the management of Kaufland should think about whether it has always been fair to Bulgarian producers over the years and whether it has had unacceptable commercial practices, Mirchev said.

Milena Dragiyska, chief executive of Lidl Bulgaria – a Lidl shop in Vidin was shut down temporarily earlier this week by the Bulgarian Food Safety Agency over alleged violations – described to the media how the pressure was affecting the daily work in the shops.

Dragiyska said there have been cases where seven, eight or nine inspectors have arrived at employees who are on their own shift.

She alleged that inspectors had apologised to staff, explaining that they were ordered to find grounds for a sanction.

“Actually, the big question is what is the goal? That is not clear to us,” Dragiyska said.

She warned that the consequences of this pressure could affect thousands of jobs and Bulgarian producers who rely on the chains for the sale of their goods. According to her, Lidl alone works with over 300 Bulgarian producers, and the volume of joint work is growing.

Dragiyska insisted that the conversation with the state focus on irrigation, labour, financing and the competitiveness of Bulgarian production.

Bulgarian food producers and processors have said that state pressure on large retail chains is also threatening their own production.

Zhivka Grozdeva from the Association of Fruit Growers in Bulgaria believes that the voice of producers who have been working successfully with the chains for years remains silenced in the public conversation.

At a conference of the Association for Modern Trade – an association of which most major retailers in Bulgaria are members – Grozdeva said that large retailers provide a market for significant quantities of Bulgarian fruits and vegetables.

” Without them, part of the production would remain unsold or even unpicked ,” said Grozdeva, who is also a fruit producer.

She said that no one is obliged to work with chains if they prefer another option.

Asked to comment on the average markups on Bulgarian fruit, she estimated that they amount to about 10 per cent-15 per cent, unlike small shops, where, according to her, it reaches 50 per cent.

Grozdeva described the relationship with the chains as a direct negotiation process: the manufacturer sends an offer, the retailer responds, and both parties specify the terms and deliveries.

According to her, the main obstacles to Bulgarian production lie elsewhere – in insecure access to water for irrigation, as irrigation systems cover 1/7 of the country’s territory, the shortage of workers, and the growing administrative burden.

“They increase costs and make it difficult to compete with producers from other countries,” Grozdeva said.

“I see a partner in the large chains,” Vladislav Mihaylov from the National Association of Dairy Processors said during the Association for Modern Trade conference.

Mihaylov described the pressure on foreign chains in recent weeks as an “undeclared war”.

“Nobody wins from any war. Neither the state nor the consumers. We, the producers, are between a rock and a hard place,” Mihaylov said.

Nikolai Vulkavnov, executive director of the Association of Modern Trade, said: “Progress is not measured solely by the price of cheese in the shop”.

He said that constant changes in rules, unpredictable enforcement and huge sanctions could lead to investments being frozen or withdrawn, with consequences for jobs and incomes.

“There will be no new jobs, existing ones may be cut, salaries may fall,” Vulkanov said.

On November 13, GERB leader Boiko Borissov sharply criticised Kaufland Bulgaria’s Petrov’s statement.

Borissov described Petrov’s words as absolutely unacceptable: “They will certainly fire him and all this has to happen, because no one will like such a statement, no one will allow it”.

The GERB leader said that he was wondering whether the government wanted to take Bulgaria back to the time of the communist-era state-owned shops.

Borissov said that he suspects that those close to the government are interested in the properties of Kaufland and other large retail chains.

“I guess because communists never do anything for their own sake, and the best properties in big cities are in these chains,” Borissov said.

In my opinion, one of Radev’s oligarchs has looked around in the chains and now they will do everything possible to expel them. They are worth chasing, I emphasise, with such behaviour, but they do nothing for their own sake,” he said.

(Photo: Bartosz Wacawski/ freeimages.com)

World.title: Bulgaria supported ‘with reservations’ declaration in Dublin on European security
World.content:
Bulgaria has supported with reservations the French initiative on key principles of European security, presented at the Ninth Summit of the European Political Community in Dublin, the government government information service said on November 13.

Radev expressed written reservations to the preamble of the declaration, requesting that the political messages be adapted to the current stage of the peace negotiations in Ukraine, the statement said.

The statement followed media reports that Bulgaria was alone among European Union member states to not have signed the declaration.

Bulgaria supports the achievement of a just and lasting peace in Ukraine through negotiations, the new round of talks in Abu Dhabi with the mediation of the United States is an important step in this direction, according to the statement.

“European positions must support this process, and the language of the common documents must reflect the dynamics of the processes and expectations from the peace negotiations,” it said.

The preamble of the document speaks of “the unprovoked full-scale Russian aggression against Ukraine and the growing threats to the stability of Europe”.

It also says that the signatories “reaffirm their firm support for the independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders”.

They emphasise that Russia’s hybrid campaigns and attempts to undermine support for Ukraine will only strengthen their commitment to Ukraine and their resolve.

The signatories recall that the path to peace in Ukraine must be decided together with Ukraine and that any issue affecting European security must be resolved together with Europeans.

It is emphasised that Ukraine’s security is an integral part of Euro-Atlantic security and that the future development of European strategic stability will be conditioned by the end of the war in Ukraine.

This is the full text of the declaration, as posted on the website of the President of France:

Committed to peace and upholding international law, and in the face of unprovoked full-scale Russian aggression against Ukraine and growing threats to Europe stability, the signatory states, gathered for the 9th Summit of the European Political Community in Dublin on the 12th of November 2026, consider strengthening European security and defending their security interests as their common objective.

The signatory states reiterate their firm support for the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognised borders

They underline the necessity to provide robust and credible security guarantees to Ukraine and reiterate, for those concerned, their intention to do so, in order to prevent the recurrence of aggression in Europe in the future.

They underline that Russia’s hybrid campaigns and attempts to undermine support to Ukraine will only strengthen their commitment to Ukraine and their resolve.

The signatory states recall that the path to peace in Ukraine should be decided with Ukraine and that any matter affecting European security should be decided with the Europeans.

They consider that the following key principles of European security can contribute to provide a path to a just and lasting peace for Ukraine, which will be of utmost importance for stability in Europe

They emphasize that Ukraine’s security is an integral part of Euro-Atlantic security and that future developments in European strategic stability will be conditional upon the conclusion of the war in Ukraine.

I. General Principles

The signatory states reaffirm the following general principles related to European security :

International law and the Charter of the United Nations are the cornerstone of this Declaration. In addition, the signatory states reaffirm the rules and principles upon which European security is and must remain founded, notably where applicable to the relevant signatory states, the North Atlantic Treaty (1949), the Statute of the Council of Europe (1949), the Treaty on the European Union and the Treaty on the functioning of the European Union (1950, 1957, 1986, 1992 and sq.), the Helsinki Final Act (1975), the Charter of Paris for a New Europe (1990), the Agreement on the European Economic Area (1992), and the Istanbul Charter for Security in Europe (1999). Common objectives contained in this Declaration are rooted in these fundamental documents and the signatories which are parties to them aim to ensure their effective implementation In this regard, the signatory states underline the importance of the following principles, which form the foundations of peace and stability on the European continent : respect for the sovereign equality of states and the rights inherent in sovereignty, such as the territorial integrity, the inviolability of borders, non-interference in domestic affairs, and the right of states to freely determine their relations with other states, and to choose whether or not to participate in treaties, alliances, or international organizations ; the refraining from the threat of or the use of force, including irresponsible nuclear rhetoric and coercion, and the peaceful settlement of disputes, in accordance with international law and good neighbourly relations ; the right to individual or collective self-defence in the event of an armed attack ; and the respect for the international law, including the international law of the sea as reflected by UNCLOS. The signatory states recognise that European states bear a primary responsibility and are assuming greater responsibility for the security of Europe, which will also contribute positively to global and transatlantic security. The signatory states reaffirm their commitment to human rights, and fundamental freedoms for all, without distinction of any kind, including on the grounds of race, sex, language, or religion, including in the digital realm, as well as the right of all nations to freely determine their political status, in accordance with international law. Democracy, rule of law, human rights and respect of the humanitarian international law are essential elements of comprehensive security and contribute to resilient societies capable of resisting both internal and external pressures. Enhanced participatory democracy, transparency and enabling civic space, including media freedom and freedom of expression, are indispensable safeguards of democratic resilience and long-term security. International law also applies to the global commons we share. Free, safe, autonomous and unhindered access to these spaces must be ensured within the limits of international law, in the air, on the seas, in outer space and in cyberspace. This declaration and the associated common objectives are in line with international mechanisms and the missions of existing multilateral organizations and forums in Europe (NATO, EU, OSCE, Council of Europe). Signatories who are members of NATO reaffirm that NATO is the foundation of their collective security and that the Alliance remains the cornerstone of their collective defence. They recall their ironclad commitment to collective defence under Article 5 of the Washington Treaty. They reaffirm their unwavering commitment to the transatlantic bond and to the Euro-Atlantic security. They recall their determination to build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO, working together with the United States and Canada which continue to play an essential role in NATO and assuming greater responsibilities for the Alliance’s collective defence. Signatories who are members of the European Union reaffirm their commitment to a stronger and more capable European Union that is better equipped to act and deal autonomously with immediate and future challenges and threats with a 360° approach, while recognizing the challenge and threats on the Eastern Flank. Enlargement of the European Union, anchored in a merit-based process and as a geostrategic investment in peace, security, stability and prosperity, also contributes – together with the European Neighbourhood Policy – to the security of the continent. In this global context, the security of the continent depends on strengthening both national and collective defence capabilities in the appropriate forums to address threats with a 360° approach, with the aim of deterring any aggressive actions and being able to defend against them. It also relies on strengthening the resilience and robustness of our democracies, as well as human rights and rule of law. International cooperation, to complement and deepen European and transatlantic frameworks, should always be pursued with a 360° approach. Diversifying partnerships with countries that are committed to upholding the principles of international law and the UN Charter, and that offer balanced and mutually beneficial relationships under the principle of good neighbourly relationships contributes to security and stability in Europe and to address shared challenges and advance common interests.

II. Common objectives

With the aim of strengthening security in Europe, the signatory states support the following common objectives in accordance with their respective international commitments and constitutional laws :

Security – the signatory states will uphold security, peace and stability in Europe in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations and their respective international commitments, including through bilateral agreements between them and for the states concerned by further strengthening the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation and the European Union, which are cornerstones for our security. National security and Defence efforts – in accordance with their respective international commitments, security and defence policies and constitutional obligations, the signatory states reaffirm their commitments to strengthening their capabilities in order to respond to their legitimate security needs, enhance their security and ensure the defence of Europe. To this end, and according to their respective commitments, they will make the most effective use of their resources and continue to develop cooperation among themselves and with relevant organizations, as each of them deems appropriate. Collective resilience – in the face of destabilizing actions conducted below the threshold of armed attack, including through cyber and hybrid activities and coercion, and the expansion of conflict into new areas, the signatory states will work in order to develop the tools necessary to prevent, deter and respond to these challenges, to strengthen the protection of their critical infrastructure, to enhance their resilience, and to cooperate on a voluntary basis to improve the detection and attribution of these attacks, with the aim of discouraging the threats and providing a coordinated response and holding to account those responsible. Risk management and reduction– the signatory states support discussions on further risk management and reduction mechanisms that contribute to stability in Europe, once the conditions are met and peace is restored in Europe. This could address particular risks, be it military or coming from actions conducted below the threshold of armed aggression, aiming at ensuring the stability of the entire continent. Operational Planning – the signatory states will continue to strengthen their collective working practices and their joint operational capabilities for the defence and security of Europe, notably through NATO for those being members of it, as well through other cooperation mechanisms and inclusive coalitions. Industrial cooperation – the concerned signatory states will continue to strengthen their defence industrial production capacity and cooperation across Europe to develop resilient, secure and more independent supply chains and infrastructure for their defence equipment, without prejudice to cooperation with trusted partners. They will promote, as appropriate, cooperation projects between all European actors and foster a competitive European defence equipment market across Europe. They will actively work to create the necessary conditions to mobilize private capital, and support the growth of European defence companies Strategic Dialogues – the signatory states will continue deepening their exchanges and dialogues on strategic issues related to European security, complementing and benefiting from existing collective security frameworks for those participating in them and bilateral arrangements. Democratic integrity – Human rights, rule of law and democratic systems, upon which European societies are fundamentally based, and must be protected and strengthened, to ensure their integrity and resilience in the face of growing deliberate campaigns aimed at undermining those values, including Foreign Information Manipulation and Interferences (FIMI). The signatory states will continue to promote solidarity, cooperation, and the use of the necessary mechanisms and institutions to achieve this goal. Fight against terrorism – the signatory states reaffirm their commitments in the fight against terrorism. In this framework, they condemn terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including state-sponsored terrorism in the strongest possible terms and will continue their cooperation to respond collectively to this threat, in accordance with international law. Response to illicit drug and human-trafficking and migrant-smuggling as well as organised crime networks in Europe – the signatory states reaffirm that illicit drug and human-trafficking as well as organized crimes networks are a major threat to the security, safety and health of the citizens in Europe. They remain committed to fighting illicit drug and human-trafficking and organised crime networks in accordance with international law with the strongest determination and to safeguard the integrity of European societies. Security of supply – the signatory states will continue to work towards the reduction of their dependencies as well as regarding supply chains for critical components or materials. By diversifying and setting up new trade partnerships, they will enable Europe to better respond to the challenges it faces. Protection of global commons – the signatory states will contribute to the protection and security of global commons, ensuring, within the limits of international law, safe, autonomous and unhindered access to these areas, and taking greater responsibility when European interests are involved. In accordance with international law, the protection of freedom of navigation on international waterways, in particular, requires upholding the high seas as a space of freedom, cooperation, and law. These same principles apply, as appropriate, to other shared global commons. Contribution of Europe to Global food security – building on the principles of protecting global commons, the signatory states reaffirm the necessity of the freedom of navigation and of the safety of commercial shipping, notably in the Black Sea, and that the uninterrupted functioning of all maritime routes is essential for global food security.

The above is without prejudice to the specific character of the security and defence policy and interests of the signatory states, and their respective constitutional laws and international commitments.

The Signatory States :

World.title: November 15 is the statutory deadline to fit vehicles with tyres suitable for winter conditions
World.content:
From November 15 to March 1, motor vehicles in Bulgaria must by law be fitted with tyres suitable for winter conditions.

According to the law, approved by Bulgaria’s Parliament in 2016, cars must have tyres designed for winter conditions or that have a tread depth of no less than or equal to four millimetres, the Interior Ministry said.

The Road Traffic Act allows the use of all-season or even summer tyres if they meet the grip requirement, but experts strongly recommend winter tyres for better safety in cold weather.

The traditional Interior Ministry “Winter” campaign, which aims to increase drivers’ attention to preparing their cars for the upcoming winter season, started on November 1.

(Photo: Clive Leviev-Sawyer)

World.title: Bulgaria issues weather warnings over strong winds forecast for November 13
World.content:
Bulgaria’s national meteorological bureau has issued the Code Orange warning of dangerous weather for several districts for November 13 because of forecast strong winds.

The districts subject to the Code Orange warning are Montana, Vratsa, Dobrich, Varna, Bourgas, Shoumen, Yambol, Stara Zagora and Haskovo.

All the remaining districts, with two exceptions, are subject to the lesser Code Yellow warning of potentially dangerous weather, also because of forecast strong winds.

The exceptions are the districts of Blagoevgrad and Smolyan, which are classified Code Green for November 13, meaning that no weather warning is in place.

In Bulgaria on November 13, minimum temperatures will be between 11° and 16° Celsius, in the Sofia region, about 12°.

There will be variable cloudiness on Friday. In the evening, from the northwest, the cloudiness will increase and thicken, and rain will begin.

It will be warm for the period with maximum temperatures between 20° and 25° Celsius, in places subject to southerly winds up to 27°-28°, and in Sofia, about 21°.

In the mountains, light rain will fall in places. A strong, stormy wind will blow from the west-southwest on the highlands and northern slopes. The maximum temperature at an altitude of 1200 metres will be about 14°, at 2000 metres, about 9°.

Over the Black Sea coast, the cloudiness will be variable. In the morning, mainly along the southern coast, there will be low layered clouds and reduced visibility. There will be a strong to stormy southwest wind. Maximum temperatures will be 21°-23°, the meteorological bureau said.

World.title: Bulgaria’s government proposes complete ban on advertising gambling games
World.content:
Bulgaria’s Cabinet approved on November 11 proposed amendments to the Gambling Act that, if approved by Parliament, will see a complete ban on the advertising of gambling games.

“The aim is to strengthen the prevention of the development or deepening of addiction, as well as to have a positive impact on the most vulnerable groups of people,” the government information service said.

A limited presence of trademarks of organisers of gambling would be allowed only in sponsorships of sports clubs, federations, associations and organisations, as well as in support of activities in the fields of culture, healthcare and education, the statement said.

The amendments propose that the activities of affiliate operators be suspended. This ensures consistency between the ban on advertising gambling games and the regime applicable to persons who promote them.

A one-time state fee is introduced for maintaining a licence for organising the activities of production, distribution and service of gaming equipment and import, distribution and service of gaming equipment.

A five-year licence would cost 50 000 euro and a 10-year licence would cost 100 000 euro.

The alternative tax under the Corporate Income Tax Act (CITA) for land-based casinos and gaming halls is increasing in 2027. From 2028, this tax will be eliminated from the CITA and will be replaced by a two-component state tax provided for in the Gambling Act.

A minimum of 100 000 euro per month will be the variable part of the two-component state fee for issuing and maintaining an online betting licence.

The amendments are also related to an increase in the one-time fees for maintaining a licence to organise gambling games, the amount of contributions for socially responsible behaviour, and fines and property sanctions.

Activities are also planned to expand the prevention of gambling addiction among individuals in the education system, including through the implementation of information campaigns, preventive programmes and the development of appropriate teaching materials, the government information service said.

The amendments introduce a new requirement, that a foreign legal entity organising online betting must have a place of business in Bulgaria.

“This creates an additional mechanism for tracking financial flows, helping to detect discrepancies between the declared activity, the amount of bets, the paid out winnings, the income and expenses, and the corporate tax due,” the statement said.

A mandatory cash contribution is also introduced for payment institutions, banks and electronic money companies that carry out payment transactions related to participation in gambling games and the payment of winnings.

The bill also proposes a complete ban on cash payments between construction companies, contractors and subcontractors under contracts, construction activities, supplies of materials and provision of services.

It is envisaged that payments will be made by bank transfer or through other traceable electronic payment instruments.

“The measure will contribute to limiting the shadow economy, increasing financial discipline and creating a level playing field for construction companies that comply with the legislation,” the statement said.
