World.title: Croatia is Facing a Waste Crisis: Waste Could End Up in Forests
World.content:
November the 13th, 2026 – Croatia is currently facing a serious waste crisis, in which waste could end up in the streets and forests. In some cases, it often already is.

The Ekologija grada (City Ecology) association recently warned of the growing problem of waste acceptance at landfills in Croatia, assessing that due to insufficient capacities and the refusal to accept waste from other areas, regular waste collection could be interrupted in part of the country. Poslovni reports that because of what they describe as a crisis of trust in the waste management system after scandals involving illegally disposed waste, a number of landfills have limited or stopped accepting waste from other cities and municipalities. Among them are Karepovac, Ploče’s Lovornik, Bjelovar’s Doline, Diklo, and Sodol.

The consequences of the lack of available capacities, they emphasise, are particularly felt by Makarska and the municipalities of the Makarska Riviera, Omiš, Kaštela, Dugi Rat, Zadvarje and Šestanovac, which have been forced to look for alternative landfills, conclude temporary agreements or organise the transport of waste to more distant counties.

Similar difficulties, they note, have also been experienced by Varaždin, Samobor, Jastrebarsko, Josipdol and Plaški, while Otočac, after the closure of the Podum landfill, redirected its waste to the Babina Gora Waste Management Centre.

The association warns that the problem does not affect only municipal waste but also industrial waste, and that public service providers and authorised companies could be left without space for its disposal and treatment. “If public service providers and authorised companies are left without a place for disposal, the waste will not disappear,” they warn, noting that it could end up on the streets, in forests and by rivers, or in overcrowded warehouses where the risk of fire increases.

They are calling on the Ministry and the Environmental Protection and Energy Efficiency Fund to adopt a binding decision on the acceptance of municipal waste from municipalities that have been left without landfills, and to draw up an urgent plan for the disposal of non-hazardous industrial and hazardous waste.

They are also requesting a check of the contractual obligations of landfills that received Fund resources, with the application of contractual measures, including the return of funds, if it is established that they are refusing to accept waste contrary to the contracts.

They further demand the public disclosure of data on landfills that have free capacities, on the extent of those capacities, and on those that refuse to accept waste. “It is time for decisions, not for politics. Every week in which parties, ministries, counties and cities accuse each other is a week closer to waste on the streets,” said the association’s president, Josip Pavlović.

World.title: Split Port Opens Brand New International Passenger Terminal
World.content:
November the 13th, 2026 – Split Port opened its brand new international passenger terminal this week, concluding a 20+ million euro project.

Split Port officially opened its new international passenger terminal this week, formally marking the completion of a project worth over 20 million euros. Poslovni reports that the extensive project was co-financed with non-repayable EU funds from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan.

a ground floor passenger reception

The former ugly, totally dilapidated building has finally been renovated into a modern passenger terminal, the construction of which has upgraded the port infrastructure and reorganised domestic and international traffic. The terminal was built due to the increase in capacity of the city port, where passenger traffic is almost four times higher and vehicle traffic three times higher than 25 years ago, the Split Port Authority pointed out. The new terminal covers more than 12,000 square metres, while the building itself has almost 3,000 square metres. On the ground floor there is space for receiving passengers, while the upper floor houses operational services, including the police, customs, and the security and port authority departments.

Vice Mihanović, director of the Split Port Authority, announced that the roof of the building will be opened to citizens and will contain public amenities such as a children’s playroom, an outdoor gym and a telescope.

“The facility is intended for international traffic, while domestic liner traffic will remain at the previous locations. With the construction of the terminal, we are relocating international traffic to the port breakwater, and we have repurposed the entire St. Duje Quay for domestic liner traffic,” Mihanović stated. St. Duje Quay spans over 10,000 square metres and six berths, and the re-purposing will improve travel conditions for islanders and domestic passengers and bring them closer to the city after disembarking from the ferry. The old terminal building has also been put into use for domestic traffic only.

the viewpoint and lungomare

Mihanović also announced four major projects of the Port Authority with a total value of almost 60 million euros, including the expansion of St. Peter’s Quay by more than 5,000 square metres and the construction of two new berths. Split Mayor Tomislav Šuta said that the construction of the terminal is a major step forward for the city and passengers, and announced the arrangement of a lungomare and viewpoint in that area.

World.title: Croatia Introduces Tougher Rules and Surveillance for Short-Term Rentals
World.content:
November the 13th, 2026 – Croatia is set to introduce much stricter rules and heightened surveillance for short-term rentals, with around 60,000 units in particular being under the state’s magnifying glass.

Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina stated recently that the Hospitality Activity Act, which has been sent for a second reading in Parliament, is one of the most important for tourism and a major step forward in its development. “With this law we want to achieve three fundamental goals: a strong step forward in suppressing unregistered activity, the complete digitalisation of all administrative procedures in tourism, and the introduction of order, transparency and an increase in the quality of the offer, especially in the category of short-term rental accommodation,” Glavina said after the government session.

Poslovni reports that he further explained that the most important goal – suppressing unregistered activity – is achieved through the law in several ways, one of which is the transposition into Croatian legislation of the European Commission regulation and the introduction of a digital registration number whose aim is to prevent service providers who do not have it from appearing and advertising on online platforms.

He assessed these platforms as very important because the largest tourist traffic comes from them, so among the goals is the introduction of more order into the ways they operate, because until now short-term rental and accommodation could be advertised and sold through them without a decision in the member state.

“The penalties for platforms that would ignore this are draconian and they will certainly make an effort across Europe, including in Croatia, to ensure that this does not happen,” Glavina said. He recalled that the new law expands the powers for supervising providers of this accommodation, in addition to the State Inspectorate, to the Customs Administration, cities and municipalities through the activities of municipal wardens, and it has also been agreed that all eventual revenues from fines will go entirely to the budgets of local and regional self-government units.

The State Inspectorate has also been given the possibility of secret supervision of classifieds, groups on social networks and similar, so that it can react and control the facilities. “This year we have significantly strengthened the activities of inspectors against unregistered activity, and when it enters into force, the law will contribute to this even more,” Glavina said. He repeated that private landlords and family accommodation are very important and that they have been accommodated.

When asked whether he knows how many registered apartments for rent to tourists there are in buildings, he said that he does not have exact data because until now no records have been kept of the type of facilities in which the apartments are located, which will change with the new law and digitalisation.

According to our estimate, that is around 60,000 facilities-apartments, Glavina said, noting that other EU countries are also struggling in various ways with short-term rental to tourists because it reduces the available housing stock.

Regarding the objections and complaints of small landlords and entrepreneurs to the draft law, he said that from 2016 until about a year and a half ago, the number of newly registered beds in short-term accommodation for tourists grew by around 25,000 every year, which led to the fact that, despite the growth of overall tourism, growth in that accommodation was smaller. That is why the steps forward with the law and responsible tourism policy were important, and that is why in the last two years we have not had growth in the number of those beds but even a slight decrease, and those beds have gone into long-term rental, which is also the goal of housing policy, Glavina concluded.

World.title: Croatia Will Need 100,000 New Hotel Beds Over the Next Decade
World.content:
November the 13th, 2026 – Croatia is going to need anywhere between 80,000 and 100,000 new hotel beds over the next decade, according to hotelier reps warn.

Croatia will need between 80,000 and 100,000 new hotel beds over the next ten years, hoteliers’ representatives warned at a recently held congress in Poreč. There’s an issue, however, as building new hotels is becoming increasingly difficult due to high land prices, expensive construction work, slow administration and shrinking opportunities for profit. Index reports that in Croatia currently, hotels currently account for only 9.2 percent of total accommodation capacity in Croatia, yet generate approximately a quarter of all tourist overnight stays. Hoteliers are therefore calling for the continuation of state incentives, better conditions for investment and measures that would attract more tourists outside the summer months.

croatia’s accommodation capacity poses an issue

Veljko Ostojić, president of the Association of Entrepreneurs in Croatian Hospitality and director of the Croatian Tourism Association, said that the hotel sector achieved good results this year, but that Croatia must change the structure of its tourist accommodation. “Croatian hospitality is the winner of this tourist year, not only according to physical indicators but also according to everything it does to raise the quality of Croatian tourism. However, the structure of our accommodation capacity is currently the biggest challenge,” Ostojić said. According to his estimate, Croatia should increase the number of hotel beds by 80,000 to 100,000 over the next decade. The problem, he warns, is that most investments relate to the renovation and reconstruction of existing hotels, while completely new hotel complexes on previously undeveloped land are almost not being built at all.

why are so few hotels being constructed in croatia?

Ostojić believes that investors are deterred by a combination of several problems, from the price of land and construction to slow administrative procedures and legal uncertainty. “The question is why there are practically no significant greenfield investments in Croatia. The reasons are numerous: the price of land, the slowness of administration, legal uncertainty, the cost of construction and the hotel business model itself. We must be open and realistic,” he said. He added that the space for new investments is getting smaller, which he considers bad for the long-term development of Croatian tourism. Hoteliers also warn of rising operating costs and declining profitability, which makes it increasingly difficult to find financially viable projects.

the interest in the height of summer is waning…

Ostojić also warned that tourist habits are changing. According to him, some guests are increasingly avoiding the busiest summer months because of the heat, high prices and excessive crowds in certain destinations. He believes Croatia must develop new tourist facilities, events and manifestations that would attract guests during spring and autumn. This would extend the tourist season, increase the occupancy of hotel capacities and reduce dependence on July and August alone, which many are now avoiding due to extreme temperatures and crowds.

Robert Pende, director of the Directorate for Entrepreneurship Development, Investments and Competitiveness at the Ministry of Tourism and Sport, said that the state has been encouraging investments in the hotel sector for years. The aim of these incentives is not only the construction of higher-quality accommodation but also the reduction of seasonality in Croatian tourism. Pende warned that Croatia still has one of the most pronounced seasonalities of tourism in the European Union.

“We want to change that, and investments are key to this,” he said, noting that 34 applications for projects with a total value of approximately 500 million euros have been received through the investment incentive system. This refers to the value of planned investments, not the amount of state support.

has croatia managed to retain its competitiveness?

Kristijan Staničić, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board, assessed that Croatia, despite global challenges and unpredictable circumstances on the tourist market, has retained its competitiveness among Mediterranean destinations. “The tourist year that is slowly coming to an end has shown that Croatia has retained its competitiveness. The results we have achieved confirm positive trends in tourist traffic, and a great deal of credit for this belongs precisely to hoteliers,” Staničić said. He added that new investments, raising the quality of service and the development of tourist destinations play an important role in the further development of Croatian tourism.

World.title: Nations League: Croatia Fall 2-1 to England at Wembley
World.content:
Croatia were beaten 2-1 by England at Wembley on Thursday night, with Morgan Rogers’ opener and a VAR-awarded penalty cancelling out Petar Sučić’s equalizer, but Slaven Bilić’s depleted side showed the fight and organization that had been so badly missing in Rijeka a month earlier.

Croatia faced England at Wembley on Thursday night in the fifth round of the Nations League, a month after the 7-0 defeat in Rijeka that Slaven Bilić and his players have since called a “collective blackout”.

Croatia went into the match on three straight defeats, though the 2-1 loss to Spain at Poljud had restored some pride. Bilić arrived in London with a depleted squad. Josip Šutalo, Marin Pongračić, Kristijan Jakić, Andrej Kramarić and Franjo Ivanović were all ruled out through injury; Luka Sučić was struggling with a virus, and Ivan Perišić was suspended after his red card against Spain.

England, without the injured Djed Spence and Ezri Konsa, marked a special night for Harry Kane, who presented his Ballon d’Or to the Wembley crowd before kick-off and was set to become England’s most-capped player.

Lineups

England (4-2-3-1): Pickford; Quansah, Burn, Hall, Alexander-Arnold; Rice, Anderson; Gordon, Rogers, Bellingham; Kane

Croatia (3-4-2-1): Livaković; Gvardiol, Vušković, Stanišić; Vlašić, Mišić, Kovačić, Smolčić; Baturina, Sučić; Matanović

Bilić switched to a back three, with Vlašić and Smolčić as wing-backs, and left Luka Modrić on the bench.

Match report

Before kick-off, Wembley celebrated a landmark night for England captain Harry Kane. He showed his recently won Ballon d’Or to the home crowd, and Sir Peter Shilton, whose record he was about to break, honored him on his 126th appearance, making Kane England’s most-capped player. Croatia captain Luka Modrić joined the ceremony to present him with a replica of the Croatian first football.

The match then got underway in front of more than 80,000 spectators.

Croatia started with real purpose, pressing England on both flanks and keeping the hosts from settling on the ball in Croatia’s half. By the 13th minute, though, England were gradually taking control of possession, even if neither side had yet created anything clear.

The first moment of danger came in the 16th minute. Trent Alexander-Arnold crossed, Croatia failed to clear properly, and Elliot Anderson hit a fierce shot from the edge of the box that flew over the bar. England threatened again two minutes later, when Alexander-Arnold tried his luck himself, but Mišić was quick to block.

Morgan Rogers sent another ball into the box in the 20th minute, but Vušković cleared. Croatia responded two minutes later with a long spell of possession that ended in a speculative shot from distance by Mišić.

England took the lead in the 24th minute. Kane switched the play to the right, Bellingham crossed into the middle, and after a poor reaction from Gvardiol, Rogers managed to bundle the ball into the net for 1-0.

England kept pushing. In the 29th minute, Lewis Hall broke forward and shot, but Mišić got across to block it behind for a corner, his second important block of the night. The hosts were proving especially dangerous from set pieces, with every corner causing alarm in the Croatian box.

Croatia finally tested Pickford in the 33rd minute, when Kovačić tried his luck from distance. Baturina also shot straight at Pickford a few minutes later.

Croatia went into the break 1-0 down. They had started the match well, and apart from the Gvardiol slip that led to Rogers’ goal, their performance looked much closer to the display against Spain at Poljud than to the collapse in Rijeka.

Neither coach made a change at the break.

England started the half on the front foot. Anthony Gordon aimed for the far corner from the inside-left channel in the 48th minute but missed the target, and two minutes later Rice arrived from deep and cut the ball back for Kane, only for Vušković to react and clear.

In the 55th minute England broke quickly, cutting through Croatia in a few passes, and Bellingham’s shot was saved by Livaković. Gordon then fired wide again from the left. At the other end, Croatia were finding out once more how hard it was to get through the England defense, with every route to goal closed off so far.

Croatia then hit back. Pushing England back as the second half went on, they equalized from a corner in the 59th minute. Quansah’s headed clearance went straight to the feet of Petar Sučić, who made it 1-1.

The lead was not level for long. Smolčić was penalized for pulling back Quansah in the Croatian box, and after a VAR review, England were awarded a penalty, with Smolčić booked. Kane scored for 2-1 in the 64th minute.

Bilić then made a double change in the 70th minute, bringing on Ante Budimir and Mario Pašalić for goalscorer Petar Sučić and Matanović.



In the 74th minute, Bilić turned to Luka Modrić and Marco Pašalić, replacing Mišić and Smolčić. A minute later, Baturina’s cross for Budimir was claimed by Pickford. Tuchel then made a triple change in the 77th minute, sending on Garner, White and Ngumoha for Rice, Gordon and Alexander-Arnold.

Croatia created their best chance of the half in the 82nd minute. Modrić found Vlašić, who turned and sent his shot just wide of the right-hand post. Two minutes later, Vlašić was involved again, crossing for Budimir, whose header went off target.

England had the ball in the net in the 86th minute through Garner, but the flag was already up for offside. It was again a Gvardiol error.

Croatia pushed for a winner in the closing minutes. In the 87th minute, Marco Pašalić played Budimir through, but Pickford made an excellent save. A minute later, there was a scramble in front of the England goal. Budimir, using Gvardiol to lift himself higher in the air, could not direct his header from close range.

In the 90th minute, Majer came on for Kovačić. A corner for Croatia came in the 90th minute, which found Budimir’s head and went just above the crossbar. After a last effort from England, the game ended 2-1.

The result went England’s way, but a month on from the humiliation in Rijeka, this was a far braver and more convincing Croatia, one that matched the hosts for long spells and gave Bilić real reason for optimism before Sunday’s game against Czechia in Osijek.

World.title: Vis Archipelago Retains Status as UNESCO Global Geopark
World.content:
November the 12th, 2026 – The Vis archipelago has successfully retained its status as a UNESCO Global Geopark for another four years as all 10 recommendations from the previous evaluation have been fulfilled.

The above was confirmed on the 4th of November at the 11th session of the UNESCO Global Geoparks Council, held at UNESCO headquarters in Paris. The Geopark Vis Archipelago has been part of the UNESCO Global Geoparks Network since 2019.

Morski reports that the re-validation, which is carried out every four years, included a review of documentation and a field mission by international evaluators from the 22nd to the 27th of June 2026.

During their stay on the Vis archipelago, the evaluators visited numerous geological sites, geotrails and visitor centres, and held talks with representatives of the local community, institutions, scientific organisations and partner organisations.

The international evaluators praised the way the sites are presented to visitors, the cooperation with schools and scientists, and the support given to local producers. They also highlighted how the geopark has connected Vis and Komiža in caring for the heritage of the entire archipelago.

World.title: New Dawn for Luxury Tourism in Kaštela With High-End Hotel Brand
World.content:
November the 12th, 2026 – A new dawn for luxury tourism in Kaštela is beginning with the arrival of one of the world’s most recognisable brands in the high-end hotel segment.

It’s genuinely no exaggeration to say that a new tourism dawn of sorts in Kaštela is now beginning. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the international Odien Group, headquartered in Prague, is bringing Sofitel, one of the world’s most recognisable brands in the luxury hotel segment, to Kaštela and Croatia. The contract with Accor, one of the world’s leading hotel groups that includes the Sofitel brand in its portfolio, was formally signed at the Renaissance Vitturi Castle in Kaštel Lukšić.

high-end tourism

Sofitel Kaštela, which will be constructed on the site of the former Zeničko resort in Kaštel Stari, is expected to open its doors in 2029 and will be managed by Odien Hotels, the hotel division of the Odien Group. The hotel will have 137 rooms and apartments, including spacious junior suites and higher-category accommodation units with private balconies or terraces overlooking the sea. Guests will have access to several restaurants and bars, a spa centre, indoor and outdoor pools, a beach club, and spaces for business meetings and various events. It goes without saying that this is an important milestone for Croatian tourism, and especially for Kaštela, which with this project is positioning itself on the international map of luxury hospitality. For the Odien Group, Sofitel represents much more than a new hotel project. It is an important part of the group’s long-term investment strategy aimed at developing Kaštela into an internationally recognisable tourist destination.

a luxury hotel brand blends with heritage

Kaštela will get an internationally recognisable luxury hotel brand, as well as an intimate heritage hotel located in a Renaissance building.

“Our ambitions go beyond the mere construction of luxury hotel facilities. We want to contribute to creating a destination with a strong international identity, recognised for quality, authenticity and the experiences it offers. Kaštela has exceptional potential: a rich history, valuable architectural heritage, an authentic Mediterranean character and an ideal location between Split and Trogir. Combining all these qualities with the international recognition and reputation of the Sofitel brand, which is synonymous with quality, will undoubtedly open a new chapter in the city’s tourism development,” said Mike Saran, owner of the Odien Group.

“Croatia has become one of the most attractive European tourist destinations, recognised for its unique combination of natural beauty, rich culture and authenticity. We are proud that, through this exceptional project with the Odien Group, we are bringing Sofitel to the Croatian market as the first international luxury hotel brand in the country. Sofitel Kaštela will embody the elegance of French luxury while embracing the spirit, heritage and lifestyle of the Adriatic coast, creating a unique destination for travellers from around the world,” said Maud Bailly, CEO of the Sofitel, Sofitel Legend, MGallery and Emblems brands. The arrival of this prestigious hotel brand is part of the Odien Group’s long-term development strategy and commitment to Kaštela. As part of that strategy, the group will, through its companies Odien Hotels and Odien Real Estate, invest more than 100 million euros over the next five years. In addition to the new Sofitel Kaštela hotel project, the company this year also purchased the historic Štafileo Castle in Kaštel Štafilić, which it plans to renovate and convert into a luxury heritage hotel.

These two projects bring two different but harmoniously connected hotel concepts: an internationally recognisable luxury hotel brand and an intimate heritage hotel located in a historic Renaissance building, which will offer guests an authentic experience of local heritage. Together with the group’s existing hotel operations in Croatia, these projects are part of its long-term vision of creating new tourism content and value in Kaštela and throughout Dalmatia.

international luxury tourism for Kaštela

“These projects give the Kaštela the opportunity for a significant step forward in the segment of international luxury tourism. The city’s growing recognition as a tourist destination, its rich cultural and historical heritage and its geographical location form solid foundations for the development of a tourism offer that goes beyond the framework of traditional seasonal tourism,” said Denis Ivanović, Mayor of Kaštela.

“This is an extremely important moment for Kaštela. The arrival of an international luxury hotel brand and the Odien Group’s investments in our city confirm that Kaštela has the potential to become a recognisable high-end tourism destination. It is particularly important to emphasise that this is not just about one hotel project, but about a series of investments that can contribute to the development of the city, open new jobs, strengthen the local economy and extend the tourist season. For us, it is of key importance that this development takes place in parallel with the preservation of Kaštela’s identity and in close cooperation with the local community,” the mayor added. The Odien Group has otherwise been present in Croatia since 2015, when it took over the Le Méridien Lav Split resort in Podstrana.

World.title: Zagreb-Podgorica Direct Flights Coming on November the 26th
World.content:
November the 12th, 2026 – New Zagreb-Podgorica direct flights are coming on November the 26th, with the two capitals being linked in this way after several years.

Travel between Croatia and Montenegro will soon become significantly faster and simpler. Index reports that Montenegro’s national airline Air Montenegro has announced the introduction of a new direct route between Zagreb and Podgorica, with the first flight scheduled for the 26th of November this year.

The flight between the two capital cities will last only 50 minutes, allowing passengers faster and simpler travel without transfers. The new route will operate three times a week, and the flights will be operated by Embraer E195 aircraft, which can accommodate 118 passengers. The introduction of this route is part of Montenegro’s Public Service Obligation (PSO) programme, whose aim is to improve Montenegro’s international transport connectivity and enable more regular air links with important European destinations.

the upcoming flight schedule

According to the announced timetable, aircraft will operate between Zagreb and Podgorica on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sundays. From Zagreb, these flights will depart at 08:50 and are expected to arrive in Podgorica at 09:40. In the opposite direction, departure from Podgorica is planned at 07:20, with arrival in Zagreb scheduled for 08:10. All departure and arrival times are given in local time, and the schedule is of course subject to change.

the price

One-way ticket prices start at around 50 euros, depending on the direction of travel and the chosen date. On the official Air Montenegro website, the currently listed price for the first flight from Zagreb on the 26th of November is 58.30 euros. The ticket price includes all mandatory fees, as well as one piece of hand luggage weighing up to eight kilograms and one piece of checked luggage weighing up to 23 kilograms. The final price will depend on the travel date, seat availability and the time of booking.

The new air route could also be interesting for travellers who want to get better acquainted with Podgorica, the capital and largest city of Montenegro. Located in the area where the Morača and Ribnica rivers meet, Podgorica combines modern city life, historical sights and natural beauty. One of the places worth visiting is Stara Varoš, the historic city quarter that preserves traces of the Ottoman past. There you will also find the Clock Tower (Sahat-kula), one of Podgorica’s recognisable landmarks. A walk through this part of the city is an opportunity to get to know traditional architecture and local culture.

Among the best-known modern symbols of the city is the Millennium Bridge, which stretches across the Morača River. Visitors can also walk to the place where the Ribnica flows into the Morača and view the old stone bridge on the Ribnica. Nature lovers can head to Gorica hill, after which the city is named, which is a popular place for walking and recreation. Near Podgorica there are also waterfalls on the Cijevna River, known as the Montenegrin Niagara, which are especially impressive when the water level is high. For those who want to explore the surroundings of the city as well, an interesting choice can be Lake Skadar, known for its rich plant and animal life, picturesque landscapes and opportunities for boat trips.

World.title: Estonian ex-NATO envoy faults US for opening door to Russia's Europe demands
World.content:
Former Estonian ambassador to NATO Jüri Luik says it's troubling that the U.S. has allowed Russia to make demands about Europe's security alongside Ukraine peace talks.

German paper Bild reported Friday that Moscow wants a new European security order that would force Finland out of NATO, require the alliance to dismantle its military bases in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, and turn Moldova into a federation.

Citing sources close to Russian leader Vladimir Putin, the paper reported that the proposed peace plan originated within his inner circle, Finnish public broadcaster Yle reported.

Luik, an Isamaa candidate for the Riigikogu next spring, urged caution over reports of Russian demands, saying that the details need clarification.

He noted that Bild had reported Moscow making the demands in behind-the-scenes discussions, but Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov had denied the claims.

"So apart from the Bild article, I currently have no other sources saying that such demands have been made," Luik said.

'That is bad'

The bigger problem, according to Luik, was Washington's decision to discuss Europe's security arrangements alongside a potential Ukraine peace deal, despite European countries' insistence that a peace agreement should come first.

"The important point, of course, is that Russia has been put in a position where it can make demands and state its positions at all," he stressed. "The Americans leading the negotiations have decided that some of the discussions on peace in Ukraine should also cover Europe's security arrangements."

Jüri Luik. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

In practice, he explained, this means the U.S. has effectively created a situation "where Ukraine's future and Europe's security arrangements are being discussed in parallel. And that, of course, is bad."

Inexperienced with Russia

The former Estonian foreign affairs and defense minister also questioned the experience of the current U.S. administration and American negotiators involved in dealing with Moscow.

"They clearly don't attach much importance to the historical baggage or to everything Russia has done in recent years, including its massive war," Luik said, noting that the U.S. negotiators appeared to view the talks as some kind of technical or market bargaining.

"It's crucial, of course, that European countries don't end up victims of such bargaining," he emphasized.

Luik said that if Europe does join Ukraine peace negotiations, its representatives should have a clear EU mandate and remain accountable to member states.

He cited Estonia's support for European Council President Antonio Costa and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who are formally required to report to member states on their work in the negotiations.

"The question isn't who is physically sitting at the table, but whether they answer to us as European countries, including Estonia," Luik said.

World.title: Elderly Jõhvi residents lose free travel on Kohtla-Järve city buses
World.content:
Elderly residents in Ida-Viru County have lost the right to free bus travel after a pilot project's budget ran out in under two months due to uptake being underestimated.

Pensioners in Jõhvi municipality aged 63 and over had been eligible to ride for free on city buses in Kohtla-Järve, whose municipality is adjacent to Jõhvi's – the two towns are a few kilometers apart.

However, starting Thursday, Jõhvi's elderly have had to start paying the €0.70 concessionary rate, Russian-language "Aktuaalne kaamera" reported.

The Jõhvi–Kohtla-Järve pilot began on September 1, primarily to allow the municipality's schoolchildren, including from the more outlying settlements of Järveküla and Kohtla-Nõmme, to get to school and back more easily. Concessions on the city buses were then extended to other Jõhvi residents, with Jõhvi municipality paying the difference in ticket price.

Aivar Kamal, head of Kohtla-Järve's finance service, said Jõhvi residents had the same conditions as Kohtla-Järve's own — pensioners traveled free, schoolchildren paid 50 cents — and that the project had been budgeted at €12,000 to year end. However, the money ran out in less than two months. The contract with Jõhvi is now being revised: the municipality wants to keep the concessions, but with pensioners paying 70 cents a trip, while schoolchildren from Jõhvi will continue to pay 50 cents.

According to Jõhvi Municipality spokesperson Ilmar Aun, free transport to Jõhvi pensioners between the hours of 9 a.m. and 9 p.m. had turned out to be the most expensive for the municipality.

He said that in October alone passengers had made almost 4,800 free trips, a level of demand the municipality had not expected. Each trip cost its budget one euro — so approximately €4,800 for the month. Maintaining the same concessions Kohtla-Järve gives its own residents would have cost Jõhvi €120,000 to €130,000 a year, Aun said.

The municipality says it intends to keep the concessionary fares next year as well. Whether free travel returns for elderly Jõhvi residents will depend on negotiations with Kohtla-Järve. Travel conditions for elderly residents of Kohtla-Järve itself are unchanged.

World.title: Microsoft services disruption highlights Estonian state's dependence
World.content:
An outage affecting services provided by Microsoft disrupted operations at numerous Estonian institutions and businesses on Friday, including government agencies, many of which use the company's office software.

Although government agencies are not required to use Microsoft products, most have opted for the company's office software. According to Taivo Tender, deputy director for technology and innovation at the State IT Center (RIT), Microsoft's services currently meet the agencies' needs, but there are plans to test alternatives in the future.

Disruptions to Microsoft services, including Outlook and Teams, began Thursday evening, affecting access to email, calendars and other tools. As of noon Friday, Microsoft had not disclosed the cause of the outages.

According to Tender, Microsoft was selected as the platform for the government's centralized workplace services when efforts began to standardize state IT services. He noted that the centralized IT service was established to improve the quality and security of government agencies' IT systems and consolidate technical expertise in one place.

86 agencies use RIT IT services

The State IT Center currently provides services to 86 institutions, although not all government agencies are covered. The transition is taking place gradually and depends on agreements reached with individual agencies.

According to Tender, Microsoft currently meets the needs of government agencies and no significant shortcomings have been identified. However, the State IT Center is monitoring trials of non-Microsoft solutions in other European countries and plans to explore alternatives in greater depth next year. The aim is to compare service costs and assess the risks of dependence on a single provider.

Entrepreneur and technology expert Taavi Kotka believes that the use of Microsoft products by government agencies is not a problem in itself. He noted that there is no blanket requirement for all government agencies to use Microsoft, as some have opted for open-source solutions.

No such thing as outage-proof service

"No one has yet managed to produce another product as good as Word and Excel," Kotka said. According to him, occasional service outages do not outweigh the benefits of good productivity tools, as there is no guarantee that alternative solutions would be free of disruptions either.

Aare Reintam, a cybersecurity expert at Cybexer Technologies, said there is currently no reason to believe the Microsoft service disruptions were caused by a cyberattack. In his assessment, the outage may have been related to server overload and the rerouting of data traffic.

Reintam explained that when some servers can no longer handle their workloads, data traffic is redirected to other servers. However, if too much traffic is concentrated in certain locations, those servers can also become overloaded. He said that in this case, a secure connection service may have become overwhelmed, making other services inaccessible as well.

Reintam added that there are currently no indications that users' personal data or passwords have been leaked or made accessible to unauthorized parties. The issue is primarily one of service availability.

State agencies dependent on tech company services

Reintam believes the incident nevertheless highlights how dependent businesses and government agencies have become on services provided by major technology companies. However, he does not consider it practical to replace the entire Microsoft ecosystem or continuously run solutions from multiple providers in parallel.

According to Reintam, switching systems would require significant financial and human resources. For a medium-sized company, this could mean hundreds of work hours, while larger companies could face thousands of hours of work.

Erik Janson, head of the national ICT infrastructure unit at the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs, said the broader transition to Microsoft's cloud-based office software services began in 2022. According to Janson, functionality, efficiency, modern features and cybersecurity capabilities have been key factors in choosing Microsoft products.

Janson said one drawback of Microsoft is its licensing costs and the way they have increased over time. He added that the State IT Center has regularly assessed the risks associated with Microsoft services.

Agencies have backup systems

Janson said government agencies also have backup systems in place, although these may not offer the same functionality as the primary systems used on a daily basis.

In the longer term, he considers the development of Europe's own sovereign cloud solutions important. The European Commission has already begun working toward this goal.

Äripäev reported that disruptions to Microsoft services are also affecting court operations. Viivika Siplane, spokesperson for Harju District Court, wrote that the outages have disrupted the courts' email service.

"As a result, it is currently not possible to submit procedural documents to the courts by email," Siplane explained. "We ask that procedural documents be submitted through the public e-File system," she added.

World.title: Janar Holm: The government must decide what level of readiness Estonia will ensure
World.content:
The government must decide what level of readiness Estonia will achieve and by when, and then secure the funding and personnel needed to reach that goal. If readiness targets are lowered, that should be stated clearly. Otherwise, a misleading impression may emerge about the state's actual level of preparedness, Auditor General Janar Holm said in his annual address to the Riigikogu.

I can once again confirm that the state's annual financial report for the previous year is materially accurate. That means that, with one exception, the report fairly and correctly reflects the state's financial position, operating results and cash flows. The government's accounting is generally well managed.

The Ministry of Defense's housekeeping is not in order

The troubling news is that the Ministry of Defense's housekeeping remains in poor order. Unfortunately, this is not new. Significant problems with military assets have accumulated over a long period.

Four years ago, in 2022, I told the Riigikogu that the accounting of Defense Forces assets was inadequate and would likely require renewed attention in the near future. That is exactly what has happened. Society has made a considerable effort to provide more money for national defense. Large quantities of fixed assets and supplies have been purchased, but persistent problems in work organization and attitudes have only deepened the confusion.

I want to emphasize that proper accounting for expenditures and inventories is not needed for the peace of mind of Estonian accountants or auditors. It is also misleading to downplay the problem by suggesting that the National Audit Office expects every cartridge and pair of boots to be counted individually. We have not even reached that level of detail.

We are talking about weapons and weapons systems, components of weapons systems, expensive ammunition, camouflage equipment, and fire-control and communications systems.

What should concern defense officials is the possibility that they do not have a sufficiently clear overview of the assets and funds under their responsibility. Accurate knowledge of existing stocks, their locations and whether they are usable is part of military readiness.

The public must have confidence that money allocated for national defense is being used wisely. The slogan "more defense capability for every euro" rings hollow if it takes years to establish how millions and millions of euros were actually used.

I have been asked whether speaking publicly about problems in the defense sector constitutes a security threat to Estonia. It certainly does not.

Estonia's strength lies in the fact that even problems in the defense sector can be openly discussed and solutions demanded. That is precisely how civilian oversight should function in a democratic state.

A major step forward would be ensuring that at least all supplies delivered to warehouses this year are properly recorded. Defense Minister Martin Herem and I have discussed this repeatedly since he took office.

"Accurate knowledge of existing stocks, their locations and whether they are usable is part of military readiness."

Today I will not spend much time discussing contracts for defense assistance procurement and related financial matters. Following our audit, the media has continued investigating artillery shell procurement deals, and law enforcement authorities are also examining the background of those transactions.

However, I do want to address how the Estonian Center for Defense Investments monitors its contracts and their implementation.

Last year we spoke about problems with advance payments. We found such problems again this year, including advance payments that had not been properly reconciled. But the issues extended beyond that.

Contract terms were not followed, or contracts had not even been signed. Due to errors in documentation, it was impossible to determine under which contract goods had been received or whether they had actually arrived. In some cases, authorities did not verify whether the goods purchased and received matched what had been agreed upon.

This may sound surprising, but auditors are human and understand that mistakes happen. However, these were not isolated errors.

We reviewed only 64 contracts, yet even within that sample we found systemic problems. In such an environment, the state may make incorrect payments, equipment may never arrive and supplier breaches may go unnoticed. The state may lose money, and the defense forces may be left without equipment they expected to have.

According to the head of the Estonian Center for Defense Investments, efforts to improve contract management have been underway since the beginning of the year. Hopefully next year's report will reflect the results of that work.

"We reviewed only 64 contracts, yet even within that sample we found systemic problems."

The goal should be straightforward: at any moment it should be known what was ordered, what was paid for, what has been delivered and whether it is usable.

The Ministry of Defense must ensure that both asset accounting and contract management have clearly assigned responsibilities and deadlines.

Budget approval has become an exercise in retroactive validation

The audit of the state's annual report also identified other issues affecting all ministries to varying degrees.

I have repeatedly spoken over the years about the quality and transparency of the state budget. I will not dwell further on the budget passed by the Riigikogu. Instead, I want to address the internal budgets approved by ministers for their ministries.

Those budgets are supposed to define how much money may be spent and for what purposes. At least that is the common understanding.

In reality, this basic principle has increasingly been abandoned.

In two-thirds of ministries, ministers approved the final allocation of their 2025 operating budgets only months after the budget year had already ended. The minister's signature authorizing spending merely confirmed that the money had already been spent. Budget approval has become an exercise in retroactive validation.

As a result, budget approval has become a formality rather than a meaningful decision-making process. If reality does not match the budget, the budget is simply adjusted afterward.

But a signature given after a budget year has ended does not legalize spending that lacked proper authorization when it occurred.

"Budget approval has become a formality rather than a meaningful decision-making process."

Naturally, budgets are easier to prepare after the fact because by then it is known exactly how much was spent. But we should take the operation of our state more seriously.

If we expect government agencies and civil servants to take budgets seriously, ministers must do so first. Otherwise, the message is clear: spend as you see fit and we will complete the paperwork later.

Compounding the issue, we still lack a clear overview of how much future budget funding has already been committed through contracts and other obligations. This comes at a time when the state's budget strategy projects deficits of up to four percent of GDP.

The Ministry of Finance does not monitor whether ministries comply with limits on long-term commitments. About half of the ministries claimed they do so, but none could provide supporting calculations. The rest openly admitted they do not monitor such commitments at all.

As a result, when future budgets are discussed, it is impossible to know precisely how much room remains for new decisions. Some choices may already have been made on behalf of future governments and future compositions of the Riigikogu.

Future policymakers may be left with little freedom beyond deciding how to pay for promises made by their predecessors.

When making future budget decisions, the government and parliament must know how much money is already tied up in contracts and how much remains available for new decisions. The Ministry of Finance and other ministries must create that overview.

Just as we do not know how much future funding has already been committed, we also fail to see how much money paid from the state budget is simply sitting unused.

An audit completed this summer of SmartCap's venture capital funds illustrated how little attention is paid to the use of state funds as a whole.

At the end of last year, those funds held more than €250 million in uncommitted cash for future investments and expenses. Much of that money sat in fixed-term deposits. At the same time, the state was borrowing money to cover day-to-day expenses and even paying SmartCap management fees on funds that remained unused.

With one hand, we set money aside; with the other, we borrow more.

This is ultimately a question of financial management. When discussing shortages of public money, we must also know where state funds are currently sitting. Better stewardship could prevent such situations.

The SmartCap example

But how can someone act as a good steward when they are simultaneously responsible for several competing interests?

In audits, the National Audit Office has often pointed to overlapping roles and potential conflicts of interest. The SmartCap case shows how overlapping responsibilities can affect decisions with direct financial consequences for the state.

These are not merely abstract or theoretical risks.

A representative of the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications simultaneously held three different roles.

As a member of SmartCap's supervisory board, that person was expected to safeguard the company's interests and oversee management.

As a member of the supervisory board of EIS, SmartCap's parent organization, the same individual was responsible for directing and overseeing the parent entity.

Within the ministry, the same person was also responsible for shaping and implementing Estonia's economic and innovation policy.

From SmartCap's perspective, receiving funding in advance provides certainty for future investments. From the state's perspective, however, the question should have been whether such advance funding was truly necessary.

Which interest prevails?

Too often, the interests of the state as a whole disappear between multiple responsibilities. Who was responsible for ensuring that the solution made sense for the state overall?

This is not merely a question about SmartCap.

When appointing representatives to supervisory boards, ministers must carefully consider which responsibilities can realistically be carried out by one person and when combining roles begins to weaken oversight.

When directing and supervising the use of public money, it must always be clear who is responsible for what.

From the annual health care report

There has already been considerable discussion in recent days about this year's National Audit Office report on health care. For that reason, I will not repeat all of its conclusions.

As it did four years ago, our annual report focuses on long-term trends in Estonia's health care system. At that time, the minister of health and labor said we had reached a point where decisions could no longer be postponed. Last year, standing here, I promised that when preparing this year's report we would examine whether those supposedly urgent decisions had actually been made.

Unfortunately, the fundamental questions surrounding the long-term financing of health care remain unresolved, even though successive government programs have repeatedly promised to address them. At the same time, the system's capacity is not growing at the same pace as people's need for care. The government and the Riigikogu must decide what level of access to medical care people will be guaranteed and how it will be financed on a sustainable basis. Those decisions have been postponed again and again.

If one opens an issue of Meditsiiniuudised from October 30, 2009, the headline reads: "Pevkur: Decisions must be made on how to move forward." The article covered a speech by the minister of social affairs at the North Estonia Medical Centre's fall conference and quoted him as saying: "We must decide how to move forward. Difficult choices lie ahead. We need to determine how Estonia's health care system will be financed in the coming decades, whether it will continue as before or whether something must change."

Now, 17 years later, I would add that making, or rather avoiding, these fundamental decisions cannot forever be replaced by annual cost-cutting measures by the Health Insurance Fund.

"The shortage of family physicians is worsening, and obtaining a specialist appointment remains difficult despite additional funding."

This does not mean nothing has improved during the past four years. Some things have. More children, significantly more children, are receiving health checkups, and more people are participating in cancer screening programs. Family physicians are increasingly able to consult specialists without requiring patients to attend separate appointments. The system for ensuring quality of care has been updated, and new ways of working have been tested. The supervisory board of the Health Insurance Fund has implemented various cost-saving measures to contain expenditure growth. These are necessary steps made possible by the work of many people.

But overall, access to health care has not improved. The shortage of family physicians is worsening, and obtaining a specialist appointment remains difficult despite additional funding. When people cannot receive timely care from family physicians, home nurses or social workers, their problems eventually end up in emergency departments or hospitals. There, attempts are made to solve problems that should have been addressed earlier and elsewhere.

Against this backdrop, more reforms are being pursued simultaneously than the health care system is capable of implementing. The goals may be correct, but they all require the same personnel, funding and functioning data systems. There simply are not enough of these resources to do everything at once.

Four years ago, development plans were presented as solutions to many of the system's problems. The plans have now been completed, yet most of the problems remain.

As of September this year, alongside the Population Health Development Plan and its programs, there were 16 additional strategy documents and seven more in preparation or planning. Patients can now choose from a fairly wide range of strategic documents. The selection of available appointment times is much more limited.

The problem is not merely the number of documents. Often, their contents fail to clearly identify who is responsible for implementation, what funding will be used and by what deadline.

The "Pharmaceutical Policy 2030" strategy took three years to prepare and was completed in 2023, yet its implementation plan has still not been approved. The three years spent drafting the strategy have now been followed by another three years waiting for the implementation plan.

One year ago, while discussing transportation policy before the Riigikogu, I pointed out that one of the main weaknesses of our strategies is the avoidance of difficult choices and the separation of promises from actual capabilities.

This year's health care report confirms the same pattern: intentions accumulate faster than the capacity to carry them out. Estonia has no shortage of people capable of drafting development plans. What is lacking is the ability to act on them.

The Ministry of Social Affairs should decide which changes can realistically be implemented first with the people, money and IT systems already available, and which previously promised reforms must therefore be postponed.

We saw the same pattern in this year's audit of development policy in southeastern Estonia. Special attention promised for the region appeared in action plans, but had little influence on actual decisions made by ministries. The special attention existed more on paper than in reality.

Rather than identifying solutions suited to the region's problems, the plan largely collected activities the state would have undertaken anyway. The special attention consisted mainly of producing a document rather than changing policy. At the same time, the ministry had already begun searching for new strategic approaches for the region, creating a situation where one low-impact plan could be followed by another before any decision has been made about what should actually be done differently.

Preparing a development plan has increasingly become a convenient way to demonstrate that work is being done without making difficult decisions. Attention shifts from unresolved problems to a document under preparation. Questions about what can realistically be achieved with existing resources and what must be abandoned are postponed. The development plan no longer helps decision-making; instead, it provides an excuse to delay decisions. Development planning has become development parking.

Are promises actually being kept?

The National Audit Office is currently completing an audit on the use of funding allocated for the civilian components of comprehensive national defense. We will discuss the results in the near future.

However, we have also audited civil protection and crisis preparedness during the past year and in previous years.

Based on the National Audit Office's experience, I have reason to agree with Meelis Oidsalu's description of Estonia's crisis management pattern: a shock, media attention and an emergency procurement process. Unfortunately, it also happens that the air begins leaking out before the emergency procurement even begins. Attention shifts elsewhere and momentum fades until the next crisis.

The gap between ambitious plans and actual implementation was also evident in an audit examining how government information systems are hosted and whether they can continue functioning during a crisis.

In response to the security situation, the government set a goal in its action program requiring critical databases and information systems to remain operational outside Estonia by the first quarter of 2027.

The audit found that this goal will not be achieved on time. By June of this year, only 13 of the 122 systems on the list had achieved the required level of readiness, about 11 percent.

The Ministry of Justice explained that the government had already revised the target in February. By the deadline, only those systems for which existing capabilities permit such readiness are expected to be completed. An updated timetable and additional funding requirements are to be submitted to the government in the first quarter of 2027, the very quarter in which the original goal should have been achieved.

The readiness deadline has become a deadline for submitting another plan.

We observed a similar discrepancy between targets and actual activity in this year's food reserve audit. In 2022, the government set a goal of maintaining food reserves sufficient for the entire population for 14 days. Four years later, the goal remained unmet because the Stockpiling Agency had been operating according to a much smaller target. One objective existed on paper, another guided day-to-day work.

"Are we doing what we promised, and can those promises be trusted?"

This pattern of generating momentum amid public attention and then quietly lowering expectations wastes both time and money while leaving important preparedness goals unfulfilled. When the next crisis arrives, shortcomings will need to be addressed in haste and at greater cost, if there is still time to do so.

The government must decide what level of readiness Estonia will ensure and by when, and then secure the money and personnel necessary to achieve it. If targets are lowered, that should be clearly stated. Otherwise, a misleading impression may emerge regarding the state's actual preparedness.

It should not be the case that setting a target becomes a major public event while abandoning it happens quietly, without explaining what the country is no longer prepared for and what risks are being accepted as a result.

Across all the issues discussed today, the same question remains: are we doing what we promised, and can those promises be trusted?

We will carry that question into the coming year.

Next year will mark 10 years since Estonia's administrative reform, and our annual report will focus on regional development. We will examine how government decisions and public spending affect the viability of life across Estonia's different regions and whether promises are reflected in real choices and actions.

World.title: Acclaimed documentary scrutinizing Israel's Gaza strikes coming to Tallinn
World.content:
"NAZA," an award-winning documentary investigating Israel's military targeting in Gaza and the role of AI in its strikes, premieres at Tallinn's Kai Cinema on November 28.

Filmed at night from rooftops in Tel Aviv, "NAZA" examines the systems used by Israel to select targets and approve strikes that have killed civilians in Gaza since October 7, 2023.

Based on investigative reporting published between 2023 and 2025 by The Guardian, +972 Magazine and Local Call, the documentary features anonymous accounts from 24 people connected to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and Israeli intelligence services. Their testimonies shed light on how decisions about strikes in Gaza were made and the consequences for civilians.

According to the Guardian, the film's title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to the number of civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.

The film also explores the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in military decision-making and who bears responsibility when algorithms help determine matters of life and death.

"NAZA" was directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, who also co-directed the 2024 Oscar-winning documentary "No Other Land."

25-minute ovation

The film received a Special Jury Prize in the main competition at the Venice Film Festival, where its premiere earned a festival record nearly 25-minute standing ovation.

"NAZA" has also won the Audience Award for Best European Film at the San Sebastián Film Festival and Best Political Documentary at the Critics Choice Documentary Awards earlier this month, among other accolades. It was likewise selected for the Main Slate at the 64h New York Film Festival.

Audiences will have ten chances to see the film in Estonia, beginning November 28 at Kai Cinema in Tallinn.

World.title: Estonia to ski federation: Russian athletes will not compete on our snow
World.content:
Estonia has told the International Ski Federation (FIS) that Russian and Belarusian athletes will not be allowed to compete on Estonian territory while the war in Ukraine continues.

A letter to that effect from the Culture Ministry follows the FIS easing restrictions in September so that neutral status alone suffices, and comes as Otepää prepares to host junior world championships in January and the biathlon world championships in February.

The FIS relaxed its rules for athletes from the aggressor states at the start of September. Before, Russian and Belarusian competitors had previously faced a much more thorough background check, but now confirmation of neutrality is enough. Restrictions have also been lifted for athletes linked to military and security-service sports clubs such as Moscow's CSKA and Dynamo.

This week the FIS also updated its list of athletes granted neutral status for the coming winter sports season, admitting Denis Spitsov, who has won five Olympic medals. However, Russia's best-known skier, Aleksandr Bolshunov, was not granted neutral status.

Estonia does not host a cross-country World Cup stage this winter as it did last season, but Otepää hosts the junior and U23 Nordic World Championships from January 18–24, and the biathlon World Championships take place at Tehvandi in February.

Sport in Estonia falls under the Ministry of Culture's remit. Source: Iris Tähema/ERR

"Estonia condemned Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine immediately, and since the start of the war the Estonian government, the Ministry of Culture and the Estonian Olympic Committee have agreed that Russian and Belarusian athletes and teams should not be taking part in international sports competitions until the war in Ukraine has ended," the ministry wrote.

"The Estonian government takes the position that competitions involving Russian and Belarusian athletes cannot take place in Estonia," the ministry letter continued. It warned that allowing them would conflict with Estonia's position as a leading supporter of Ukraine and give Russia and Belarus a chance to use international media coverage for propaganda.

The ministry noted that Estonia stopped issuing tourist visas to Russian citizens on March 10, 2022, and that since August 18 of the same year, Russian citizens who already had tourist visas — including those obtained to take part in sports competitions or cultural events — have not been allowed to enter the country. It called on all event organizers to show full support for Ukraine and to condemn Russia's war.

To compete under neutral status in International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) events, Russian and Belarusian athletes and support personnel must sign a declaration of neutrality and participate as a neutral athlete, which would include no display of Russian or Belarusian flags or other national symbols. They can only compete in individual events. Other requirements include no military or security agency links and compliance with anti-doping regulations and checks.

World.title: Tallinn to use satellite imagery to detect illegal buildings
World.content:
Tallinn's Urban Planning Department will begin using satellite imagery to identify illegal structures. The system will be ready for use in January.

Tallinn's Urban Planning Department has signed a contract with technology company Datel to use satellite imagery-based analysis in construction oversight. The tool will compare satellite images with data from the national building register to identify illegal structures.

Older orthophotos will also be available through the platform to help determine when a particular building or extension was constructed, the Urban Planning Department said.

The platform will generate a list of buildings that are either missing from the building register or incorrectly registered, as well as unregistered structures and buildings whose footprints differ significantly from the information recorded in the register. The analysis will cover the entire territory of Tallinn, except for the island of Aegna.

Satellite imagery will be produced this year and the system will be ready for use in January.

Deputy Mayor Tiit Terik said the introduction of satellite data will provide better opportunities to monitor changes in the urban environment and make construction oversight more efficient.

"Smart solutions allow us to process large amounts of information more quickly and direct officials' attention to where it is needed most," Terik said.

Eva-Maria Meristo, head of the Urban Planning Department's construction oversight division, said the satellite-based tool will help officials detect changes to buildings in the urban environment earlier and devote more attention to resolving complex cases.

"From space, we get a view of the city that isn't visible from the street. Satellite data helps us identify where construction activity warrants closer inspection. If an inspection reveals a discrepancy, we assess whether the structure can be brought into compliance with regulations and under what conditions," Meristo said.

Oliver Stimmer, head of Datel's space division, said Tallinn's decision to adopt the Catanova service, developed jointly by Datel and the European Space Agency (ESA), marks an important step for the company.

"Until now, we have primarily offered this innovative machine learning-based object detection solution to municipalities in Spain. One of the biggest advantages of satellite-based remote sensing is its cost-effectiveness, as large areas can be analyzed using a consistent methodology without the need for on-site inspections every time a potential discrepancy needs to be identified," Stimmer said.

World.title: 'World's only volunteer cyber reserve' drills Tallinn Airport defense
World.content:
Volunteers have been rehearsing this week how to keep Tallinn Airport running during a large-scale cyber attack, with a scenario of check-in and baggage systems being down.

Volunteers have been rehearsing this week how to keep Tallinn Airport running during a large-scale cyber attack, with a scenario of check-in and baggage systems being down.

The volunteer IT specialists come from Estonia's cyber reserve, and this week's exercise is the fifth of its kind involving a critical infrastructure operator; it tested a situation in which hundreds of passengers are left without their baggage at a time when flights are delayed or canceled.

This was the fifth exercise for the state Information System Authority's (RIA) cyber reserve in cooperation with an Estonian critical infrastructure operator. No comparable network of volunteer IT specialists exists elsewhere in the world, "Aktuaalne kaamera" reported.

Members of RIA's cyber reserve worked through a set scenario: the passengers cannot check in, and the baggage system is not working. Whereas in real life, resolving an attack of this kind could take a week; in the exercise each team was given just one day.

Passengers at Tallinn Airport. Source: Patrik Tamm / ERR

In the scenario: "Hundreds of air passengers are left essentially without luggage, luggage does not reach the plane, real people's lists do not reach the airlines, real people have to be checked by hand," said RIA chief expert Armani Pogosjan.

Pogosjan explained how flights are delayed or canceled and compensation claims follow, in the case. This need not be abstract either – an actual cyber attack affected passengers much closer to home as recently as this year. "A few months ago there was a very similar attack in our neighboring country Latvia. A few years ago there was an even bigger attack at Dublin Airport," he noted.

In any case, Estonian critical service providers face cyber attack attempts every day. Most are repelled, and incidents with impact are rare — though Selver's refrigeration systems hacked earlier this month is a high profile recent exception.

Riivo Tuvike, CEO of Tallinn Airport, said all major and well-known infrastructure companies are potential targets in the current security situation, meaning airports are no different.

"The growth began when Russia attacked Ukraine. Perhaps what has now happened with AI has simply increased the number of these attacks. Because it is easier and cheaper to do, there are also more of them."

Despite having just a day to resolve things, the exercise was judged to have been a success.
