Speaking at the COP31 UN climate conference in the Turkish city of Antalya, Bektenov said Central Asia faced growing challenges from rising temperatures, shrinking glaciers, desertification and water scarcity, requiring closer regional cooperation.

He invited international partners to support the initiative, which was proposed by Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

Swiss rail maker Stadler steps up Kazakhstan expansion

The company has put its first “Charme” sleeper carriages – produced locally in Astana – into service on behalf of the Kazakhstan Railways (KTZ), reported swissinfo on Nov. 11.

The contract provides for the delivery of 557 sleeper carriages and their maintenance over 20 years, with commissioning scheduled to continue until the end of 2030.

More than 100 carriages, manufactured locally, were already taken delivery of in October. They will operate, in particular, on the 1,300-kilometer line linking Astana to Almaty.

Kazakhstan’s AI ambitions open a new chapter in its economic ties with Europe

Growing technology exports and major investment in computing infrastructure are giving Kazakhstan a stronger foothold in the digital economy. The challenge is to turn that momentum into lasting gains for businesses and workers, according to an EU Reporter article published on Nov. 3.

In Ekibastuz, Kazakhstan is preparing to put its energy resources to a new use: powering the computing systems behind artificial intelligence. The planned Data Centre Valley represents an attempt to build another export industry, selling access to advanced computing alongside the country’s established trade in natural resources.

For European businesses and policymakers, the development raises an increasingly practical question. Could Kazakhstan become a significant partner in digital services, industrial AI and the infrastructure connecting European and Asian markets?

National Bank of Kazakhstan sells its first tokenized notes

The National Bank of Kazakhstan sold short-term notes in the form of digital tokens for the first time at a November 9 auction on the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE). The tokenized notes accounted for 10 billion tenge (about $22.3 million), or one-fifth of the issue’s total face value of 50 billion tenge (about $111.7 million), reported the Times of Central Asia on Nov. 11.

The central bank said selling conventional and tokenized notes together allowed it to apply the same pricing rules to both forms and test how the digital platform worked alongside the existing securities market. It sees the trial as a step toward tokenizing other government securities.

Kazakhstan inks new deals to supply Uranium to Indian cos

Kazakhstan, the world’s largest producer of uranium, has signed new contracts to supply natural uranium to major energy companies in India in 2026, as the country seeks to expand its international partnerships and diversify its uranium export markets, reported The Economic Times on Nov. 10.

World.title: IMF: Uzbekistan’s Next Growth Challenge is Productivity and Regional Integration
World.content:
ASTANA – Uzbekistan’s strong economic growth is creating opportunities to strengthen its position as a regional trade and logistics hub, but sustaining the momentum will require deeper structural reforms, greater private sector participation and closer economic integration across Central Asia, International Monetary Fund (IMF) officials said Nov. 13 at a roundtable at the Central Bank of Uzbekistan in Tashkent.

Roberto Cardarelli, assistant director of the IMF’s Middle East and Central Asia Department, and Koba Gvenetadze, the fund’s resident representative in Uzbekistan, discussed the country’s growth prospects, inflation risks and structural reform priorities, highlighting the need to translate strong economic performance into higher productivity and sustainable job creation.

Uzbekistan’s economy has expanded strongly over the past five to six years, supported by domestic demand and continued structural reforms. However, the strength of domestic consumption also creates potential overheating pressures, making the coordination of fiscal and monetary policies increasingly important, Gvenetadze said. He cautioned against treating a particular growth rate as the ultimate measure of economic success. Instead, the priority should be to ensure that growth is sustainable, increasingly productivity-driven and supported by private businesses rather than the state.

“It’s a very important moment for Uzbekistan to make sure that all this performance and very impressive performance in terms of growth is translated into higher productivity,” Gvenetadze said.

The IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook projects Uzbekistan’s economy to grow by 7.8% in 2026, up from its previous forecast of 6.8%. Growth is expected to moderate to 6.5% in 2027, compared with the earlier projection of 6%. The revised outlook reflects the country’s strong economic performance and places Uzbekistan among the region’s fastest-growing economies. The improved forecast comes as the country seeks to accelerate annual economic growth toward 9%-10%. Achieving such ambitions without intensifying inflationary pressures will depend on the country’s ability to strengthen its economic foundations and improve productivity.

Moving beyond first-generation reforms

The next phase of Uzbekistan’s economic transformation will require moving beyond the initial wave of liberalization toward more difficult institutional and structural changes. Cardarelli described this as a broader challenge facing economies across the region. Having implemented many first-generation reforms, including market liberalization, countries now need to address more complex issues related to private sector development, state-owned enterprises, financial markets and human capital.

For Uzbekistan, reducing the state’s economic footprint remains a central priority. Gvenetadze identified stronger corporate governance, stricter budget constraints for state-owned enterprises, transparent privatization and stronger competition as key areas for reform.

The financial sector also requires further modernization. The IMF sees a need to phase out directed and preferential lending, strengthen banking supervision and improve the regulatory framework, alongside advancing the long-discussed capital markets law.

These reforms are closely connected. A more competitive banking system and deeper capital markets could improve access to financing for private businesses, reduce reliance on state-directed credit and create conditions for more efficient investment.

Governance improvements will also matter. Gvenetadze noted that Uzbekistan had already adopted a conflict-of-interest law, while legislation on whistleblower protection and asset declarations would further strengthen institutional accountability.

The IMF also highlighted the importance of expanding women’s and young people’s participation in the labor market. For an economy with a growing young population, creating jobs will depend not only on investment and infrastructure but also on developing the skills required by a more diversified economy. Cardarelli stressed that human capital would be particularly important as countries seek to move toward services and higher-value economic activities. Diversification into these sectors is difficult without a workforce equipped with the necessary skills.

Growth, inflation and fiscal discipline

Maintaining macroeconomic stability will be another test for Uzbekistan as economic activity remains strong. The IMF identified inflation as a major macroeconomic stability challenge across the region, driven by domestic demand pressures and external shocks. Cardarelli noted that bringing inflation down from double-digit levels is generally easier than achieving further reductions, requiring monetary policy to remain appropriately tight.

In Uzbekistan, strong domestic demand and higher-than-budgeted gold revenues have created additional fiscal policy considerations. Higher commodity revenues can encourage governments to increase spending, potentially reinforcing demand-driven inflation.

Gvenetadze said Uzbekistan had so far demonstrated fiscal discipline. He noted that the budget deficit was set at 3% of GDP for this year and said he expected the actual figure to come in below that level. He also referred to discussions with the authorities on analyzing the non-mineral budget deficit. Such an indicator would help assess how much public finances depend on gold revenues and provide a clearer picture of the underlying fiscal position. Gvenetadze clarified that the IMF had not recommended establishing a separate sovereign wealth or stabilization fund for Uzbekistan. The broader challenge is to prevent temporary revenue gains from translating into permanent spending commitments while maintaining sufficient fiscal space to respond to future shocks.

Uzbekistan’s regional role and the Middle Corridor

Beyond domestic reforms, Uzbekistan’s geographical position gives it an opportunity to become an increasingly important link in regional and international trade, Gvenetadze said. Stronger economic links with neighboring countries could generate positive spillovers across the region by expanding trade, investment and market opportunities.

The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, currently under construction, illustrates the potential of improved regional connectivity. The project could open new trade routes and strengthen Central Asia’s links with global markets.

However, the benefits extend beyond transit. Better transport connections can lower trade costs, attract investment and give businesses access to larger markets. Cardarelli also pointed to the changing geography of global trade as an opportunity for the region. Disruptions linked to conflicts in the north and south have pushed businesses to explore alternative routes, increasing Central Asia’s strategic importance. The Middle Corridor is part of this wider shift.

Yet infrastructure alone will not determine whether the region can capitalize on changing trade patterns. The IMF’s analysis highlights the importance of improving logistics and governance, lowering trade and regulatory barriers, streamlining customs procedures, digitalizing trade processes and harmonizing standards across countries. These measures are essential to turn transport connectivity into deeper economic integration.

World.title: Kazakhstan Considers Unified Strategy for Three Financial Platforms
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is considering a unified strategy to coordinate the development of three financial platforms, the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE), the Astana International Financial Center (AIFC) and Alatau City, while preserving their distinct specializations, according to the National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov, who announced it, speaking at the 14th Congress of Financiers of Kazakhstan on Nov. 13.

Under the proposed framework, cooperation would include mutual recognition of participants across platforms, regular exchange of supervisory information between regulators, harmonized regulatory approaches and a clear division of responsibilities, Atameken Business reported.

National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov also emphasized the importance of keeping the three financial markets interconnected as they develop independently. He said Alatau City was emerging as another source of financial innovation, with its own regulatory and tax frameworks, alongside the capital market developing within the AIFC.

“In our view, it is extremely important to ensure synergy between these markets through mutual recognition, mutual compatibility and mutual circulation, so that they can develop while remaining interconnected,” Suleimenov said.

He stressed that the proposed strategy would not involve micromanagement or dictate specific actions to each platform. Instead, it would set common strategic priorities and define each market’s specializations.

“It is extremely important to ensure that each market does not become confined within its own jurisdiction or geographical location. Capital and money are liquid by nature; they are fluid and therefore cannot be locked in,” he said.

AIFC and Alatau City: complementary roles

The potential relationship between the AIFC and Alatau City was also discussed at the congress, amid questions about whether the new city could compete with the financial center for foreign investment.

AIFC Governor Renat Bekturov said the two jurisdictions had different objectives, including at the legislative level, according to the National Business Agency.

The AIFC focuses on attracting investment, developing the capital market and innovative financial products, and providing an independent regulatory framework. Alatau City, meanwhile, is intended to accelerate urban development through special regimes covering investment, construction, science and innovation.

“This involves special regimes for attracting investment, as well as for the construction industry, science and innovation. The foundation of Alatau City’s legal system is territoriality. Financial products, however, are extraterritorial. For example, how could you create a token linked to a specific property that would be traded only in Alatau City? Naturally, this would not be the case,” Bekturov said.

He said the AIFC did not expect competition with Alatau City but rather an exchange of experience. The regulatory and institutional practices developed by the financial center could support the new city’s future development and create opportunities for cooperation between the two jurisdictions.

“The argument that the AIFC was established solely for foreign investment is incorrect. Our task is also to facilitate the development of the capital market in Kazakhstan,” Bekturov said.

World.title: Cultural Weekend: Music, Art and More
World.content:
ASTANA – As winter approaches, warm up your weekend with art, music and theater. From multimedia exhibitions and classical concerts to ballet performances, The Astana Times editorial team has curated a list of events to enjoy with friends and family.

Astana

“Fallen Angels” and “Bolero X” ballets, Nov.13 – 14

Three choreographic works come together in a programme that explores different emotions and styles of movement. Inspired by the music of Edith Piaf, the first work tells stories of love, heartbreak and loss. The programme also features Jiří Kylián’s energetic Fallen Angels and Bolero X, a contemporary interpretation of Maurice Ravel’s famous composition, bringing together around 50 dancers in a powerful display of movement and rhythm.

Venue: Astana Ballet; 43 Uly Dala Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Classical concert, Nov. 14

The concert celebrates the sound of the flute through works by Kazakh and international composers. Audiences can hear the instrument in a variety of styles, from classical compositions to more contemporary works.

Venue: Astana Opera; 1 Konayev Street. Tickets are available here.

Concert featuring Ludovico Einaudi’s greatest hits, Nov. 15

Fans of film music can enjoy a concert dedicated to the work of composer Hans Zimmer. Performed by a symphony orchestra and choir, the programme features familiar soundtracks from films such as Interstellar, Inception, Pirates of the Caribbean, The Lion King and The Dark Knight. The performance brings some of cinema’s most memorable musical moments to the concert stage.

Venue: Qazaqconcert; 10/1 Mangilik El Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“The Mysterious Worlds of Hieronymus Bosch” exhibition, Nov.14 – Jan.31

Visitors can explore the unusual artistic world of Dutch painter Hieronymus Bosch through a multimedia exhibition featuring some of his most famous works. Large-scale projections bring his imaginative creatures, mysterious landscapes and symbolic details to life, offering a closer look at paintings created more than five centuries ago.

Venue: Lumiere-Hall Multimedia Museum; 8 Abay Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Almaty

Andrea Bocelli concert, Nov. 14-15

The programme pays tribute to the music of Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli, featuring some of his best-known songs performed by the Otyrar Sazy Academic Folklore and Ethnographic Orchestra. The repertoire includes Time to Say Goodbye, The Prayer, Vivo per Lei and Besame Mucho, alongside other popular melodies. The concert offers an evening of familiar songs and orchestral arrangements.

Venue: 35 Kaldayakov Street. Tickets are available here.

“Anna Karenina” ballet, Nov.15

Boris Eifman’s ballet brings Leo Tolstoy’s classic novel Anna Karenina to the stage through expressive choreography and dramatic movement. The production explores the complicated relationships, passion and personal struggles of its characters, offering a new interpretation of one of Russian literature’s best-known stories.

Venue: Abay Opera Theater; 110 Kabanbay Batyr Street. Tickets are available here.

“The Duenna” performance, Nov. 14

This adventurous comedy by British playwright Richard Brinsley Sheridan follows a series of romantic intrigues, unexpected twists and amusing misunderstandings. Directed by Alexey Shemes, the production promises a lighthearted theatrical evening filled with humour and lively characters.

Venue: 117 Abay Avenue. Tickets are available here.

World.title: Kazakhstan-China Freight Traffic Rises 8% in First 10 Months of 2026
World.content:
ASTANA – Freight traffic between Kazakhstan and China reached 31.8 million tons in the first 10 months of 2026, an 8% increase compared to the same period last year, when 29.4 million tons were transported, reported Kazakhstan’s national railway company Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ).

Growth was recorded in both directions. From January through October, 12.1 million tons of cargo were transported from China to Kazakhstan, up 9% year on year. Of this volume, 5 million tons passed through the Dostyk border crossing, marking a 13% increase. Another 7.1 million tons were transported through Altynkol, up 6%.

In the opposite direction, Kazakhstan shipped 19.7 million tons of cargo to China, an 8% increase compared to the same period in 2025.

At the border crossings, 13.1 million tons were transported through Dostyk, up 12%, while traffic through Altynkol reached 6.6 million tons, a 1% increase.

The growth in freight traffic reflects ongoing efforts to strengthen transport and logistics links between Kazakhstan and China. Further development of international rail connections is focused on modernizing border infrastructure, increasing the capacity of border crossings and improving logistics processes.

World.title: Tokayev Orders Measures to Curb Corruption in Kazakhstan’s State-Owned Companies
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has ordered the government and oversight bodies to submit proposals to reduce corruption in state-owned companies by Nov. 24, following the detention of senior executives at Samruk-Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund and Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), the national railway company.

Speaking at an operational meeting of the Security Council on Nov. 13, Tokayev described the detentions as “an extremely serious signal” indicating widespread corruption in state-owned companies.

He stressed that the Constitution is the country’s supreme law and that violations of its provisions would be addressed under the Law and Order principle.

“The Constitution is the Basic Law of our state, the legal passport of the people. Disregarding the Constitution and its fundamental provisions is tantamount to discriminating against the people. Such actions will be suppressed in accordance with the Law and Order principle. No one is allowed to violate the Constitution or even mock this, one could say, sacred document,” Tokayev said.

He also emphasized that officials entrusted with public authority must act decisively to protect national interests.

“All of us entrusted by the people with public authority must demonstrate unwavering commitment to upholding national interests. This is our civic and political duty,” he said.

He noted that Samruk Kazyna manages Kazakhstan’s strategic assets, implements major investment projects and cooperates with leading foreign companies and international financial institutions.

“Behind each such agreement and partnership are numerous years of negotiations, Kazakhstan’s commitments and the trust of the international community in our country,” he said.

State-owned companies continue operations

Tokayev stressed that the detention of executives would not affect the operations of Samruk Kazyna or state-owned companies, including KTZ. All institutions and enterprises under their management continue to operate as usual.

“This serious incident is not a reason for disruptions in the operations of the Fund and state-owned companies. Moreover, I am confident that the fight against corruption should, on the contrary, increase the confidence of investors and creditors in this institution, and its work will become more efficient, transparent and productive,” he said.

Tokayev also highlighted the recovery of illegally acquired assets, noting that the Prosecutor General’s Office had secured the return of more than 1.3 trillion tenge (US$2.9 billion). The funds were allocated to building 466 social and infrastructure facilities, including medical institutions, water supply systems, schools and sports complexes. Of these, 383 have been completed.

He said the quality of completed facilities should also be assessed, pointing to recurring problems with infrastructure quality, particularly roads.

Corruption statistics and investigations

According to Tokayev, authorities identified 3,168 corruption offenses between 2023 and 2025. Of these, 2,165 were committed by civil servants, while the remaining cases involved other individuals, including employees of the quasi-public sector. The total amount involved exceeded 248 billion tenge (US$550 million).

In the first 10 months of 2026, authorities recorded 751 corruption-related offenses, including 546 committed by civil servants and 205 by other individuals, including employees of quasi-public sector entities.

Tokayev acknowledged that the corruption situation remained challenging and said the authorities would continue to report publicly on the situation and measures being taken to address it. He said all reports of corruption offenses involving officials at different levels would be promptly and thoroughly investigated by the National Security Committee’s Anti-Corruption Service, with the participation of the Prosecutor General’s Office.

“Naturally, there will be no division into ‘our own,’ ‘not quite our own’ and, even more so, ‘outsiders.’ Our Constitution has established the principle of equality of all citizens before the law. We must comply with this requirement,” Tokayev said.

“No one, regardless of their position, achievements or personal connections, should expect exemptions from the law,” he added.

President Tokayev instructed the government and oversight bodies to submit concrete proposals by Nov. 24 to reduce corruption offenses and improve the performance of quasi-public sector companies and their staff.

World.title: IMF, Development Partners Support Early Pension Reform Work in Uzbekistan
World.content:
ASTANA – The International Monetary Fund (IMF), together with the Asian Development Bank (ADB), International Labour Organization (ILO) and World Bank, is working with Uzbekistan’s authorities on an early-stage concept for pension reform, IMF Resident Representative in Uzbekistan Koba Gvenetadze said Nov. 13.

Speaking at a roundtable at the Central Bank of Uzbekistan in Tashkent, Gvenetadze said the reform remains at an early stage, with authorities examining international experience and assessing different approaches to pension system management. He stressed that any future reform should be financially sustainable and avoid creating additional or unforeseen pressure on the state budget.

Responding to a question about the management of pension savings, including the possibility of involving external investment companies, Gvenetadze said the authorities had not yet developed a detailed reform plan. He added that the development of domestic capital markets could also be relevant to pension reform, as pension funds and capital markets often develop alongside each other.

The IMF will continue working with the authorities as the reform process advances, he said.

World.title: ‘Armenia is replacing one dependency with another’: Former Security Council Secretary Armen Grigoryan’s assessment
World.content:
Article by Armenia’s former Security Council secretary

“Armenia is replacing one dependency with another”: Former Security Council Secretary Armen Grigoryan’s view

“The idea of Armenia joining the European Union seems attractive at first glance. But we often confuse what we want with what is possible,” says Armen Grigoryan, a former secretary of Armenia’s Security Council.

He published an article arguing that EU membership is an unrealistic prospect and contradicts the formula Armenia’s authorities have declared. That formula calls for “replacing dependence on a few with dependence on many”.

“This is not a genuine alternative or a diversification of foreign policy. It is simply a way to replace one dependency with another, one that offers fewer prospects and ignores regional realities,” he writes about Armenia’s prospects for European integration.

In Grigoryan’s view, the EU membership agenda once again leads Armenia into a dead end. It forces the country back towards forms of dependence that “have proved unsustainable”.

“Just as we once believed that Russia would solve our security problems, we now mistakenly expect the EU to solve the economic problems that will arise on the path to EU membership,” he argues.

Discussing potential risks, the former official said Armenia could once again face the harsh reality it has experienced since 2020. That was when the 44-day war in Nagorno-Karabakh began. He argues that “an external partner may not take responsibility for solving the problems we expect it to address”.

Grigoryan also raises the question of “how to reduce dependence on Russia without deepening that very dependence even further”. However, he does not offer a direct answer under this subheading. Instead, he speaks of the need for independent decision-making and closer cooperation with the EU, the US and other countries.

Below, we publish an abridged version of the article by the former Security Council secretary, which has sparked considerable debate in Armenia’s political circles.

Historical overview

“If we look at Armenia’s recent history, a very clear and harsh pattern emerges. Every time Yerevan has tried to move closer to the West, it has faced mounting pressure from Russia and ultimately ended up even more firmly in Moscow’s ‘embrace’.

In the 1990s, under Levon Ter-Petrosyan, attempts to build closer ties with European and Euro-Atlantic institutions ended with Armenia joining the Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO) and signing a Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance with Russia in 1997. This strengthened Armenia’s military and political ties with Moscow.

In the 2010s, under Serzh Sargsyan, an attempt to sign an Association Agreement with the EU ended with the decision on 3 September 2013 to join the Customs Union. Armenia subsequently joined the Eurasian Economic Union.

Today, this history appears to be repeating itself, but under a much more dangerous scenario.

“While Armenia continues negotiations and takes steps towards EU membership, I see a growing risk that the country could become involved in the Russia-Belarus Union State.”

Armenia has no immunity against pressure from Moscow

“Statements and steps towards EU membership are sharply worsening relations between Armenia and Russia.

Faced with Russia’s harsh and aggressive countermeasures, Armenia’s state immune system simply cannot withstand Moscow’s economic, political and hybrid pressure.

As a result, without real security guarantees from the West, Armenia cannot reduce its dependence on Russia. Instead, it becomes even more vulnerable to Russian pressure.”

The European integration agenda contradicts regionalisation

“An unrealistic EU membership agenda runs counter to the natural process of regionalisation. Armenia lies at the crossroads of three major regional powers: Russia, Iran and Turkey. Yerevan’s relations with each of them are closely interconnected and require a delicate balance.

Iran has repeatedly outlined its ‘red lines’, opposing any expansion of Western military and political presence in the region. Given its strained relations with the West, Tehran views the EU as part of the collective West.

Armenia’s attempts to join the EU could jeopardise its friendly relations with Iran. And Iran is not just a neighbour for Armenia, but a vital ‘lifeline’.

Although Turkey is a NATO member, it pursues an independent regional policy. Together with Azerbaijan, Ankara seeks to resolve regional issues with the participation of countries in the region. The ‘3+3’ format is one example of this approach.

Yerevan’s attempts to expand the West’s presence in the region could create further tensions in its relations with Turkey and Azerbaijan.

Russia views Armenia’s EU membership agenda as a threat to its interests in the region and responds with strong opposition.”

Armenia risks losing the foundations of its economic stability

“In spaceflight, a rocket must reach the second cosmic velocity of 11.2 km per second to escape Earth’s gravitational field. If it fails to reach the required speed, it cannot remain in orbit and falls back under the force of gravity.

Armenia lacks the ‘speed’ it needs to escape the economic gravitational pull of the Russia-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) and Russia itself.

If Armenia finds itself in an ‘intermediate’ position during a prolonged and drawn-out EU accession process, it risks losing the foundations of its current economic stability: cheap energy supplies and access to the Russian market. It could then fall back even more painfully into complete dependence on Russia.”

Will Yerevan consider imposing sanctions on Russia and Iran?

“On its path towards EU membership, Armenia will also face the question of whether to join sanctions against Russia and Iran. This could seriously damage relations with these two countries, which are vital to Armenia’s security and economy.

Amid discussions about possible increases in the price of Russian gas, and even supply cuts in some cases, Armenia is increasingly exploring ways to import more gas from Iran. However, this raises an important contradiction.

Under the sanctions imposed on Iran, the European Union prohibits the purchase, import and exchange of Iranian natural gas. At some point on its path towards EU membership, Armenia will have to align its legislation and foreign policy with EU requirements.

This means Armenia will have to stop importing gas from Iran. The future of the Armenian-Iranian ‘gas-for-electricity’ programme will also come into question.

This creates a contradiction. Armenia needs alternative suppliers to reduce its dependence on Russian gas. Yet, on its path towards EU membership, it may have to limit its access to Iranian gas as well.”

Cooperation should extend beyond the EU and US

“Armenia can develop political, economic and security cooperation with European partners without making EU membership a foreign policy goal.

Our task is not to replace dependence on Russia with dependence on another power centre, but to strengthen Armenia’s independence.

We can deepen cooperation not only with the EU and the US, but also with India, China, Central Asian states, the Gulf countries, Japan, South Korea and other partners, each through its own agenda.

Armenia’s foreign policy options are not limited to choosing between two geopolitical centres.

The more diverse our economic, political and security ties become, the more opportunities we will have to balance external dependencies.”

Article by Armenia’s former Security Council secretary

World.title: Abkhazia’s capital temporarily bans high-rise construction in city centre. What happens next?
World.content:
Authorities have temporarily banned buildings taller than 18 metres, or roughly six storeys, in the historic centre of Sukhum.

The decision, proposed by Mayor Timur Agrba and approved by the city council, will remain in force until the city adopts a new master plan.

Abkhazia’s capital last approved a master plan during the Soviet era, in 1987. Since then, the authorities have not adopted a comprehensive new urban development plan, although both officials and the public have periodically called for one.

Whenever another high-rise appears near the waterfront, Sukhum residents grow increasingly vocal in demanding tighter controls on construction. They believe these buildings are damaging the city’s historic character.

According to Timur Agrba, the city administration receives proposals for buildings of various heights. Officials reject some of them, but without a proper master plan, the city authorities have virtually no regulatory grounds for refusing projects, apart from the need to preserve the city’s historic character.

The authorities plan to start drawing up a new master plan in 2027, a process that could take several years. That is why Agrba proposed temporarily restricting the height of new buildings. However, the measure effectively contradicts existing legislation: the coefficient set out in the current Urban Planning Code allows buildings taller than 18 metres.

The restriction may therefore prove to be purely temporary and, possibly, not particularly effective.

Authorities cannot revoke construction permits they have already issued, so the new restriction will apply only to future projects.

They may also grant exceptions for certain buildings that serve an important social purpose or are significant for the republic or the city.

Sukhum’s chief architect, Bislan Bagateliya, confirms that the city centre’s architectural character calls for low-rise development. He supports restricting high-rise construction until the authorities have a clear understanding of how the city should develop.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Children in cars without car seats: Why are child car seats unpopular in Armenia?
World.content:
Why are child car seats unpopular in Armenia?

In Armenia, you can often see children travelling in cars without special child seats. They sit in the back or on their parents’ laps. Although traffic rules require parents to use child seats to transport children safely, few people follow this rule.

Under Armenia’s current traffic regulations, children under the age of seven must travel in a special child car seat. The seat must match the child’s height and weight. Children aged seven to 12 should use special booster seats. Boosters are designed for children weighing 15–36 kg or 22–36 kg. They position the seat belt correctly across the child’s body. Boosters raise children so that the standard seat belt runs across their shoulders and hips, rather than their necks. However, children in this age group can also travel in the back seat without a child seat. In that case, they must wear the standard seat belt. Children under 12 must never travel in the front passenger seat without a child seat or booster.

Experts warn that even a low-speed collision can have serious consequences for a child in a road accident.

A properly selected and installed car seat significantly reduces the risk of serious injury and death.

Why do parents in Armenia refuse to use child car seats? How effectively does the Patrol Service enforce the rules? What do official road accident figures tell us, including cases with tragic outcomes?

To answer these questions, a JAMnews journalist contacted the Ministry of Internal Affairs, examined official statistics and spoke to parents.

Child car seats often go unused, even when families have them in their cars

Stepan Grigoryan’s child is two years old. He bought a special child car seat, but the toddler often refuses to sit in it. He cries and struggles. His mother has to sit next to him to calm him down. When she cannot, the child cries and climbs onto her lap.

“If we first distract him with toys or something else, he sits in the car seat calmly. But if that doesn’t work, he starts crying until we pick him up. I understand how important it is for him to sit in a car seat, but on short trips he often sits on his mother’s lap,” Stepan explains.

He knows that accidents can happen even on short journeys. He also admits that the parents are at fault for giving in to their child’s demands.

Stepan drives frequently and has noticed that more children now travel in car seats. Even so, he believes that no more than 10% of parents follow the rules:

“In the mornings, I often see children aged 10 or 12 travelling with their parents in taxis or school buses. They don’t use child car seats or seat belts. The authorities either do very little to enforce the rules or do nothing at all.”

He believes that raising the fine from 5,000 drams [$13] to 20,000 drams [$55], a proposal now widely discussed on social media, will not solve the problem:

“That’s not enough to make drivers think twice. The fine should be higher. If drivers know they could face a 50,000-dram [$138] fine, get caught at least once a year or temporarily lose their driving licence, they will take greater care.

Let me tell you about my own experience. Patrol officers have stopped me for speeding and talking on the phone while driving. But they have never checked whether my child was sitting in a car seat or on his mother’s lap. Strict enforcement and hefty fines could help make life-saving child car seats the norm.”

He also proposes that the government provide free car seats to low-income and large families through a social programme, or organise donations:

“I’m sure many parents would gladly give their old car seats to families in need. They are durable and last a long time, but children outgrow them, so their parents no longer need them. Social workers could register vulnerable families and help them apply to local authorities or the government for a car seat.”

Child road deaths

The number of children killed in road accidents in Armenia remains alarming. In 2023, 13 children under the age of 12 died. The figure fell to 11 in 2024 and remained at 11 in 2025.

The authorities do not keep detailed statistics on deaths linked to the absence of child car seats. The Ministry of Internal Affairs does not track these cases separately. As a result, it is impossible to determine exactly how many children died because they were not using car seats.

How much do car seats cost in Armenia?

Prices for child car seats vary significantly depending on the manufacturer, model, the child’s age group and the seat’s technical specifications.

A review of local online shops shows that booster seats (boosters) cost up to 10,000 drams ($27).

Prices for standard child car seats start at 28,000–33,000 drams ($77–91). Some models cost 80,000 drams ($222) or more.

Second-hand seats are cheaper. You can find them for between 10,000 and 20,000 drams. However, when choosing a car seat, parents should consider more than just the price. They should also check whether it meets safety standards. The seat must match the child’s height and weight. Parents must also install it correctly in the car.

Enforcement steps up

Narek Sargsyan, a spokesperson for the Minister of Internal Affairs, said a recent fatal accident had reignited public debate about child car seats. The crash killed both parents and one of their young children. Two other children suffered critical injuries.

He confirmed that the authorities plan to quadruple the fine for failing to follow child passenger safety rules. The current fine stands at 5,000 drams. The proposed legislative amendments would also add one penalty point to the driver’s record.

“The National Assembly will discuss this issue. Lawmakers may also revise the fine or introduce other regulations. The problem remains a priority. Statistics on administrative offences over recent years show that enforcement has gradually increased,” Sargsyan said.

He presented figures covering 2024–2026. Authorities recorded 3,773 violations involving the transport of children without appropriate safety equipment in 2024. The figure rose to 9,067 in 2025 and reached 10,844 in the first nine months of 2026.

“We welcome the public debate that has started around this issue. It encourages the authorities to step up enforcement and consider additional regulations,” Sargsyan said.

Why are child car seats unpopular in Armenia?

World.title: Can electronic salary monitoring eliminate under-the-table payments in Azerbaijan?
World.content:
Electronic salary monitoring in Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan plans to pay salaries through an electronic payment system selected by the Central Bank, based on data from the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection of the Population. Employees will still be able to choose which bank receives their salary. Deputy Labour and Social Protection Minister Zaur Aliyev announced the plans on 11 November at a meeting of the Milli Majlis Committee on Labour and Social Policy.

Aliyev said the aim of the new system was to monitor not only the salaries specified in employment contracts but also the actual amounts paid to workers.

“This will create a more effective monitoring mechanism to identify and prevent cases of delayed salary payments, underpayment or concealment of part of an employee’s earnings.”

Under proposed amendments to the Labour Code, employers will have to pay salaries in full into a bank account chosen by the employee. The Report news agency reports that the government expects the new system to strengthen oversight of timely salary payments and compliance with labour laws.

The initiative forms part of the same package of legislative amendments as the introduction of hourly pay. We have previously reported on who could benefit from such a system.

Will electronic monitoring put an end to under-the-table salary payments, or will it simply lead to new ways of concealing income?

What are under-the-table salary payments?

Under this arrangement, employers transfer part of an employee’s salary to their bank account and pay the rest in cash, unofficially. The salary stated in the employment contract is lower than the employee’s actual earnings. As a result, employers pay taxes and social security contributions only on the officially declared amount. Some workers do not have employment contracts at all.

Samed Shikhi, who has worked at various companies in Azerbaijan for around ten years, said that most of his employers had not offered him an employment contract.

“Getting an extra 50 manats (around $30) today is more beneficial for me than counting on a higher pension after the age of 65.”

He said most workers do not try to change the situation. Seeing the pensions that current retirees receive, they do not expect to get substantial payments when they grow old.

How widespread is the problem?

There are no precise figures, but official statistics offer an indication of the scale of the problem. According to the State Statistics Committee, Azerbaijan has more than 5.1 million employed people, while the number of salaried employees stands at 1,776,800. Of these, 942,600 work in the private sector.

At a parliamentary committee meeting, MP Vugar Bayramov said that 65% of employed people work without employment contracts. According to an International Monetary Fund report on Azerbaijan published this year, only 23% of private-sector workers have official employment contracts. The IMF estimates that the shadow economy accounts for around half of the country’s GDP.

Economist Rashad Hasanov believes that underreporting salaries is most common in the private sector, where it affects more than 40% of employment contracts.

“It is difficult to give an exact figure, but this is a fairly widespread phenomenon,” he said.

Independent economists consider the widespread practice of declaring minimum wages in employment contracts one indication of unofficial payments. This is particularly common in profitable industries such as construction, hospitality and retail.

For comparison, the State Statistics Committee reported that Azerbaijan’s average monthly nominal salary stood at 1,173 manats (around $690) in January–August this year. The minimum wage, meanwhile, is 400 manats (around $235).

According to figures published last year by the State Tax Service, the private non-oil sector had the highest number of registered employment contracts in retail (299,000), services (232,000) and construction (98,000).

Taxes rise as oversight tightens

The introduction of electronic salary monitoring comes alongside an increase in the tax burden. For seven years, starting in 2019, employees in Azerbaijan’s private non-oil sector were exempt from income tax on monthly earnings of up to 8,000 manats (around $4,705).

According to the State Tax Service, the number of employment contracts in the sector increased by around 470,000, or 87%, during this period. It exceeded one million in September last year. The agency attributes this growth to economic development and the tax incentives that remained in place for seven years.

The tax exemption expired at the end of 2025. Employees now pay income tax on monthly earnings of up to 2,500 manats (around $1,470) at a rate of 3% in 2026, 5% in 2027 and 7% from 2028 onwards. The first 200 manats (around $118) remain tax-free.

Last year, Bayramov wrote about how tax rules affect the number of employment contracts. He believes the decline in their number in the private sector is linked to a 2025 change that allowed micro-entrepreneurs to receive tax benefits without having to employ staff.

Hasanov warns that if the move towards official salary payments increases employers’ tax and social security costs, companies may try to pass the additional expenses on to workers:

“Given the high level of competition in the labour market, unemployment and the shortage of medium- and high-paying jobs, this could reduce the amount employees actually take home after taxes and contributions.”

What will the electronic system fail to detect?

Hasanov believes the new system will primarily monitor payments made under existing employment contracts, rather than bring undeclared salaries into the formal economy:

“This mechanism does not require employers to legalise under-the-table salaries, nor does it prevent them from declaring minimum wages in employment contracts.”

This means that if an employment contract specifies a salary of 400 manats and the employer transfers exactly that amount to the employee’s bank card, the system will not detect any violation. The remaining earnings, paid in cash, will remain outside its oversight.

Economist Akif Nasirli considers the new mechanism an “important step”. He believes that fully declaring salaries will increase workers’ pension savings. However, Nasirli also points to another practice:

“Sometimes an employer transfers the official salary to an employee’s bank card but pays the remaining amount in cash or demands that the employee return part of the money transferred.”

The economist says the authorities should compare salaries declared in employment contracts with actual pay levels, taking into account the industry, job position and workload. He also calls for an effective complaints mechanism for workers and measures to hold employers who break the law accountable.

Why don’t workers complain?

In response to a separate enquiry from Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, the State Labour Inspectorate said it could investigate violations in job s if someone filed a complaint. If it confirmed a violation, “measures would be taken against the employer in accordance with the law”. This means that oversight largely depends on workers themselves reporting abuses.

Samed Shikhi believes the main reasons workers do not complain are fear of losing their jobs and a lack of faith that their complaints will achieve anything:

“The problem is that companies often have connections with certain officials or influential people.”

The electronic system will be able to monitor only salaries officially declared by employers. Detecting cash payments will largely depend on workers themselves. As long as employees are afraid to complain, under-the-table salary payments may continue with their tacit consent. The practice is becoming an even more pressing issue as the tax burden increases.

Electronic salary monitoring in Azerbaijan

World.title: Tbilisi mayor considers restricting traffic in city
World.content:
Possible traffic restrictions in Tbilisi

Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze has outlined several possible ways to tackle traffic congestion in the capital. These include restricting vehicle traffic, introducing an alternating-day driving system based on odd and even number plates, and charging drivers to enter certain parts of the city.

He said the growing number of cars was one of Tbilisi’s main problems. Infrastructure projects, such as building flyovers, would not be enough to solve it.

Kaladze did not say that the authorities had decided to introduce any of these measures. However, he noted that restrictions might be necessary to address the problem. In that case, the public would have the final say.

On 11 November, Kaladze told the pro-government Imedi TV channel that 900,000 vehicles had been on Tbilisi’s roads during peak hours.

He rejected claims that dedicated bus lanes were the main cause of traffic congestion. As an example, he cited Agmashenebeli Avenue, where traffic becomes almost impossible at certain times despite the absence of a dedicated public transport lane.

“The biggest problem is our dependence on cars and the sheer number of vehicles, not that the city government is doing nothing. There are specific solutions, just as there are in other countries,” Kaladze said.

Asked by the presenter whether the city could restrict traffic based on whether a vehicle’s number plate ends in an even or odd digit, the mayor described this as one possible option.

“If we want to solve this problem, we could agree on measures such as allowing only cars with number plates ending in an even or odd digit on certain days. Another option would be to install cameras in specific areas and introduce congestion charges, as many European cities have done,” the mayor said.

Kaladze said that although the public might find such decisions difficult to accept, residents themselves would need to play a part in addressing the situation.

“When we make a decision, it is important that everyone understands and accepts it. Society must be ready for it. The city authorities cannot simply do nothing while the problem persists. No — we must make a decision, and we will all have to make certain sacrifices,” Kaladze said.

Traffic congestion and growing pressure on the urban environment

Traffic congestion and overcrowded public transport have remained among Tbilisi’s main transport problems for many years. Rapid urban growth, the development of new residential neighbourhoods and heavy reliance on private cars are putting additional pressure on the existing transport infrastructure.

Didi Dighomi is Tbilisi’s fastest-growing residential district, followed by Navtlughi and Varketili. A study by Danish consultancy Ramboll, commissioned by Tbilisi City Hall, forecasts that Didi Dighomi’s population will at least double between 2022 and 2042.

The study’s authors identify the development of rail transport as one possible long-term solution to the district’s transport problems.

Against this backdrop, Tbilisi City Hall is working on a tram line project. On 7 September 2026, the municipality signed a design and construction contract with a consortium of Turkish companies, EYE Group. The project envisages a tram line connecting Didi Dighomi with Didube metro station. The contract is worth 287,654,321 lari (approximately $111,089,941), and the municipality expects construction to finish by 2030.

At the same time, in recent years, City Hall has introduced dedicated bus lanes on several major streets in the capital. The aim is to speed up public transport and reduce reliance on private cars. Some categories of taxi were subsequently also allowed to use these lanes.

The possible restrictions Kaladze mentioned suggest a shift towards a stricter transport policy aimed at curbing the growth in the number of cars in Tbilisi. However, the mayor has yet to specify when the measures might take effect or how the authorities plan to implement them.



Possible traffic restrictions in Tbilisi

World.title: Why has Abkhazia been unable to resolve its waste crisis for 20 years?
World.content:
Waste crisis in Abkhazia

The history of the waste crisis in Abkhazia resembles an endless, absurdist tragicomedy: the problem is clear, experts have worked out technical solutions, yet for years the authorities have directed their efforts towards the wrong measures and on an insufficient scale.

Presidents and mayors come and go, expert commissions are convened, but each time another fire breaks out at an illegal rubbish dump or residents take to the streets to protest against the unbearable stench, the authorities are forced to revisit the issue. And each time, it emerges that the problem has only grown worse.

Timeline of waste protests

Public debate over Abkhazia’s waste problem intensified following a protest in the village of Alakhadzy, near the resort town of Pitsunda, when it became clear that the authorities’ assurances that they had the situation “under control” were far from reality.

On 27 October, residents of Alakhadzy blocked access to a rubbish dump. They were driven to take action by persistent smoke from burning waste, an unbearable stench and the risk of a major fire. Nearly 1,000 people signed a petition calling for the dump to be closed.

The head of the district administration, Yury Khagush, arrived at the scene, along with members of the district assembly, local officials, police officers and even representatives of the State Security Service. The protesters dispersed after being promised that the issue would be resolved.

This was far from the first such incident. The history of “waste protests” in Abkhazia dates back to July 2007, when residents of the Mayak neighbourhood in Sukhum first blocked rubbish trucks from entering a municipal landfill located within the city limits.

In the years that followed, the landfill continued to catch fire repeatedly, engulfing Sukhum in toxic smoke. In August 2011, city authorities promised to bring the site up to an “acceptable standard” by November that year.

However, nothing had changed by November, and in December, then-President Alexander Ankvab openly acknowledged that the republic was facing a waste crisis.

“We need to find the courage either to reach agreements with investors or to make savings elsewhere and build at least two large waste-processing plants ourselves,” Ankvab said at the time.

Two years later, he described purchasing Italian equipment as the most cost-effective option. However, the plans never materialised.

From one landfill to another

In 2018, the landfill in the Mayak neighbourhood was finally closed. However, the problem did not disappear – it was simply relocated. Waste from the capital began to be transported daily to a landfill in the village of Shashakuara, in Gali district, 72km away, resulting in significant costs and wear and tear on vehicles.

“The Sukhum landfill contains hundreds of thousands of cubic metres of waste. But most of that volume is air. Only 15% consists of solid and liquid waste, while 85% is air. So these trucks keep driving back and forth, transporting air and burning fuel,” Russian hydraulic engineer Alexander Tsekhovoy explained to specialists in Sukhum in 2019.

According to his calculations, rather than endlessly transporting waste between landfills, each district should establish special compaction stations capable of compressing waste four- to fivefold. This would reduce the number of trips to the central landfill to just four truckloads a day.

However, instead of introducing these technologies, the authorities have continued simply transporting waste from one district to another.

Costly and pointless landfill in Katsikyt

A new waste management complex in the village of Katsikyt, in Gulripshi district, was supposed to provide a breakthrough solution to the waste problem.

The 5.5-hectare site was equipped with a waste disposal pit featuring a multilayer insulating base, treatment facilities and a conveyor belt for sorting waste. Construction proved extremely challenging, both technically and financially, with the project costing more than 150m roubles [$1.81m].

However, by the time the facility was nearly complete, it turned out that nobody wanted it.

Sukhum refused to use the complex, while the authorities in Gulripshi district were also reluctant to take responsibility for it. Security personnel were soon withdrawn from the site, which has since been effectively abandoned and remains unused.

Waste processing complex in the village of Katsikyt

The landfill in the village of Katsikyt was intended to be a financially sustainable facility. During its construction, Timur Agrba, then head of the Capital Construction Department and now mayor of Sukhum, said the facility could become self-financing by sorting, compacting and selling recyclable materials, including plastic, paper and metal.

According to Agrba, if properly managed, the facility could not only cover its operating costs but also generate revenue for further development.

However, in practice, the main obstacle is the tariff for household waste disposal.

“The current tariff policy does not reflect the realities or the costs incurred by our companies. International practice shows that waste collection and transportation should be funded through payments made by the residents who generate that waste,” Beslan Eshba, then head of the Sukhum city administration, explained back in 2014.

He promised that city authorities would seek to introduce relevant amendments to a new housing code. However, 12 years later, the new code has still not been adopted.

The current waste collection fee in Abkhazia is 27 roubles [$0.33] per person per month, a relatively modest amount. Yet most urban residents do not even pay this, as there is no clearly established system for collecting utility payments.

To obtain an objective assessment of the situation, Abkhazia’s Public Chamber held a series of meetings with Russian specialists, local environmental experts and representatives of district administrations.

As a result, an expert report was drawn up, providing a comprehensive assessment of the entire household waste management system. The report has already been submitted to the president, parliament, executive authorities and the Institute of Ecology.

For now, however, it represents little more than another faint glimmer of hope on the horizon. No tangible progress has been made towards resolving the problem.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Проблема мусора в Абхази

World.title: Special forces officers convicted of assaulting protesters jailed for five years each
World.content:
Special forces officers jailed for assaults

A court has sentenced special forces officers convicted of physically assaulting journalist Guram Rogava and protester Zviad Maisashvili during demonstrations in November and December 2024 to five years in prison each.

The special forces officer convicted of assaulting Guram Rogava, a journalist with Formula TV, was also banned from professional duties for three years. Lasha Gamkrelidze, the new prosecutor in the case, informed the journalist of the verdict by telephone.

According to Formula, Rogava had expected to testify as a victim during the trial. However, the prosecutor explained that his testimony was unnecessary because the court and the defence had accepted the charges as undisputed. Rogava himself believes that the person who directly assaulted him remains at large.

Two other special forces officers arrested in connection with the assault on Zviad Maisashvili were each sentenced to five years in prison. Lawyer Dimitri Mchedlishvili confirmed the information to Tabula.

On 30 November 2024, at around 06:30, special forces officers kicked Zviad Maisashvili in the face during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue, causing him to lose consciousness. Footage of the assault circulated on social media.

On 7 May 2026, Georgia’s Prosecutor’s Office announced that it had identified and detained five people in connection with assaults on Rogava, Maisashvili and opposition politician Levan Khabeishvili.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, four of those detained were current or former special forces officers, while the fifth was a serving officer with the Interior Ministry’s Security Police Department. Two of the suspects were already serving prison sentences at the time of their arrest.

Prosecutors said that on 29 November 2024, during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue, an officer from the Interior Ministry’s Special Tasks Department assaulted Guram Rogava while the journalist was carrying out his professional duties.

The detainees were charged under Article 333(3) of the Criminal Code with abuse of official powers involving violence. The officer detained in connection with the assault on Rogava also faced an additional charge of unlawfully obstructing a journalist’s professional activities.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office’s initial statement, the charges carried prison sentences of five to eight years.

Maisashvili said both special forces officers detained over the assault on him had admitted their guilt and apologised to him.

Guram Rogava and Zviad Maisashvili

Background

The assaults on Guram Rogava and Zviad Maisashvili were among several high-profile incidents of police violence during pro-European protests in Tbilisi in November and December 2024.

The protests began on 28 November 2024, after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that the government would take the issue of opening EU accession talks off the agenda until the end of 2028.

In the following days, law enforcement officers used water cannon, tear gas and other crowd-control measures against protesters on Rustaveli Avenue and near the parliament building. Numerous incidents of physical violence against demonstrators, journalists and human rights defenders were documented.

Both protesters and members of the media sustained injuries during the demonstrations. The assault on journalist Guram Rogava attracted particular attention. On 29 November 2024, a special forces officer attacked Rogava while he was reporting live from Rustaveli Avenue, leaving him seriously injured.

Media representatives and human rights organisations called for investigations into these incidents. On 30 November 2024, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) said the police’s use of water cannon, pepper spray and batons, including against peaceful demonstrators and journalists, had been disproportionate.

According to Georgia’s Public Defender’s 2024 report, the ombudsman and his representatives visited 624 people who had been detained or injured during protests between 15 April 2024 and 1 March 2025. Of those, 360 reported ill-treatment.

The report also noted that no police officers had been held accountable for violence committed by law enforcement personnel during that period.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office statement of 7 May 2026, more than 550 witnesses were questioned and thousands of investigative and procedural actions were carried out as part of the investigations into the cases involving Zviad Maisashvili, Levan Khabeishvili and Guram Rogava.

The Prosecutor’s Office said the investigations would continue to identify other possible perpetrators and bring them to justice.

World.title: Strategic partnership signed in Dublin: What does London want from Baku, and what does Baku gain?
World.content:
Azerbaijan-UK partnership

Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham signed a joint declaration on strategic partnership on 12 November at the European Political Community summit in Dublin. The British government published the text of the document on the same day.

The declaration covers three main areas: defence and security; trade, investment and economic growth; and education and innovation. The two countries agreed to hold annual strategic partnership meetings to assess progress in these areas.

The document builds on a 1994 friendship and cooperation agreement and a 1998 declaration on friendly relations and partnership between the two countries.

Six months earlier, the UK signed a similar declaration with Armenia. A comparison of the two documents raises the question:

What does the UK prioritise in its strategic partnership with Azerbaijan, and which issues does it leave unaddressed?

What does the document entail?

Defence and security. The two countries intend to expand defence cooperation in training, capacity building and interoperability, as well as explore opportunities for cooperation in the defence industry. The document also provides for cooperation between law enforcement agencies, collaboration on border control and judicial and legal cooperation aimed at strengthening the rule of law and institutional resilience.

Trade and energy. The UK will support the development of the Middle Corridor, a transport route linking China to Europe via Central Asia, the Caspian Sea and the Caucasus. The two countries also intend to cooperate on renewable energy, green finance and low-carbon technologies. The main platform for cooperation in these areas will be the bilateral Intergovernmental Commission on Trade and Economic Cooperation.

Education and innovation. The document provides for cooperation in higher and vocational education, digital skills development, civil servant training, artificial intelligence and digital governance.

In the declaration, the UK welcomes steps towards normalising relations between Azerbaijan and Armenia and expresses support for efforts to achieve a “lasting peace”.

However, the implementation of all commitments is subject to the availability of resources and the domestic laws of each country.

How does the declaration signed with Armenia differ?

The declaration, signed on 5 May by then UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, also identifies three main areas of cooperation. The first two are similar to those outlined in the declaration with Azerbaijan: defence and security, and economic growth and development.

However, the third area differs. In the declaration with Armenia, it is titled “Governance and Democratic Resilience”, while the document with Azerbaijan focuses on “Education and Innovation”.

In the declaration with Armenia, the two countries commit to protecting democracy, human rights and the rule of law. The document also provides for creating an enabling environment for independent media and civil society.

By contrast, the declaration with Azerbaijan makes no mention of democracy, human rights or the media. The term “civil society” appears only once, in the context of strengthening people-to-people ties between the two countries.

Furthermore, the declaration with Armenia provides for the development of a joint “Results Framework” to monitor the implementation of the agreements. No equivalent mechanism is included in the declaration with Azerbaijan, with the two countries agreeing only to hold annual meetings.

The declaration with Armenia also explicitly states that it does not constitute an international treaty and that either party may terminate cooperation by giving six months’ written notice.

What is the wider context behind these differences?

The declaration was signed amid continuing international criticism over the arrests of journalists in Azerbaijan. According to Amnesty International, 12 people detained in connection with the Meydan TV case are being persecuted for their journalistic work. The human rights organisation has also reported serious health problems among some of those detained.

In February this year, the detained journalists appealed to diplomatic missions in Baku, including the British embassy, asking them to monitor the court proceedings.

In response to calls for the journalists’ release, Azerbaijani officials have said that the legal proceedings are ongoing and that a fair decision will be reached.

The British government’s statement announcing the signing of the declaration makes no mention of the issue.

What do the two countries expect from each other?

The UK has long been one of the largest foreign investors in Azerbaijan, largely through BP, which operates the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli and Shah Deniz oil and gas fields. According to Azerbaijani officials, British investment in the country’s economy has exceeded $39bn.

However, the two countries’ figures for bilateral trade differ. According to Azerbaijan’s State Customs Committee, trade turnover between the two countries reached $3.72bn in the first nine months of this year.

According to official UK government statistics, trade in goods and services totalled £1.2bn in the 12 months to June, making Azerbaijan the UK’s 89th-largest trading partner.

British exports to Azerbaijan amounted to £724m, down 2.9% from the previous year. Imports from Azerbaijan, meanwhile, increased more than 2.6-fold to £453m.

Preparations for the declaration began well before its signing. In August 2025, UK Minister for Europe Stephen Doughty announced during a visit to Baku that the two countries had agreed to upgrade bilateral relations to a strategic partnership.

In December, UK Minister of State for Defence Lord Coaker visited Baku. In October this year, UK Trade Minister Lord Anas Sarwar announced at a meeting of the Intergovernmental Commission in Baku that the text of the declaration had been agreed.

The two countries also signed a roadmap for developing transport and digital infrastructure. Sarwar outlined the areas the partnership would cover:

“Of course, it will include energy and port infrastructure, investment, education and other areas.”

The UK government’s statement on Doughty’s 2025 visit also mentioned the peace process, the Russia-Ukraine war, the Middle Corridor, energy, defence, cybersecurity and education.

Human rights and media freedom were not mentioned on that occasion either.

What meetings took place in Dublin?

The signing of the declaration was one of several events on Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev’s busy schedule in Dublin. On the same day, he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and the prime ministers of Bulgaria, Greece and the Czech Republic. His meeting with the Bulgarian prime minister focused on a proposed electricity corridor between the two countries.

According to the Azerbaijani side, Aliyev and Pashinyan discussed the peace agenda under the joint declaration signed in Washington in August 2025, border delimitation, transport links and the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP).

The two leaders also welcomed the transit of goods through Azerbaijan to Armenia and in the opposite direction.

The UK signed strategic partnership declarations with Armenia and Azerbaijan six months apart. Both documents provide for support for the peace process in the South Caucasus. However, the third area of cooperation differs: the declaration with Armenia focuses on democracy, while the one with Azerbaijan emphasises education.

Azerbaijani human rights activists and opposition figures have yet to comment on the signing of the declaration.

World.title: Azerbaijani judoka Gultaj Mammadaliyeva wins bronze at Zagreb Grand Prix
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. Azerbaijani judoka Gultaj Mammadaliyeva has won a bronze medal at the Grand Prix tournament in Zagreb, the capital of Croatia.

Competing in the under-52 kg weight category, Mammadaliyeva defeated Croatia’s Tihea Topolovec and Chinese Taipei’s Pin-Hsien Tseng to reach the quarterfinals.

At this stage, she lost to Hungary’s Róza Györtyás and moved into the repechage round, where she defeated Kosovo’s Fatjona Kasapi. In the bronze medal bout, the Azerbaijani judoka overcame Italy’s Ilaria Finestrone to secure third place.

Another Azerbaijani representative, Nizami Imranov, competing in the under-66 kg category, also came close to winning a medal. He defeated France’s Daki Bouba, Italy’s Matteo Piras, and Morocco’s Abderrahmane Boushita.

However, Imranov lost to Brazil’s Ronaldo Lima in the semifinal. Due to an injury, he was unable to compete in the bronze medal match and finished fifth overall.

Two other Azerbaijani judokas were eliminated in their opening bouts. Turan Bayramov (66 kg) lost to Germany’s Florian Bekeri, while Murad Muradli (60 kg) was defeated by France’s Luka Mkheidze.

The Grand Prix tournament in Zagreb will run until November 15.

World.title: Leyla Aliyeva attends discussions on environmental challenges of Caspian Sea at COP31 (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. An event titled “A Sea in Retreat: Climate, Nature and People on the Caspian Frontline” was organized in partnership with the IDEA Public Union and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) on the sidelines of the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31).

Addressing the opening ceremony, Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, founder and head of the IDEA Public Union, noted that the declining water level of the Caspian Sea threatens the survival of rare species inhabiting the region, including sturgeons and Caspian seals. She underscored the importance of expanding scientific research, enhancing international cooperation, and pursuing joint action to address the sea’s environmental challenges.

Highlighting the projects implemented by the IDEA Public Union in this field, Leyla Aliyeva mentioned that scientific expeditions have been organized to investigate the causes behind the decline in the Caspian seal population, while fingerlings of various fish species have been released into water bodies to replenish fish stocks.

Leyla Aliyeva also highlighted IDEA’s initiatives aimed at cleaning up the Caspian Sea coastline. It was noted that nearly 7,000 volunteers have joined coastal cleanup campaigns organized since 2011, collecting over 120 tons of waste for recycling. Noting that the future of the Caspian Sea depends on decisions made today, she called for protecting its rich nature for future generations.

Stewart Maginnis, IUCN Deputy Director General, and Dario Liguti, Director of the Sustainable Energy Division at the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE), also addressed the opening ceremony.

The following panel discussions featured Caspian research expert at the IDEA Public Union Elnur Safarov, representative of the UK’s University of Leeds Simon Goodman, founder and Executive Director of the Great Whale Conservancy Michael Fishbach, as well as representative of the University of Geneva and Chair of the Caspisnet network Alexandre Hedjazi.

Discussions focused on climatic factors driving the decline in the Caspian Sea’s water level, biodiversity conservation, adapting marine ecosystems to changing conditions, and strengthening regional collaboration.

The event concluded with the screening of a short documentary produced by the IDEA Public Union highlighting the current environmental situation of the Caspian Sea.
