World.title: TRIPP moves toward implementation — Azerbaijan's peace agenda reshapes S. Caucasus
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. The developments in the South Caucasus in recent years have increasingly made one truth clear: the region’s future should no longer be shaped by conflict and confrontation, but rather by cooperation, transportation links, and economic integration. Azerbaijan’s political will, particularly that of President Ilham Aliyev, and the peace agenda he has put forward play a decisive role in shaping this new phase.

Following the historic victory in the 44-day Patriotic War, Azerbaijan set itself a new goal: to consolidate the results of the war in accordance with international law, achieve lasting peace in the region, and transform the South Caucasus from an arena of confrontation into a platform for cooperation. Baku has sought to achieve this goal not only through political statements, but also through concrete proposals, diplomatic initiatives, and economic projects. Today, we are already seeing individual elements of this agenda being implemented.

President Ilham Aliyev’s meeting with Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, which took place on November 12 in Dublin, also marked another important milestone in this very process. At the meeting, which took place within the framework of the 9th Summit of the European Political Community, the parties discussed advancing the peace agenda, building on the outcomes of the Peace Summit held on August 8, 2025, in Washington, and the signed Joint Declaration.

The significance of the meeting lay not only in the fact that the two leaders came together. The substance of the discussions showed that relations between Azerbaijan and Armenia are gradually shifting from the stage of political agreements to that of practical cooperation aimed at transforming everyday life and economic ties. Transportation and transit routes, trade and economic relations, border delimitation, confidence-building measures, the future integration of power grids, and the management of transboundary water resources—these are the issues that today constitute the true substance of peace.

Baku is the architect of the peace agenda; cooperation is the key condition for the next phase

The peace proposals put forward by Azerbaijan after the war are based on the fundamental principles of international law: mutual recognition of sovereignty and territorial integrity, the inviolability of state borders, the renunciation of territorial claims against one another, and the non-use of force. This was precisely the essence of the five principles announced by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in 2022.

As a result of negotiations conducted based on these principles, the text of a peace agreement was initialed in Washington on August 8, 2025. This marked a historic step toward resolving the decades-long conflict in the political and legal spheres. At the same time, it should be noted that the initialed text is not yet an officially signed and entered into force agreement. For the agreement to be signed and enter into force, it is essential to complete the required legal procedures.

Azerbaijan’s position is clear: lasting peace is possible only on the basis of mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, the renunciation of territorial claims, and normal good-neighborly relations. Accepting this reality and integrating Armenia into regional integration processes are crucial for its own economic and political future. A peace agreement is the primary legal and political foundation for this path.

In essence, through the new reality created by the Patriotic War, Azerbaijan has opened up opportunities for the development of all countries in the region, including Armenia. Armenia, which for many years operated under a logic of blockade and confrontation, is now beginning to see the benefits created by trade, transit, energy, and transportation links with its neighbors. This demonstrates that the peace agenda put forward by Azerbaijan is beneficial not only to Baku but to the entire region.

TRIPP - An Economic Pillar of Peace and a Slow-Moving Process

One of the notable topics at the Dublin meeting was the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP) project. President Ilham Aliyev and Nikol Pashinyan discussed the planning and design of the project’s rail and road components, as well as the prospects for transit connections along the route.

The significance of TRIPP extends far beyond that of a single transportation route. In addition to establishing a connection between Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan, this project has the potential to reshape the transportation landscape of the South Caucasus, accelerate freight transport between the East and West, and expand opportunities for regional trade. The development of rail and road infrastructure could create conditions for reducing freight transit times and costs, diversifying routes, and expanding economic ties.

The project also opens up significant economic opportunities for Armenia. The country could gain the opportunity to connect to the regional transit system, attract new investments, modernize its infrastructure, and expand trade ties with its neighbors. For Azerbaijan, ensuring unimpeded transport links with Nakhchivan and strengthening its position along the East–West corridor are of strategic importance.

Notably, the TRIPP project is already moving forward on the legal and organizational fronts. The Armenian Parliament has enacted the necessary legislative changes to implement the project.

The announcement that the project will enter the construction phase in early 2027 indicates that TRIPP is moving beyond the realm of political debate and approaching the stage of practical implementation.

The main reason TRIPP is becoming a difficult process to reverse is that it is driven not only by political agreements but also by economic interests. Along with Azerbaijan and Armenia, Türkiye, Central Asian countries, as well as European and Asian markets could benefit from this route. Transporting cargo via shorter, safer, and more efficient routes will enhance the region’s competitiveness.

105,000 metric tons of cargo and transboundary rivers: peace is already yielding tangible results

One of the most significant outcomes of the Dublin meeting was the positive assessment of cargo transit to Armenia through Azerbaijani territory. According to official data, a total of 105,000 metric tons of cargo has been transported through Azerbaijani territory to Armenia from last November to the present. This figure demonstrates that the peace agenda is already yielding concrete results in the economic sphere. By creating conditions for transit through its territory as part of this process, Azerbaijan is helping to give peace economic substance.

Another important development is the establishment of working groups on the management of transboundary rivers. This area, which at first glance appears to be a technical and environmental issue, is in fact a crucial component of regional security. The protection of river water resources, water allocation, pollution prevention, and environmental risk management are issues that cannot be resolved within the borders of a single country.

The establishment of working groups on transboundary water cooperation between Azerbaijan and Armenia demonstrates the parties’ willingness to discuss even more complex issues through dialogue.

Turkish-Armenian relations are also part of the regional agenda being shaped jointly with Baku.

Another important aspect of regional developments is the normalization of Turkish-Armenian relations. At a meeting between Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, held on November 11 as part of COP31, the two leaders discussed the normalization of relations and the establishment of transportation and communication links between the two countries.

Türkiye’s position in this process also highlights the crucial importance of Azerbaijani-Armenian relations. Turkish Minister of Transport and Infrastructure Abdulkadir Uraloğlu stated that Ankara has completed preparations to reopen the land border and restore rail service with Armenia; however, the opening of the border is contingent upon the conclusion of a comprehensive agreement between Armenia and Azerbaijan. This statement by the Turkish side once again demonstrates the importance of coordination between Ankara and Baku on regional issues.

Thus, the normalization of Armenian-Turkish relations is also inseparable from the Azerbaijani-Armenian peace process. This shows that complementary political and economic processes are taking shape in the region.

The opening of the border between Türkiye and Armenia, the restoration of rail service, and the expansion of trade ties will increase the economic potential of the South Caucasus. However, for this process to be sustainable, it is important to take Azerbaijan’s security interests into account and maintain coordination with Baku.

Azerbaijan’s regional strategy: not external dependence, but cooperation through its own efforts.

Today, against the backdrop of ongoing political and military conflicts, instability, and economic risks in the Middle East, a historic opportunity has emerged to transform the South Caucasus and Central Asia into a region of stability and interconnectedness. With its rich natural resources, energy potential, transportation capabilities, and advantageous geographic location, Central Asia is attracting the attention of the world’s leading powers. China, Russia, the US, and the EU are seeking to expand their economic and political ties with this region.

In this geopolitical landscape, Azerbaijan is one of the key connecting countries linking Central Asia with Europe. The routes passing through the Caspian Sea, the Middle Corridor, port and railway infrastructure, and energy and logistics capabilities make Azerbaijan’s role indispensable. Without Azerbaijan’s participation, it is difficult to envision a large-scale and sustainable system of interconnectivity that would enable Central Asia to access European markets.

This is the very essence of the regional approach being shaped under the leadership of President Ilham Aliyev: the three states of the South Caucasus – Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Armenia – must rely first and foremost on their own will and regional dialogue when resolving their problems, ensuring security, and establishing economic cooperation. The interests of external powers must not become the sole factor determining relations among the countries of the region. On the contrary, cooperation among the three countries based on mutual benefit, respect for each other’s sovereignty, and shared economic interests must form the foundation of stability in the South Caucasus.

This does not mean rejecting cooperation with external partners. US participation in the TRIPP project, the European Union’s interest in regional infrastructure, and Türkiye’s support for the normalization process demonstrate that the new economic architecture of the South Caucasus also creates broad opportunities for international partnership. However, the countries of the region themselves must be the primary architects of regional solutions.

The events of recent days at COP31 and the Dublin Summit have once again demonstrated this reality. Azerbaijan is one of the key players in promoting a peace agenda with Armenia, normalizing Turkish-Armenian relations, and developing transportation and economic ties between the East and the West.

At the heart of all this lies the political course set forth by President Ilham Aliyev. Following its military victory, Azerbaijan put forward a peace initiative, proposed opening regional transport routes, and placed opportunities for economic cooperation on the agenda; today, we are seeing the practical results of these initiatives.

The future of the South Caucasus can no longer be assessed solely through the lens of past conflicts. The region now has the prospect of building new transportation routes, trade opportunities, energy cooperation, and a common security system. In this process, Azerbaijan is not merely a participant but the leading regional force shaping its direction. Having initiated the peace process, Baku has now moved on to the stage of transforming that peace into economic prosperity, regional integration, and long-term stability.

World.title: Azerbaijan, Vietnam discuss trade, investment, business cooperation (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. As part of the Azerbaijani delegation’s visit to Vietnam, discussions were held on expanding trade and economic ties, promoting mutual investment, and exploring opportunities for business partnerships, the Azerbaijani Ministry of Economy said.

Moreover, it was noted that the Azerbaijani delegation, led by First Deputy Minister of Economy Elnur Aliyev, visited Hanoi, the capital of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam.

As part of the visit, a meeting was held with Nguyen Viet Son, Vietnam’s Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade. During the meeting, the importance that Azerbaijan attaches to the development and diversification of trade and economic ties with Vietnam was emphasized. The parties exchanged views on opportunities to increase mutual investment and expand cooperation between business communities. They also discussed prospects for cooperation in industry, energy, tourism, and other areas of mutual interest.

A meeting was held with Nguyen Quoc Tuan, Deputy Chairman of the Vietnamese company “Vingroup” and Chairman of the Board of GSM (Green Smart Mobility), the company’s global green transportation division. The meeting focused on opportunities for cooperation in various areas, including the assembly of electric vehicles in Azerbaijan and real estate development.

During the visit, a meeting was also held with Nguyen Viet Son, Deputy Chief Executive Officer of the Vietnamese company ROX Group. The discussion focused on the company’s investment opportunities in the real estate and renewable energy sectors in Azerbaijan, as well as the prospects for implementing potential projects in these areas.

World.title: Istanbul hosts event marking Azerbaijan's Victory Day anniversary (PHOTO)
World.content:
Photo: State Committee on Work with the Diaspora of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. An event marking the 6th anniversary of November 8, Victory Day, was held in Istanbul and organized by the Istanbul Turkish-Azerbaijani Society for Solidarity and Culture (İSTAD), the State Committee for Diaspora Affairs reported.

In addition, the report notes that the event was attended by representatives of civil society organizations operating in Türkiye, intellectuals, scholars, figures from the arts and business communities, as well as numerous guests.

The program began with the national anthems of Azerbaijan and Türkiye, followed by a minute of silence to honor the memory of the martyrs.

Delivering a welcoming speech, Sefer Karakoyunlu, chairman of İSTAD and spokesperson for TADEF, noted that the glorious Victory is an important historical event not only for Azerbaijan but also for the entire Turkic world. He spoke about how, over the past 30 years, Azerbaijan’s just cause has been championed on various platforms, and emphasized the significance of liberating the occupied territories as a result of the 44-day Patriotic War. The Chairman emphasized that the historic Victory achieved by the Azerbaijani Army under the leadership of President and Supreme Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev has instilled a profound sense of pride in the people; he paid respectful tribute to the memory of the martyrs and expressed his gratitude to the veterans.

A special guest at the event, the mother of martyr Tapdig Babashov and Vice Chair of the “Support for Mothers of Martyrs” Public Association, Kifayat Türksoy, in her speech, shared the experiences of the martyrs’ families, spoke of their devotion to the Motherland, and described the spiritual significance of the Karabakh Victory for the Azerbaijani people. The martyr’s mother’s speech provided the participants with some deeply moving moments.

Under the direction of conductor Tekin Büyükkaya, the Turkish-Azerbaijani Brotherhood Choir performed musical pieces reflecting the national and cultural values of both countries.

In conclusion, the participants exchanged views, emphasizing the importance of Azerbaijani-Turkish brotherhood and strengthening solidarity within the Turkic world.

The event concluded with the chanting of slogans dedicated to Azerbaijani-Turkish brotherhood.

World.title: Homes with architectural designs that cost just $1 near completion
World.content:
Construction costs might be soaring across the country but on a building site at Corrimal, north of Wollongong, no-one is complaining about the price that was paid for an architect's plans.

Builder James Forrest and his team are putting the finishing touches on four new row homes, following designs purchased for just $1 from a pattern book launched by the NSW government in July 2025.

If he meets the November deadline, he will be the first in the state to complete a home under the scheme.

Mr Forrest said using the design saved him an extraordinary amount of time, because it included planning controls and a 10-day complying development pathway.

"All the rigours of the design work have been done already. It's just matching it to the site, and it's approved," he said.

" If we were building this through the traditional pathway it would take about 12 months to get it approved — this was approved in eight weeks. "

James Forrest aims to complete the project by the end of November. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

The Corrimal development used one of eight low-rise designs available for the nominal fee of $1 in the first six months of the scheme.

They now cost $1,000.

The program was sold as a way to get more high-quality housing built faster and cheaper. So far, 25,000 designs have been purchased.

Harry Catterns says the designs can be adjusted to different sizes and configurations. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Architect Harry Catterns co-owns the company that designed the row homes.

"We thought it would be a more helpful contribution to the housing mix if we could provide small house-like dwellings with their own front door, their own garden, rather than the typical apartment you might see on a site like this," he said.

Mr Catterns said the design could be adjusted to one, two or three bedrooms and offered different bathroom configurations.

All are two-storey, with balconies and sliding glass doors.

The builder is hoping to have the homes ready for tenants, and owners, by Christmas. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Mr Forrest said he hoped to have three homes occupied by Christmas, and the fourth, larger home on the market shortly after.

"These will be cheaper for buyers than ordinary builds for a number of reasons, but primarily because of its speed and cost-saving," he said.

Mr Forrest estimated the Corrimal build was around $600,000 cheaper than an ordinary project.

Uptake scrutinised

The Pattern Book now offers 17 designs after nine mid-rise options were added in November 2025.

They cost up to $2,500 and do not have the same planning controls or fast-track as the low-rise designs.

Tom Forrest says the scheme has been a "dud". (ABC News: Sam Foster)

The Urban Taskforce's Tom Forrest said the mid-rise developments would still need final development approval from councils and faced the same planning timelines as a typical build.

"Nobody is building and it hasn't improved the number of new dwellings brought to the market," he said.

So far, the entire Housing Pattern Book program has translated to fewer than 60 applications, with 45 of them approved.

"As of now it would have to be marked down as a dud," Mr Forrest said.

The Housing Industry Association does not agree, with NSW chief executive Brad Armitage saying it was working for builders.

"When you take those [economic] factors into consideration, so many approvals with this relatively new pattern book is actually quite strong," he said.

Brad Armitage says the pattern book is a success. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

Election promise

The NSW opposition has promised to overhaul the scheme with new designs and review planning controls if it is elected next March, describing it as a "failure".

"We want to see a lot more builders like this one at Corrimal rolling out a lot more housing as part of the pattern book and clearly it's not working at the moment," Shadow Housing Minister Chris Rath said.

"We need to make it much easier to actually build the pattern book designs.

"It's just far too slow and far too restrictive."

NSW Planning Minister Paul Scully defended the outcome.

"We're seeing challenging economic conditions for new home building, higher interest rates, higher building costs, shortages of skilled labour," he said.

"But I'm pleased with the level of interest there was, and I think you'll start to see more coming out of the ground as we start to see the proof in the builds themselves."

The Corrimal project will not be James Forrest's last. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Mr Forrest said he was already planning another Housing Pattern Book build.

"We've done it, we've landed this," he said.

"Generally speaking, this is a goer."

World.title: The must-see artworks at the Clarice Beckett exhibition
World.content:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, the National Gallery of Australia's conservation team toiled away on a number of small studies and paintings by tonal artist Clarice Beckett, who captured the life and scenery of her coastal home in south-east Naarm/Melbourne.

The works, which were donated to the gallery by Beckett's sister Hilda Mangan in 1972, had been stored in boxes for years and, because of the materials Beckett favoured, were weathered and cracked, the paint peeling.

"Beckett often worked on cardboard. She would go out into the landscape and she would take her paintboxes and be outdoors, so it was easy for her to carry these small pieces of cardboard with her but because of that the condition of the works had through time become compromised," NGA senior curator of Australian art Elspeth Pitt tells ABC News.

The paintings were painstakingly restored, finished with custom frames, and a group of 27 of them taken on the road, touring regional Australian galleries.

Clarice Beckett: Paintings from the National Collection is currently at Goulburn Regional Art Gallery.

Here are three works to see at the exhibition:

Not titled (Seascape)

"Seascape is a gorgeous work because it's really evidence of Clarice being in nature and being in weather," Pitt says.

Not titled (Seascape), c1919–1935. (Supplied: National Gallery of Australia, Kamberri/ Canberra, gift of Mrs Hilda Mangan, 1972)

"She would often use the tea-tree which was endemic to the area as a framing device for her works, and in this small painting you can see this tea-tree, it's being whipped around in the wind. Also you can see in the top right-hand corner of the work her fingerprint.

"She liked to paint in storms — and very sadly this is how she passed away [in 1935]; she was painting in a storm and she contracted double pneumonia — I think that fingerprint suggests that she was painting in weather and had to gather up her paints and cardboard and other paraphernalia quite quickly to make the walk home.

"You can see all through she is working very quickly — she works carefully but with haste."

Not titled (Sunset)

This was one of the first works from the Beckett collection that the conservation team spent time bringing back to life.

Not titled (Sunset), c 1919–1935. (Supplied: National Gallery of Australia, Kamberri/ Canberra, gift of Mrs Hilda Mangan, 1972)

"This was an example where the fluctuation in relative humidity had caused the painting surface to crack over time. [Conservator] Jocelyn [Evans] over a period of many months undertook extensive conservation work very, very carefully gluing the surface back together, filling in and then painting it with very specific reference to Beckett's mode of painting and the colours she would use," Pitt says.

"The surface now looks really exquisite and such a wonderful example of a conservator bringing a work back to life."

Pitt says the dreamy haze of the colour and tones are "typical Clarice".

"She would often paint at the beginnings and the ends of the day," she says.

"They're so simple but they have a magic about them and I think there's great poetry in her work. She was able to cut through the humdrum and the monotony and she was able to see truth."

Not titled (Seascape with boat and reflection)

Painted some time between 1920 and 1930, this minimalist work has an expanse of still grey water and a very small boat, a wooden rowing boat or a dinghy. The horizon is suggested by a very pale blue band of paint that just rests at the upper periphery of the painting

Not titled (Seascape with boat and reflection), c 1919–1935. (Supplied: National Gallery of Australia, Kamberri/ Canberra, gift of Mrs Hilda Mangan, 1972)

"What I find so impressive about this particular work, despite its scale … is that minimal nature with which it has been articulated," Pitt says.

"This kind of work precedes abstraction. In the very early 20th century she was already gesturing towards minimalism and abstraction, and those ideas and movements only really came to the fore in an Australian context a couple of decades later.

"She was really anticipating these future directions of Australian art quite early on."

Clarice Beckett: Paintings from the National Collection is at the Goulburn Regional Art Gallery until November 21.

World.title: Boots Riley is ready for the working class to rise up
World.content:
Boots Riley was born into activism.

The son of prominent US civil rights attorney Walter Riley, a teenage Boots led 2,000 of his fellow students in a walkout over cutbacks that were set to affect all the schools in the area, except the one with predominantly white students.

According to Riley, the school board capitulated as soon as they understood the size of the congregation heading towards them. It was one of Riley's first tastes of the power of collective action.

Riley's rise to international fame was as the lead vocalist of The Coup, a political hip-hop group that layers critique and lampoonery of capitalism, worker exploitation, police brutality and white patriarchy over irresistible bass-driven back beats.

Boots Riley (left) with Tupak Shakur and The Coup members DJ Pam The Funkstress (Pam Warren) and E-Roc (Eric Davis) in 1993. (Getty: Al Pereira/Michael Ochs Archives)

In 2018, Riley parlayed into film, delivering the award-winning Sorry To Bother You, the dystopian tale of an African American telemarketer who is swept into a corporate conspiracy after learning how to utilise his "white voice".

His next screen project, the 2023 limited series I'm A Virgo, starred a 3.9-metre-tall teenager (Emmy-winner Jharrel Jerome) who becomes an unlikely folk hero for a community fighting against a tyrannical billionaire cosplaying as a Marvel-esque superhero.

Now, Boots is back on the big screen with I Love Boosters.

Inspired by a song from The Coup's 2006 album Pick A Bigger Weapon, I Love Boosters follows the efforts of The Velvet Gang, a group of professional shoplifters targeting cut-throat, materialistic, billionaire fashion mogul Christie Smith (Demi Moore).

The through-line of Riley's work is clear: power lies with the people; they just have to rise up and take it.

The Velvet Gang (from left Naomi Ackie, Keke Palmer, Poppy Liu and Taylour Paige) are philanthropic shoplifters. (Supplied: Neon)

A lot of people turn to you for absurdism, but what do you find most absurd about the world we're currently living in?

They call it absurdism, but it's really just analysis. Like, if you really point out the contradictions that exist in our world, it would be called absurd. We're talking about a world which, at its core … is based on just a tiny amount of people exploiting the labour of most of us; the ruling class exploiting the working class.

We all know it, but when you point out the fact that the people that have the power are the working class and we're just giving it to the ruling class, it's an absurd situation.

[It's absurd] when you point out the fact that there's a genocide going on and the folks that are defending themselves against a multi-decade genocide are the only ones called the terrorists, right?

We have all these things that are ironies, that we just live with, but I would say the big absurd thing is the fact that the working class hasn't yet organised to change this.

The Velvet Gang's work encourages a full-on worker uprising with a major fashion chain. (Supplied: Neon)

What do you think the biggest roadblock is for collective action in 2026?

There are a lot of competing narratives that tell us we don't need collective action, that tell us that it won't work, that tell us that there's nothing that we can do.

There is that like, 'Oh, maybe I'm gonna lose my job'. That's one [fear].

But then the next one is this idea that maybe it's not gonna do anything anyway.

The biggest thing is nihilism and the way that we fight that is showing it's not that every time you fight, you're gonna win. We're gonna lose a bunch of times, right? Because, you know, there's a chant where they're like, 'when we fight, we win'. And that's not true, but the only time we're gonna win is when we fight.

Boots Riley on the red carpet at the 2026 Rome Film Festival. (Getty: Vittorio Zunino Celotto)

Show these victories that we're seeing around the world … Let's take Italy. Prime Minister [Giorgia] Meloni is as right wing as Trump, maybe a little bit more.

They have to go head-to-head on stuff around the Pope because she's in Italy, right? But other than that, she's pretty right wing on almost everything. [Italy] had a general strike for a few days and shut down shipping and were able to get her to concede and send out a naval ship to protect the flotilla to Gaza.

Could you imagine Trump doing that? No, and it's not because he's nicer. It's because we haven't forced them to through shutting down industries.

When people know that that happened, they're more interested in: "How can I be part of that? What would it take to get to over there from here?"

Demi Moore's Christie Smith in Boosters follows in a line of sharply written, ultra-rich characters from you. Her dangerously tilted office is a great representation of the mindset of these people, just pure inconvenience to satiate narcissism. What is in the forefront of your mind when you write billionaire characters?

Power, and what people feel like they're doing with that power, because none of them think they're the villain. Many times they think they're doing something that pushes humanity forward. They think there are very few billionaires in the world and they think they're the chosen ones. Therefore, any answer that someone's gonna come up with that one person can do is going to really be at the misfortune of everyone else.

Christie Smith keeps her office at a dangerous tilt, to the struggle of her staff. (Supplied: Neon)

The truth is that all these supposed things like, to solve world hunger, I'm gonna make a pill that everybody can take or something like that. Who knows what it is; everybody's running away from what we have to have, which is class struggle.

It's an incredible visual representation of that idea. You had the horse people in Sorry To Bother You, you have another incredible body transformation in Boosters. What interests you about transformations of the body?

I like a lot of weird movies that make you feel uncomfortable. At the same time you're being uncomfortable, you're in it and that's why you're uncomfortable.

You're also thinking that somebody decided to put me through this, you know? I want people to be inside the art, but also be pushing back and forth with it, to be engaging with it.

If I wanna push people away while making them still wanna be in it and feel in it, then I make an extra obstacle for myself. I have to make it awesome for people to wanna go through all of this stuff.

In Sorry To Bother You, it was for one reason, which was that I needed him to experience a mortal terror, a mortal danger, and in film, death is not enough.

It would be an almost peaceful ending really.

Yeah, like, you're not afraid that the character is gonna die. Really, you're afraid of what's gonna happen before that. That terror of how is the world changing me? How do I change the world? We're dealing with that back and forth and it's always gonna change us.

We can't get away from that, you know? But are we able to keep changing the world as it's changing us?

Loading Instagram content

Before I let you go I have to ask about Boosters' incredible costuming. Was there an outfit from the film that you really loved?

The exploding plaid is maybe my favourite, but that's a combination of costume and production design.

The turquoise dress obviously is one that's not only because of the colour and the thematic connection to the rest of the movie, but just the different textures that are in the one dress. Yeah, like Shirley [Kurata, I Love Boosters costume designer] really came through with that one.

I just have one more question for you. And that is, what do you ultimately hope people take away from I Love Boosters?

Some of what that answer would be might give away that might be spoilers.

I think the movie is about loneliness and ways that we can defeat it.

I Love Boosters is in Australian cinemas now.

Quotes have been edited for clarity and brevity.

World.title: Registered psychologist accused of recruiting for Universal Medicine cult
World.content:
Cynthia Hickman advertised herself as a "soul psychologist".

She wrote columns about her approach for a wellness magazine that hinted at her spiritual bent.

Reading these articles was a Victorian woman, who asked the Background Briefing podcast to use the name "Helen" so she could share sensitive details of her personal history.

Helen was impressed by what seemed like Hickman's "non-blame" approach to her clients.

She'd long put off seeing a psychologist, fearing it would "unleash and probably unravel in me an incredible family history" involving violence and sexual abuse.

But Hickman's columns made her seem like the ideal therapist and confidant.

So, Helen took the plunge, embarking on a 400-kilometre round trip from regional Victoria to Hickman's home in an affluent suburb of South Melbourne.

Her first impression was that the psychologist was "a very elegant person, in terms of her presentation".

"So I thought, 'OK, there's going to be quite a formality around this," Helen said.

She says she wanted to attend monthly, but was told "No, you must come weekly", and agreed to the 400km round trip each week, hoping to finally "let this grief go".

Cynthia Hickman conducted sessions from her home in the southern suburbs of Melbourne. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

At the time, she couldn't foresee how her relationship with the psychologist would go on to derail her life.

Helen has shared her experience exclusively with the Background Briefing podcast, in the hopes of protecting other vulnerable people seeking care.

"I didn't want her to continue hurting and damaging people under the registration of a psychologist in this country," Helen says.

She hopes to "throw a spotlight" wider than her psychologist and onto a predatory organisation that includes more than 40 Australian healthcare professionals, as medical advocates call for their deregistration.

A network of practitioners

Helen's early sessions with Cynthia Hickman, in 2006, seemed like fairly conventional therapy.

They stirred up memories Helen had not shared with anyone else, from a childhood fractured by multiple instances of sexual abuse, and a violent father.

But once the rapport had been established, Hickman told Helen she'd benefit from attending talks by spiritual healers, and receiving "esoteric breast massage" from a former corporate lawyer named Serryn O'Regan.

"I was very nervous but I just went with it," Helen says.

" I felt like a kid again, trusting and being naive. "

She says that as she lay on the massage table, O'Regan explained that a woman's breasts told the story of her life, and Helen's breasts indicated her "body was dead".

Helen "felt like less than a person in that instant". She "went right back to feeling traumatised" and sat on a nearby beach crying for three hours.

Serryn O'Regan also acted as a lawyer for Universal Medicine. (Supplied)

Still, Helen thought her trauma was the problem, and followed O'Regan's suggestion of further treatment from allied health practitioners who worked from her house.

Helen estimates she spent $35,000 over about three years between therapy with psychologist Cynthia Hickman and the alternative therapies and talks.

"I saw myself as needing to be better, to be more in control of my sadness or my grief," Helen says.

Uncovering the cult

And then in her third year of therapy, at O'Regan's urging, Helen flew to Byron Bay for a talk by another spiritual healer.

She saw familiar faces in the crowd: O'Regan, the health practitioners who treated Helen at her house, and up the front, psychologist Cynthia Hickman, "fully participating in what was going on up on stage".

"Things started to click into my mind that she actually was involved in this thing."

Helen learnt it was called Universal Medicine, and it revolved around the man on stage, Serge Benhayon.

"Everyone seemed to love him," she says.

Serge Benhayon, who has no medical qualifications, has followers around the world. (Facebook: Serge Benhayon)

It was about three years before news outlets revealed Benhayon was a formerly bankrupt tennis coach claiming to be the reincarnation of Leonardo Da Vinci after a divine revelation on the toilet.

It would be another three years before medical experts decried Benhayon, who had no medical qualifications but built a business empire on bogus therapies like "ovarian readings" and "chakra puncture".

And it would be over a decade before a NSW jury found he led a socially dangerous and sexually manipulative cult.

Benhayon had surrounded himself with influential people who lent him credibility, from executives to lawyers, members of UK nobility and, crucially, health professionals.

Medical advocate Professor John Dwyer has counted dozens of registered healthcare workers among the cult's devotees, including one of Australia's leading paediatric specialists and a respiratory physician who referred lung cancer patients to Benhayon.

Dwyer has spent more than a decade lobbying governments and regulators to take action, but says the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) has done little to "rein these people in".

John Dwyer is critical of Universal Medicine. (ABC News: Josh Robertson)

" There are, to my knowledge, maybe registered health professionals [in Australia] practising Universal Medicine's nonsense as we talk," he says.

"They're not fit people to be registered health professionals."

Meeting Serge

Helen says the network of therapists she became entangled with led her to believe she had "bad energy", a damaging belief that was reinforced when she came face to face with the cult leader himself.

Helen says that at a Universal Medicine retreat, Serge Benhayon touched her on a massage table and told her: "You are full of poison."

"I felt less than human," Helen says.

"Did he mean I was a snake or a poisonous animal or something? That's how I felt."

Serge Benhayon has claimed he contains all of the knowledge in the universe inside of him. (Supplied)

Helen says she was so distressed she didn't emerge from her room until the next morning.

Still, she continued treatment.

"I needed to prove to myself that I was capable of not running away from things that frightened me, because I'd probably done that all my life," she says.

As she continued her journey with Universal Medicine, she says Hickman began lacing her therapy sessions with its concepts, using the "same phrases" as Benhayon and "almost instructing" her.

Do you know more? Contact backgroundbriefing@abc.net.au

Or, send an encrypted email from a Protonmail account to backgroundbriefing@protonmail.com

Send us documents anonymously through SecureDrop

An 'unhinged' therapy session

It would take years for Helen to extricate herself from the cult, and it started with a letter from her mother.

"My mum wrote everything in capital letters," she recalls. "'Dear Helen. Something is wrong. I know not what.'"

Helen says that when she raised the letter in a therapy session, Hickman instructed her to "dig a hole and burn" it.

"I thought, 'I can't do that. It's from my mum,'" Helen says.

For Helen, this was concerning advice.

She'd begun therapy hoping to strengthen her relationship with her family.

Finally, after more than three years of Hickman's therapy, a session in late 2009 prompted a reckoning that's still hard for Helen to talk about.

"She said to me, 'Helen, do you know why you were sexually abused as a child? Because you've sexually abused other people [in a past life].'"

This idea was straight out of the Universal Medicine belief system. Benhayon has told followers that, "If you have been sexually abused, then you have been an abuser."

Serge Benhayon has falsely claimed that abuse survivors and people with disabilities are being punished for their actions in a "past life". (Supplied)

Helen says for her registered psychologist to propose this in therapy was "unhinged" and "absolutely morally reprehensible".

"It almost had the potential to undo everything I'd tried to do to work through and share those issues with someone for the first time in my life," Helen says.

"I thought she'd gone crazy. That's when I thought, 'I'm not coming back here.'"

Helen travelled from regional Victoria for sessions with Cynthia Hickman in Melbourne. (ABC News: ABC News)

Purging Serge

While Helen managed to cut off her relationship with Hickman, she continued following Universal Medicine's teachings, even taking the drastic step of discarding most of her personal belongings on Serge's advice, some "1,500 books, 200 CDs" and 76 "paintings and little treasures".

The next year, Helen suffered a breakdown when her mother died within weeks of being diagnosed with cancer.

She had a moment of clarity about what she'd done under the cult's influence.

"I blamed myself … I really crucified myself for being so stupid," she says.

"'Where's your stuff? Where's the things you loved that you let go?'"

She felt Cynthia Hickman had groomed her to join an exploitative cult.

Cynthia Hickman has described herself as a "soul" psychologist. (Supplied)

"I was encouraged by a psychologist who's registered, who advertised, who I trusted, and all these connections that I was introduced to led me down that path," Helen says.

" If you're a vulnerable person, you're drawn along with it. These are the people who are going to save your life. "

Helen had a sophisticated understanding of trauma, having worked for decades in domestic violence policy. Yet she says "no matter your professional background" the practitioners are "really good at sowing doubt in human beings … they do it in a very insidious way".

For more stories like this follow the podcast Listen for free on ABC Listen on your mobile device.

Helen raises the alarm

It took more than a decade for Helen to come to terms with her experience and resolve to take action.

By now, Helen was in her 70s and living on the pension in public housing in Melbourne.

Propelled by a "mixture of extreme outrage … and sadness and grief", she decided to formally complain to AHPRA about her former psychologist.

"I had to do this," she says.

"It is so important to hold people to account, particularly people who carry an oath, who carry the imprimatur of the regulators in this country to say 'you are suitable and qualified to practice', and what do they do?"

She learned the regulator had taken a complaint from another more recent client of Hickman's, who also alleged the psychologist tried to recruit them into the cult.

AHPRA placed conditions on Hickman's practice, including supervision about maintaining evidence-based practice, professional boundaries, and keeping her role as a psychologist separate from alternative therapies and spiritual advice.

Under the conditions, Hickman can no longer call herself a "soul psychologist".

Cynthia Hickman had practising conditions placed on her by the Psychology Board of Australia in 2023. (Supplied)

The Background Briefing podcast has discovered that the Psychology Board of Australia has referred Hickman to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal, asking the tribunal to determine whether she engaged in professional misconduct. A finding of professional misconduct can lead to a psychologist being deregistered.

Action 'should be commonplace'

Professor Dwyer believes anything short of deregistering health professionals promoting the cult will fail to address the risk to patients.

"In these cults, once you're hooked onto it … being just wrapped over the knuckles by AHPRA, it's just not reasonable to think that's going to actually change you," he says.

Universal Medicine first came to the attention of John Dwyer more than a decade ago. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

In 2021, UK authorities stripped the professional accreditation of a social worker who publicly promoted the cult leader Benhayon.

Professor Dwyer says this kind of action "should be commonplace" in Australia, but AHPRA had acted against only a "very small number" of registered health professionals who were devotees of the cult.

Cynthia Hickman, Serryn O'Regan and Serge Benhayon did not respond to questions from Background Briefing.

World.title: Albanese's salad days have wilted into a long list of woe
World.content:
There's a telling moment in The Tony Blair Story, a three-part political documentary currently on ABC iview. For political junkies, it is a must-watch.

Blair's early years in the 1990s as UK prime minister were a whirlwind of change and political wins: he granted the Bank of England independence, ushered in devolution in Wales and Scotland, began work on the eventually successful Northern Ireland peace process, and spearheaded the West's intervention in Kosovo.

The documentary portrays the latter as being the moment when Blair attained a near-messianic moral triumph over evil as he walked through large cheering crowds in Kosovo after convincing BIll Clinton to intervene.

British novelist and journalist Robert Harris observes in the documentary that Blair's ascendancy confirmed an "almost cyclical natural rule of politics".

"Whenever something in politics looks at its zenith, the termites are at work on the base," Harris muses.

Watch The Tony Blair Story on ABC iview The extraordinary, personal story of Tony Blair's rise and fall.

That moment in Kosovo, he adds, was when "for the first time maybe a slight parting from reality began to take place".

"In that triumph the seeds of tragedy were sown," Harris cautions in a nod to what would unfold only a few years later in Iraq.

Twelve months ago this columnist noted that "these are Anthony Albanese's salad days".

"He can do no wrong," even as the threat of stagflation and roaring bills already darkened the government's political horizon.

Still brimming with confidence from his defenestration of Peter Dutton in the May 2025 landslide, the prime minister was on a political and personal high.

About to marry his partner Jodie Haydon at the Lodge, he'd banished any doubts that he could manage the mercurial Donald Trump, and was just a few weeks away from passing devilishly challenging environmental approvals laws as well as a spate of historic alliances and defence pacts with Pacific states.

"In political terms, this moment may well be as good as it gets. The real question: are these sunlit uplands a long plateau for the government or a peak where everything now goes downhill?" that column noted.

The first signs of damage

We now know the answer, if only because nothing stays static in politics for long.

Outrage over Communications Minister Anika Wells's hugely expensive trip to New York set off weeks of media headlines and social media meltdowns at the end of last year over MPs' travel entitlements.

Something in the government was "beginning to rot at the core", a Sydney Morning Herald editorial declared in early December in reference to the travel row and suggestions the "wily Albanese government is suffering from a hubris previously unseen".

The first signs of termite damage were already becoming apparent. Then came the devastating Bondi killings and months of fallout that left the government — in the eyes of its critics — on the defensive, reactive and shaken.

Anthony Albanese, with wife Jodie Haydon, at the Bondi Beach memorial service on December 21, 2025. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

It was also around this time that One Nation's rise in the polls began to steepen.

In February came the first big blow to the Albanese government's economic management with the first of what would become five Reserve Bank interest rate hikes.

Despite managing well the fallout from the war against Iran, next came the May budget which involved breaking election promises on changes to negative gearing and capital gains taxation — reforms that continue to bedevil the government, with legislation due before the Senate next week on trusts.

Winter was marred by Bush Barbie and Japanese royal melons. The less said the better.

More recently, the prime minister has been seared by ABC News-led coverage of a $6 million federal grant to the Marrickville Golf Club.

Big shifts in the political economy

And now the treasurer is facing the big pile-on over the government's fiscal settings, which the opposition has successfully linked in the minds of many to high inflation and rising interest rates.

It's a long list of woe, and barely includes more recent setbacks such as the government's backdowns on the sale of some Defence properties and a plan — mere weeks old — to crack down on backpacker visas.

Little wonder things look crooked for the government.

Anecdotally it's hard to find people willing to speak warmly of the prime minister, even among Labor diehards.

Survey data for the government has been bleak. This column has been told by one prominent pollster to brace for even gloomier figures early next week.

"It's the worst set of numbers. Everything is bad," he said.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

So bad that the danger for the government is that it becomes self-reinforcing and self-perpetuating by drowning out successes and good news — the political equivalent of a bank run.

Underlying the grimness inside the government is the realisation that there are few easy policy options to hand.

The notion of spending more money to appease grumpy voters appears to have become toxic.

Whereas it wasn't long ago that both the government and the Coalition regarded fiscal sugar hits as pragmatic politics.

This is a big shift in the political economy.

Another is the growing corridor chatter about the need for the government to undergo a reset and refresh, both of the ideas it pursues and the personnel leading those debates.

Talk of a Cabinet reshuffle appears to be taking on greater urgency. It was previously considered a second-half-of-next-year issue.

As the government flounders, that timeline has shifted towards the first half of the year, perhaps the opening months of 2027.

Loading

Talk of Albanese's future

Albanese's own future and his remaining goals as prime minister are also increasingly coming up in conversations.

A leadership upheaval of that magnitude seems unlikely any time soon. But the chances are also not zero anymore, like they have been over the past five years or so.

Labor's most prominent backbench provocateur, Ed Husic, told Nine newspapers last month that the prime minister should ensure rank-and-file members get to vote on the party's next leader if he resigned next year or after the election.

The story was published on the day that independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car outside her electorate office, so it didn't get much wider notice.

For now, Ed Husic is a lone public voice inside the government. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

But Husic's remarks made him the first MP to openly speculate about the prime minister's political longevity.

"If you do it more than 12 months from the next election, you've got that opportunity [to hold a vote with party members]," he told the papers, adding that it was important the next leader is selected by a "wider base" to ensure a "debate about the direction of the party" and the "big issues confronting Australia."

For now, Husic is a lone public voice inside the government.

It would be foolhardy to bet on the prime minister pulling up stumps before the next election. Albanese insists to his caucus that he has what it takes to turn the ship around before the next election, due in 2028.

He's also got an eye on becoming the second-longest serving Labor prime minister in history behind Bob Hawke and Andrew Fisher, whose total over three stints in the job was just under five years.

That milestone for Anthony Albanese would arrive in mid-March.

Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

World.title: As the world's calamities converge climate talks tread water
World.content:
Estimates vary, but the organisers of this year's UN climate talks in Türkiye said earlier this week that there were 94,866 people in Antalya for the two-week COP 31conference.

That includes all the official delegations, observers and media, not all the other groups who come along for the climate jamboree.

Given that climate change seems to be so far down the list of world leaders' priorities these days, the numbers — which include 34,000 delegates of the various nations attending — seem even more staggering.

The United States, at least at a national level, isn't here since Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris Agreement for a second time after regaining office.

Neither are a lot of other world leaders.

China's President Xi Jinping is missing; Vice-President Han Zheng has come instead.

There's no sign of India's Narendra Modi, Canada's Mark Carney or Japan's Sanae Takaichi.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham turned up very briefly.

Despite this, those who keep the faith on climate change say coming to the COP meetings each year and seeing such huge numbers of people in attendance, gives them hope.

"At least it shows that the rest of us are sticking together," one attendee said.

But pragmatists concede that the process of annual international talks feels like it is, at best, treading water for now.

This week's meeting was the first time it had been conceded that the 1.5°C target had been blown. (Reuters: Wolfgang Rattay)

A '35 by 35' plan

We are a long way from the grand (and failed) ambition of Copenhagen in 2009, when an attempt to set up an entire world regulatory and pricing structure for carbon seemed (briefly) possible.

We are also a long way from Paris in 2015, where a legally binding international agreement was signed by nearly 200 countries to hold the global average temperature increase to "well below 2 degrees Celsius" above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit the increase to 1.5°C.

This week's meeting was the first time it had been conceded that the 1.5°C target had been blown.

The forecast of a 2.6°C increase in warming has also now snuck up to 2.7°C..

In that context, the central plank of this year's talks seems not only starkly unambitious but more rubbery and accommodating of differences.

Australia's climate credibility questioned at UN conference Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has put the Pacific at the centre of his COP31 pitch, but Australia's continued expansion of coal and gas is drawing criticism from climate advocates.

The trajectory of what can be achieved keeps falling, even as the number of climate-related disasters around the world keeps growing.

Turkiye and Australia — as co-presidents of this year's conference — have proposed the world adopt a "35 by 35" plan.

That is, a plan for electricity's share of final energy consumption to increase to around 35 per cent by 2035.

While there is talk of this being a "pledge", the language of the proposal speaks of "advancing the shared ambition" of increasing electricity's share "while recognising different national circumstances and development priorities, and encouraging broader participation and implementation through national action, international partnerships and investment".

In other words, the "pledge" is not only not binding, but it also puts no strictures on just what sort of energy is used to generate this electricity.

In the language of international diplomacy, 35 by 35 "aims to mobilise political support, investment and international cooperation to accelerate electrification in line with national circumstances".

Australia and Turkiye, by happenstance, are among the countries currently most reliant on fossil fuels to generate electricity.

(Also by happenstance, Turkiye announced on the day the climate talks opened that new oil discoveries would help lift daily production to over 100,000 barrels a day in the second half of next year.)

Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen, who is chairing the negotiations, says the 35 by 35 target would require countries to quadruple the current pace at which they are electrifying. (Reuters: Murad Sezer)

Not an ambitious target

Some countries, notably France, say the pledge is not worth anything if it is made on the back of fossil-fuel sourced electricity.

Critics say it may lock in fossil fuel use for longer.

Advocates argue that the plummeting cost of renewable energy means the only rational decision to reach when considering future electricity supplies is clean energy.

But it is not always that simple. The complications of individual countries energy systems, the structure and age of electricity grids and infrastructure, let alone the cost, can also limit a country's capacity to switch.

No-one seems entirely sure how this proposal will end up after two weeks of negotiations: will it be an "ambition" or some form of binding pledge?

Electricity currently accounts for about 23 per cent of energy consumption.

It is forecast to rise to 30 per cent on the basis of technology changes already underway.

The international think tank the Energy Transitions Commission has estimated that if the whole 35 by 35 pledge was powered by clean energy it would only cut global warming by about 0.3°C.

With the 1.5°C target already blown, that doesn't sound particularly ambitious.

Climate and energy minister Chris Bowen, who is chairing the negotiations between 190 countries, rejects that, saying the target would require countries to quadruple the current pace at which they are electrifying their energy systems.

That means four times faster take up of electric cars, renewable energy like wind and solar, greener buildings and transport systems.

In a world where global political will on climate adaptation feels like it is on life support, focusing on electrification offers the political advantage that it can be sold as directly addressing household energy costs at a time when a world energy crisis has made that a rather important issue.

COP31 summit targets major electrification push The climate summit will push for nations around the world to electrify their energy faster and move away from fossil fuels.

Matt Kean, who chair's Australia's Climate Change Authority, was briefly in Antalya at the conference. The Authority's brief relates only to Australia's climate tasks, but he reflected both the reasons why focusing on electrification might make sense in policy terms, but also the political ones in global terms.

"For Australia to hit it's ambitious emissions reduction targets, there are three things that we need to do: decarbonise the grid [that is move away from fossil-fuel based electricity]; electrify as much as we can; and use our landmass to sequester as much carbon as possible," he says.

"Doing those three things largely gets us to 62 to 70 per cent [emissions reduction]. Then we need to invest in research and development, to try and solve the problems of steel and cement, that is, the very-hard-to-abate parts of the economy.

"But let's focus on the things where the technologies are available to us now.

"If you were to electrify, not only is it going to be good for our emissions, but it will also be good for families and businesses through lower bills.

"Every time you drive past the bowser at the moment, you're reminded about the need to get off energy supplies coming from very volatile parts of the world."

The plight of Palestinians in Gaza has been raised this week in environmental terms as well as human terms, and not just by activists like Greta Thunberg. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The calamities of the world are converging

Meetings like the one in Antalya run on compromise and meetings with eye-glazing titles like the "High Level Event on Matters Related to the Global Implementation Accelerator".

For those who want such meetings to completely shift the dial on the climate discussion, they seem like what Greta Thunberg described in 2021 as just a lot of "blah, blah blah".

There is outrage here that the agenda doesn't even mention cutting fossil fuels directly — a deliberate decision by Turkiye and Australia because talks in so many previous years have foundered on setting any targets or plans to do it.

If you put this year's climate talks in the prism of broader world events, rather than just arguing the questions of what should be done about the climate, they are happening in a world without US leadership, where the international order has been crumbling, and where there seems to be an inverse relationship between the need to solve conflicts and the ambitions or capacity to do so.

It's somehow appropriate that the plight of Palestinians in Gaza or conflicts in Lebanon, Ukraine and Africa have been raised this week in environmental terms as well as human terms. And not just by activists like Thunberg, but by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in his opening address as host of the conference.

"What has taken place in Gaza is not only a genocide; it is also an ecocide," he said.

"Centuries-old olive trees have been cut down in Gaza. The soil and water have been polluted in Gaza. And cities in Gaza have been turned into enormous piles of rubble."

All the calamities of the world seem to be converging.

Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

World.title: Why you will pay for Jensen Huang's indiscretions
World.content:
The reaction was swift and brutal.

Jensen Huang's resignation, while expected, sparked yet another nosedive in the value of the company he has led for 33 years, initially shedding another 14 per cent before recovering to end the day down almost 5 per cent.

For the past week, ever since revelations that he had been romantically involved with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, Nvidia's share price has been pummelled on fears the founder may be forced out.

Once reports of a second extramarital affair emerged, with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, his fate was sealed. Now, reports have surfaced of at least another in-house relationship.

Since October 6, the company has been stripped of 30 per cent of its value, as the scandal surrounding Huang added to broader concerns that higher interest rates and a less benign US government after the midterms would slow the rollout of AI.

The Economist magazine was typically blunt in its assessment of Huang's cavalier disregard for the consequences of his behaviour.

"Mr Huang's Chinese affair could go down as the most expensive shag in history," it declared.

The sun king flames out

Nvidia is no ordinary company.

It sits smack in the middle of the AI revolution.

It is the sun that powers the AI solar system, as governments and corporations revolve around it.

For the past four years, a stock market boom has been driven by a single technology, underpinned by one company, driven by just one person, Huang.

Nvidia, which began life making chips for computer games, was thrust into the spotlight by an insatiable demand for its product, as the only supplier of the chips that could power the next industrial revolution.

Nvidia chips are powering the AI revolution. (Reuters: Ann Wang)

Huang not only put himself front and centre of that boom, he has meticulously ensured that no-one else is equipped to run the operation.

He, and he alone, has controlled everything from financing to chip design, ruling over his domain with complete authority.

Where most chief executives would have a handful of senior executives reporting to them, Huang has 60. Or had, until yesterday.

Justin Wolfers, the Australian-born professor of economics at the University of Michigan, says Huang's management style has left the company deeply exposed.

"He has so many direct reports, he has made himself irreplaceable, but he hasn't done the work a CEO should do, which is creating a successor," he told the ABC

"When you run a company worth $US4.5 trillion that is powering the next industrial revolution and you can't be bothered to figure out a coherent management structure, so that when you get caught with pants down, your company is worth much less, that is an extraordinary fail of management and the board."

Justin Wolfers says Jensen Huang's management style has left the company deeply exposed. (Supplied)

Huang's demise raises questions about the long-term future of the company and adds to the fears that the AI investment boom is ripe for a fall.

Alice Huang, the suspected spy, has gone to ground and is reportedly back in China.

Beijing has since denied all accusations of espionage. But it would appear to have been one of the most successful honey-trap missions in history.

Long live … who?

After emergency meetings until late last night Australian time, the company passed on the mantle to its chief financial officer of 13 years, Colette Kress.

Colette Kress is the interim chief executive of Nvidia. (Supplied: Nvidia)

At this stage, she is simply keeping the seat warm while the board looks for a permanent replacement. But she would have a better handle on the complexity of the operation than anyone else.

Nvidia's high powered chips don't come cheap. And to keep that solar system running, the firm has helped finance many of its customers to ensure their expansion also ensures ongoing demand for its technology.

The Australian group Firmus, which spectacularly failed last month to raise funds for a listing on the Australian Securities Exchange, is one such group.

Another is the US firm CoreWeave — with a similar operation to Firmus — which this week announced it would be relying less on traditional debt finance and more towards Nvidia, its main supplier.

How the biggest IPO in three decades fell over There were high hopes for the Firmus float, but it sunk amid concerns about debt and ambitious expansion plans.

Kress will also need to navigate the now-treacherous waters in Washington as a more hostile Senate and House come to grips with Huang's indiscretions and the potential fallout from the spy scandal.

Nvidia is due to release its results next week which, if the money-making machine continues its spectacular performance, may give her an opportunity to soothe investor fears.

But the very next day, on November 18, Huang will appear at a congressional hearing to be interrogated over his relationship with Alice Huang, the alleged spy who loved him.

An executive at a Singaporean firm call Megaspeed, which was a customer of Nvidia, Alice Huang is suspected of funnelling billions of dollars of Nvidia chips through to Chinese AI firms, circumventing a US ban on sales to China.

Loading

Chipping away

Australians have a lot riding on the AI boom and, by default, Nvidia.

More than $1 trillion of Australian superannuation funds are invested offshore, the bulk of which has been directed to the biggest American technology companies.

And for the past four years, that money has chased the AI boom, explains Jun Bei Liu, portfolio manager and founder of Sydney investment firm Tencap.

Jun Bei Liu says Nvidia has been central to the AI build-out. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"Nvidia has been central to the whole build-out of the AI infrastructure," she says.

"They have been a big investor into businesses like cloud businesses and neoclouds and then also the data centre businesses."

The 20 per cent fall in Nvidia's stock in the past week would be enough to impact super fund returns, she says, but she is more concerned about the long-term impact, given the company's central role in the future of AI.

Huang was the visionary that created the company and drove every key decision it made regarding its technology and its strategy.

Without him, the future has just become a great deal less certain.

"There are a lot of ramifications around what is to come if a company like Nvidia changes its strategy," she says.

The uncertainty over Nvidia has added to the turmoil already engulfing the technology industry as pressure builds on governments to rein in the industry's power and its reach over the lives of ordinary citizens.

As Wolfers explains, the US tech giants have far more power than any other corporations in history.

"We have a very small number of firms run by a small number of executives that are set to power the next industrial revolution," he said.

"They have more power than governments, they are cosy with Washington and they will shape the lives of Australians no less than they will reshape US lives."

Jensen Huang (left) has a close relationship with Donald Trump. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

While the Trump administration may be unwilling to stand in the way of the industry, given the president's close personal relationships with its leaders, it may well be financial markets that pull the handbrake.

Growing doubts over profitability, the enormous amounts of capital being poured into AI development, and the prospect of delays to the physical rollout forced on the industry by seething community anger over data centres have already rattled confidence.

And now this. A pillar of the entire edifice has been shown to be defective.

World.title: The bikie boss, the $800,000 Ferrari and an $18 million Brighton mansion
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaCrime The bikie boss, the $800,000 Ferrari and an $18 million Brighton mansion Cameron Houston and Marta Pascual Juanola November 14, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Police have raided an $18 million Brighton mansion occupied by a bikie boss following a campaign of violence against embattled property developer Simon Pitard and his family’s aged care empire. Detectives from Taskforce Echo searched the luxury residence of Finks national president Mark Balsillie on November 6, just hours after two masked men fired 10 shots at an Arcare aged care facility in Maidstone. Later that day, police publicly identified the gang as an “organised crime priority”. The multimillion-dollar mansion in Brighton where Balsillie has been living. The police raid also followed the firebombing of Pitard’s Brighton property on October 27 when two luxury cars were destroyed. On October 28, an innocent 52-year-old woman sustained serious burns when her Cheltenham townhouse was firebombed in a case of mistaken identity, which is also under investigation. Detectives carried out firearm prohibition order compliance searches at another five properties in Narre Warren North, Safety Beach, Mount Eliza and Dallas as part of their November 6 blitz on the Finks, but no arrests were made.



This masthead does not suggest Balsillie is involved in the campaign of violence against Pitard. He did not respond to requests for comment. An investigation by this masthead can also reveal that federal law enforcement agencies have been investigating the ownership of Balsillie’s opulent home and a recent application for an $11 million loan in the name of a 23-year-old associate of the bikie enforcer. Balsillie (centre) at slain underworld figure Sam “The Punisher” Abdulrahim’s funeral in 2025. The Age According to land title records, the registered owner of the mansion is self-described taxi driver-turned-billionaire property developer Pankaj “Harry” Goyal, whose construction company Harcon Projects built the four-level home, replete with rooftop garden, indoor pool, sauna and climate-controlled cellar. Balsillie has lived in the mansion for the past six months and has told associates he was in the process of buying it from Goyal, according to five underworld and property industry sources who asked not to be identified because of safety concerns.



The sources said the potential transfer of the mansion came to the attention of law enforcement agencies, when a 23-year-old associate of Balsillie was named as the applicant for an $11 million loan. Harcon Projects boss Pankaj “Harry” Goyal. The man, who The Age has decided not to name for safety reasons, lives with his parents in Bentleigh East and would have been required to make monthly repayments of almost $70,000 if the loan proceeded. On September 9, the 23-year-old replaced Balsillie as the sole director and shareholder of a company called AP Global Aust Pty Ltd, which was first registered by the Finks boss in January. The 23-year-old is expected to be interviewed next month by the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission over his alleged involvement in the sale. The commission declined to comment when contacted by this masthead.



Goyal’s close connection with Balsillie has seen him allow the Finks president access to an $800,000 blue Ferrari Purosangue. The 46-year-old businessman, who has a penchant for expensive cars, drives a black version of the luxury car himself. Goyal confirmed he owned the Brighton property when contacted by this masthead, but did not respond to repeated questions about his arrangement with Balsillie and denied the bikie had ever driven his car. He said Balsillie “might be living” in the mansion, but “is definitely not on the lease”. “I’ve got another 100 [properties]. So what has that got to do with me?” Goyal said. The construction boss has previously claimed he went from having 60 cents in his pocket, after gambling away money his father had given him to settle in Australia, to making a billion dollars and rubbing shoulder with Australia’s wealthiest through financing and land banking.



He told a podcast in 2023 he worked as a dishwasher and waiter at Crown Casino, while also working 16-hour shifts as a taxi driver to raise the funds to start his finance company, Loans Direct. The Brighton mansion features an indoor pool, glass lift and home movie theatre. “I used to eat the soft serves or the biscuits for 10 cents back then to fill my tummy up,” he said. Land title records show the 46-year-old has amassed expansive property interests that include shares in dozens of units in Brighton, Shepparton, Rockbank, Craigieburn, Thornhill Park, Moorabool, Truganina, Little River, and Charlemont worth more than $400 million. This masthead does not suggest any wrongdoing by Goyal or any involvement with the Finks OMCG.



Three underworld and property industry sources told this masthead that Goyal had also been involved in a botched $95 million deal with Balsillie to redevelop a former cattle farm in Sydney’s west into a cemetery. However, the deal fell over earlier this year after they failed to settle on the property, forfeiting a $9.5 million deposit. The 73-hectare site, in the semi-rural suburb of Wallacia, 70 kilometres west of Sydney, had been earmarked for a cemetery development since 2020. Earlier plans for the land, which is on a flood plain that backs onto the Nepean River, included 775,000 burial plots, a chapel, a crematorium and several mausoleums. The property on Greendale Road, Wallacia. The deal to develop the old cattle farm into a cemetery fell over earlier this year. Wolter Peeters



Goyal confirmed his involvement in the cemetery proposal, but denied Balsillie had a role in the deal. Balsillie has held various leadership roles with several outlaw bikie gangs for more than a decade, despite coming from an unconventional background. Related Article Exclusive

Organised crime Melbourne nursing homes under police guard as bikies target prominent aged care chain The 42-year-old is the son of retired police officer Andrew Balsillie, who served more than 40 years with Victoria Police and helped uncover a drug lab run by slain gangland figure Carl Williams out of a Broadmeadows commission building in 1999. Balsillie originally joined the Comancheros, and rapidly ascended to senior ranks within the gang.



When Balsillie pleaded guilty to extortion and possessing counterfeit money in 2016, a County Court judge described his involvement with the Comancheros as the beginning of his “fall from grace”, having grown up in a “caring and loving family”. Balsillie later defected to the Mongols, who sent him to Russia to patch over Comanchero members. Balsillie has held several senior positions in three different bikie gangs. Instagram In 2017, the 39-year-old survived a murder attempt when he was shot seven times in the arms, leg and stomach by a former Comanchero associate who fled to Turkey after the attack. Balsillie pleaded guilty to possessing and trafficking cocaine in the County Court in 2022, after claiming he had used two grams of cocaine a day to manage chronic pain caused by the shooting.



Judge David Brookes accepted he had undergone “genuine reformation” since his arrest in 2020, when detectives from the Echo and Trident taskforces found 127 grams of cocaine concealed inside a cereal box, encrypted mobile phones and syringes filled with growth hormone and testosterone at Balsillie’s property. Since taking over the leadership of the Finks in 2024, Balsillie has helmed a rapid expansion of the once fringe club recruiting several former associates from the Comancheros, including Ahmad “Rocky” Niazi and Thomas Laslo. Last Friday, Victoria Police said it had created a specialist taskforce made up of officers from Taskforce Echo, Operation Phoenix and the Viper Taskforce to target the gang. “My message to the Finks ... is very clear: if you choose to continue your involvement in serious and organised crime, Victoria Police is coming after you,” Detective Superintendent Wayne Cheesman said. World.content:
SportSoccerAustralian soccer Socceroos take another positive step with 3-0 rout of defending Asian champions Vince Rugari November 14, 2026 — 5:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
