If only there were an Asian Cup around the corner. The Socceroos have taken another assured step in the right direction, dominating two-time reigning Asian champions Qatar in a commanding 3-0 friendly victory in Doha on Saturday morning (AEDT). Nestory Irankunda and Connor Metcalfe celebrate a goal. Getty Images Originally booked as a warm-up match ahead of a tournament which has now been delayed by 12 months, there was little riding on the match aside from the opportunity to advance the team’s overall development and blood some new faces. Both boxes were sufficiently ticked.



Coach Tony Popovic rolled out his strongest available team, and their first-half performance was as aggressive and dominant as they have been during his tenure, proving that the recent promise of the Brazil friendly series at home was no flash in the pan. They went 3-0 up before the break, with all three goals – from Riley McGree, Tete Yengi and Nestory Irankunda – coming on the back of mistakes forced by the Socceroos’ high press, which a hapless Qatar failed to deal with. Two of them came directly from errant passes by Qatar’s goalkeeper, Mahmud Abunada, who endured a nightmare performance. View post on X Popovic rang the changes in the second half, handing debuts to Eli Adams, Sam Klein, Kasey Bos and Diesel Herrington, while the returning Gianni Stensness also came off the bench for his first minutes for Australia in more than four years. Naturally, the Socceroos lost a bit of momentum as a consequence of all of those substitutions, but while they could not find an additional goal, they still kept a clean sheet while denying Qatar a single shot on target for the match; they did not fire their first shot until the 72nd minute.



Tony Popovic. AP Photo/Hussein Sayed Popovic had little to complain about afterwards, aside from the fact they could and should have scored more. “We were very aggressive,” Popovic said. “It was testing conditions, wasn’t easy for the players. We could see that they were finding it hard to breathe and move in these conditions. The pitch was quite hard underneath. It’s not what they’re accustomed to in Europe. “I think [we could have added] a few more goals from our good play, and we started the second half well, and I think when we made all the changes, I think we lost a lot of cohesion and we lost our way a little bit. But it was important for those boys to get minutes and to rest some of the boys that need to back up against Jordan, and some debutants, which is always a special moment.”



Related Article Olympics Matildas to face fearsome Japan in Olympic qualifying mission Another positive was Connor Metcalfe’s performance in central midfield next to Paul Okon jnr, which further cemented the FC St. Pauli star as a viable option to play there at international level instead of his usual wide attacking position. With first-choice players Mohamed Toure, Cristian Volpato, Jordan Bos, Jackson Irvine, Lewis Miller and Aiden O’Neill all currently sidelined through injury, the performance showcased the growing depth of the Socceroos and hinted again at the serious potential of this current generation of players. They will play again next week in another friendly against Jordan, the team Qatar beat in the last Asian Cup final four years ago, which will also take place in Doha - the result of several days of delicate behind-the-scenes negotiations by Football Australia, after Socceroos players expressed their unwillingness to travel to Amman due to security fears. That game could prove to be Popovic’s final match in charge of the Socceroos if he is unable to come to an agreement with Football Australia over a contract extension. World.title: Kate Atkinson’s new novel shouldn’t work. Somehow it does
World.content:
CultureBooksReview Kate Atkinson’s new novel shouldn’t work. Somehow it does Helen Elliott November 14, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Kate Atkinson’s unclassifiable novels could be seen as a succession of cartwheels: now upside down, now vertical, in endless motion, teetering on imbalance, adjusted in the nick of time. Or not. Atkinson’s element is speed. That said, it is a very British speed. Open her novels, adjust your reading. Her latest, Our Noble Selves, is the full cartwheel. The novel follows Harry Flynn, a sometime London journalist, now – as with half the world – back from World War II. Harry had been one of the millions presumed dead; at times he presumes he might be, wonders why he isn’t, or simply thinks: why not? Women don’t seem to notice anything odd about Harry, though he has no idea why they like him so much – which is obviously part of the appeal. Novelist Kate Atkinson. Getty Images Harry is the sort of man Atkinson specialises in: believable, yearnable, imbued with charm both sexual and otherwise. Perhaps he has Trevor Howard’s voice in Brief Encounter. The novel opens around the time that film arrived in cinemas. But charm, sexual or otherwise, natural or manufactured, won’t keep a man upright. And Harry likes to drink. The trouble is that it makes him blot out his memory. Drinking is, after all, the obvious root of blotto. Harry, captured after the fall of Singapore in 1942, was a prisoner of the Japanese on the Burma Railway. Not that anyone will ever know, because he sees no point in speaking about those years. Returned men and women acknowledged the unspeakable through a mutual silence. There is nobility in not saying how much a human soul can endure. Yet not saying, like nobility, is an old-fashioned virtue. Perhaps it is the result of cauterised emotion? Or perhaps it is simply being British?



Five years after the end of the war, Harry is editing an anthology of poems for the entirely marvellous Festival of Britain which is to occur in 1951. Devised by the Labour government to celebrate the centenary of the 1851 Great Exhibition, the Festival of Britain embodied the idea of shrugging away the war years and installing hope in a future. The aim was to find pride in the details of a specifically British life. As Harry’s boss, Gerald Barry (Atkinson uses the historical figure), says: “This is our story… Our love of country, love of freedom, love of nature, pride in craftsmanship, our reputation for tolerance and fair play. Farming, industry and science – production rather than products. Harry listens but privately thinks: All this for a summer festival? It sounded exhausting. And such faith in a brave new world.” Photo: The poems are routinely awful, leaving Harry time for other corners of the festival: pageantry, homes and gardens, beauty parades, fashion and cooking – which proves especially eccentric. There is some absorbing office politics as well, alongside lovely glimpses of friendship, even if Harry’s private life remains dismal. Atkinson cartwheels all over the place, and such is her skill that the droll frequently turns dazzling. Now and again, though, you might feel as if you are staring at an upside-down head between two flailing arms, shouting at you: “Keep up! Keep up!” Keeping up is both entertaining and provoking as you register the underpinnings of human life. These arrive as stills frozen out of the surface pageant, lively with details any curious reader might want to pursue. Atkinson is an historical novelist whose brain teems with the ordinary particulars of the last century; Our Noble Selves can be read simply for the sheer texture of how life felt during those grim years, when a country tried to recover from the shock of the war. It can also be read as a vanishing-woman mystery, if that is your fancy. Harry? A murderer? Mmmm. Or it can be taken as straight history, charting the miraculous Festival of Britain in the very nation that invented pageantry – as anyone who has read Mapp and Lucia or tuned into Midsomer Murders understands without needing a word of explanation.



Editor's pick Review I hated this book. Then I realised just how brilliant it was In an afterword, Atkinson says she originally intended to write a novel about the experience of the POWs on the Burma-Siam Railway but, tough as she is, she could not go on. The experience of real men, in a real hell, felt exploitative, and she was intending a relatively light-hearted novel. So she turned her head away and wrote something different. But she recommends J. G. Farrell’s The Singapore Grip for those who want to know what the word harrowing might mean to people like charming Harry. She’s right. But if Farrell is too inconvenient, Our Noble Selves might strike exactly the right note in these not-quite harrowing days. Our Noble Selves by Kate Atkinson is published by Doubleday ($35). World.title: I worked part-time at David Jones. I know exactly why the business failed
World.content:
BusinessConsumer affairsDavid Jones collapse Opinion I worked part-time at David Jones. I know exactly why the business failed Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist November 14, 2026 — 5:30am

November 14, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I’m told that admitting you are upset about the demise of David Jones is an admission that you are middle class. Well, maybe. Then again, I have a nostalgic regard for many icons of the past. Not all are posh. Aside from David Jones, they include Chiko Rolls, Alpine cigarettes when stored by a young female friend in the space between her arm muscle and her T-shirt, and KB beer (providing it was being derided as “Kids’ Beer”, on account of its sweetness). David Jones is expected to close many of its 38 stores and make thousands of staff redundant. Eddie Jim And when it comes to David Jones, I have the experience of being a middle-class shopper but also one of the workers. I don’t want to overstate my claim to fame. I won’t be claiming a late-issue redundancy payment from the receiver. I was there for months, not years. All the same, in 1980, when I was attempting to convince the University of Sydney that I deserved a history degree, I worked part-time as a lift operator at David Jones’ Market Street store. I was required to operate the antique machinery and to simultaneously intone the usual catechism: “Ground floor: perfumery, stationery and leather goods, wigs and haberdashery, kitchenware and food. Going up …”



Actually, those are the words of the lift operator in Are You Being Served? Our floors were a little different, but I can’t remember. My point: across continents, department stores were famous and so were their lift operators. My fellow Herald writer Peter FitzSimons, when offering his own recollections about the demise of DJs, made special mention of we lift operators. The lift, he wrote, “came complete with an old attendant with a peaked cap and crimson uniform. There were no buttons in the lift to denote floors and instead this kindly old fellow had his hand on a dial like the one used on the bridge of a ship – full steam ahead, steady astern, etc – to get it moving. And as it stopped at each level, he would portentously make announcements. ‘Children’s wear, shoes, toys … Dining, kitchen and bridal wear… Women’s designer fashion, men’s formal wear ...’ And so on.” Well, of course, I take offence at Pete’s “kindly old fellow”. I was, and am, only three years older than Fitz. In fact, my main problem with the job was the older male customers. We were required to laugh at their jokes. Sorry, I should have said: “We were required to laugh at their joke.” Every time it would be the same. An old chap would hop into the lift. His lips would start twitching as he readied the witticism, and then it would come, somewhere between first floor (women’s etc) and third floor (kitchen’s etc).



“Well, son, I’m guessing this is a pretty up and down sort of job.” Dutiful employee, that was me, I would chortle away as if comedy itself had reached a new plateau. After this, the fellow would exit the lift full of cheer, with a desire to spend as much time and money as possible. The business pages of this newspaper are full of analysis of why DJs finally came unstuck, but none have mentioned the obvious: the departure of the lift operators and our readiness to laugh at “the joke”. Working all day inside the lift, I was also aware that for many customers David Jones meant only one thing: bras. Later in life, this was confirmed. When I mentioned my lift-operator job to female friends, their memories of DJs were always connected to that one department. A lift operator at David Jones’ Market Street store in 1984. Trevor James Robert Dallen/Fairfax Media They’d recount how they’d been dragged in there by their mothers because David Jones supposedly had the best bra-fitters. These were no-nonsense women who would grab the breasts of the terrified teenage girl, assess their weight and shape, before they issued a first bra.



Related Article Opinion

Pop culture Will and Kate’s kids’ names? I’m sick of being told I’m supposed to know about these things Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist I remember asking: “Did they do a good job?” “Who knows,” would be the reply, “I was just mortified that I had breasts in the first place.” Later still, I had my own experience of the glory days of David Jones. I’d started going on TV for five minutes a week – 7’s Sunrise program – and I needed a proper suit so I looked OK next to Kochie. I went to DJs and, Anglophile that I am, I was attracted to a display of suits by some young British designer. They were what one might call “slim-fit”. A DJs sales assistant, a woman of a certain age, appraised my appearance as I stood there with my chosen slim-fit suit on its hanger. “We often find,” she said, “that these British suits are not built for our broad Australian shoulders.” She never called me fat. She never said, “Mate, you’ve let yourself go.” But, when I walked out that afternoon, I was holding a suit which fitted me. And my ego was still intact. What a glorious woman.



Is it any surprise the David Jones business has failed? The positive suit lady, that woman with the talent for bare-faced lies, is no longer there. The brusque bra-fitters with their rough, breast-appraising hands, are no longer there. And nor are the lift guys, with our willingness to laugh at a joke we have heard 4000 times before. I mourn them all. Although, speaking for myself, it certainly was an up and down sort of job. Need more Richard Glover in your life? World.title: Your retirement savings shouldn’t be someone else’s sales target
World.content:
November 14, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

You’re 55 or 60, you’ve spent decades building up your super, and you’re wondering whether you’ve saved enough. Then you come across an ad that promises to tell you if you’re on track for retirement. So you click. You answer a few questions, leave your phone number or email, and wait to hear back. Retirees are being pressured into financial advice they don’t understand. Simon Letch What you might not realise is that you just entered a sales funnel. Your details could be passed on to a business whose job is to turn your curiosity and fear of not having enough into an appointment with a financial adviser. And that appointment could ultimately lead to a recommendation that you move your savings out of a conventional super fund into a much higher risk investment approach. Welcome to the world of financial services lead generation. It’s a business model that most Australians don’t know anything about, and shouldn’t have to. Yet they’re being drawn into it, hook, line and sinker, often without understanding who’s behind the offer, who’s making money from their inquiry, or what the business ultimately wants them to do with their retirement savings.



After reading ASIC’s latest investigation into the worst of these practices, I think it’s time we banned the kind of lead generation that financially rewards businesses for funnelling Australians towards financial advice, financial products and super switching, whether directly or through a chain of intermediaries. There really is a world of difference between helping someone understand their real retirement options and helping them make good decisions, and making money from steering them towards a financial decision that might not be in their best interests. To understand the problem, all we need to do is follow the money. ASIC’s latest investigation shows just how lucrative this business model has become. The corporate regulator examined 15 financial advice licensees using lead generators between January 2025 and June 2026. During that period these businesses acquired 7639 new clients through lead generation arrangements, or about 35 per cent of new clients.



And here’s where it gets really juicy. ASIC found that some lead generators were being paid between 80 and 100 per cent of the upfront advice fee when they successfully turned someone into a client. That’s a lot of money. Thousands and thousands of dollars. And that’s going to the business responsible for getting everyday Australians through the door of these advice businesses. And that upfront advice fee could be deducted entirely from your superannuation savings. Some were telling people their funds weren’t performing well enough, or frightening them about what could happen if the market crashed. So why would a financial advice business be willing to sign on for a deal like that? You have to wonder just how much money they expect to make from a customer over the years ahead. Once the customer signs up, the advice business can collect ongoing fees potentially for years. And if the customer is persuaded to switch their super, substantial sums can flow into investment management and platforms potentially generating even more revenue for the businesses involved in the arrangements.



Across the 15 licensees – the businesses legally responsible for the financial advice provided under their licence – clients paid $9.8 million in upfront advice fees and agreed to another $4.5 million in annual ongoing fees. From that you can see why getting someone to click on a free super check can be such a valuable business. And we’re not talking about small amounts of money changing hands here. ASIC found that more than $678 million was switched or invested after referrals from lead generators across these 15 businesses alone. And about 90 per cent of that money came from superannuation savings. Now, that $678 million isn’t money that’s been lost. But it’s an enormous amount of retirement savings being moved around because of introductions by businesses that are being financially rewarded for delivering new customers to advisers. That makes my blood boil. We’re talking about money people have spent 30 or 40 years accumulating, potentially being redirected into investments they may not fully understand, through a process they might not even realise is designed to sell them something.



The problem starts long before someone sits down with a financial adviser. Related Article Superannuation The ‘immediate warning sign’ to protect your super ASIC’s report shows just how far some of these businesses will go to get people to move their super, too. Some were telling people their funds weren’t performing well enough, or frightening them with warnings about what could happen to their savings if the sharemarket crashed. And some of the people making these claims weren’t even qualified to give financial advice – they’re effectively salespeople, flogging fear to get people through the door. I’ve been writing about these problems for years, and this week I sat down with ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland to discuss them on the Prime Time podcast, too.



I have to say it: I’ve had enough. We’ve seen far too many examples of Australians being frightened, pressured and persuaded into making decisions about their life savings that might not be in their best interests. It really is time for the government to step up and make illegal all forms of financial lead generation that steer someone into switching their super. Free courses, free super checks, free retirement assessments, online quizzes, calculators, lead generation forms with incentives, or even ‘paid mates who refer unknowing consumers’. The Super Members Council’s Misha Schubert. Eamon Gallagher I don’t care what the bait looks like. If the real purpose is to funnel people towards advisers who plan to switch their super, and someone is being financially rewarded for getting them there, it’s time for it to stop. Consumers don’t understand that it’s happening. And I don’t think burying the details of these financial arrangements in disclosure documents that nobody reads makes them more acceptable. Telling someone in the fine print that you’re being paid to steer them towards an adviser doesn’t make the practice right. It shouldn’t be happening in the first place.



I’m not the only one calling for a ban. Super Members Council chief executive Misha Schubert says these practices have no place in the financial services industry. She’s also warning that the government’s proposed restrictions on unlicensed lead generators don’t go far enough. Dodgy businesses will just find another way. Editor's pick Opinion

Superannuation Super funds are finally overhauling retirement. Here’s what’s changing Bec Wilson Money contributor As Schubert puts it, parliament needs to “shut and bolt the door on this harmful practice – not leave it ajar to continuing harm”. That doesn’t mean banning genuine financial education, or making it harder for people to find good advice from an adviser they arrive at by genuine referral where no money changes hands. It means drawing a clear line between helping people understand their options and using a helpful-looking offer to sell them something they might not actually need.



Meanwhile, while the government faffs about on this, Australians need to be a lot more wary about what they are clicking on in the financial services world. If you see an ad offering a free super check, or retirement assessment, ask yourself who’s behind it and what they want from you. Before handing over your phone number or email to be connected into an advice referral, find out whether anyone is being paid to refer you. Then ask yourself if there’s a better way to get the help you need. There almost always is. And if someone starts telling you your super isn’t performing, or that you need to move your money urgently, please be careful. Don’t let these very slick salespeople frighten you into deciding about savings you’ve spent decades building. Good financial advice should help you understand your options, not scare you into taking action. I believe wholeheartedly that people should be able to find an adviser without someone else making money from steering them through the door. There’s plenty of demand out there for good advice and plenty of good advisers. So why can’t we just let good advice win?



Bec Wilson, bestselling author of How to Have an Epic Retirement, is a retirement educator and founder of the Epic Retirement Institute. She writes a weekly newsletter about modern retirement at au.epicretirement.net. She has various commercial arrangements with a range of organisations, including superannuation funds. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: The two debt traps to avoid this Christmas – and what to do instead
World.content:
MoneySavingChristmas Opinion The two debt traps to avoid this Christmas – and what to do instead Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor November 14, 2026 — 5:01am

November 14, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

With five rate rises this year, petrol near $2 a litre and Christmas coming, it’s possible you might be really feeling the cash crunch. It’s also possible you’re desperately trying to figure out how to solve it. And there are tools available, but there are right and wrong ways to try and ease the financial squeeze. Let’s lay them bare. Christmas spending can tighten the screws on household budgets. Luis Ascui Buy now, pay later: The season may have you thinking something silly: buy now, pay later. With Christmas just over a month away, could you instead curb the spend and use old school pay-in-advance lay-by? This will stop you dealing with a Christmas repayment hangover well into the New Year.



At least it is lightly regulated now, with some credit checks and responsible product approval guidelines. But it’s possible that this very thing has pushed people from Afterpay to advance-pay products. Wage advance: Anything of this ilk, where you get your money before you have earned it, comes with a steep interest or fee cost. That this product usually carries the latter is why it escapes the National Credit Code. I’ve lost track of the number of people who’ve said to me: ‘My costs are going up and up, but my income is staying the same.’ And not only does it cost you extra money to get access to cash you haven’t yet earned, you are getting into a downward spiral of playing catch up – with each transaction, you are eroding the money you have to spend from your future pays. This is just a terrible strategy. So, let’s look at better ones, starting with investigating where you could cut expenses.



Relationships and hardship: You’ve no doubt taken a razor to your spend, but most people pay too much on what they believe to be ‘fixed’ costs – think utilities and insurances, and many other financial products. Start by playing the ‘relationship’ card: pick up the phone and ask your providers if you can get a loyalty discount to match the better new products on the market (give this a Google first). If no dice, get disloyal and switch. You also absolutely qualify for concessions with your existing providers, if your situation has escalated beyond your ability to cope. And leniency should apply even to loans. Every financial and service provider needs to have a dedicated financial hardship department and they must extend you help. But what if the price pressures are across the board, and you feel financially maxed out?



One Stop One Story: The OSOS hub is a free service designed to help in times of financial distress, to advocate for you for a better deal. Operated by the Thriving Communities Partnership, it was launched with a focus on domestic and family violence victim-survivors but has expanded to cover general financial hardship and related crises. Rather than having to explain your financial situation to each one of the providers in your life, this service does it for you. There is also help available to rebuild your finances long term. The National Debt Helpline: The National Debt Helpline administers and matches thousands of free financial counsellors around the country with people in need. You can register online at ndh.org.au or 1800 007 007. It may take a while for an appointment, but your finances will get a once-over which could give them a second wind.



Similar to the OSOS hub, counsellors can advocate for you with financial providers, and also with Services Australia for any benefits you might be entitled. They can get you streamlined access to the no-interest loan scheme too. Editor's pick Opinion

Interest rates Most Australians don’t have a mortgage. Rate rises could leave them better off Max Yong Money contributor They will also look bigger picture and see what else could be optimised and future-proofed for financial comfort for your family. If you are really at crisis point with the cost of living, know that there is help at hand from a centralised portal. Ask Izzy: Ask Izzy is a free, anonymous website that connects people in crisis or experiencing hardship with local support services as immediately as possible. It aggregates 450,000 services that can come to your assistance for survival necessities from food and shelter, to financial help and mental health counselling –



whatever it is that you need to run your life and just can’t seem to afford right now. You can access it on mobile and without phone credit or Wi-Fi on select networks. Ask Izzy is a practical lifeline that gets people over the line to get their finances sorted out. Beyond Blue: The mental health and suicide prevention charity also has great resources on its website to help you in times of financial crisis. You can access free mental health and financial support through the Beyond Blue Financial Wellbeing Hub, which combines emotional care with practical money management tools. I’ve lost track of the number of people who’ve said to me: “My costs are going up and up, but my income is staying the same.” That is a stressful position and one in which many Australians find themselves right now. What may help is to know that you are not alone. You are also certainly not without access to significant practical help. The thing to do – whatever you do – is to reach out for it.



Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: Too many boundaries are behind the ‘sex recession’, warns Esther Perel
World.content:
The world-famous psychotherapist on midlife marriage, infidelity and how to manage the tension between love and desire.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This story is part of the November 14 edition of Good Weekend. See all stories .

Esther Perel pops onto the screen looking exactly as her devoted legions of fans would expect. Her asymmetrical blonde bob is perfectly swept to one side, her silk shirt (black today) is opened just so, revealing one of her favoured drop necklaces from a range called “ladders to bliss”. The twinkle in her eyes is enchanting even in two dimensions. For the most ardent of Esther Perel’s millions of followers, all of these hallmarks must be as familiar as freckles on their partner’s face. Esther Perel: “There is a way to take accountability for hurt and to bring back the good things in the relationship.” Women and men have been drawn to the Belgian-raised, French-sounding psychotherapist with cult-like devotion for decades. They come seeking reassurance and reasons for hope when their romantic relationships hit the toughest of times, her charismatic wisdom offering the promise of everything from repair after a seismic betrayal of trust, to advice on returning vitality to garden-variety marriages. Podcaster, author, TED talker and most recently consultant to Olivia Wilde’s box office hit, The Invite, Perel is such a global star of sex, intimacy and relationships advice that some online dissect her every aphorism. But if Perel, 68, is aware of the weight of the expectations of lovelorn hordes, she wears it as lightly as the hand-harness chain she often sports on TikTok, Instagram or live: it looks as delicate as gold thread but also as steely as chain mail. For someone attributed with borderline supernatural powers to peer into the heart, her words are down to earth. I open with a question based on the Australia’s recently published longitudinal study, known as HILDA, which examined 17,000 people’s attitudes to their relationships. It exposed a satisfaction gap between genders starting as soon as a couple move in together.



Overall the findings were positive; people in very long-term relationships are highly satisfied. But an odd happiness gap widens between men and women as perceived relationship quality descends until the 24-year mark. That’s when it bottoms out for both, before bouncing back up again as decades advance. Related Article Good Weekend Rachel spent five years ‘quiet quitting’ her marriage. Her husband didn’t see it coming I wonder what insights or solutions the New Yorker who shot to fame 20 years ago with her global bestseller, Mating in Captivity, may add to established understandings of why men seem happier than women, and what it is about midlife that triggers this big dip for both. “On some level, this is an old finding – that life satisfaction and health increases for men in committed relationships and life satisfaction for women often decreases, and her health for that matter because she’s busy taking care of everybody else’s health, and she forgets her own very often,” she says. Women are more likely to struggle to maintain a sense of autonomy and individuality because they enter the care-taking and executive role in the family, assuming “a sense of responsibility for the wellbeing of others, the home and the domestic, and they often have two jobs,” she says. “But that doesn’t mean that it’s glorious for the men.” ‘Family life wants routine, and consistency and repetition. Desire doesn’t want to return to the same spot day after day.’ Esther Perel Experience has shown Perel that “family life and domesticity, and intimate relationships, are challenging in and of themselves”, leading her to conclude that what family life thrives on is also “what eroticism defends against”, as she puts it to Good Weekend. “There is this notion that if you love, you desire,” she says. “But in fact in a long-term relationship, what love wants – which is consistency and familiarity and safety – are elements that are preconditions for desire. But desire basically lives in the space that is more playful, less responsible.”



“If family life wants routine, and consistency and repetition, desire doesn’t want to return to the same spot day after day. So there is an inherent tension in reconciling love and desire in the same place – because it addresses a set of needs that … are actually polarities.” In a time when far longer life-expectancies mean couplings are expected and required to bridge more decades of challenge and routine – as well as happy stability – mining the daily conflict between excitment, freedom, and a craving for security remains a super-rich seam. At the many women’s conferences where she is invited to speak, Perel is often asked to articulate how those exhausted by demands of work and home can make space to be themselves and regroup. “When you find yourself mired in tasks and responsibilities and to-dos and lists, it is not so obvious that at the end of the day, and a long list of things, number 27 will suddenly be ‘connect with my desires and my playfulness and erotic self’.” She cites a study for which men and women in heterosexual couples were invited to write down the family duties they complete between 5pm and 11pm. Men typically had five to 10 on their lists, Perel says, while women had up to 30 – including ensuring their partner carried out his. Men felt more relaxed at night generally because they expected to do fewer tasks, but also felt stressed that their partner was monitoring them: a passion-killing burden by 11pm if ever there was one. ‘Midlife often means a time when we say, “Is this it? Is there more? Is this going to be my life for the next 25 years?” ’ Esther Perel “So then the issue is: How do you create an erotic space where that part of you can express itself?” asks Perel. No wonder her audiences love her when she makes them feel so seen. Western couples now expect their romantic partner to fulfil all the roles in life that a whole village once sustained, Perel famously says, and this is too much to ask. And she is openly compassionate when addressing the fallout when things go bad, which includes people having affairs.



Perel emphasises the pivotal role of trust in sustaining authentic connection. But she also says that people can decide to effectively “marry each other again” after their original partnership is shattered by betrayal, for example with an affair – effectively a second marriage to the same person, if the damage or disappointment can be overcome. The million-dollar question is how you achieve that – as the stultified couple in The Invite is advised to do by Piña, the luscious and liberated sex therapist character played by Penelope Cruz. Penelope Cruz, left, plays a sex therapist who provokes a reckoning in the marriage of her neighbor (Olivia Wilde) in the movie heavily influenced by Esther Perel’s insights, The Invite. A24 “There is repair after rupture,” says Perel, who has been married to psychologist, family therapist and author, Jack Saul, for more than 40 years. “There is a way to take accountability for hurt and to bring back the good things in the relationship, because not all infidelity is the end of the relationship.” This idea of a new marriage to the same person was a line Perel actually coined some time ago, after working with many post-infidelity couples. “And from there came this thinking that many of us want something different at a certain point,” she says. “There’s your 24-year mark – we want something different, and 24 years often means midlife.” ‘We’ve had a sex recession for quite a while. But it has taken up way more proportions at this point.’ Esther Perel “Midlife often means a time when we say, ‘Is this it? Is there more? Is this going to be my life for the next 25 years? I have one more chance for something different, better, more satisfying. My children are gone, my career is somewhat established’,” she says. “And then the question is: Do you need to be with someone else … or can you imagine a new story for the two of you, and is that something you aspire to?” The “how?” doesn’t turn out to be simple. It can involve any number of changes. Physically moving to a different place. Doing something professionally different. Starting an entirely different life. “Organising one’s life in a different quadrant,” she says, comes with questions. “What is important that I do that brings me joy? What is important for me to learn and grow and give back? It also depends on what happened in the 24 years before.”



The movie Perel heavily influenced happily discusses sex styles enjoyed by the fresh – but still solidly middle-aged – couple who live above our time-worn, married heroes (played by Wilde and Seth Rogen). It traverses practices incorporated into the mainstream from what was traditionally considered porn territory – for example “pegging”. But surprisingly for someone unflustered by airing so-called taboo topics in her content, Perel’s team advises Good Weekend that asking what she makes of the fact sexual choking has become normalised, especially among younger Australians, is off the table. And the implications of the way women are depicted in commercial porn now (often very demeaningly), aren’t up for discussion either. Even in the midst of a global debate about why so many young men have been caught up in online worlds that warp their ideas of healthy relationships with women and themselves, a question about whether porn can reduce desire is similarly a no-go. Perel: “We are less and less connecting to people ... increasingly avoiding each other and sleep-walking into isolation.” But Perel is happy to discuss the so-called “sex recession” being experienced in the west, and if repeated claims that young people are less sexually active than ever before are really true. The answer is yes, and the reasons complex. “One of the big shifts or challenges to our romantic pursuits is romantic consumerism. More and more the heart thinks like a market when we look at relationships, we have brought to it the language of optimisation, maximisation,” she says. “It is one big transactional vocab.” But sex, Perel says, comes with a plot. And the plot is the relationship. “If you don’t approach people, you’re constantly ‘boundarying’ yourself out of living. If you make sure constantly to protect yourself to not be vulnerable … then you are going to have a sex recession. We’ve had a sex recession for quite a while. But it has taken up way more proportions at this point.” What she wants to discuss is “relational thinness” – the loss of deep connections, and disembodiment – the fact that so much of what was once experienced in person is now delegated to online personas.

World.title: ‘No, no, no, no, no!’: Teeks answers the question I couldn’t resist asking
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend ‘No, no, no, no, no!’: Teeks answers the question I couldn’t resist asking It may not be a deadly sin but lust ‘can lead you astray’, says the Maori singer-songwriter sensation. Benjamin Law November 14, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This story is part of the November 14 edition of Good Weekend. See all stories .

Each week, Benjamin Law asks a public figure to discuss three subjects we’re typically told to keep private, by getting them to roll a die. The numbers they land on are the topics they’re given. This week, he talks to Teeks. The Kiwi singer-songwriter, 33 (non-stage name: Te Karehana Gardiner-Toi) hit #1 in New Zealand with his multi-platinum- and multi-award-winning 2021 debut album Something To Feel. His new album is Lovers Comet. Teeks: “I was a very skinny and lanky kid … So I didn’t always feel that I loved my body.” RELIGION You grew up in a Maori family in New Zealand’s Northland. What beliefs were you raised with? We weren’t necessarily raised religious. My grandfather was an archdeacon in the Anglican church, but we didn’t actively go to church as a family. For the most part, I was raised with a Māori worldview. In our culture, we have many gods, but it’s not organised religion. The ocean, the land and the sky: these are entities with names. We have this understanding that we belong to the land, not the other way around. Is there a relationship between being Maori and your songwriting and singing? Singing, music and dance: they’ve just always been around. There’s a ceremonial aspect to them: the way I approach music and songwriting is that I feel they’re sacred acts. And singing live in front of people, on stage, is incomparable to anything. For me, it’s the closest thing to prayer and meditation.



When you’re having that extreme moment of spiritual connection with the audience on stage, does it make you feel like a cult leader? [Laughs] Sometimes! But I love being on stage – the reciprocity of energy. I feel as if it’s one of the few times in my life where I’m completely in control. I’m conscious of the fact that all these people are gathered in front of me, in this room, to witness and to experience music. To be in the driver’s seat is a privilege and responsibility that I take very seriously. Related Article Dicey Topics

Good Weekend What pushed Marlon Williams to record his latest album in Maori To which of the seven deadly sins are you the most susceptible? Oh, definitely lust. Is that such a sin, though? No, I don’t think it’s a sin. But I do think that it can lead you astray. It can be dysfunctional and self-destructive, if you let it take over. I’m already seeing the headline “Teeks is dangerously horny”. [Laughs] Sometimes you make dumb choices when you’re in lust. That’s all I’m saying!



DEATH When was the last time that you grieved over something or someone? My [maternal] grandmother passed away only a few months ago. Oh, I’m so sorry to hear that. Thank you. That one was definitely difficult: she has always been around. I couldn’t imagine her not being there for our family gatherings. She was definitely the matriarch of our family. The biggest thing is going home to where my family live and feeling the absence: there’s definitely a void. But one thing I’m so, so grateful for is being Maori because our grieving process is so beautiful. I think it’s probably the best way to grieve somebody. What’s the approach? What can the rest of us learn from it? We call it tangihanga: basically, we spend time with the body. So we go back to the marae – our tribal meeting house – and we lay the body there for a few days, and we’ll just sit and sing. Waves and waves of people from different tribes and different parts of the country come onto the marae to pay their respects. It’s important for us to cry and encourage the release of emotion. If you’re not from the culture, it might sound strange, but proximity to – and spending time with – the body is important. How would you like to die, ideally? Peacefully, with not too much suffering. Isn’t drowning supposed to be peaceful? I love the ocean. If I was going to go, I think that’s how I’d want to be taken out. I feel like the ocean’s home for me.



Related Article Good Weekend ‘I actually cried quite a lot’: Macy Gray on the complicated grief of losing an ex What’s your least ideal way? Any way that’s embarrassing. Any song requests for your funeral? Some of the classics, like Landslide by Fleetwood Mac. Sade, because I love her so much. And I’m always going to refer back to my culture: on the last night of the tangi [tangihanga is commonly shortened to tangi], which is usually where all the singing happens, we have kapa haka groups that come onto the marae. It’s like choral singing and it’s such a beautiful experience. So that’s a given. BODIES You’re photogenic and not afraid to pose shirtless. Have you always been confident in your body? No, no, no, no!



Really? No, because I was a very skinny and lanky kid. The hardest thing for me is to put on weight. So I didn’t always feel that I loved my body. Eventually, though, I started going to the gym and I found a love and appreciation. It’s a form of therapy for me, but I’m also able to see progress and feel good. When you look good, you feel good. What’s your workout regimen? The past couple years, I’ve definitely spent more time at the gym. Honestly, I probably do that more than making music. Also, eating is half the job. ‘Isn’t drowning supposed to be peaceful? I love the ocean. If I was going to go, I think that’s how I’d want to be taken out.’ Teeks You have the word “Surrender” tattooed on your neck. Tell me about that. I read The Power of Now, by Eckhart Tolle, years ago, at that age when you’re trying to find meaning and purpose. It left a big impression on me. “Surrender” is full acceptance and understanding that resistance is the root of all suffering. I wanted a little reminder of that. What’s the superpower that you wish you had? To be able to control time. It would be nice just to hit pause and have the world stop.



What superpower do you actually have? [Very long pause] Hmm … Next year you’ll sing at the Sydney Opera House. Isn’t that a superpower? I guess so! But it sounds weird to me to say that my singing is a superpower. Well, I think it’s a superpower! I guess standing on stage and having everybody in the palm of your hand is a superpower. And when I go on stage, I do feel powerful. Teeks’ new album, Lovers Comet, is out now. He will perform at the Sydney Opera House on April 15, 2027. World.title: The bikie boss, the $800,000 Ferrari and an $18 million Brighton mansion
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaCrime The bikie boss, the $800,000 Ferrari and an $18 million Brighton mansion Cameron Houston and Marta Pascual Juanola November 14, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Police have raided an $18 million Brighton mansion occupied by a bikie boss following a campaign of violence against embattled property developer Simon Pitard and his family’s aged care empire. Detectives from Taskforce Echo searched the luxury residence of Finks national president Mark Balsillie on November 6, just hours after two masked men fired 10 shots at an Arcare aged care facility in Maidstone. Later that day, police publicly identified the gang as an “organised crime priority”. The multimillion-dollar mansion in Brighton where Balsillie has been living. The police raid also followed the firebombing of Pitard’s Brighton property on October 27 when two luxury cars were destroyed. On October 28, an innocent 52-year-old woman sustained serious burns when her Cheltenham townhouse was firebombed in a case of mistaken identity, which is also under investigation. Detectives carried out firearm prohibition order compliance searches at another five properties in Narre Warren North, Safety Beach, Mount Eliza and Dallas as part of their November 6 blitz on the Finks, but no arrests were made.



This masthead does not suggest Balsillie is involved in the campaign of violence against Pitard. He did not respond to requests for comment. An investigation by this masthead can also reveal that federal law enforcement agencies have been investigating the ownership of Balsillie’s opulent home and a recent application for an $11 million loan in the name of a 23-year-old associate of the bikie enforcer. Balsillie (centre) at slain underworld figure Sam “The Punisher” Abdulrahim’s funeral in 2025. The Age According to land title records, the registered owner of the mansion is self-described taxi driver-turned-billionaire property developer Pankaj “Harry” Goyal, whose construction company Harcon Projects built the four-level home, replete with rooftop garden, indoor pool, sauna and climate-controlled cellar. Balsillie has lived in the mansion for the past six months and has told associates he was in the process of buying it from Goyal, according to five underworld and property industry sources who asked not to be identified because of safety concerns.



The sources said the potential transfer of the mansion came to the attention of law enforcement agencies, when a 23-year-old associate of Balsillie was named as the applicant for an $11 million loan. Harcon Projects boss Pankaj “Harry” Goyal. The man, who The Age has decided not to name for safety reasons, lives with his parents in Bentleigh East and would have been required to make monthly repayments of almost $70,000 if the loan proceeded. On September 9, the 23-year-old replaced Balsillie as the sole director and shareholder of a company called AP Global Aust Pty Ltd, which was first registered by the Finks boss in January. The 23-year-old is expected to be interviewed next month by the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission over his alleged involvement in the sale. The commission declined to comment when contacted by this masthead.



Goyal’s close connection with Balsillie has seen him allow the Finks president access to an $800,000 blue Ferrari Purosangue. The 46-year-old businessman, who has a penchant for expensive cars, drives a black version of the luxury car himself. Goyal confirmed he owned the Brighton property when contacted by this masthead, but did not respond to repeated questions about his arrangement with Balsillie and denied the bikie had ever driven his car. He said Balsillie “might be living” in the mansion, but “is definitely not on the lease”. “I’ve got another 100 [properties]. So what has that got to do with me?” Goyal said. The construction boss has previously claimed he went from having 60 cents in his pocket, after gambling away money his father had given him to settle in Australia, to making a billion dollars and rubbing shoulder with Australia’s wealthiest through financing and land banking.



He told a podcast in 2023 he worked as a dishwasher and waiter at Crown Casino, while also working 16-hour shifts as a taxi driver to raise the funds to start his finance company, Loans Direct. The Brighton mansion features an indoor pool, glass lift and home movie theatre. “I used to eat the soft serves or the biscuits for 10 cents back then to fill my tummy up,” he said. Land title records show the 46-year-old has amassed expansive property interests that include shares in dozens of units in Brighton, Shepparton, Rockbank, Craigieburn, Thornhill Park, Moorabool, Truganina, Little River, and Charlemont worth more than $400 million. This masthead does not suggest any wrongdoing by Goyal or any involvement with the Finks OMCG.



Three underworld and property industry sources told this masthead that Goyal had also been involved in a botched $95 million deal with Balsillie to redevelop a former cattle farm in Sydney’s west into a cemetery. However, the deal fell over earlier this year after they failed to settle on the property, forfeiting a $9.5 million deposit. The 73-hectare site, in the semi-rural suburb of Wallacia, 70 kilometres west of Sydney, had been earmarked for a cemetery development since 2020. Earlier plans for the land, which is on a flood plain that backs onto the Nepean River, included 775,000 burial plots, a chapel, a crematorium and several mausoleums. The property on Greendale Road, Wallacia. The deal to develop the old cattle farm into a cemetery fell over earlier this year. Wolter Peeters



Goyal confirmed his involvement in the cemetery proposal, but denied Balsillie had a role in the deal. Balsillie has held various leadership roles with several outlaw bikie gangs for more than a decade, despite coming from an unconventional background. Related Article Exclusive

Organised crime Melbourne nursing homes under police guard as bikies target prominent aged care chain The 42-year-old is the son of retired police officer Andrew Balsillie, who served more than 40 years with Victoria Police and helped uncover a drug lab run by slain gangland figure Carl Williams out of a Broadmeadows commission building in 1999. Balsillie originally joined the Comancheros, and rapidly ascended to senior ranks within the gang.



When Balsillie pleaded guilty to extortion and possessing counterfeit money in 2016, a County Court judge described his involvement with the Comancheros as the beginning of his “fall from grace”, having grown up in a “caring and loving family”. Balsillie later defected to the Mongols, who sent him to Russia to patch over Comanchero members. Balsillie has held several senior positions in three different bikie gangs. Instagram In 2017, the 39-year-old survived a murder attempt when he was shot seven times in the arms, leg and stomach by a former Comanchero associate who fled to Turkey after the attack. Balsillie pleaded guilty to possessing and trafficking cocaine in the County Court in 2022, after claiming he had used two grams of cocaine a day to manage chronic pain caused by the shooting.



Judge David Brookes accepted he had undergone “genuine reformation” since his arrest in 2020, when detectives from the Echo and Trident taskforces found 127 grams of cocaine concealed inside a cereal box, encrypted mobile phones and syringes filled with growth hormone and testosterone at Balsillie’s property. Since taking over the leadership of the Finks in 2024, Balsillie has helmed a rapid expansion of the once fringe club recruiting several former associates from the Comancheros, including Ahmad “Rocky” Niazi and Thomas Laslo. Last Friday, Victoria Police said it had created a specialist taskforce made up of officers from Taskforce Echo, Operation Phoenix and the Viper Taskforce to target the gang. “My message to the Finks ... is very clear: if you choose to continue your involvement in serious and organised crime, Victoria Police is coming after you,” Detective Superintendent Wayne Cheesman said. World.title: Socceroos take another positive step with 3-0 rout of defending Asian champions
World.content:
SportSoccerAustralian soccer Socceroos take another positive step with 3-0 rout of defending Asian champions Vince Rugari November 14, 2026 — 5:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If only there were an Asian Cup around the corner. The Socceroos have taken another assured step in the right direction, dominating two-time reigning Asian champions Qatar in a commanding 3-0 friendly victory in Doha on Saturday morning (AEDT). Nestory Irankunda and Connor Metcalfe celebrate a goal. Getty Images Originally booked as a warm-up match ahead of a tournament which has now been delayed by 12 months, there was little riding on the match aside from the opportunity to advance the team’s overall development and blood some new faces. Both boxes were sufficiently ticked.



Coach Tony Popovic rolled out his strongest available team, and their first-half performance was as aggressive and dominant as they have been during his tenure, proving that the recent promise of the Brazil friendly series at home was no flash in the pan. They went 3-0 up before the break, with all three goals – from Riley McGree, Tete Yengi and Nestory Irankunda – coming on the back of mistakes forced by the Socceroos’ high press, which a hapless Qatar failed to deal with. Two of them came directly from errant passes by Qatar’s goalkeeper, Mahmud Abunada, who endured a nightmare performance. View post on X Popovic rang the changes in the second half, handing debuts to Eli Adams, Sam Klein, Kasey Bos and Diesel Herrington, while the returning Gianni Stensness also came off the bench for his first minutes for Australia in more than four years. Naturally, the Socceroos lost a bit of momentum as a consequence of all of those substitutions, but while they could not find an additional goal, they still kept a clean sheet while denying Qatar a single shot on target for the match; they did not fire their first shot until the 72nd minute.



Tony Popovic. AP Photo/Hussein Sayed Popovic had little to complain about afterwards, aside from the fact they could and should have scored more. “We were very aggressive,” Popovic said. “It was testing conditions, wasn’t easy for the players. We could see that they were finding it hard to breathe and move in these conditions. The pitch was quite hard underneath. It’s not what they’re accustomed to in Europe. “I think [we could have added] a few more goals from our good play, and we started the second half well, and I think when we made all the changes, I think we lost a lot of cohesion and we lost our way a little bit. But it was important for those boys to get minutes and to rest some of the boys that need to back up against Jordan, and some debutants, which is always a special moment.”



Related Article Olympics Matildas to face fearsome Japan in Olympic qualifying mission Another positive was Connor Metcalfe’s performance in central midfield next to Paul Okon jnr, which further cemented the FC St. Pauli star as a viable option to play there at international level instead of his usual wide attacking position. With first-choice players Mohamed Toure, Cristian Volpato, Jordan Bos, Jackson Irvine, Lewis Miller and Aiden O’Neill all currently sidelined through injury, the performance showcased the growing depth of the Socceroos and hinted again at the serious potential of this current generation of players. World.title: Kate Atkinson’s new novel shouldn’t work. Somehow it does
World.content:
CultureBooksReview Kate Atkinson’s new novel shouldn’t work. Somehow it does Helen Elliott November 14, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Kate Atkinson’s unclassifiable novels could be seen as a succession of cartwheels: now upside down, now vertical, in endless motion, teetering on imbalance, adjusted in the nick of time. Or not. Atkinson’s element is speed. That said, it is a very British speed. Open her novels, adjust your reading. Her latest, Our Noble Selves, is the full cartwheel. The novel follows Harry Flynn, a sometime London journalist, now – as with half the world – back from World War II. Harry had been one of the millions presumed dead; at times he presumes he might be, wonders why he isn’t, or simply thinks: why not? Women don’t seem to notice anything odd about Harry, though he has no idea why they like him so much – which is obviously part of the appeal. Novelist Kate Atkinson. Getty Images Harry is the sort of man Atkinson specialises in: believable, yearnable, imbued with charm both sexual and otherwise. Perhaps he has Trevor Howard’s voice in Brief Encounter. The novel opens around the time that film arrived in cinemas. But charm, sexual or otherwise, natural or manufactured, won’t keep a man upright. And Harry likes to drink. The trouble is that it makes him blot out his memory. Drinking is, after all, the obvious root of blotto. Harry, captured after the fall of Singapore in 1942, was a prisoner of the Japanese on the Burma Railway. Not that anyone will ever know, because he sees no point in speaking about those years. Returned men and women acknowledged the unspeakable through a mutual silence. There is nobility in not saying how much a human soul can endure. Yet not saying, like nobility, is an old-fashioned virtue. Perhaps it is the result of cauterised emotion? Or perhaps it is simply being British?



Five years after the end of the war, Harry is editing an anthology of poems for the entirely marvellous Festival of Britain which is to occur in 1951. Devised by the Labour government to celebrate the centenary of the 1851 Great Exhibition, the Festival of Britain embodied the idea of shrugging away the war years and installing hope in a future. The aim was to find pride in the details of a specifically British life. As Harry’s boss, Gerald Barry (Atkinson uses the historical figure), says: “This is our story… Our love of country, love of freedom, love of nature, pride in craftsmanship, our reputation for tolerance and fair play. Farming, industry and science – production rather than products. Harry listens but privately thinks: All this for a summer festival? It sounded exhausting. And such faith in a brave new world.” Photo: The poems are routinely awful, leaving Harry time for other corners of the festival: pageantry, homes and gardens, beauty parades, fashion and cooking – which proves especially eccentric. There is some absorbing office politics as well, alongside lovely glimpses of friendship, even if Harry’s private life remains dismal. Atkinson cartwheels all over the place, and such is her skill that the droll frequently turns dazzling. Now and again, though, you might feel as if you are staring at an upside-down head between two flailing arms, shouting at you: “Keep up! Keep up!” Keeping up is both entertaining and provoking as you register the underpinnings of human life. These arrive as stills frozen out of the surface pageant, lively with details any curious reader might want to pursue. Atkinson is an historical novelist whose brain teems with the ordinary particulars of the last century; Our Noble Selves can be read simply for the sheer texture of how life felt during those grim years, when a country tried to recover from the shock of the war. It can also be read as a vanishing-woman mystery, if that is your fancy. Harry? A murderer? Mmmm. Or it can be taken as straight history, charting the miraculous Festival of Britain in the very nation that invented pageantry – as anyone who has read Mapp and Lucia or tuned into Midsomer Murders understands without needing a word of explanation.



Editor's pick Review I hated this book. Then I realised just how brilliant it was In an afterword, Atkinson says she originally intended to write a novel about the experience of the POWs on the Burma-Siam Railway but, tough as she is, she could not go on. The experience of real men, in a real hell, felt exploitative, and she was intending a relatively light-hearted novel. So she turned her head away and wrote something different. But she recommends J. G. Farrell’s The Singapore Grip for those who want to know what the word harrowing might mean to people like charming Harry. She’s right. But if Farrell is too inconvenient, Our Noble Selves might strike exactly the right note in these not-quite harrowing days. Our Noble Selves by Kate Atkinson is published by Doubleday ($35). The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: I worked part-time at David Jones. I know exactly why the business failed
World.content:
BusinessConsumer affairsDavid Jones collapse Opinion I worked part-time at David Jones. I know exactly why the business failed Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist November 14, 2026 — 5:30am

November 14, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I’m told that admitting you are upset about the demise of David Jones is an admission that you are middle class. Well, maybe. Then again, I have a nostalgic regard for many icons of the past. Not all are posh. Aside from David Jones, they include Chiko Rolls, Alpine cigarettes when stored by a young female friend in the space between her arm muscle and her T-shirt, and KB beer (providing it was being derided as “Kids’ Beer”, on account of its sweetness). David Jones is expected to close many of its 38 stores and make thousands of staff redundant. Eddie Jim And when it comes to David Jones, I have the experience of being a middle-class shopper but also one of the workers. I don’t want to overstate my claim to fame. I won’t be claiming a late-issue redundancy payment from the receiver. I was there for months, not years. All the same, in 1980, when I was attempting to convince the University of Sydney that I deserved a history degree, I worked part-time as a lift operator at David Jones’ Market Street store. I was required to operate the antique machinery and to simultaneously intone the usual catechism: “Ground floor: perfumery, stationery and leather goods, wigs and haberdashery, kitchenware and food. Going up …”



Actually, those are the words of the lift operator in Are You Being Served? Our floors were a little different, but I can’t remember. My point: across continents, department stores were famous and so were their lift operators. My fellow Herald writer Peter FitzSimons, when offering his own recollections about the demise of DJs, made special mention of we lift operators. The lift, he wrote, “came complete with an old attendant with a peaked cap and crimson uniform. There were no buttons in the lift to denote floors and instead this kindly old fellow had his hand on a dial like the one used on the bridge of a ship – full steam ahead, steady astern, etc – to get it moving. And as it stopped at each level, he would portentously make announcements. ‘Children’s wear, shoes, toys … Dining, kitchen and bridal wear… Women’s designer fashion, men’s formal wear ...’ And so on.” Well, of course, I take offence at Pete’s “kindly old fellow”. I was, and am, only three years older than Fitz. In fact, my main problem with the job was the older male customers. We were required to laugh at their jokes. Sorry, I should have said: “We were required to laugh at their joke.” Every time it would be the same. An old chap would hop into the lift. His lips would start twitching as he readied the witticism, and then it would come, somewhere between first floor (women’s etc) and third floor (kitchen’s etc).



“Well, son, I’m guessing this is a pretty up and down sort of job.” Dutiful employee, that was me, I would chortle away as if comedy itself had reached a new plateau. After this, the fellow would exit the lift full of cheer, with a desire to spend as much time and money as possible. The business pages of this newspaper are full of analysis of why DJs finally came unstuck, but none have mentioned the obvious: the departure of the lift operators and our readiness to laugh at “the joke”. Working all day inside the lift, I was also aware that for many customers David Jones meant only one thing: bras. Later in life, this was confirmed. When I mentioned my lift-operator job to female friends, their memories of DJs were always connected to that one department. A lift operator at David Jones’ Market Street store in 1984. Trevor James Robert Dallen/Fairfax Media They’d recount how they’d been dragged in there by their mothers because David Jones supposedly had the best bra-fitters. These were no-nonsense women who would grab the breasts of the terrified teenage girl, assess their weight and shape, before they issued a first bra.



Related Article Opinion

Pop culture Will and Kate’s kids’ names? I’m sick of being told I’m supposed to know about these things Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist I remember asking: “Did they do a good job?” “Who knows,” would be the reply, “I was just mortified that I had breasts in the first place.” Later still, I had my own experience of the glory days of David Jones. I’d started going on TV for five minutes a week – 7’s Sunrise program – and I needed a proper suit so I looked OK next to Kochie. I went to DJs and, Anglophile that I am, I was attracted to a display of suits by some young British designer. They were what one might call “slim-fit”. A DJs sales assistant, a woman of a certain age, appraised my appearance as I stood there with my chosen slim-fit suit on its hanger. “We often find,” she said, “that these British suits are not built for our broad Australian shoulders.” She never called me fat. She never said, “Mate, you’ve let yourself go.” But, when I walked out that afternoon, I was holding a suit which fitted me. And my ego was still intact. What a glorious woman.



Is it any surprise the David Jones business has failed? The positive suit lady, that woman with the talent for bare-faced lies, is no longer there. The brusque bra-fitters with their rough, breast-appraising hands, are no longer there. And nor are the lift guys, with our willingness to laugh at a joke we have heard 4000 times before. I mourn them all. Although, speaking for myself, it certainly was an up and down sort of job. Need more Richard Glover in your life?
