World.title: Your retirement savings shouldn’t be someone else’s sales target
World.content:
November 14, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

You’re 55 or 60, you’ve spent decades building up your super, and you’re wondering whether you’ve saved enough. Then you come across an ad that promises to tell you if you’re on track for retirement. So you click. You answer a few questions, leave your phone number or email, and wait to hear back. Retirees are being pressured into financial advice they don’t understand. Simon Letch What you might not realise is that you just entered a sales funnel. Your details could be passed on to a business whose job is to turn your curiosity and fear of not having enough into an appointment with a financial adviser. And that appointment could ultimately lead to a recommendation that you move your savings out of a conventional super fund into a much higher risk investment approach. Welcome to the world of financial services lead generation. It’s a business model that most Australians don’t know anything about, and shouldn’t have to. Yet they’re being drawn into it, hook, line and sinker, often without understanding who’s behind the offer, who’s making money from their inquiry, or what the business ultimately wants them to do with their retirement savings.



After reading ASIC’s latest investigation into the worst of these practices, I think it’s time we banned the kind of lead generation that financially rewards businesses for funnelling Australians towards financial advice, financial products and super switching, whether directly or through a chain of intermediaries. There really is a world of difference between helping someone understand their real retirement options and helping them make good decisions, and making money from steering them towards a financial decision that might not be in their best interests. To understand the problem, all we need to do is follow the money. ASIC’s latest investigation shows just how lucrative this business model has become. The corporate regulator examined 15 financial advice licensees using lead generators between January 2025 and June 2026. During that period these businesses acquired 7639 new clients through lead generation arrangements, or about 35 per cent of new clients.



And here’s where it gets really juicy. ASIC found that some lead generators were being paid between 80 and 100 per cent of the upfront advice fee when they successfully turned someone into a client. That’s a lot of money. Thousands and thousands of dollars. And that’s going to the business responsible for getting everyday Australians through the door of these advice businesses. And that upfront advice fee could be deducted entirely from your superannuation savings. Some were telling people their funds weren’t performing well enough, or frightening them about what could happen if the market crashed. So why would a financial advice business be willing to sign on for a deal like that? You have to wonder just how much money they expect to make from a customer over the years ahead. Once the customer signs up, the advice business can collect ongoing fees potentially for years. And if the customer is persuaded to switch their super, substantial sums can flow into investment management and platforms potentially generating even more revenue for the businesses involved in the arrangements.



Across the 15 licensees – the businesses legally responsible for the financial advice provided under their licence – clients paid $9.8 million in upfront advice fees and agreed to another $4.5 million in annual ongoing fees. From that you can see why getting someone to click on a free super check can be such a valuable business. And we’re not talking about small amounts of money changing hands here. ASIC found that more than $678 million was switched or invested after referrals from lead generators across these 15 businesses alone. And about 90 per cent of that money came from superannuation savings. Now, that $678 million isn’t money that’s been lost. But it’s an enormous amount of retirement savings being moved around because of introductions by businesses that are being financially rewarded for delivering new customers to advisers. That makes my blood boil. We’re talking about money people have spent 30 or 40 years accumulating, potentially being redirected into investments they may not fully understand, through a process they might not even realise is designed to sell them something.



The problem starts long before someone sits down with a financial adviser. Related Article Superannuation The ‘immediate warning sign’ to protect your super ASIC’s report shows just how far some of these businesses will go to get people to move their super, too. Some were telling people their funds weren’t performing well enough, or frightening them with warnings about what could happen to their savings if the sharemarket crashed. And some of the people making these claims weren’t even qualified to give financial advice – they’re effectively salespeople, flogging fear to get people through the door. I’ve been writing about these problems for years, and this week I sat down with ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland to discuss them on the Prime Time podcast, too.



I have to say it: I’ve had enough. We’ve seen far too many examples of Australians being frightened, pressured and persuaded into making decisions about their life savings that might not be in their best interests. It really is time for the government to step up and make illegal all forms of financial lead generation that steer someone into switching their super. Free courses, free super checks, free retirement assessments, online quizzes, calculators, lead generation forms with incentives, or even ‘paid mates who refer unknowing consumers’. The Super Members Council’s Misha Schubert. Eamon Gallagher I don’t care what the bait looks like. If the real purpose is to funnel people towards advisers who plan to switch their super, and someone is being financially rewarded for getting them there, it’s time for it to stop. Consumers don’t understand that it’s happening. And I don’t think burying the details of these financial arrangements in disclosure documents that nobody reads makes them more acceptable. Telling someone in the fine print that you’re being paid to steer them towards an adviser doesn’t make the practice right. It shouldn’t be happening in the first place.



I’m not the only one calling for a ban. Super Members Council chief executive Misha Schubert says these practices have no place in the financial services industry. She’s also warning that the government’s proposed restrictions on unlicensed lead generators don’t go far enough. Dodgy businesses will just find another way. Editor's pick Opinion

Superannuation Super funds are finally overhauling retirement. Here’s what’s changing Bec Wilson Money contributor As Schubert puts it, parliament needs to “shut and bolt the door on this harmful practice – not leave it ajar to continuing harm”. That doesn’t mean banning genuine financial education, or making it harder for people to find good advice from an adviser they arrive at by genuine referral where no money changes hands. It means drawing a clear line between helping people understand their options and using a helpful-looking offer to sell them something they might not actually need.



Meanwhile, while the government faffs about on this, Australians need to be a lot more wary about what they are clicking on in the financial services world. If you see an ad offering a free super check, or retirement assessment, ask yourself who’s behind it and what they want from you. Before handing over your phone number or email to be connected into an advice referral, find out whether anyone is being paid to refer you. Then ask yourself if there’s a better way to get the help you need. There almost always is. And if someone starts telling you your super isn’t performing, or that you need to move your money urgently, please be careful. Don’t let these very slick salespeople frighten you into deciding about savings you’ve spent decades building. Good financial advice should help you understand your options, not scare you into taking action. I believe wholeheartedly that people should be able to find an adviser without someone else making money from steering them through the door. There’s plenty of demand out there for good advice and plenty of good advisers. So why can’t we just let good advice win?



Bec Wilson, bestselling author of How to Have an Epic Retirement, is a retirement educator and founder of the Epic Retirement Institute. She writes a weekly newsletter about modern retirement at au.epicretirement.net. She has various commercial arrangements with a range of organisations, including superannuation funds. World.title: The two debt traps to avoid this Christmas – and what to do instead
World.content:
MoneySavingChristmas Opinion The two debt traps to avoid this Christmas – and what to do instead Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor November 14, 2026 — 5:01am

November 14, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

With five rate rises this year, petrol near $2 a litre and Christmas coming, it’s possible you might be really feeling the cash crunch. It’s also possible you’re desperately trying to figure out how to solve it. And there are tools available, but there are right and wrong ways to try and ease the financial squeeze. Let’s lay them bare. Christmas spending can tighten the screws on household budgets. Luis Ascui Buy now, pay later: The season may have you thinking something silly: buy now, pay later. With Christmas just over a month away, could you instead curb the spend and use old school pay-in-advance lay-by? This will stop you dealing with a Christmas repayment hangover well into the New Year.



At least it is lightly regulated now, with some credit checks and responsible product approval guidelines. But it’s possible that this very thing has pushed people from Afterpay to advance-pay products. Wage advance: Anything of this ilk, where you get your money before you have earned it, comes with a steep interest or fee cost. That this product usually carries the latter is why it escapes the National Credit Code. I’ve lost track of the number of people who’ve said to me: ‘My costs are going up and up, but my income is staying the same.’ And not only does it cost you extra money to get access to cash you haven’t yet earned, you are getting into a downward spiral of playing catch up – with each transaction, you are eroding the money you have to spend from your future pays. This is just a terrible strategy. So, let’s look at better ones, starting with investigating where you could cut expenses.



Relationships and hardship: You’ve no doubt taken a razor to your spend, but most people pay too much on what they believe to be ‘fixed’ costs – think utilities and insurances, and many other financial products. Start by playing the ‘relationship’ card: pick up the phone and ask your providers if you can get a loyalty discount to match the better new products on the market (give this a Google first). If no dice, get disloyal and switch. You also absolutely qualify for concessions with your existing providers, if your situation has escalated beyond your ability to cope. And leniency should apply even to loans. Every financial and service provider needs to have a dedicated financial hardship department and they must extend you help. But what if the price pressures are across the board, and you feel financially maxed out?



One Stop One Story: The OSOS hub is a free service designed to help in times of financial distress, to advocate for you for a better deal. Operated by the Thriving Communities Partnership, it was launched with a focus on domestic and family violence victim-survivors but has expanded to cover general financial hardship and related crises. Rather than having to explain your financial situation to each one of the providers in your life, this service does it for you. There is also help available to rebuild your finances long term. The National Debt Helpline: The National Debt Helpline administers and matches thousands of free financial counsellors around the country with people in need. You can register online at ndh.org.au or 1800 007 007. It may take a while for an appointment, but your finances will get a once-over which could give them a second wind.



Similar to the OSOS hub, counsellors can advocate for you with financial providers, and also with Services Australia for any benefits you might be entitled. They can get you streamlined access to the no-interest loan scheme too. Editor's pick Opinion

Interest rates Most Australians don’t have a mortgage. Rate rises could leave them better off Max Yong Money contributor They will also look bigger picture and see what else could be optimised and future-proofed for financial comfort for your family. If you are really at crisis point with the cost of living, know that there is help at hand from a centralised portal. Ask Izzy: Ask Izzy is a free, anonymous website that connects people in crisis or experiencing hardship with local support services as immediately as possible. It aggregates 450,000 services that can come to your assistance for survival necessities from food and shelter, to financial help and mental health counselling –



whatever it is that you need to run your life and just can’t seem to afford right now. You can access it on mobile and without phone credit or Wi-Fi on select networks. Ask Izzy is a practical lifeline that gets people over the line to get their finances sorted out. Beyond Blue: The mental health and suicide prevention charity also has great resources on its website to help you in times of financial crisis. You can access free mental health and financial support through the Beyond Blue Financial Wellbeing Hub, which combines emotional care with practical money management tools. I’ve lost track of the number of people who’ve said to me: “My costs are going up and up, but my income is staying the same.” That is a stressful position and one in which many Australians find themselves right now. What may help is to know that you are not alone. You are also certainly not without access to significant practical help. The thing to do – whatever you do – is to reach out for it.



Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram. World.title: Too many boundaries are behind the ‘sex recession’, warns Esther Perel
World.content:
The world-famous psychotherapist on midlife marriage, infidelity and how to manage the tension between love and desire.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This story is part of the November 14 edition of Good Weekend. See all stories .

Esther Perel pops onto the screen looking exactly as her devoted legions of fans would expect. Her asymmetrical blonde bob is perfectly swept to one side, her silk shirt (black today) is opened just so, revealing one of her favoured drop necklaces from a range called “ladders to bliss”. The twinkle in her eyes is enchanting even in two dimensions. For the most ardent of Esther Perel’s millions of followers, all of these hallmarks must be as familiar as freckles on their partner’s face. Esther Perel: “There is a way to take accountability for hurt and to bring back the good things in the relationship.” Women and men have been drawn to the Belgian-raised, French-sounding psychotherapist with cult-like devotion for decades. They come seeking reassurance and reasons for hope when their romantic relationships hit the toughest of times, her charismatic wisdom offering the promise of everything from repair after a seismic betrayal of trust, to advice on returning vitality to garden-variety marriages. Podcaster, author, TED talker and most recently consultant to Olivia Wilde’s box office hit, The Invite, Perel is such a global star of sex, intimacy and relationships advice that some online dissect her every aphorism. But if Perel, 68, is aware of the weight of the expectations of lovelorn hordes, she wears it as lightly as the hand-harness chain she often sports on TikTok, Instagram or live: it looks as delicate as gold thread but also as steely as chain mail. For someone attributed with borderline supernatural powers to peer into the heart, her words are down to earth. I open with a question based on the Australia’s recently published longitudinal study, known as HILDA, which examined 17,000 people’s attitudes to their relationships. It exposed a satisfaction gap between genders starting as soon as a couple move in together.



Overall the findings were positive; people in very long-term relationships are highly satisfied. But an odd happiness gap widens between men and women as perceived relationship quality descends until the 24-year mark. That’s when it bottoms out for both, before bouncing back up again as decades advance. Related Article Good Weekend Rachel spent five years ‘quiet quitting’ her marriage. Her husband didn’t see it coming I wonder what insights or solutions the New Yorker who shot to fame 20 years ago with her global bestseller, Mating in Captivity, may add to established understandings of why men seem happier than women, and what it is about midlife that triggers this big dip for both. “On some level, this is an old finding – that life satisfaction and health increases for men in committed relationships and life satisfaction for women often decreases, and her health for that matter because she’s busy taking care of everybody else’s health, and she forgets her own very often,” she says. Women are more likely to struggle to maintain a sense of autonomy and individuality because they enter the care-taking and executive role in the family, assuming “a sense of responsibility for the wellbeing of others, the home and the domestic, and they often have two jobs,” she says. “But that doesn’t mean that it’s glorious for the men.” ‘Family life wants routine, and consistency and repetition. Desire doesn’t want to return to the same spot day after day.’ Esther Perel Experience has shown Perel that “family life and domesticity, and intimate relationships, are challenging in and of themselves”, leading her to conclude that what family life thrives on is also “what eroticism defends against”, as she puts it to Good Weekend. “There is this notion that if you love, you desire,” she says. “But in fact in a long-term relationship, what love wants – which is consistency and familiarity and safety – are elements that are preconditions for desire. But desire basically lives in the space that is more playful, less responsible.”



“If family life wants routine, and consistency and repetition, desire doesn’t want to return to the same spot day after day. So there is an inherent tension in reconciling love and desire in the same place – because it addresses a set of needs that … are actually polarities.” In a time when far longer life-expectancies mean couplings are expected and required to bridge more decades of challenge and routine – as well as happy stability – mining the daily conflict between excitment, freedom, and a craving for security remains a super-rich seam. At the many women’s conferences where she is invited to speak, Perel is often asked to articulate how those exhausted by demands of work and home can make space to be themselves and regroup. “When you find yourself mired in tasks and responsibilities and to-dos and lists, it is not so obvious that at the end of the day, and a long list of things, number 27 will suddenly be ‘connect with my desires and my playfulness and erotic self’.” She cites a study for which men and women in heterosexual couples were invited to write down the family duties they complete between 5pm and 11pm. Men typically had five to 10 on their lists, Perel says, while women had up to 30 – including ensuring their partner carried out his. Men felt more relaxed at night generally because they expected to do fewer tasks, but also felt stressed that their partner was monitoring them: a passion-killing burden by 11pm if ever there was one. ‘Midlife often means a time when we say, “Is this it? Is there more? Is this going to be my life for the next 25 years?” ’ Esther Perel “So then the issue is: How do you create an erotic space where that part of you can express itself?” asks Perel. No wonder her audiences love her when she makes them feel so seen. Western couples now expect their romantic partner to fulfil all the roles in life that a whole village once sustained, Perel famously says, and this is too much to ask. And she is openly compassionate when addressing the fallout when things go bad, which includes people having affairs.



Perel emphasises the pivotal role of trust in sustaining authentic connection. But she also says that people can decide to effectively “marry each other again” after their original partnership is shattered by betrayal, for example with an affair – effectively a second marriage to the same person, if the damage or disappointment can be overcome. The million-dollar question is how you achieve that – as the stultified couple in The Invite is advised to do by Piña, the luscious and liberated sex therapist character played by Penelope Cruz. Penelope Cruz, left, plays a sex therapist who provokes a reckoning in the marriage of her neighbor (Olivia Wilde) in the movie heavily influenced by Esther Perel’s insights, The Invite. A24 “There is repair after rupture,” says Perel, who has been married to psychologist, family therapist and author, Jack Saul, for more than 40 years. “There is a way to take accountability for hurt and to bring back the good things in the relationship, because not all infidelity is the end of the relationship.” This idea of a new marriage to the same person was a line Perel actually coined some time ago, after working with many post-infidelity couples. “And from there came this thinking that many of us want something different at a certain point,” she says. “There’s your 24-year mark – we want something different, and 24 years often means midlife.” ‘We’ve had a sex recession for quite a while. But it has taken up way more proportions at this point.’ Esther Perel “Midlife often means a time when we say, ‘Is this it? Is there more? Is this going to be my life for the next 25 years? I have one more chance for something different, better, more satisfying. My children are gone, my career is somewhat established’,” she says. “And then the question is: Do you need to be with someone else … or can you imagine a new story for the two of you, and is that something you aspire to?” The “how?” doesn’t turn out to be simple. It can involve any number of changes. Physically moving to a different place. Doing something professionally different. Starting an entirely different life. “Organising one’s life in a different quadrant,” she says, comes with questions. “What is important that I do that brings me joy? What is important for me to learn and grow and give back? It also depends on what happened in the 24 years before.”



The movie Perel heavily influenced happily discusses sex styles enjoyed by the fresh – but still solidly middle-aged – couple who live above our time-worn, married heroes (played by Wilde and Seth Rogen). It traverses practices incorporated into the mainstream from what was traditionally considered porn territory – for example “pegging”. But surprisingly for someone unflustered by airing so-called taboo topics in her content, Perel’s team advises Good Weekend that asking what she makes of the fact sexual choking has become normalised, especially among younger Australians, is off the table. And the implications of the way women are depicted in commercial porn now (often very demeaningly), aren’t up for discussion either. Even in the midst of a global debate about why so many young men have been caught up in online worlds that warp their ideas of healthy relationships with women and themselves, a question about whether porn can reduce desire is similarly a no-go. Perel: “We are less and less connecting to people ... increasingly avoiding each other and sleep-walking into isolation.” But Perel is happy to discuss the so-called “sex recession” being experienced in the west, and if repeated claims that young people are less sexually active than ever before are really true. The answer is yes, and the reasons complex. “One of the big shifts or challenges to our romantic pursuits is romantic consumerism. More and more the heart thinks like a market when we look at relationships, we have brought to it the language of optimisation, maximisation,” she says. “It is one big transactional vocab.” But sex, Perel says, comes with a plot. And the plot is the relationship. “If you don’t approach people, you’re constantly ‘boundarying’ yourself out of living. If you make sure constantly to protect yourself to not be vulnerable … then you are going to have a sex recession. We’ve had a sex recession for quite a while. But it has taken up way more proportions at this point.” What she wants to discuss is “relational thinness” – the loss of deep connections, and disembodiment – the fact that so much of what was once experienced in person is now delegated to online personas.

World.title: ‘No, no, no, no, no!’: Teeks answers the question I couldn’t resist asking
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend ‘No, no, no, no, no!’: Teeks answers the question I couldn’t resist asking It may not be a deadly sin but lust ‘can lead you astray’, says the Maori singer-songwriter sensation. Benjamin Law November 14, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This story is part of the November 14 edition of Good Weekend. See all stories .

Each week, Benjamin Law asks a public figure to discuss three subjects we’re typically told to keep private, by getting them to roll a die. The numbers they land on are the topics they’re given. This week, he talks to Teeks. The Kiwi singer-songwriter, 33 (non-stage name: Te Karehana Gardiner-Toi) hit #1 in New Zealand with his multi-platinum- and multi-award-winning 2021 debut album Something To Feel. His new album is Lovers Comet. Teeks: “I was a very skinny and lanky kid … So I didn’t always feel that I loved my body.” RELIGION You grew up in a Maori family in New Zealand’s Northland. What beliefs were you raised with? We weren’t necessarily raised religious. My grandfather was an archdeacon in the Anglican church, but we didn’t actively go to church as a family. For the most part, I was raised with a Māori worldview. In our culture, we have many gods, but it’s not organised religion. The ocean, the land and the sky: these are entities with names. We have this understanding that we belong to the land, not the other way around. Is there a relationship between being Maori and your songwriting and singing? Singing, music and dance: they’ve just always been around. There’s a ceremonial aspect to them: the way I approach music and songwriting is that I feel they’re sacred acts. And singing live in front of people, on stage, is incomparable to anything. For me, it’s the closest thing to prayer and meditation.



When you’re having that extreme moment of spiritual connection with the audience on stage, does it make you feel like a cult leader? [Laughs] Sometimes! But I love being on stage – the reciprocity of energy. I feel as if it’s one of the few times in my life where I’m completely in control. I’m conscious of the fact that all these people are gathered in front of me, in this room, to witness and to experience music. To be in the driver’s seat is a privilege and responsibility that I take very seriously. Related Article Dicey Topics

Good Weekend What pushed Marlon Williams to record his latest album in Maori To which of the seven deadly sins are you the most susceptible? Oh, definitely lust. Is that such a sin, though? No, I don’t think it’s a sin. But I do think that it can lead you astray. It can be dysfunctional and self-destructive, if you let it take over. I’m already seeing the headline “Teeks is dangerously horny”. [Laughs] Sometimes you make dumb choices when you’re in lust. That’s all I’m saying!



DEATH When was the last time that you grieved over something or someone? My [maternal] grandmother passed away only a few months ago. Oh, I’m so sorry to hear that. Thank you. That one was definitely difficult: she has always been around. I couldn’t imagine her not being there for our family gatherings. She was definitely the matriarch of our family. The biggest thing is going home to where my family live and feeling the absence: there’s definitely a void. But one thing I’m so, so grateful for is being Maori because our grieving process is so beautiful. I think it’s probably the best way to grieve somebody. What’s the approach? What can the rest of us learn from it? We call it tangihanga: basically, we spend time with the body. So we go back to the marae – our tribal meeting house – and we lay the body there for a few days, and we’ll just sit and sing. Waves and waves of people from different tribes and different parts of the country come onto the marae to pay their respects. It’s important for us to cry and encourage the release of emotion. If you’re not from the culture, it might sound strange, but proximity to – and spending time with – the body is important. How would you like to die, ideally? Peacefully, with not too much suffering. Isn’t drowning supposed to be peaceful? I love the ocean. If I was going to go, I think that’s how I’d want to be taken out. I feel like the ocean’s home for me.



Related Article Good Weekend ‘I actually cried quite a lot’: Macy Gray on the complicated grief of losing an ex What’s your least ideal way? Any way that’s embarrassing. Any song requests for your funeral? Some of the classics, like Landslide by Fleetwood Mac. Sade, because I love her so much. And I’m always going to refer back to my culture: on the last night of the tangi [tangihanga is commonly shortened to tangi], which is usually where all the singing happens, we have kapa haka groups that come onto the marae. It’s like choral singing and it’s such a beautiful experience. So that’s a given. BODIES You’re photogenic and not afraid to pose shirtless. Have you always been confident in your body? No, no, no, no!



Really? No, because I was a very skinny and lanky kid. The hardest thing for me is to put on weight. So I didn’t always feel that I loved my body. Eventually, though, I started going to the gym and I found a love and appreciation. It’s a form of therapy for me, but I’m also able to see progress and feel good. When you look good, you feel good. What’s your workout regimen? The past couple years, I’ve definitely spent more time at the gym. Honestly, I probably do that more than making music. Also, eating is half the job. ‘Isn’t drowning supposed to be peaceful? I love the ocean. If I was going to go, I think that’s how I’d want to be taken out.’ Teeks You have the word “Surrender” tattooed on your neck. Tell me about that. I read The Power of Now, by Eckhart Tolle, years ago, at that age when you’re trying to find meaning and purpose. It left a big impression on me. “Surrender” is full acceptance and understanding that resistance is the root of all suffering. I wanted a little reminder of that. What’s the superpower that you wish you had? To be able to control time. It would be nice just to hit pause and have the world stop.



What superpower do you actually have? [Very long pause] Hmm … Next year you’ll sing at the Sydney Opera House. Isn’t that a superpower? I guess so! But it sounds weird to me to say that my singing is a superpower. Well, I think it’s a superpower! I guess standing on stage and having everybody in the palm of your hand is a superpower. And when I go on stage, I do feel powerful. Teeks’ new album, Lovers Comet, is out now. He will perform at the Sydney Opera House on April 15, 2027. World.title: Country Life:  A glimpse into country life for Kiwi kids
World.content:
From videos on the small screen as people scroll, to opening up her farm to the public, Sally Newall is on a mission to share what life's like on a working farm.

The veterinarian and farmer lives on a 500-hectare farm operation in Pātoka, about 40 kilometres north of Napier, and is the woman behind Kiwi Country Kids.

In a new on-farm learning facility, she hopes to take this from the world of social media to real life.

"Part of it is about getting people on the farm and sharing what we do on the farm," she told Country Life.

Audio player for " Kiwi Country Kids: A glimpse into country life " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/country/2586939%2Fcountry-life-a-glimpse-into-country-life-for-kiwi-kids

Kiwi Country Kids: A glimpse into country life Country Life Download MP3 11m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

Newall started the social media page back in 2020 and it now has more than 26,000 followers across Facebook and Instagram.

"We've got awesome followers. They're great because they're really engaged."

In a new barn, the three calf bays are filled with new arrivals. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Most of their followers are based in New Zealand, and include a real "cross section of society".

"We've got loads of ex-farmers, farmers, lifestylers, loads of people that live in town," she explained.

"We've got people that love following the page because they are retired now but they grew, you know, they lived on a farm for years and it's a lot of sort of reminiscing for those people.

"And then I hope there's a piece in there which is people that live in town and don't have any connection with farming whatsoever and we're able to show them what we do on a day-to-day basis."

Kiwi Country Kids was started six years ago to highlight life on a working farm and now has more than 26,000 followers across Facebook and Instagram. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The purpose-built barn is divided into three sections, with a milking area on one side and a larger enclosed space in the middle which Sally hopes to use for farm skills workshops and visits from groups like local schools. The other side houses three calf pens. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The learning facility in a three bay barn just next to the family homestead is the "next step".

Newall said in an age where AI videos feed into misinformation online, it's more important than ever to get people out on the farm.

"Show them that you're genuine and show them that farmers do care about their animals and they do care about the environment and just so that people can cut through the nonsense a little bit and see for themselves."

The new build features a milking and wet area on one side, a covered indoor education and function space in the middle, and three calf pens on the other side - filled with hungry new arrivals.

From the centre space she hopes to run farm skills workshops, recently hosting a women's butchery skills night, and host visits from groups like local schools.

People will be taught about life on the farm and offered the opportunity to get up close with the menagerie of surrounding animals - goats, cows, pigs and sheep, dogs, horses, geese, rescue chooks from commercial farms, and even a few guinea fowl.

Activities range from helping feed the chickens and collecting eggs, feeding the goats and pigs, interacting with the horses, helping feed lambs or calves to watching a cow being milked and even helping make butter.

It's not all Instagram and cute animals though. The barn is also an important part of the working farm's operations.

"I put it up as a decent agricultural shed because we don't actually have indoor sort of accommodation for animals here. So nice, small, small area for our calves to be reared in."

The new arrivals have to be taught how to drink from the feeders. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

From a few days to month old Charolais and Friesian calves. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Three calf pens were filled with new arrivals, freshly born calves, when Country Life paid a visit.

"We're Friesian bull farmers so we usually just get the straight Friesians, but we wanted to have a nice group of beef crosses so that I can steer them and then we'll have a nice big group of steers on the farm in amongst all the crazy Friesian bulls."

Sourcing them had proven challenging this year, Newall said, largely due to such strong beef and dairy returns leading to increased interest in calf rearing.

"Prices for calves have just been absolutely through the roof, especially these beef boys."

Calf rearing is no easy job. Without access to fresh milk it involves mixing up milk powder for twice daily feedings, 2.5 litres each time, dropping to once a day when they're a bit older.

Being so young, there's also a fair bit of training involved in getting the calves to feed.

"They take a while to figure out where the feeder is and it's a new shed and they don't know you and it only takes them a couple of days and then you're away."

World.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang and the 'most expensive affair in history' - but not the only one
World.content:
It's been called the most expensive affair in history.

Jensen Huang is stepping down from his role at the helm of Nvidia after it was revealed he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman accused of spying.

While commentators online have speculated about how US$140-ish billion fortune would be split if he and his wife, Lori, were to separate, the financial impacts are being felt much more widely.

Shares in the company have fallen more than 10 percent, cutting its value by hundreds of billions of dollars.

But his resignation has caused ripples across the wider AI sector, too, because Huang had been instrumental in investing back into other cloud providers, suppliers and labs. There are concerns his departure could mean trouble for a sector that is already facing wariness about its share prices and prospects.

Audio player for " What's the biggest risk to our economy right now? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2585017%2Fnvidia-s-jensen-huang-and-the-most-expensive-affair-in-history-but-not-the-only-one

This may be one of the most dramatic cases but it's not the first time human failings have had significant financial implications.

In 2010, Hewlett-Packard chief executive Mark Hurd stood down after he was found to have made false expense claims to cover up a relationship with a contractor.

The Guardian reported that the company's shares doubled in value during his time at the top, but his resignation sent them down 10 percent.

McDonald's share price dropped about 3 percent after Steve Easterbrook was fired as chief executive in 2019 after he engaged in a consensual relationship with an employee. Rail company Norfolk Southern had a 4 percent share price drop after its chief executive and chief legal officer were both sacked in 2024 for an affair.

Massey University marketing expert Bodo Lang said it was to be expected that poor behaviour by a chief executive would have an impact on the way consumers and investors viewed a company.

"There's definitely a halo or a trickle-down effect where a behaviour, particularly if it's repeated, there's a sense that might be something that's accepted and that it reflects not just the values of the individual, but also the values of the company.

"Many rational consumers will just go, 'that's just the person at the top doing things that he shouldn't have been doing'. But it will undoubtedly cause a minor correction in some people's attitude and perception of Nvidia."

He said the effect was stronger with Nvidia because Jensen Huang was so well known.

"He probably has nearly more brand awareness than the brand itself, the company itself. He is the brand in a way because he's been very vocal, he's very out there. If he was some quiet little person that people have never thought about, I think it would have had much less impact. But because he is so well known, particularly by insiders, I think there will be an impact."

He said the best thing companies could do was to eliminate as much uncertainty as possible.

"Less informed and less willing consumers or shareholders or stakeholders will go with peripheral cues like, oh, this is a bit of a disaster and maybe I should sell my shares. And I think more informed people will take a more informed decision path."

Stanford University research found shareholders usually reacted negatively to news of chief executive misconduct, and share prices declined by a market-adjusted 3 percent over the three days before including and the the initial news broke.

"However, stock price reactions are not uniformly negative," researchers David Larcker and Brian Tayan wrote. "Eleven out of the 38 companies in our sample exhibited positive abnormal stock price returns when CEO misbehaviour made the news. Perhaps unexpectedly, there is no discernible relationship between the type of behaviour and stock price reaction."

The misconduct cases it looked at included affairs, questionable financial practices, lying to the board, using objectionable language or exhibiting objectional behaviour and expressing controversial views publicly.

There have been other cases where human failings have had expensive consequences.

Expensive typo

A typo proved extremely expensive in 2006 when a trader with Mizuho Securities tried to sell one share his company held for 610,000 yen but instead entered an order to short-sell 610,000 shares for one yen each.

It was reported to have cost at least NZ$300 million, as reported at the time by the NZ Herald.

It also caused the Nikkei index to fall 300 points. Mizuho was quoted as saying it tried to cancel the order three times but was unsuccessful.

Software deployment error

A software problem at Knight Capital meant old code clashed with new software, creating a flood of stock exchange orders that put the organisation in a position where it had to sell at a loss.

Other companies had to step in with a US$400 million investment to keep it afloat.

Reuters reported that the company said its loss was just under US$390m.

World.title: Country Life: Woodchester Station 10 years after the Kaikōura quake
World.content:
Dave and Rebekah Kelly were in their mid 20s when they took over Woodchester Station in North Canterbury.

They were 12 years into a 30-year plan to develop Rebekah's family farm, including installing kilometres of new fencing, a water reticulation system, and diversifying their income streams into sheep, wool, beef, and honey.

It was working out fine, but then suddenly, it wasn't.

Ten years ago, on 14 November, 2016, the Kaikōura earthquake struck, and the couple's world was turned upside down, almost literally.

It was two minutes past midnight when the 7.8 magnitude quake struck.

"I woke up to Dave yelling as he was watching a piece of furniture leaping across the floor at him," Rebekah told Country Life.

Audio player for " Woodchester Station: 10 years on after the Kaikōura quake " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/country/2585888%2Fcountry-life-woodchester-station-10-years-after-the-kaikoura-quake

Woodchester Station: 10 years on after the Kaikōura quake Country Life Download MP3 22m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

"It was incredibly loud, and we just leapt out of bed and raced down the hallway to the kids.

"We definitely didn't feel safe in the house.

"We have four children and we grabbed them and got outside, and then just stood there because it was a 90-second earthquake and that is a really long time."

They then drove to flat ground and huddled together in the car in the pitch black. When the dawn broke Dave went out for his first recce.

"It was just a shock, an intense feeling of vulnerability," he recalled.

"There are a lot of parts of the farm that, if we had been going about our daily work, we would have been buried alive, so the fact that it was at midnight I think saved hundreds of lives. We felt like we'd dodged a bullet."

In a minute and a half their plan to future-proof the farm against droughts and lean seasons had all changed.

"Well, I think there's two disasters," Dave said.

"There's the natural disaster, and then the looming financial disaster, which comes when your business has just been turned upside down. We spent close to $200,000 on unbudgeted repairs in the first six weeks. We had two bulldozers, a couple of diggers going, men fixing water pipes. We lost all our water tanks. We had no power, and you know now, 10 years later, with really good prices, those decisions to reinvest are paying off really well."

Dave said the farm had become a pretty dangerous place very quickly.

A view of the landslide at Woodchester Station North Canterbury. RNZ / Mark Leishman

"You'd be coming over a brow of a hill, and wouldn't know that on the other side of that brow the whole thing had dropped up to four metres.

"I was pretty lucky a couple of times when out surveying the damage."

When the enormity of the disaster hit home Rebekah admits to having had thoughts of leaving the land she grew up on.

"I questioned whether I felt safe to be here anymore, with four children. You think you know a place quite well, and it turns out that it's got this other underbelly.

"My whole life's been here, and I very quickly rationalised that where else would I live. This place is a place that I know myself the best, and it's a place that I was really enjoying bringing up with children and living here with Dave."

The recovery meant diversifying their income streams further.

They had 320 Angus beef, 3500 breeding ewes, a forest in the Emissions Trading Scheme, and 250 beehives on the property and then Rebekah began attracting tourists to Woodchester to see the damage from the quake.

Rebekah guides tourists on the farm to see damage from the quake. RNZ Mark Leishman

Recovery from the quake included diversification into tourism. RNZ Mark Leishman

One of the main features of the farm tour is Lake Rebekah, a one kilometre long, 150 metres wide, 30 metres deep lake formed when the earthquake dammed the Leader River.

Its outlet is a 25 metre waterfall affectionately named the Victoria Falls after Rebecca and Dave's daughter Victoria.

Rebekah named the lake after herself as a joke.

"The children thought that Lake Quake would be quite a good idea, but after I mentioned the name on the Kim Hill Show, Lake Rebekah has stuck."

Lake Rebekah was formed when the quake dammed the Leader River. RNZ Mark Leishman

For Dave and Rebekah the last 10 years have continued to be challenging.

"Only two years ago we were on our hands and knees," Dave said.

"We'd had our driest six months ever. We were in drought, sheep prices had crashed, lambs were down to $10 a head. Wool was $1 [per kg].

"That was only two years ago and we just knew we had to play the long game. We got capital stock, fed them, and you know we looked after them, and then things started to turn around."

Dave is a believer in technology and loves using his drone to survey his farm and herd his stock.

"Yeah, dogs tend to create an argument with young cows and calves so drones are pretty much a game-changing kit. As much as I love traditional farming, drones sort of become like a third man. You're sort of farming in 3D … and it even barks, through a small speaker on the front."

Back at the homestead, sitting around the family table, Dave and Rebekah reflect on where they are now 10 years on.

"It's not so much the farm or the land. It's the relationships and knowing that you're going to hand this business on because you really only learn by doing."

As for Rebekah, Woodchester is an inheritance she does not take lightly.

World.title: The 16 MPs (likely) voted out of Parliament
World.content:
Even as Parliament looks likely to grow to 131 MPs, several who have been there for the last term have been saying goodbye this week.

Because they were involuntarily ejected by voters, these 16 departing MPs probably won't get the chance to deliver valedictory speeches - so this will have to do for now.

National

Nicola Willis, the deputy leader and finance minister who also championed National's economic growth and social investment strategies, is the highest-profile exit, and one of National's hardest-working and most effective ministers.

She had worked as a staffer for both John Key and Bill English, and built a reputation as a fierce debater, going on to be a general manager at Fonterra and a director at the New Zealand Initiative, before returning to Parliament as an MP in 2018 on National's list, after the resignation of Steven Joyce.

After previously attempting campaigns in traditionally left-leaning Wellington electorates - against Grant Robertson in Wellington Central in 2017 and 2020, and Ōhāriu's Greg O'Connor in 2023 - she chose not to contest an electorate this time, ending up a victim of National's overhang.

Paul Goldsmith and Nicola Willis were key members of Christopher Luxon's cabinet. Fiona Goodall/Getty Images

At third on the list, Chris Bishop is another victim of National's electorate success, after conceding Hutt South to Labour's Ginny Andersen on election night and acknowledging his chances of returning in the final count were "extremely unlikely".

A former lobbyist for Philip Morris, and staffer for Gerry Brownlee and Steven Joyce, Bishop entered Parliament in 2014 on National's list, claimed Hutt South in 2017 after the departure of Labour's Trevor Mallard, who he'd previously worked for, and lost it to Andersen in the 2020 'red wave' election, before winning it back in 2023.

Another of National's hard-working front bench, Bishop has led National's revision and replacement of Labour's Resource Management Act reforms, housing, infrastructure and transport, and became Attorney-General this year, while losing his role as National campaign chair in April, after rumours of an attempted leadership spill.

With National's low polling in 2026, Paul Goldsmith shifted from the one-tick strategy he'd run in Epsom against a succession of ACT leaders since 2011 to an explicit two-tick campaign against David Seymour, but appears to have fallen short, winning 30.5 percent of electorate votes on the night, compared to Seymour's 36.8.

A historian, biographer, pianist and taekwondo black belt, the trusted Luxon loyalist ended up with 10 portfolios (with GCSB and NZSIS being one combined role) - believed to be the most held by a minister this century - after Chris Penk's August attempt to topple the leader and sudden exit.

After being an Auckland councillor criticised for attempts to have homeless people removed from the CBD, he went on to become a National minister under John Key, had a stint as finance spokesperson under Judith Collins, and under Luxon, has led broadcasting, electoral and justice changes, including the move-on orders and removal of same-day voter enrolment.

Gerry Brownlee leaves Parliament as the father of the House - the longest continuously serving male MP - and Parliament's Speaker.

Gerry Brownlee leaves Parliament as father of the House. VNP / Phil Smith

He became MP for Ilam in the first MMP election of 1996, after unsuccessfully challenging Jim Anderton in '93, holding the seat until the red wave of 2020. He was deputy leader under both Don Brash and Judith Collins, and was a Leader of the House, defence minister, foreign minister, transport minister and led the response to the Canterbury earthquakes under Key.

His past life as a woodwork teacher stood him in good stead in the Speaker's chair, but whether his family's Olympic rowing history had much impact is unclear.

Nancy Lu was National's highest-ranked new MP in 2023, after Andrew Bayly's by-election win in Port Waikato saw him move to an electorate seat, freeing up a spot for a list seat.

Born in Guangzhou, China, she moved to Auckland at age 10 and became a chartered accountant, before becoming the party's only Chinese-heritage candidate in 2020.

Melissa Lee was the first Korean elected to Parliament - and the first Korean-born woman to enter a country's Parliament outside Korea - when she came in on National's list in 2008. She came close to unseating Labour's Helen White from Mt Albert in 2023, falling short by just 18 votes in a judicial recount.

After being a journalist for 23 years, including writing for the NZ Herald and the Listener, she was replaced as media and communications minister, and dumped out of Cabinet in Luxon's first reshuffle in 2024.

Carlos Cheung will hope special votes tip his way in Mt Roskill, with just 262 votes separating him and Michael Wood, who was dumped from cabinet in 2023 for repeatedly failing to declare shares and lost the previously safe Labour seat, as the red tide swept back out.

Cheung was born in Hong Kong and moved to New Zealand as a teenager, he has a PhD in diabetes and cardiac disease, and made it a point of pride to visit every junior, intermediate, secondary and special school in his electorate.

Vanessa Weenink had probably the most explosive comments of any departing MP, saying she would not miss the abuse from members of the public and expressing frustration at National's rightward shift.

A general practitioner for 20 years and an army medical officer for 22 - including deployments to Afghanistan and East Timor - Weenink was a Labour member, until the NZ Medical Association she chaired was disestablished in 2022, after which she joined National, narrowly taking Banks Peninsula in '23, before losing it again to Labour's Tracey McLellan.

Vanessa Weenink switched allegiances to National, after the Labour government disestablished her NZ Medical Association. VNP/Phil Smith

Labour

Deborah Russell was first elected in 2017, as MP for New Lynn, replacing former leader David Cunliffe, but after two terms, had to return on the list in 2023, after losing to Paulo Garcia.

An academic with a PhD in philosophy and co-writer of a book on tax fairness, she was minister of statistics and the Earthquake Commission under Chris Hipkins, and occasionally landed in hot water for expressing tax views out of line with the party's.

Rachel Boyack was an organiser for First Union, before reclaiming the Nelson electorate in the 2020 red wave from National's Nick Smith, who had held the seat since 1996, and narrowly held it in '23 by just 26 votes against National's Blair Cameron, before losing it to him by more than 1200 votes this election.

Her Plain Language Bill that aimed to make government documents easier to understand was reversed by the National-led coalition last term.

Dan Rosewarne was an army mechanic, who attained the rank of captain - with two deployments to Afghanistan, one to Solomon Islands and one responding to the Kaikōura earthquake - and survived leukaemia, before entering Parliament in 2022 on the list, after Kris Faafoi's retirement.

He was ejected again, after losing Waimakariri to National's Matt Doocey in '23, but returned to Parliament briefly this year, after the resignation of Peeni Henare in March.

Georgie Dansey entered Parliament on Labour's list, after Adrian Rurawhe's resignation in February, before the former Speaker's death in September.

Georgie Dansey's stay in Parliament may be brief, unless special votes save her seat. VNP / Phil Smith

She had lost the Hamilton West by-election, caused by Gaurav Sharma's resignation, to National's Tama Potaka in 2022, and fell short in Hamilton East in '23 and '26, but with just 456 votes separating her and incumbent Ryan Hamilton, she'll hope special votes land in her favour.

Green

At 19th on the Greens list in 2023, Mike Davidson never really expected to be an MP, but entered in October 2025, after the resignation of Benjamin Doyle capped off a now well-traversed string of MP replacements for the party in the last term.

A former Christchurch City Councillor who advocated for cycleways and public transport, his 2026 list placing at 20th means a return to Parliament seems very unlikely - almost as unlikely as the first time.

NZ First

Jamie Arbuckle controversially stayed on as a Marlborough district councillor - a role he'd held since 2010 - after coming to Parliament on New Zealand First's list in 2023.

He's 13th on the list - so, next in line - after placing behind rising stars Craig Stobo and Taine Randall, and former National MPs like Alfred Ngaro, Harete Hipango-Brownlie and Michael Laws. He could yet return, if Laws is eventually dumped and the party doesn't lose support in special votes.

Independents

Mariameno Kapa-Kingi and Tākuta Ferris were both removed from Te Pāti Māori during its internal ructions a year ago.

Kapa-Kingi - who had helped develop iwi health services, and worked in homelessness and suicide prevention - had defeated Labour deputy Kelvin Davis and was later re-instated to Te Pāti Māori, after a court battle.

Mariameno Kapa-Kingi's term was tumultuous, after she was banished from and then re-instated to Te Pāti Māori. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

However, she ultimately stood under the banner of her own Te Tai Tokerau party for the election, losing to Te Pāti Māori's Aperahama Edwards.

Ferris - nicknamed 'Doc' (Tākuta means 'doctor', he was named for the man who saved his and his mother's life during a difficult birth) never sought a court battle to return to the fold and ran as an independent this year.

An expert in Māori art and design, and mātauranga Māori, he was considered an outside chance to defeat Labour's Rino Tirikatene, who had beat him in 2020, but won in 2023 with a 2800-vote margin, after a campaign where he went toe to toe with the likes of Winston Peters and David Seymour in The Press leaders debate.

Pre-election exits

Lest we forget, some honourable mentions for the MPs that chose to leave on their own terms, resigning within the final six months, so as to not trigger by-elections.

World.title: Young smashes ton, Henry takes six as Black Caps crush India in fourth ODI
World.content:
Will Young hit a century and Matt Henry took six wickets as New Zealand sealed a dominant 244-run victory by bowling India out for 89 in the fourth one-day international in Mount Maunganui on Friday to remain afloat in the series.

The hosts trail India 2-1 and can no longer win the five-match series, but they can avoid defeat if they win the final match at the same venue on Sunday. The third match was abandoned due to rain.

Chasing 334 for victory, India got off to a disastrous start as paceman Henry ripped through their top order in a lethal first over, taking the wickets of Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and Shreyas Iyer to leave the visitors reeling on 0-3.

Ruturaj Gaikwad also departed shortly afterwards, but a steely 44-run partnership between Ishan Kishan (27) and Axar Patel (21), and a quickfire 21 from Naman Dhir helped ensure they did not lose by a record margin in terms of runs.

Henry took three more wickets as India were bundled out for their sixth-lowest ODI total.

Earlier on Friday, New Zealand opener Young made up for his single-digit scores of 9 and 6 in the opening two matches of the series with an assured knock of 125 from 108 balls - his best-ever ODI score and his fifth century in the format.

The 33-year-old profited from some lax fielding by India, with Rohit and Kishan dropping him on consecutive deliveries in the second over of New Zealand's innings.

Young was supported by Tim Seifert (58) and Finn Allen (41), while India's Patel, Gurnoor Brar and Auqib Nabi each picked up two wickets.

India were without captain Shubman Gill and batter KL Rahul, who will also miss the final ODI as they prepare for the upcoming two-test series against New Zealand beginning on Wednesday. - Reuters

World.title: 'Always helpful': Close friend pays tribute to BurgerFuel crash victim
World.content:
A longtime friend of one of the trio killed in the BurgerFuel crash in South Auckland has remembered him as a kind and charming man who was always willing to help others.

The trio killed in Sunday night's crash in Takanini have been named as Sukhdeep Singh, 33; his wife, Sukhvir Kaur, 29; and their brother-in-law, Gurpreet Singh, 38.

Mandeep Singh said Sukhdeep Singh had lived in New Zealand for seven years and operated an NZ Post courier business, while his wife had arrived just six months earlier.

Gurpreet Singh, who had lived in New Zealand for three years, worked as an NZ Post courier driver, he said.

His wife and young son had remained in India, according to the Supreme Sikh Society.

Three people died after a car crashed into a BurgerFuel outlet in South Auckland on Sunday. RNZ / Nick Monro

The newlywed couple and their brother-in-law died after the car they were travelling in lost control at a roundabout on Great South Road, left the road and crashed through a BurgerFuel restaurant in Takanini.

RNZ understands the vehicle is believed to have been travelling at more than 150 km/h.

Mandeep Singh said he had known Sukhdeep Singh since 2015 and the two had been close friends for more than a decade.

He described his friend as "not too extroverted, but always helpful".

"I lost my job back in 2023," he said. "He asked me, 'If you want to come with me, we can deliver parcels together. I'll help you'."

Mandeep Singh said Sukhdeep had married in February this year, and the two had travelled to India on the same flight.

"When he came back, he was really happy because he got married," he said.

He recalled the newlyweds visiting his home, where they spent time watching movies and enjoying each other's company.

Mandeep Singh described Sukhdeep's wife as "lovely and nice".

When Mandeep Singh saw news of the crash on Sunday night, he thought the car involved looked familiar.

"We [had] bought the car together," he said.

"Then I thought,'Why does the car look so similar to the one we bought?'"

Mandeep Singh said he later confirmed with a local temple that Sukhdeep and his family had attended Diwali celebrations on Sunday night.

He then learned that his friend was among those killed in the crash.

"I was terrified because my hands were shaking," he said.

Mandeep Singh urged the public not to speculate whether his friend had been speeding or was responsible for the crash, while the investigation was ongoing.

"He did not use to drink alcohol," he said.

"Police are doing their best to investigate what happened, and we have to wait until the results comes."

Emergency services were called to the crash just after 10:15pm on Sunday night.

All three occupants were pronounced dead at the scene, police said.

No one inside the building was injured.

World.title: Former RNZ board member says she knew ministerial approval was needed for overdraft
World.content:
A former RNZ board member says she was aware ministerial approval was required for a $5 million overdraft and is questioning why it wasn't sought.

On Monday, the public broadcaster revealed a shock $11.8 million budget blow-out, after a litany of financial blunders that included the overdraft that allegedly breached the Crown Entities Act.

By law, RNZ requires ministerial sign-off to set up such an overdraft.

In an email sent to media, former board member Jane Wrightson said she knew the approval was required under law, however, she did not know why it wasn't sought, adding, "it should have been".

She said she had stipulated to RNZ's board that ministerial sign-off would be required, adding the full board was aware of this.

Wrightson said that as her term was ending, she wasn't involved in any subsequent correspondence.

On Thursday board chair Brent Impey told Checkpoint a director did ask RNZ chief financial officer Hilary Parker in writing whether ministerial approval was required.

The query came after the board signed off on the overdraft, but before it was formally entered into.

"The assurance given at that time was that RNZ did not require approval from either the minister of finance or the shareholding ministers to establish the facility," Impey said.

"This matter will form part of what the independent review needs to consider and it is important that this process is undertaken with consideration of all relevant information in due course.

World.title: Students face 'derived grades' process after online glitch disrupts NCEA English exam
World.content:
The NZ Qualifications Authority (NZQA) will use a 'derived grades at scale' process to assess students affected during this week's online exam glitch.

About 40,000 students were sitting NCEA level 2 English on Thursday - many of them online - when the malfunction disrupted the exam, forcing many to revert to using paper exams.

While many students were given additional time to complete their exams, others will now be judged on internal work or assessments throughout the year.

NZQA has posted on social media to reassure these students about the process.

"You don't need to apply like with an individual derived grade," it said.

"Your school will submit this on your behalf.

"Your school will handle the evidence. This will come from the recent practice/mock exams or other stand-specific work.

"Your best result will count. If you complete the exam, we will compare your exam result with your school-assessed grade and award whichever is higher."

NZQA said Friday's Microsoft email outage had slowed communication, but assured students the process was underway with their schools.

Derived grades at scale are designed for "extraordinary circumstances" like earthquakes, flooding, blocked roads, medical emergencies or power cuts.

NZQA deputy chief executive Jann Marshall said, despite extensive testing, the online assessment platform used didn't perform as it should have.

"We are sorry for the disruption and the stress that students, as well as teachers and parents, experienced," she said.

"It's unacceptable.

"Students have worked hard for the examination and recently expected the platform to perform well."

She said their vendor had assured them that glitches that "slowed" and "locked people out" of the system would not happen again.

Secondary Principals' Association president Louise Ānaru told Morning Report that students had shown amazing resilience in the face of this setback.

"The good news is, of course, there are systems in place to make sure they're not disadvantaged," she said.

World.title: Spectacular try helps England to Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup glory
World.content:
England is Wheelchair Rugby League World champion for a third time after triumphing in a fiery, exhilarating final against France in Wollongong.

A spectacular try on the cusp of half-time proved pivotal for the English, with superstar Jack Brown rolling half the length of the pitch to collect a perfectly weighted Rob Hawkins kick and put his side ahead.

England kept the advantage for most of a hotly contested second half before surging clear late to triumph 50-38 and prompt a rousing rendition of the English sporting anthem Three Lions.

Earlier, Australia's Wheelaroos finished their campaign on a high, beating Ireland 70-24 in the third-place play-off.

Brown's superb effort came after a topsy-turvy first-half between wheelchair rugby league's two great powers, who have now combined for all five World Cup titles to date.

England raced to a 10-0 lead within the first 10 minutes, but was pegged back quickly, with French livewire Leo Hivernat scoring a try and providing a brilliant no-look pass to set up Damien Dore.

Tempers flared in the first period when England's Mason Billington shoved Hivernat to the ground, prompting a mid-court coming-together between the two teams.

Being a non-disabled player in elite wheelchair sport Leading out Australia at this month's Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup will be a dream come true for Bayley McKenna, the Wheelaroos first non-disabled skipper.

A flurry of quick points followed for the French, but England eventually regained its composure, with Hawkins levelling things up in the right corner before setting up Brown in the half's dying moments.

France's Dany Denuwelaere crossed for a second-half hat-trick, but England proved too strong, with Brown scoring twice to complete his treble and Joe Coyd finishing with four tries.

Wheelaroos finish campaign on a high

Still licking their wounds from the 86-18 loss to England in Tuesday's semifinal, the Wheelaroos were out to finish their campaign on a high against an Irish side ranked one place ahead of them in the world rankings.

And Australia raced out of the blocks in the evening's curtain raiser, with Cory Cannane crossing within a minute and Toby Popple completing a quickfire double to have the tournament hosts 16-0 ahead after just seven minutes of play.

Ireland's Cian Horgan proceeded to hit back barely 60 seconds later, but his four-pointer would prove to be Australia's only concession in a dominant first half.

Wheelaroos captain Bayley McKenna was a surprise omission from coach Brett Clark's starting five, but returned early on to score his ninth try of the competition as the Australians reached the break with a 36-point advantage.

Ireland's Oran Spain, forced to rely on the kindness of an Irish tourist to replace a wheelchair broken on the eve of the tournament, suffered a heavy first-period fall but returned after half-time to score his side's second try in an improved showing from his side.

However, McKenna continued to influence the game, providing a deft assist for Daniel Anstey before tumbling over for two late tries to complete both his hat-trick and Australia's 70-24 victory.

Anstey also finished with a treble as the Wheelaroos secured a third-place finish, their equal, second-best finish in tournament history.

World.title: Australia's next fast bowling star blows England away on ODI debut
World.content:
Mahli Beardman has stamped his reputation as the next big thing in Australian cricket by slicing his way through England during a memorable ODI debut in Perth.

On a day when Australian cricket was still knee-deep dealing with the ghosts of Sandpapergate, Beardman snared 6–24 as England was skittled for 131 in 33.4 overs at Perth Stadium.

Australia chased the runs down with ease, led by captain Mitch Marsh's explosive 50 from 30 balls at the top of the order.

The 21-year-old Beardman was nearly unplayable at times, with England collapsing from 2–38 to 7–60 on the back of Beardman's burst.

It marked just the second time an Australian has produced a five-wicket haul in their ODI debut, following on from Tony Dodemaide's haul of 5–21 against Sri Lanka at the WACA Ground in 1988.

Only some late handy runs from Gus Atkinson (29 not out off 32 balls) and Will Jacks (25) ensured England made it to triple figures, with the visitors 8–65 at one stage.

"It all happened very quickly," Beardman told Fox Cricket when asked about his big haul.

"It's just a great privilege and honour to be able to represent my country. And to go out and take a few wickets as well is the cherry on top.

"Harry Brook was a nice wicket to get off the mark. Anytime you get your first one it's a weight off your shoulders, so that was awesome."

The right-arm paceman snared his first ODI wicket in his second over when he found the edge of England captain Brook (1).

Hitting speeds of up to 145.4 kilometres per hour, Beardman was able to entice 200-game milestone man Joe Root (17 off 36 balls) to drive on the up to gift wicketkeeper Josh Inglis his third catch of the innings.

And Beardman was on a hat-trick when he collected the scalp of Jordan Cox at the start of his fourth over — again with another pearler of a delivery that caught the edge.

Sam Curran's attempted pull off Beardman's bouncer gave Adam Zampa a catch on the boundary rope and Beardman his fourth wicket.

And Beardman's five-wicket haul was complete when Liam Dawson was caught at gully, giving the West Australian figures of 5–13 off 4.4 overs at that point.

Spencer Johnson (3–42) ensured the party continued by jumping high in the air to pull off a one-handed catch off his own bowling to send Jamie Overton packing.

Atkinson and Jofra Archer (11) struck a series of boundaries in a 29-run last-wicket stand before Beardman completed the demolition job by having Archer caught at gully.

Beardman's figures were the fourth best by a debutant in ODI world cricket, with Charlie Cassell's effort of 7–21 for Scotland against Oman in 2024 still the best.

Marsh's early burst made sure the result was never in doubt for Australia, despite Travis Head being bowled for a golden duck by Gus Atkinson.

Marsh hit a series of enormous sixes in a thrilling but brief knock, before Cooper Connolly (27), Matt Renshaw (26*) and Josh Inglis (23*) helped steer Australia home in just the 24th over.
